#6316. Planning Your First Trip to New Zealand? Here's Where to Go

Living in Sydney, I’m guilty of thinking of New Zealand as somewhere I can always go next month. It’s close enough for a skiing trip, which is usually my first excuse to book. I love Queenstown for that, but what I’ve particularly enjoyed discovering on my travels is how naturally New Zealand brings together its spectacular outdoors and a tradition of luxury hospitality, in every season.

Aotearoa is easy to admire from a car window, but I’ve found that the places I remember most are those where I’ve stopped and spent a little more time. Wellington is overdue for another visit, and Fiordland is somewhere I'd like to explore properly. Then there are the lodges, each with its own character and reasons to return: Huka Lodge for its history, Cabot Lodgefor its working-farm roots, and many others worth discovering.

Below are the five places I’d build a trip around, leaving enough room in the itinerary to linger a little longer wherever I find myself wanting to stay.

I’d start with Queenstown if you’re coming for the mountains, with time allotted for Arrowtown and a few days in Fiordland National Park. For the North Island, Auckland is a useful starting point before heading towards Rotorua for its geothermal landscapes and Māori culture, then Lake Taupō. If food is your priority, I’d make Wellington part of the trip. My main advice is to choose a few places you’re interested in and give each at least a few days.

It can be, although a luxury lodge and a helicopter aren’t compulsory parts of an itinerary. I’d spend on a stay I really wanted, then balance it with somewhere simpler, ideally with a kitchen so you can cook some of your own meals. Skiing and guided activities can take a sizable bite out of the budget, so decide which matter most before booking everything else. If you’re considering a camper van, compare the total hire cost, including fuel and campsite fees, with a car and accommodation. I’d also leave room on the budget for eating out and wine tasting.

Seven days is sufficient for a trip, but I wouldn’t try to cover both islands in that time. On the South Island, you could spend the week around Queenstown and Arrowtown, adding Te Anau if Milford Sound is a priority. Or drive from Christchurch to Lake Tekapo and spend time in the Mackenzie region. On the North Island, Rotorua and Taupō work well together.

I always prefer to spend an extra night somewhere than keep repacking. Leave some flexibility, too: if you’ve come for stargazing and the sky clouds over, you’ll appreciate having another evening available.

Arrowtown, 20 minutes from Queenstown, is an idyllic place to visit.

Queenstown is great for the skiing, but I’d make time for nearby Arrowtown even if it meant losing a day on the slopes. I love the old cottages and shopfronts, and how much of its gold-mining history is still visible. The partially restored Chinese miners’ settlement beside Bush Creek is worth walking through before lunch.

Food is another reason to stay. At Aosta, northern Italian cooking makes good use of Central Otago produce. Nearby Ayrburn occupies a former 150-acre farm, with restaurants spread across its restored buildings. Billy’s, in the original homestead, serves modern Chinese food. I’ve visited both Arrowtown and Ayrburn, and would happily organize another Queenstown trip around eating here, with some skiing fitted in.

Where to stay: Arrowtown House is a small boutique hotel in town, making walking to dinner easy. Millbrook Resort, nearby, has more of a resort feel, with apartments as well as rooms and a spa for sore ski legs.

I still think about the water outside Huka Lodge. The Waikato River is this extraordinary emerald color, and I could have spent much of my stay watching it. Huka also got me interested in New Zealand’s lodge history: it began as a fishermen’s camp in 1924. There’s something appealing about discovering that a place has been welcoming people for the same reason for more than a century.

You don’t have to stay there to spend time beside the river. Follow the riverside walks towards Huka Falls, where the water forces its way through a narrow rock channel. I’d also get out on Lake Taupō, with a boat or kayak trip to the Ngātoroirangi Mine Bay Māori rock carvings. Created by Matahi Whakataka-Brightwell and his team, they’re a striking example of contemporary Māori art.

Where to stay: Huka Lodge has a certain stateliness, with its manicured grounds beside the Waikato River and a history of royal guests. I have dreams of running away to Poronui Safari Camp, in the wider Taupō region. Its two canvas tents sit beside the Mohaka River, with hot showers and food supplied by the kitchen. It’s booked exclusively for up to four people.

The Cairns Alpine Resort’s Alpine Lodges on crystalline Lake Tekapo

I visited Dark Sky Project while reporting on quiet destinations for Traveler and loved having someone explain what I was looking at. The indoor experience brings Māori astronomy and science together, and houses an enormous restored 19th-century telescope. It gives you a way into the subject even if your astronomical knowledge is limited. For nighttime stargazing, book the Summit Experience at Mount John Observatory, within the Aoraki Mackenzie International Dark Sky Reserve. I’d arrange it early in the stay, leaving another night available if the weather doesn’t cooperate.

There’s plenty to look at during the day, too. Lake Tekapo gets its milky turquoise color from fine glacial rock flour floating in the water. It’s a good place to spend a few days on a South Island drive from Christchurch, with time for the Southern Alps and a separate excursion into Aoraki/Mount Cook National Park.

Where to stay: The Cairns Alpine Resort’s Alpine Lodges take their inspiration from musterers’ huts. Inside, there are two bedrooms and a kitchen, with timber-lined rooms and a wood-burning fireplace. After a late night stargazing on Mount John, you can have a lie-in and cook breakfast whenever you’re ready.

The city of Wellington, a great place to visit for good eating and galleries.

New Zealand received its first Michelin restaurant selection in 2026, although you hardly need the guide to eat well here. For me, Wellington would be a few days of galleries and restaurant bookings, with enough time between them to walk around and see what’s changed since my last visit some years ago City Gallery’s reopening has moved it up my list and is the sort of thing I’d build a weekend around. I’d leave plenty of time for eating, though.

Puffin is on my list for a glass of natural wine. I’m also keeping an eye on Rita, a small restaurant in an Aro Valley cottage known for its changing set dinners. The team is also opening a daytime deli called Super Rita, expected to open in early next year.

Where to stay: The Intrepid Hotel is the one I’d book: 18 rooms in Te Aro, near Cuba Street, with Puffin downstairs. I like the idea of a nightcap in a locals-filled wine bar and a short walk upstairs to bed.

The Cabot Lodge, a working farm, is an intriguing stay in Fiordland

Milford Sound and Doubtful Sound are still on my list, and I’d like to give Fiordland a trip of its own. I’d stay around Te Anau rather than make the long journey out and back from Queenstown. There are glowworm caves across Lake Te Anau, while nearby Manapouri is the starting point for the most direct land-and-water route to Doubtful Sound: a boat across Lake Manapouri, followed by a coach over Wilmot Pass to the fjord.

I also have a shopping recommendation for the journey. At The Key, on the approach to Te Anau, Davaar sells knitwear (that has a cult following) made from wool grown on the family’s working sheep station, Davaar Station. Founder Kate Macdonald is the fifth generation, and her sister Anna runs the food caravan next door. I bought a jumper a few years ago when she had a pop-up in Arrowtown that I still love. It’s exactly the sort of place I want to find when traveling: a homegrown product with a family story; make the best souvenirs.

Where to stay: Cabot Lodge interests me because it’s on a working farm overlooking Lake Manapouri, and near Doubtful Sound departures. For a night at Milford itself, Milford Sound Lodge has chalets overlooking the river and rainforest. I’d decide which sound I wanted to spend more time exploring before choosing where to stay.

#6315. Southwest Denies A 787 Order. Remember Its Bag Promise?

On its October 22nd, 2026 earnings call, CEO, Bob Jordan, shot down reports of a widebody order as having “no credibility.” The reports came from a Reuters exclusive two weeks earlier, citing three unnamed sources who said Southwest was looking at Boeing 787s for a long-haul push, possibly leased or second-hand, with a launch window of roughly three years. At the time, Southwest’s only comment was that it had no news forthcoming on its fleet plans. We have heard this before.

His reasoning was mostly that it would require significant changes in the business model. Operating aircraft with more than 175 seats would send the airline back to its pilots, and the pilot contract likely opens next year. Another 737 variant would be “significantly easier” than a widebody. Long-haul flying would be upside “if we decide to pursue that.” My eyerolls are likely audible at this point.

I know how this goes because I have watched the free bag story (and every other unique characteristic that Southwest would “never” change) play out. In July 2024, Jordan told investors that bags flying free was the number one reason customers choose Southwest, behind only fare and schedule. On September 17, 2024, a Southwest spokesperson told The Points Guy there was “no work currently underway” to change the policy, and Jordan, pressed on the question, would only say never say never, as CBS reported.

Six months later, on March 11, 2025, Southwest ended the policy. The airline set fees of $35 for the first checked bag and $45 for the second on flights booked on or after May 28, 2025. Jordan’s explanation was that bags flying free was not part of the airline’s DNA, and that open seating was not either. What he should have said was that it wasn’t part of Elliott Management’s DNA and they were running the show – at least while they were still heavy investors. Analysts warned at the time that dropping the policy could damage the brand and turn Southwest into just another airline. It most certainly did that, but as reported in recent weeks, it has, in fact, helped the stock price and financials significantly.

But there is no demonstrable difference between Southwest and any of the top 5 US carriers except one, no long haul international service.

The bags went first, and assigned seating arrived on January 27, 2026, with eight boarding groups, four fare tiers and extra-legroom rows on every flight. Basic fares board last. Open seating, which was the other half of the cattle-call charm, was gone. This has all been covered over the last 18 months but it’s important preamble when considering the next logical step for the airline, and the claims it is denying. What remains uniquely Southwest is one fleet type, and a partially point-to-point map and a reputation for friendliness, and the fleet may be next. Jordan said Southwest is not building toward any one thing, but the addition of 11 lounges, a premium credit card, and first class tell a different story.

It’s a sea of sameness (to steal another industry trope.) Delta and United sell the same choices at similar prices, and Southwest sells them with a smaller map and limited international reach. Every concession after the bag fee was an admission that the discount model was not enough on its own, even though I personally believe that it was.

The numbers explain why management keeps moving the goalposts. In the third quarter, revenue per available seat mile jumped a record 21.6%, but capacity fell 0.4% and unit costs excluding fuel rose 3.8%. Capacity for 2026 is up only about 1.2%. That mix tells me growth came from price and fees, not from flying more, but in order to keep up that frothy pace it will have to find new markets to enter.

Domestic markets are mature, and Southwest’s biggest rivals already own the best international partners. Southwest has partnerships with Icelandair, China Airlines, EVA Air and Turkish Airlines, and Jordan said international loyalty partnerships and partner redemption launch next spring (I can’t wait to see what the redemptions look like.) Partners only go so far, though. Will some EVA Air customers book connecting flights on Southwest for its customers, maybe, probably, but that’s not going to move the needle.

Alaska already saw this writing on the wall and made a move. The rest of the premium push doesn’t come close to working if Southwest customers still buy tickets to Rome on another carrier. Chicago Midway can technically accommodate a 787, as can Dallas Love, and at LAX and Baltimore that’s a very easy fit. But all of those markets have real competition from major carriers. Other Southwest hubs like Fort Lauderdale face serious challenges with nearby Miami, Houston Hobby against United at Intercontinental, Denver for both international carriers and United.

But Southwest wanted to assimilate the carrier to every other carrier so it has to compete with every other carrier too. And in that regard, I can’t see a lounge program as aggressive as 11 locations working without it. If the fleet was exclusively Airbus, the international case is easier with longer legs and a JetBlue-like model (though that’s not working out well for them at the moment and they already have premium cards, lounges, and international partners.)

Unless Southwest sees unprecedented growth from what it’s already doing – possible, but not probable – this is the last frontier. So why deny it? Doesn’t that indicate a lack of forward thinking?

I will take the other side of the denial. My prediction is that Southwest announces a widebody order or lease within eighteen months of the pilot contract opening, and that Jordan or his successor will explain it as a natural evolution of the brand. The pattern is set. Every sacred cow gets slain once the numbers demand it, and the statement of the day is always true until the day it is not. Travelers should treat Southwest’s promises the way they treat any airline’s, as information about the current quarter and not a commitment about the next one.

#6314. A New York City Weekend Guide for Design Lovers

The thing that makes visiting (or living in) New York worth every penny is that you don’t have to go out of your way looking for inspiration. You might be struck by a vintage sign advertising color TVs in the East Village; a grandpa on the Upper East Side pairing bright red socks with his loafers; or that never-gets-old view of the Brooklyn Bridge from an elevated subway track. Design is, indeed, everywhere in NYC, but sometimes you need a bit of a roadmap to plot your next moment of awe.

Like many New Yorkers, I derive a lot of joy from looking at pretty things and existing in cool spaces. When I feel like I’m staring at a blank page—or I just want to spend a weekend more intentionally—the places below are the ones I turn to for a creative spark. These spots span boroughs and cover art, architecture, and fashion—from former artist residences and Japanese-inspired stationery stores to restaurants and spas with covetable interiors.

For the aesthetes who have already seen the latest exhibition at MoMA, this weekend guide for design lovers is intended to point you in a few other directions (and no, this does not include that viral room full of dirt in SoHo).

The Cooper Hewitt is the only museum in the United States devoted exclusively to both historical and contemporary design.

For many New Yorkers, to go uptown is to go to the museum. And while the Metropolitan Museum of Art holds down the fort, there are a few other players along Museum Mile that always seem to take me by surprise whenever I visit. The Cooper Hewitt, for instance, showcases “design objects” in the broadest sense that span across centuries—you might find an Egyptian ceramic from 1100 BCE in one room, and a Swedish midcentury-modern lamp in another. It’s also a lovely hangout spot; earlier this year, the museum hosted a Hi-Fi listening room, and when the weather’s nice, visitors can take advantage of the garden (tickets are not required and Wi-Fi is free), admiring the gorgeous architecture of Andrew Carnegie’s former mansion.

The “Einspänner” at Sabarsky—double espresso with whipped cream.

A short walk away, the Neue Galerie, which specializes in early 20th-century German and Austrian art, is where I go to gush over furniture designed by the likes of Josef Hoffmann and Adolf Loos. The museum is set to reopen on November 12 for its 20th anniversary, but in the meantime, you can visit the stunning Café Sabarsky—the Viennese restaurant located within the museum—and pretend you’re at the helm of the next great intellectual movement with your friends over fancy whipped-cream-topped coffees.

Further downtown, in Midtown East, the Paul Rudolph Institute is a must for anyone who enjoyed The Brutalist. Join the monthly open house at the Rudolph-designed duplex within the iconic Modulightor building, once the headquarters of the lighting company the architect co-founded with his life partner, Ernst Wagner. Docents are on-site to answer any questions as you wind your way through the all-white apartment, with its disjointed staircases and built-in shelving units, though private tours are also available.

When it comes to shopping, I believe one can gain a lot from staring into the windows along Madison Avenue, or even heading inside to get a feel for the luxe fabrics, sans purchase. But for second-hand designer clothing, Upper East Vintage (by appointment only) and Designer Revival (Gentleman’s Resale is also right next door), both on the Upper East Side, are your best bet. I’m also always delighted by what I find at Spellman Gallery, a small showroom owned by an art appraiser with fantastic taste—you can discover all kinds of treasures, from a rare vinyl record to a painting worth a few thousand.

Browsing beautiful items will inevitably stir up an appetite, and for a restaurant that has tables equipped with landlines during live art auction sales, check out Marcel 945 Madison, housed inside the historic Breuer Building that is now the global headquarters of Sotheby’s. While the restaurant serves (very expensive) French bistro fare, it’s all about the rotating art on the walls—including works by Roy Lichtenstein and Willem de Kooning, to name a few past residents—which are also available for purchase.

With its glass blocks, chrome light fixtures, and black leather booths, Bridges in Chinatown is a design-lover's dream.

If you prefer to walk amongst grittier cast-iron buildings or people-watch from plastic stools, then it’s best you head downtown. Start with a trip to the Judd Foundation, where you can book a slot to explore 37 of minimalist Donald Judd’s artworks, each permanently installed in the late artist’s former residence and studio on Spring Street, and get a glimpse of how an artist lived and breathed in SoHo before the luxury flagships arrived. Over in Greenwich Village, the Renee and Chaim Gross Foundation boasts over 12,000 of American artist Chaim Gross’s sculptures, drawings, and prints, as well as his personal collection of global art. The late artist’s personal home, which he shared with his wife Renee, is light-filled and lived-in—an intimate experience that cannot be replicated at a traditional museum.

The Lower East Side, specifically Orchard Street, is where to go to shop independent designers. Browse Colbo—more of a multidisciplinary space than a retail store—for unisex neutrals as you sip an espresso. Adjacent to the shop, Colbo Next Door is a great spot to grab a glass of wine and listen to vinyl. Further along Orchard Street, you’ll find Lara Koleji for vintage Miu Miu, as well as Tumbao, a curation of the very best in Latin American fashion design. On East Broadway, also in the LES, Aeon Bookstore is one of my favorite bookstores in New York, a basement-level shop with a small-but-mighty selection of used titles, whether you’re looking for a coffee table book on the Bauhaus or a beautiful edition of Lolita.

Gem Home on Mott Street saves the day whenever I’m in need of a unique, last-minute gift—say, a stainless steel ice cream bowl or spiral toothbrush holder—and the shop, which is also a café, has recently started hosting dinners in collaboration with French pop-up Mon Petit Canard. Continuing on with the theme of downtown cool, Bridges is a swoon-worthy restaurant space that’s bound to get your interior design wheels turning, and there’s a famous Comté cheese tart that’s a work of art in and of itself.

If you've ever wondered what the subway looked like decades ago, the New York Transit Museum has your answer.

If you’re spending a day in Brooklyn, make sure to pop over to the New York Transit Museum in Downtown Brooklyn—talk about a celebration of design. In addition to touring over 20 different vintage train cars, you’ll view an otherwise quotidian part of New York City life in a new light. Graphic design nerds in particular will geek out over the exhibits dedicated to Massimo Vignelli, who designed the 1972 subway map we love and use today. For a different kind of museum experience, Pioneer Works in Red Hook was born out of a former 1866 red-brick warehouse, and today it’s dedicated to all kinds of arts and science programming. On view right now, for instance, is a multimedia exhibition by Helsinki-based artist Tuomas A. Laitinen, drawing on more than a decade of research on octopus intelligence, sleep, and consciousness.

There’s only one place I trust for buying jeans, and it’s Front General Store's Outpost, which boasts an entire wall of vintage Levi’s and then some—think worn-in Burberry trench coats, military deadstock, and new shoes from Japanese or British brands you might not have heard of. The vintage shopping in Brooklyn, of course, doesn’t stop there: 10 ft Single by Stella Dallas in Williamsburg is a reliable favorite for threadbare T-shirts and Ralph Lauren sweaters, and if you’re on the hunt for a conversation starter of a chair, Dream Fishing Tackle in Greenpoint is part fishing supply center, part midcentury-modern furniture store. If it wasn’t already clear, NYC loves a retail space that’s also something else: Chyelle in Bushwick and Apartment Ra’el in Bed-Stuy both serve up coffee and beautiful homeware. For those obsessed with paper and pens (guilty), Yoseka Stationery in Greenpoint stocks the very best in Japanese stationery design—from Hobonichi journals to Kaweco fountain pens.

In a sea of white-marbled wellness spaces, Spencer’s Spa in Williamsburg proves good design is integral to relaxation. I’ve had excellent facials at both the Brooklyn and SoHo locations, lingering for as long as possible afterwards in the lounge areas, which seem to take inspiration from traditional Japanese, Art Deco, and Scandinavian design (I like to take pictures of all the unique lamps and objects so I can reverse image search them for my apartment later on). But if you’d rather find your zen within New York City’s nightlife scene, James Murphy–owned club Nightmoves in Williamsburg, music venue Public Records in Gowanus, and listening bar Eavesdrop in Greenpoint all boast incredibly impressive custom sound design.

The Noguchi Museum is one of the most peaceful pockets of the city.

Akari Light Sculptures abound at the Noguchi Museum, and you can even bring one home.

A trip to Queens would not be complete without a visit to the Noguchi Museum in Astoria, where you can feel a sense of serenity walking around Isamu Noguchi’s biomorphic sculptures, then buy one of his Akari light sculptures in what is perhaps the best museum gift shop in New York City. While the museum is home to its own sculpture garden, there’s also one practically across the street—make sure you allot some time to strolling Socrates Sculpture Park, where you’ll encounter a whole host of experimental installations (they’re always rotating), with the Manhattan skyline as the backdrop.

In Long Island City, the industrial hub-turned-creative enclave in western Queens, MoMA PS1 is at once nostalgic and of-the-moment, showcasing contemporary art within former elementary school halls—it’s especially fun in the summer when it's running its Warm Up series, when everyone gathers outside for DJ sets and music performances. Also in the neighborhood, Somerset House is a staging and interior design gallery that sells collectible furniture and art—think Pierre Jeanneret armchairs and Poul Henningsen lamps—by appointment only. For something a bit more accessible, Lichen in Ridgewood sells a similar catalog of vintage furniture, plus its own in-house designs ranging from glass coffee tables to futuristic sconces.

This bank-turned-hotel features original vaulted ceilings that rival those of Grand Central Station. Sip a martini at the Swan Room, the property's see-and-be-seen lobby bar.

Situated in NoMad, The Fifth Avenue Hotel gives you access to both Museum Mile and downtown shopping. The 19th-century, Renaissance-style mansion is dressed in maximalism.

Once a barrel factory in the early 1900s, this hip Williamsburg hotel is your gateway to industrial-chic rooms, a cinema with red velvet seats, and the acclaimed Le Crocodile restaurant.

The Mercer is SoHo in a nutshell, with loft-like suites, a neutral color palette, and a buzzy restaurant. Minimalists, this one’s for you.

#6313. Don't make these time-change mistakes when planning travel

A few years ago, on a damp evening in late March in London, I learned the hard way that countries don't all change their clocks for daylight saving time simultaneously. After ordering a glass of white wine at a cozy bar in Bermondsey, I mindlessly scrolled on my phone while the bartenders chatted about the clocks jumping forward that coming Sunday. I nearly spit out my Chablis.

Back home in New York City, I had already skipped ahead one hour on the second Sunday in March. As I frantically Googled, I learned that in the United Kingdom, the clocks go forward one hour on the last Sunday in March (and back one hour on the last Sunday in October).

Don't be like me and lose two hours of sleep in one month. When you travel, remember the following to avoid daylight saving time-related snafus and other time zone mistakes — and if you're in the U.S., most states fell back one hour on Sunday, Nov. 1.

The U.K. isn't the only country that changes its clocks on a different weekend than we do in the U.S. For example, most European countries follow the same calendar as the U.K., moving clocks forward one hour on the last Sunday in March and back one hour on the last Sunday in October.

Generally, when traveling in the spring and fall, it's always best to check when the country you're going to falls forward or backward — and also whether that country observes daylight saving time at all. In fact, according to the Pew Research Center, about 66% of the world doesn't.

Though daylight saving time is commonly observed in North America and Europe, many non-European Union countries in Europe — including Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Iceland, Russia and Turkey — stay on standard time year-round.

In 2023, Egypt became the only country in Africa to change its clocks when it reintroduced daylight saving time for the first time in seven years. Now, each year, its clocks move forward one hour on the last Friday in April and backward one hour on the last Thursday in October.

It's also worth double-checking these things even if you're traveling within the U.S. In 48 states, daylight saving time runs from the second Sunday in March to the first Sunday in November. Arizona and Hawaii are the outliers that stay on standard time year-round. While it's less of an issue on an island like Hawaii, Arizona shares enough borders with other states that do observe daylight saving time that it can be problematic.

"Always double-check timing when flying in/out and on road trips through the state," Becky Blaine, TPG's newsletter managing editor and former Arizona resident, said. Otherwise, you can risk missing a flight or a reservation.

To keep it simple, remember that Arizona is in the Pacific Daylight Time zone from mid-March to early November, and the rest of the year it's in the same time zone as other states in Mountain Standard Time.

It's a similar situation in Canada. Generally, Canada follows the same daylight saving schedule as the U.S., but most of Saskatchewan, the Yukon and some parts of Quebec and British Columbia stay on standard time year-round.

In Australia, daylight saving time starts the first Sunday in October and ends the first Sunday in April in the Australian Capital Territory, New South Wales, South Australia, Tasmania and Victoria; meanwhile, the Northern Territory, Queensland and Western Australia don't observe it.

Outside of daylight saving time changes, there are some general time zone issues to be aware of while traveling.

In countries as large as the U.S., Canada and Australia, it's easy to see why there are so many time zones. But Eric Rosen, TPG's director of travel content, also pointed out that the airport in the Maldives is in a different time zone than some resorts in the tiny island nation.

Technically, the Maldives has only one official time zone: Maldives Time, which is five hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). However, some of the archipelago's private island resorts add an hour to Maldives Time to maximize their guests' evening light.

For example, The St. Regis Maldives Vommuli Resort sets its clock one hour ahead of the official clock to what it calls "Island Time," but also provides guests with butlers who coordinate transfers to and from the airport so nobody accidentally misses a flight.

Before you go to the Maldives, be sure to check if your resort also does this.

Due to its geographic location, the Canadian island of Newfoundland is 90 minutes ahead of Eastern Time instead of just 60 minutes ahead, as in the rest of Atlantic Canada. On a July trip, Nick Ewen, TPG's editor-in-chief, found this challenging for calendar purposes.

While traveling in Newfoundland, he received an Outlook invitation to a 7:30 p.m. dinner meeting the following week and accepted it without much thought. However, the actual dinner back home in the U.S. started at 6 p.m. — a detail he completely missed until the reminder popped up 15 minutes before. At that point, he realized he would be late.

Other places offset from UTC by 30 minutes include India, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, Iran and some states in Australia. Want to be confused even more? Nepal's time zone is offset by 45 minutes due to its geography.

Even when not dealing with half-hour time zones, it can be easy to make similar mistakes when adding events back home to your digital calendar while traveling in a different time zone.

"Last year, I brought my middle son to a birthday party. We were running a few minutes late, but when we arrived, it seemed like the party was almost over," Tarah Chieffi, a senior writer at TPG, said. "While the kids were eating cake, I double-checked my calendar to make sure we had gotten the time right, and it seemed like we had. But then I went to check the invitation, and we had, in fact, arrived one hour late."

Her mistake? When she entered the party into her calendar while traveling, her calendar app defaulted to the time zone she was in and showed her the incorrect time back home.

"Now, I always toggle the time zone to my home time zone if I enter appointments into my calendar while I'm traveling," she said.

"Outlook lets you have up to three time zones showing on the calendar," Madison Blancaflor, a managing editor at TPG, said.

Go to "Settings," then "Calendar," then "Time zones." Then, check the box for "Show second time zone in Day and Week view" underneath your default time zone. If you need a third one, you can also check that box.

It's also important to remember that it's possible to quickly encounter multiple time zones on cruises — especially on transoceanic cruises, where you'll change time zones daily or almost daily. And if you're on a cruise traversing the Pacific Ocean, you could lose an entire day if you cross the international date line, like Clint Henderson, TPG's principal spokesperson, did when he sailed from Seward, Alaska, to Tokyo last year.

Related: I made a rookie travel mistake that nearly cost me $4,000 — here's how I fixed it

Even on shorter cruises, check if you'll have to change time zones. When I was on a five-day Alaska cruise earlier this summer, I changed time zones twice as we moved in and out of Alaska Daylight Time on a round-trip sailing from Vancouver (which was one hour ahead, on Pacific Daylight Time).

Cabin stewards usually leave notes on your bed at turndown to remind you of upcoming time changes. Clint said he had to set his clocks back between one and two hours each night on his cruise. But you can't always rely on your cellphone to display the correct time when it's in airplane mode and using satellite-based internet. Bring an analog watch or an alarm clock to ground you if you're unsure whether your device will update properly.

However, some cruise ships may ignore time changes at select ports. "I've had that happen on Royal Caribbean ships in the Caribbean, for example, to avoid the ship time changing three days in a row," said Christine Gallipeau, a senior editor on TPG's points and loyalty team. "So if you're doing shore excursions, make sure you know what time the ship is following, as it may not necessarily match the local time."

Related: Can a cruise help with jet lag? The answer might surprise you

When traveling, don't assume every country or state follows the same daylight-saving-time rules and schedules as where you live, and be mindful of time zone anomalies. Losing or gaining an unexpected hour can lead to lost sleep, arriving late to an event and, worst of all, missed flights.

#6312. Lufthansa Now Requires An Account Just To Check In Online

Buying a ticket and having your booking confirmation will no longer be enough to check in online for many Lufthansa Group flights. The airline group is making a Travel ID account mandatory, adding another requirement to a process that should be simple. A major expansion takes effect today, with departures from the United States following later this month.

According to Lufthansa Group’s notice to travel partners, passengers will increasingly need a Travel ID to check in through the websites and apps of Lufthansa, SWISS, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, Air Dolomiti, Edelweiss, and Discover Airlines.

The rollout is phased by departure point:

One person can check in multiple travelers using their own Travel ID. Someone assisting another passenger may also use their own account for personal assistance.

Lufthansa presents Travel ID as a convenient way to use one login across its airlines, with stored information and fewer forms to complete. It also promotes personalized offers.

Certainly, a frequent Lufthansa Group passenger would likely find that useful. If you regularly fly Lufthansa, SWISS, and Austrian, having your information available across those airlines can save the annoying hassle of have to re-enter personal details.

A booking reference and surname have long been enough to retrieve a reservation and begin check-in. If additional identity or travel-document checks are necessary, an airline can request those during that process. I don’t understand why creating an account must now be part of obtaining a boarding pass, other than for the collection of data.

I already have more travel accounts than I care to count, but count me in here…I already have a Lufthansa Travel ID and I welcome this. But for an occasional traveler who simply wants to check in for a flight, it creates another step with another password or login process to manage.

Passengers who do not want an account can still check in at the airport. Good, but it does not make the online requirement particularly customer-friendly. Online check-in lets passengers helps passengers save time. Someone traveling with only a carry-on may have no reason to visit a check-in counter at all.

Why make that person choose between opening an account and completing check-in at the airport?

Airlines have spent years encouraging passengers to handle more tasks themselves. That works best when the digital process is easy to use. Adding an enrollment requirement seems like an odd way to improve it.

The exception for tickets issued by other airlines is also worth highlighting….an odd disincentive to book away, it seems to me.

Lufthansa Group is expanding its mandatory Travel ID requirement for online check-in throughout November, including US departures beginning November 16.

I have no objection to a shared account that makes traveling across the group easier. But passengers should be able to decide whether they want one. Buying a ticket ought to be enough to access the basic tools needed to use it like online check-in…

#6311. Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture, Gastronomy, and Local Life

Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand why Madrid is one of Europe’s top destinations.

Like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow. It’s a city for night owls, where dinner starts late and the parties even later. But if you can embrace the laid-back pace of life, the slow meals, and the late-night vibes, you’ll have a more authentic visit and uncover the true beating heart of the city’s culture.

I love all my visits to Madrid. I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me. The food, the energy, the art (so much art!). Madrid is just cool.

Being such a big city, I know it can be easy to feel lost. Where do you start with what you want to do? Where do you go? It took me a few visits to figure it out.

In this post, I’ll help you plan an epic five-day visit to Madrid that will ensure you not only see the main sights but that you also get off the beaten path and see just what makes Madrid so popular — and all without breaking the bank either!

This first day focuses on a prestigious area designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021. There are over 40 monuments and over 40 buildings on the site. It’s easily one of the most picturesque and historic areas of the city.

The route begins at the Prado Museum, one of the best museums on the planet. Here you’ll find works from El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya, as well as many other masters (such as Rubens, Botticelli, and Caravaggio to name a few). If you only visit one museum in Madrid, this is the one. It’s incredible and worth taking the time to explore. It’s one of the biggest museums in the world, too. Make sure you spend a few hours here at a minimum.

Just a 10-minute walk along the Paseo del Prado, the journey continues at the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, a private collection spanning from the Renaissance to Pop Art, and culminates at the Reina Sofía Museum. The Reina Sofía National Art Center offers a fantastic collection of modern art. Works by masters like Picasso, Miró, Kandinsky, Dalí, and Bacon can all be found here. The centerpiece is Picasso’s famous Guernica, a 1937 oil painting considered the most moving anti-war painting in the world. While I don’t love modern art, even I enjoyed this museum.

After museum hopping, it’s time to dive into Madrid’s culinary scene. Try Taberna La Fragua de Vulcano for a rustic atmosphere perfect for sampling cocido madrileño. If you are near the Reina Sofía Museum, don’t miss the vibrant garden terrace at Arzábal, renowned for having some of the best croquetas in the city. Finally, for a unique setting, Bodega de los Secretos lets you dine in restored 17th-century wine caves, making it the most atmospheric choice near the Prado Museum.

After a late lunch, spend some time exploring Madrid’s unique ‘House Museums. These are former private palaces that preserve the intimate atmosphere of their original owners. The crown jewel of this collection is the Sorolla Museum, the sun-drenched former residence of ‘the painter of light.’ Following a major architectural renovation, this underrated museum is set to reopen its doors in 2026, offering a refreshed look at its stunning gardens and Mediterranean canvases.

Or if you want something else, there is also the nearby Museum of Romanticism, where you can enjoy a coffee in its secret garden, or visit the Lázaro Galdiano Museum to marvel at a private collection of Goya, Murillo, Velázquez, El Greco, or Bosch housed in a magnificent neo-Renaissance mansion.

In the evening, enjoy some food and relaxation.

The second day delves into the medieval and Renaissance layout of the city, famously known as Habsburg Madrid (Madrid de los Austrias). The central hub is Puerta del Sol, where a photo at Kilometer Zero and the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue are mandatory for a traveler’s geographic check-in. Kilometer Zero is the official starting point of all the highways and railways in the country, making this effectively the center of the entire country. There’s a small plaque you can snap a photo of.

Nearby is the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue (El Oso y el Madroño). The statue shows a bear reaching up to eat fruit from a madroño tree, symbols which come from Madrid’s coat of arms (the bear represents the city and the tree represents the land and nature surrounding it that has helped make it prosper).

From here, walk toward the iconic Plaza Mayor, highlighting its porticoed architecture and the Casa de la Panadería. Plaza Mayor once hosted bullfights, markets, symphonies, tournaments, and even executions. Now it’s ringed with tourist shops, cafés, and restaurants. It’s a good place from which to indulge in some people-watching, offers some good (though overpriced) bars, and occasionally has concerts and events.

For a true “Local Life” experience, stop for a calamari sandwich in the nearby alleys. Your taste buds will thank you.

After a relaxing lunch and some people watching, head to the Royal Palace of Madrid. The largest palace in Western Europe, the Baroque-style palace was built in the 18th century and is home to over 3,400 lavishly decorated rooms. It was originally built on a former 9th-century Muslim fort and today functions much like an art museum with numerous works, including pieces by Caravaggio, Juan de Flandes, and Francisco Goya. Though it’s the official residence of the royal family, they don’t actually live here anymore, and the palace is only used for official state functions. You can walk through the palace (both self-guided and guided tours are available), starting at the grand stairway, and wander through lavishly decorated staterooms. There’s also the Royal Armory, which houses a collection of medieval weapons and armor.

To end the day, head to the Almudena Cathedral. Unlike many of the famous medieval churches in Europe, this one was constructed in the late 19th century. It was finally completed in 1993 and was consecrated by Pope John Paul II. While the exterior has a Neo-Classical design (to match the nearby palace), the cathedral also has a Neo-Romanesque crypt with over 400 columns that you can explore. Be sure to head up to the dome for stunning views out over the city.

Madrid is a paradise for foodies. It’s one of the reasons I keep coming back. While there are plenty of food tours to take in Madrid, I suggest heading off on your own to explore. Begin at the city’s iconic gastronomic markets. The glass-walled Mercado de San Miguel is a must for gourmet tapas near Plaza Mayor. It’s popular with the after-work crowd and is a place I usually visit a few times on my trips. Additionally, local favorites like Mercado de San Antón in Chueca and Mercado de Vallehermoso offer a deeper dive into regional flavors. Just make sure to bring an appetite.

If you do want to take a food tour, consider doing a food tour. This post has more of my suggestions.

For dinner, head to Sobrino de Botín, officially recognized by the Guinness World Records as the world’s oldest restaurant. It was actually a favorite of Ernest Hemingway during his time in Madrid. For a more casual vibe, go ‘tapas crawling’ through the historic streets of La Latina or Barrio de las Letras.

As the sun sets, head to the Gran Vía to experience Madrid’s world-class rooftop culture. Venues like The Roof at Picalagartos or RIU, 360º sky bar offer signature cocktails and dinner with breathtaking 360-degree views of the skyline.

For those who don’t eat meat, Madrid has actually evolved into one of Europe’s best veg hubs, boasting a vibrant vegetarian and vegan scene in neighborhoods like Malasaña, where plant-based versions of traditional Spanish dishes are now a staple of the city’s diverse culinary identity.

Madrid is the only European capital where nature, science, and royal history converge in a UNESCO World Heritage oasis known as the ‘Paisaje de la Luz‘ (Landscape of Light). But this prestigious area, encompassing the iconic El Retiro Park and the Paseo del Prado, is just the beginning of Spain’s monumental legacy. For more UNESCO wonders, take a day trip out of the city.

One popular destination worth visiting is the Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, a sprawling imperial masterpiece recognized by UNESCO for its historical significance. El Escorial is located just one hour from the city by car and was commissioned by Philip II in the 16th century. It’s a massive palatial complex that includes a monastery, library, palace, basilica, and tomb for Spanish monarchs. Yet as massive as it is, it feels more austere than other palatial complexes, likely owing to its granite walls and symmetrical layout.

Another option for a day trip is the Royal Palace and Gardens of Aranjuez, a World Heritage Cultural Landscape that rivals the beauty of Versailles. Located just one hour south of the city, this was originally a hunting lodge, also commissioned in the 16th century by Philip II. It’s a blend of Renaissance and Baroque styles, with lavish rooms filled with tapestries, porcelain, and ornate decorations. There is lots of greenery and gardens here, which is partly why the royal family used this as their spring residence.

Lastly, there’s the historic university city of Alcalá de Henares, the birthplace of Spanish novelist, poet, and playwright Cervantes (he wrote Don Quixote). Just 45 minutes away by car, it also holds its own UNESCO World Heritage status, offering a perfectly preserved look into the Spanish Golden Age (1492–1659).

On your last day, it’s time to get further off the beaten path. Step back into the Golden Age at the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales and the nearby Royal Monastery of La Encarnación, two hidden palaces that house breathtaking royal art collections behind their cloistered walls.

The Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales is a convent founded in 1559 by Joanna of Austria (sister of Philip II). The name “Descalzas Reales” (which means “Royal Barefoot Ladies”) refers to the Order of Saint Clare nuns who lived here in relative austerity. What makes this monastery unique is that many aristocratic women took refuge here, often bringing their artworks and other valuables. Over the years, this turned the convent into a veritable treasure trove of art.

The Royal Monastery of La Encarnación was founded in 1611 by the wife of Philip III, Margaret of Austria. It was a royal convent, meaning it had the direct support of the monarchy. While the exterior has an austere Baroque style, the interior is quite lavish, with ornate chapels, colorful frescoes, and lots of religious sculptures and paintings. It’s also home to several notable relics, including a vial said to contain the blood of Saint Januarius. While tours are available, it’s still an active convent so parts are not open to the public (which, honestly, makes it all the more interesting to see).

To end your day with a local touch, head to the vast Casa de Campo park. This is the largest public park in the city, created in 1931. It covers a whopping 17 square kilometers (6.5 square miles) and includes an artificial lake, lots of paths, a zoo, and even an amusement park. Here, you can enjoy a scenic lunch or dinner at one of the lakeside terraces, offering an unrivaled view of the Royal Palace and Almudena Cathedral across the skyline. It’s the perfect place to end your trip.

While Barcelona tends to get more attention, I think Madrid is one of the best cities in Europe. It boasts a mouthwatering culinary scene, a raucous nightlife, and tons of things to see and do — no matter your interest or budget. I’ve been visiting the city for almost two decades and never get tired of the tapas, architecture, and history. The city just packs so much in and there really is something for everyone here. By following the itinerary above, you’ll see all the main sights while also getting off the beaten path in Spain’s historic capital.

#6309. Is airline elite status still worth it?

Is airline elite status worth it anymore? It's an age-old question that's back on plenty of travelers' minds — especially after two of the four largest U.S. carriers overhauled their loyalty programs this month.

And one theme is becoming clear: To get the best rewards, members are going to have to spend ... a lot.

Starting in 2027, taking the most United Airlines flights won't necessarily translate to the highest United MileagePlus status.

Instead, the airline's top elite members will be the customers who spend the most money — either on flights or the airline's cobranded credit cards.

Top-tier 1K status will also be harder to earn.

Meanwhile, Southwest Airlines took its biggest step yet toward nudging flyers toward its lineup of credit cards.

Beginning next year, every dollar its members charge to their Southwest Rapid Rewards cards will count toward status.

Southwest also closed a key shortcut to its most alluring perk: the Companion Pass. Going forward, members hoping to score the "buy-one, get-one" flight pass will have to spend their way to the airline's top status tier (or take 100 flights in a year).

These changes weren't entirely surprising.

Over the past decade, airline status has become less about the time you spend in the sky and more about the cash you're willing to spend.

For years, American Airlines and Delta Air Lines have awarded status based purely on the money their frequent flyers spend.

And across the industry, carriers have become more agnostic about whether those dollars come in the form of a flight booking or card swipe at the grocery store.

On some airlines, you can now technically swipe your way to status without ever setting foot on a plane.

Here's how much you'd need to pay for top-tier airline status in 2027 — if you went exclusively by credit card spending.

*Note: American has not announced what its status thresholds will be in 2027.

Note: United requires a minimum of four United-operated flights for members to be Premier-eligible.

Note: Cardholders earn a one-time 10,000 TQP boost upon hitting 130,000 TQPs in 2027.

Note: Elite credit earned by flying or other eligible spending reduces the card spending needed to qualify for elite status. Southwest still also offers elite qualification via flight segments.

It's not just the eye-popping dollar amounts travelers must now spend to reach status.

Airlines have also made carrying a credit card a more important part of the overall loyalty experience.

United and Delta cardholders now get access to better mileage redemptions than members who don't carry a card.

JetBlue will soon offer exclusive elite perks to JetBlue TrueBlue loyalty members who carry its top-tier card.

And even more airlines offer cardholders shortcuts to elite status.

Delta this month said it's on track to pull in a record $9 billion through its banking partnership with American Express.

American expects to make $8 billion this year through its tie-up with Citibank.

Those are eye-popping numbers, of course.

Beyond the raw cash flow, though, airlines also see turning flyers into cardholders as one of the best ways to become part of customers' day-to-day lives, even when they're not on a trip.

"It really is about making sure that we are top of mind for our members every single day, whether or not they're able to be on board our aircraft," Jarad Fisher, United's president of MileagePlus, said in a recent interview.

On one hand, airline status still offers a host of ways to save money, get better seats and travel with more flexible policies.

And, in some ways, qualify has become more realistic for travelers who aren't true "road warriors," since everyday spending counts toward status.

At the same time, free first-class upgrades have gotten harder to score and status benchmarks keep getting pricier to earn.

It's created a real dilemma for travelers who fly a lot — but only have so much money they're willing to put toward earning status: Is it worth dumping tens (or hundreds) of thousands of dollars onto your favorite airline's credit card to reach your status goal?

Think about what you're getting out of status, and whether it's worth the investment.

If not, you could be a candidate to hop off the status "hamster wheel" and be an airline "free agent."

But if you've crunched the numbers and decided status is still worth it, you may need to double down on your favorite airline.

And that might mean prioritizing credit card spending on that carrier's card. Because in 2026, that is almost as important as flying when it comes to unlocking the best perks.

Here's how much you'd need to pay for entry-tier airline status in 2027 if you went exclusively by credit card spending.

*Note: American has not announced what its status thresholds will be in 2027.

$25,000 with the Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® (see rates and fees)

Assumes 12 flight segments on American to fully unlock the card's "Flight Streak" benefit.

$25,000 with the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card

Note: United requires a minimum of four United-operated flights for members to be Premier-eligible.

$35,000 with any cobranded credit card, including the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card

Of course, the most efficient way to earn status is by combining your card spending with flying.

Spending on flights does typically earn you more elite credit (and points) than you'd get with typical credit card spending.

While airline credit cards can offer strong value with that carrier, other cards may offer a stronger return for your spending.

For instance, there's basically no airline card that truly competes with the American Express® Gold Card on rewards for dining worldwide and grocery purchases.

And some Capital One credit cards offer 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase.

Most of us only have so many dollars to dole out, and sometimes the best rewards to earn are the flexible points you can transfer to a wide range of partners.

Plus, as a frequent traveler, I also carry hotel cards that are key to unlocking perks once I arrive at my destination.

If you're rethinking your loyalty with a particular airline, there are status matches you can take advantage of to effectively "change airlines."

Just remember: Most U.S. carriers are now playing the "spending to status" game in some form. So, you may encounter similar sticker shock with your new carrier of choice.

Plus, even after matching, you'll likely have to hit an ambitious challenge goal to keep your status for the entire year.

While United and Southwest announced major overhauls to their loyalty and status programs, Delta opted to stay the course for next year.

Its Medallion qualification requirements will not change in 2027.

Delta's last major shake-up to its Delta SkyMiles program came in 2023, which led to significant backlash among its SkyMiles members.

American likely won't update its AAdvantage members for a few months since its loyalty year technically doesn't begin until March 1.

So, it remains to be seen whether the status game will continue getting harder for more flyers in the new year.

#6308. Sleep Under the Stars at These Incredible Igloo-Like Airbnbs Around the World

Few travel experiences are as otherworldly as watching the night sky from the cozy cocoon of a glass-topped igloo. In the far north, that might mean watching the aurora borealis shimmer overhead, surrounded by pine forests and frozen lakes. But you don't have to travel to the Arctic Circle to experience an igloo-like stay. From snow-covered mountain landscapes in Germany to peaceful corners of Spain, these unusual stays can be found in some unexpected places across Europe and beyond.

The impressive northern lights in Finnish Lapland

Many interiors lean into a Nordic theme—think Scandi-style decor, underfloor heating, faux-fur throws, and panoramic windows designed to maximise stargazing. In Nordic destinations, many of these igloos give you the chance to enjoy classic experiences nearby, such as husky and reindeer sledding, cold-water swimming, or a spell in a geothermal spa. Elsewhere, the appeal might be waking up to mountain views, exploring the surrounding countryside, or simply enjoying the novelty of sleeping inside a transparent dome.

Wrap up, pour a hot chocolate, and settle in—here are the best igloos to bed down in for a memorable night under the stars.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pet-friendly, private deck, hot tub

Set within 45 acres of secluded private woodland, this spacious dome is a cozy base for exploring the surrounding walking trails by day and stargazing after dark, thanks to the area's limited light pollution. Inside, there's a king-size bed, two fold-out single beds, armchairs, and a dining area, as well as a private bathroom with a hot shower and a small kitchenette equipped with a microwave, kettle, toaster, and fridge. Outside, the deck has plenty of seating and a barbecue, while a covered Scandinavian wood-fired hot tub overlooking the surrounding countryside can be used for an extra charge. Dogs are welcome too, making this a good option if you don't want to leave four-legged family members behind.

Location: Shropshire, United KingdomThings to do nearby: Ludlow Castle, Tenbury Museum, Mortimer Forest

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Lake views, fireplace, air-conditioning, hot tub

Perched on a hillside above Lake Superior, this geodesic dome combines the feel of camping with all the comforts of home. Designed to be enjoyed year-round, it has a gas fireplace and heating for chilly Minnesota winters, as well as air-conditioning for warmer summer days. There's room for up to four guests, with a queen bed and a second lofted bed, plus a fully equipped kitchen and bathroom with a walk-in shower. The highlight, though, is the large private deck, where a hot tub overlooks the lake and can be used throughout the year. The town of Two Harbors is also just a short drive away, with cafés, restaurants, shops and a local brewery.

Location: Two Harbors, MinnesotaThings to do nearby: Two Harbors town, Pierre the Voyager, Two Harbors Pierhead Light, Rock Beach

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: Studio, shared bathWhy we love it: Fjord views, secluded location, terrace

Perched on rocky terrain above Trondheim Fjord, Dome Smiberget makes the most of its spectacular waterfront setting. The geodesic dome feels wonderfully secluded, surrounded by trees with little between you and the water below. Inside, a wall of honeycomb-shaped windows wraps around the bed and seating area, framing sweeping views across the fjord and letting you watch the sky change without stepping outside. Come evening, you can stargaze from bed, while a small private terrace overlooking the water makes an idyllic spot to sit out when the weather plays along.

Location: Indre Fosen, NorwayThings to do nearby: Ulvestøtta monument, Sukkertoppen mountain hikes

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Outdoor grill, swimming pond, boules court

Drive through the scenic Dresden Elbe meadows to reach this rüdehof, which serves as both the headquarters of a family distillery and a tranquil countryside retreat—best enjoyed under a layer of icing-sugar snow in winter. The igloo is more like a hobbit house, with all you need to shelter from the cold, including a double bed, compact kitchen, shower room, and a dining area with panoramic, bucolic views. You're secluded as can be, around 90 minutes from Hamburg within a two-hectare wild and rugged estate, now yours to explore at your leisure. Stoke the fire and grill outdoors at suppertime, then settle in for some stargazing. If you're feeling brave, there's a swimming pond; then warm up in the hot tub afterwards. A boules court is available for a few leisurely games before supper.

Location: Amt Neuhaus, Niedersachsen, GermanyThings to do nearby: Stixer Wanderdüne hiking paths, Alte Eiche Forsthaus grüner Jäger momumental oak tree, Hamburg

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Fireplace, sledding, northern lights viewing

This is glamping, but not as most know it. On the cusp of Rovaniemi's thick pine forests, this igloo is furnished in true Nordic style with thick down blankets, plenty of wool rugs, cozy bedding, and a crackling log fireplace to huddle around in the evenings. Wrap up and head into the garden for wintry fun, including sledding—or simply huddle under the duvet to watch as frost forms and snow falls gently behind the windows.

Location: Rovaniemi, FinlandThings to do nearby: Ounasvaara Ski Oy ski resort, Ounasvaara Winter Trail, Forestry Museum of Lapland

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Panoramic views, breakfast included, kitchenette station

Spain isn't the first place you'd think of for igloo adventures, but this Airbnb might just change your mind. Deep in Spain's Selva de Irati forest, this immersive retreat pairs stylish design with wild beauty, perched on a hilltop overlooking the lush Aezkoa Valley. Interiors are simple and sparse, leaving space to focus on the comfortable silence and the nature that surrounds—there are dreamy panoramic views over the mountains from every angle. Previous guests have loved this experience, saying the sunsets from here are especially lovely. For something a little different, it's hard to beat.

Location: Orbaizeta, SpainThings to do nearby: Mirador de Zamariain viewpoint, Museo de Roncesvalles, Irati Forest

#6307. Faye Travel Insurance: The Best New Company Out there

We may receive compensation from Faye as an advertising partner. However, this does not influence our evaluations. Our opinions are our own.

I’ve been writing about travel for nearly two decades and, in that time, I’ve watched the travel insurance industry change at roughly the speed of a glacier. For years, the pitch was always the same: buy a policy, hope you never need it, and if something goes wrong, prepare for a paperwork marathon and a check that arrives somewhere between “eventually” and “you’ve forgotten you ever filed.”

I’ve personally been on the receiving end of that runaround. So have most travelers I know. It’s just something you kind of deal with. After all, you should never, ever, ever, EVER travel without travel insurance. You don’t want to end up needing a GoFundMe to pay your bills and get home if something goes wrong. (You can’t predict the future!)

Now, there’s a lot of players in this space but one I want to highlight today is Faye Travel Insurance, which I think is doing something unique.

Faye is a digital-first travel insurance company that launched coverage in the U.S. in 2022 so it’s pretty new to the US market when you consider that brands like World Nomads or Allianz have been offering coverage for over twenty years.

Faye is based on a pretty simple idea: travel insurance shouldn’t just sit there waiting for things to go wrong. It should actively help things go right.

That means whole-trip protection (your trip, your health, your stuff, even your pet), an app that’s actually useful while you’re traveling, 24/7 access to real human customer support, claims that get processed in days instead of months, and a digital wallet that pays you back almost instantly instead of waiting around for a check in the mail, which some companies still do in this day and age.

Faye has one plan for domestic and international trips, which makes things super easy. A lot of travel insurance companies have lots of plans and you end up squinting at coverage tables trying to figure out which one isn’t going to leave you stranded and has the coverage minimums you need. Faye built a single comprehensive plan that covers most of what travelers actually need:

These limits are pretty standard, especially on the medical coverage. If you want to add stuff on, they have a few optional addons that I think are really good and unique:

The CFAR insurance is really useful and I’ve rarely seen a company allow you to add it on to a policy. Usually, it’s already incorporated at a higher fee but this creates an affordable add on. I also love the pet care add on as more and more people travel with their pets.

Here’s where Faye really separates itself. Faye built something completely different! Here’s what you can actually do inside the Faye app:

Buy a policy in as little as 60 seconds – Plug in your trip details, get a quote, get covered.

Get real-time flight tracking and alerts – You’ll get delay info, gate changes, or baggage carousel numbers when you land! A lot of apps do this but this is a nice add on.

Telemedicine – Faye gives you access to a network of 20,000 telemedicine doctors in 21 languages when you travel abroad. If you wake up with food poisoning in a town where you don’t speak the language and don’t trust the local hospital reviews, you can talk to a doctor from your hotel bed. (As someone who has had to find doctors in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Find a doctor, pharmacy, ER, or ATM nearby – The app does the work of figuring out where to go when you’re disoriented and just need to find the closest open pharmacy at 11 p.m. in a city you arrived in five hours ago. (As someone who has had to do this in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Get free airport lounge access – If your flight is delayed by three hours or more, Faye gets you into a lounge – and who wouldn’t want lounge access with free food and drinks for a long delay?

Store your documents in Safekeeping – Securely u     pload your passport, visa, insurance card, vaccination records. If anything gets lost or stolen, you’ve got digital copies.

Check destination essentials before you go – Visa requirements, plug adapter types, local emergency numbers, weather, currency conversion, even local apps worth downloading.

Chat with real humans, 24/7 – Actual customer experience specialists, available every day of the year, including weekends and holidays.

Buy an eSIM – The app also enables you to purchase an eSIM meaning you can avoid pesky physical SIM swaps and get connected to the internet right when you land.

Here’s how Faye works: something bad happens. You open the app. You file a claim in a few minutes by uploading photos of your receipts. If it’s a qualifying issue like a baggage delay or flight delay, you may get reimbursed almost instantly. Funds go straight into Faye Wallet, a digital payment card built into the app that connects to Apple Pay or Google Pay. You tap and pay, right then and there, for whatever you actually need: a new outfit, toiletries, dinner, a hotel.

For larger or more complex claims, Faye aims to resolve them within 48 hours. of receiving the necessary documentation.

If you don’t want to use the digital wallet, you can transfer the funds to your bank account or get a paper check.

Pricing depends on your trip cost, destination, length, state of residence and age (same as every insurance product) but prices start at around $5.16 a day for international trips, which is a lot more competitive than other companies out there.

I’ve used a lot of travel insurance companies over the years. Most of them are fine. A few are awful. Faye is the first one that feels like it was designed by people who actually understand modern travel and get that we’re booking trips on our phones, communicating in apps, and expecting the same digital convenience from insurance that we get from everything else.

The combination of whole-trip protection, the app, Faye Wallet, real human support, and fast claims has genuinely changed how I think about this category. Travel insurance used to be the thing I bought and forgot.

If you’re heading out on a trip soon, check it out at withfaye.com, get a quote, and see for yourself.

#6306. The 4 Amex cards I’d use to earn Membership Rewards points faster

Here's the fun part about American Express Membership Rewards: You don't necessarily need to spend more to earn more points. You need the right card in your hand at the right time.

The best Amex setup shouldn't require a flowchart. It should feel almost effortless, with your points balance growing in the background while every card earns its keep.

These are the four Amex cards I'd choose to maximize your Membership Rewards balance, whether you're looking for one great earner or a multifaceted points strategy.

These cards made my list because each has a distinct job. Most people won't need all four, but picking the right one (or complementary pair) can help your existing spending earn 2, 4 or even 5 points per dollar instead of just 1 point per dollar.

Want a single card to handle your personal expenses? For that, the American Express Gold Card is the workhorse of an Amex points strategy.

It earns 4 points per dollar at U.S. supermarkets on up to $25,000 in purchases each calendar year and at restaurants worldwide on up to $50,000, then 1 point per dollar. If groceries and dining are a large share of your budget, these bonus categories can build your points balance quickly.

The Gold isn't limited to food, either. It earns:

That range makes it my strongest one-card recommendation for someone who wants to earn Membership Rewards points across both everyday spending and travel.

The card has a $325 annual fee (see rates and fees), but includes up to $10 monthly Uber Cash for eligible U.S. Uber and Uber Eats orders†, up to $10 monthly dining statement credit with select partners and up to $50 biannual statement credits at U.S. Resy restaurants. (Enrollment is required for select benefits.)

That makes the fee easiest to justify for someone who will use the statement credits naturally and put the earning categories to work. Still, the credits are supporting actors here: The strong bonus categories are why the Gold deserves top billing.

If, like me, you spend about $800 per month at the grocery store, that alone will earn you 38,400 points annually. If you also spend $500 per month on dining, $3,000 per year in flights and $1,000 in prepaid hotels booked through Amex Travel, your annual haul climbs to 76,400 points.

That's worth over $1,500 according to TPG's October 2026 valuations.

Personally, I'd be tempted to transfer 60,000 of those points to Air France-KLM Flying Blue for a one-way business-class saver award between the U.S. and Europe. Those seats can be difficult to find, but that's the kind of redemption that makes my grocery runs feel more rewarding.

†Uber Cash will only be deposited into one Uber account when you add the Amex Gold as a payment method and redeem with any Amex card.

To learn more, read our full review of the American Express Gold Card.

Airfare is where the American Express Platinum Card gets its chance to flex.

The card earns 5 points per dollar on flights purchased directly from airlines or through American Express Travel®, including through AmexTravel.com and the Amex Travel App, on up to $500,000 in these purchases each calendar year (then 1 point per dollar). It also earns 5 points per dollar on prepaid lodging booked through Amex Travel and 1 point per dollar on all other eligible purchases.

Spending $4,000 on airfare each year would earn 20,000 Membership Rewards points on the Platinum card. That's worth about $400 according to our valuations, compared to just $40 earned on a 1% cash-back credit card. That level of spending isn't outlandish: A family of four paying $500 per ticket for two trips a year would reach it. I usually travel more than twice a year, so that difference can add up even faster.

Don't overlook the fact that these rewards come from booking flights directly with the airline, either. Buying straight from the source instead of through a travel portal can make it easier to change or cancel your reservation if your plans change, or when you have to make last-minute adjustments due to delays or operational cancellations.

The Platinum carries an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), so it makes the most sense for frequent flyers who can pair the airfare earnings with benefits they'll also use. My favorites are its broad airport lounge access through the American Express Global Lounge Collection, up to $200 in annual airline fee statement credits for incidental charges with one selected qualifying airline and complimentary Hilton Honors Gold status. Enrollment is required for select benefits.

To learn more, read our full review of the American Express Platinum Card.

Every business has expenses that refuse to cooperate with bonus categories. The Blue Business Plus Credit Card from American Express makes sure those purchases still pull their weight.

The card earns 2 points per dollar spent on the first $50,000 in eligible purchases each calendar year, then 1 point per dollar. It also earns 2 points per dollar spent on prepaid hotels and other eligible travel purchases booked through amextravel.com (and those purchases don't count toward the $50,000 annual threshold). There's also no annual fee (see rates and fees).

That makes the Blue Business Plus an excellent catch-all card for eligible business owners. Rather than worrying about whether each purchase falls into the right merchant category, you can use it for general business spending and know you're earning twice the standard rate until you hit the annual cap.

Maxing out the threshold with $50,000 in business expenses would earn 100,000 Membership Rewards points. If your business values simplicity more than squeezing every last penny out of a redemption, one of the easiest options is to use those points to cover $1,000 in airfare booked through Amex Travel. Transferring your points to travel partners might be worth even more.

It isn't the flashiest card in the Amex portfolio, but quietly doubling your points on broad business spending is a skill worth having.

To learn more, read our full review of the Blue Business Plus Credit Card.

Related: Who qualifies for a business credit card?

Some businesses spend a little everywhere. Others have two or three expense categories that swallow the budget whole.

The American Express Business Gold Card is built for the latter. It automatically earns 4 points per dollar in the two eligible categories where your business spends the most each billing cycle, on up to $150,000 in combined purchases each calendar year, then 1 point per dollar.

My favorite part: Amex automatically identifies your two highest eligible spending categories each billing cycle, so you don't need a crystal ball to make a selection in advance, and you don't have to analyze your expenses line by line to choose a category after the fact. The strongest categories can even change from month to month, allowing the card to adapt to your business rather than forcing your business to follow the card.

A business putting $50,000 of qualifying expenses on the card would earn 200,000 Membership Rewards points, even without maxing out the full annual bonus threshold. One way I'd put those points to work is by transferring them to Aeroplan. That balance would cover two round-trip tickets from Miami to Rio de Janeiro — in business class.

The card has a $375 annual fee (see rates and fees), so its sweet spot is a business with enough qualifying spending to put the 4-point-per-dollar rate to serious use. For smaller or more varied expenses, the Blue Business Plus may be the easier fit.

To learn more, read our full review of the American Express Business Gold Card.

For most customers, holding all four cards is overkill, but pairing two together can supercharge your earnings compared to carrying a single card.

For personal spending, the Gold does most of the earning work on its own with its generous earning rates. Adding the Platinum improves your rewards on flights, but the combination is better evaluated as using the Gold as your primary earner and the Platinum as a way to enhance your experience through its many benefits and statement credits.

The business pairing is much easier to defend. Use the Business Gold for purchases in your two highest eligible bonus categories and the Blue Business Plus for everything else. One handles the obvious expenses; the other cleans up everything left behind.

If you're juggling both personal and business expenses, my pick is for the personal Gold and Blue Business Plus. Between the two, you'll earn 2 to 4 points per dollar on an impressive number of charges while paying only one annual fee.

Welcome offers are exciting, but short-lived. Long-term point maximization comes from paying with the right card.

And the best Amex card for earning Membership Rewards points depends on where you spend the most.

I may dream of an infinite points balance, but the goal isn't to collect every shiny Amex card; it's to make more of my spending earn 2, 4 or 5 points per dollar.

For personal spending, the Gold is a strong choice for groceries and dining, while the Platinum can provide additional value for frequent flyers who use its premium travel benefits. Business owners may prefer the Blue Business Plus for everyday purchases or the Business Gold for concentrated spending in its bonus categories.

Once your biggest expenses earn more than 1 point per dollar, all that's left is remembering which card to use when it's time to pay and letting the points pile up from spending you were already doing.
