#6305. The 15 Most Haunted Places in the World and How to Visit Them

The most haunted places in the world may seem like something out of a fable that defies all logic. They're places where UFOs hover over Transylvanian forests, headless queens roam through castle corridors, and ghosts take shape of bears, children, and any other creature imaginable. No matter where you’re traveling, you’re sure to find some sort of haunted landmark, hotel, even landmark-turned-hotel—and usually a ghost tour to go along with it.

You might be guided more by scholarly than ghastly pursuits, though these locations are still worth your time. Spectral hauntings often come with spectacular history, architecture, and artwork, not to mention proximity to incredible cities and natural beauty. Whether you’re scheming up a Halloween trip or simply want to entertain the chills with a dash of the macabre, explore 15 of the most haunted places in the world below, if you dare.

Over the span of nearly one millennium, the Tower of London has served as an armory, prison, menagerie, and palace. Though best known today for its housing of the Crown Jewels, the UNESCO World Heritage Site also falls among the most haunted places in the United Kingdom. It's not uncommon to hear strange noises echo through the White Tower, while over a dozen ghosts—with backstories that range from ridiculous to outright tragic—are said to lurk in its limestone hallways.

The most infamous apparition is that of Anne Boleyn, Henry VIII's second wife, who was executed in the tower in 1536 for being found guilty for treason and adultery. Today, some visitors may encounter her headless body roaming about, head in hand. Other specters include two young princes who were mysteriously murdered in the 1400s and even multiple accounts of a phantom bear, who made multiple appearances in the 1800s and was said to leave any witness dead.

There are two long-running explanations for the curses that plague this 16th-century fort in Rajasthan. The first is that a religious ascetic had destroyed the fort and nearby towns after its height surpassed that of his own home, casting Bhangarh in perpetual shadow. The second, equally melodramatic, is that a black magic priest fell in love with a princess and was crushed to death by a boulder after she rejected him; right before he passed, however, he condemned the premises to a fate of destruction.

Today, the scene at the fort is quite serene, and visitors can wander throughout royal palace ruins, Hindu temples such as Gopinath and Hanuman, as well as old marketplaces and townhouses like Nartakiyon Ki Haveli. The fort is open each day from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., as no visitors—those living, at least—can legally stay after sunset.

Built by lumber magnate Carl Beck for his family in the late 1800s, this house in Penetanguishene is one of Ontario's most troublesome. Legend goes that after Beck's wife passed away, his eldest daughter Mary was put in charge of raising her younger siblings. Years later, when Carl died, he inexplicably left Mary $1 in his will. Today, an angry female ghost—presumably Mary—is said to appear in the upstairs windows (you’d probably haunt the house too if your dad gave you a $1 inheritance). For any travelers curious about Victorian architecture with a side of paranormality, consider renting the Carl Beck House on Airbnb.

What's far scarier than a haunted graveyard? A haunted graveyard 50 feet underwater. Micronesia’s Chuuk Lagoon (formerly Truk Lagoon) served as a fortified base for the Japanese Navy during World War II and was attacked by American forces during a three-day air strike in 1944. Dozens of warships, planes, tanks, and railroad cars sank to the bottom of the lagoon, where they still remain in what is known as the “Ghost Fleet of Truk Lagoon.”

The ship graveyard is immensely popular amongst scuba divers, with PADI dubbing it “one of the best wreck diving destinations on the planet.” Underwater explorers can swim up close to the wartime vessels, which are littered with weapons, gas masks, and, according to some superstitious divers, a few waterlogged ghosts.

This Victorian-era prison in Belfast is often referred to as Europe’s Alcatraz and for good reason. During its 150 years of operation, the jail contained some 25,000 inmates (men, women, and children), publicly hung many prisoners, and buried their bodies within the prison walls. The institution officially shut its doors in 1996, but the ghosts of deceased inmates are said to still roam the iron walkways today.

If this sounds like the sort of place you want to spend time in, you’re in luck—Crumlin Road Gaol offers daily tours, live concerts, and reasonably priced meals at its in-house (in-prison?) restaurant. It even serves as a venue for conferences and, believe it or not, weddings.

Though travelers have been coming to Estes Park since 1909 to enjoy The Stanley Hotel’s stately Georgian architecture and world-renowned whiskey bar, its reputation took a dark turn on October 30, 1974, when Stephen King and his wife, Tabitha, checked in. The hotel was about to close for the season, and the couple were the only guests there. King was particularly struck by the endless empty corridors that he walked through after dinner, and the property as a whole ended up serving as inspiration for The Shining’s Overlook Hotel.

Of the eerie stay, King said, “[The hotel] seemed the perfect—maybe the archetypical—setting for a ghost story. That night I dreamed of my three-year-old son running through the corridors, looking back over his shoulder, eyes wide, screaming. He was being chased by a fire-hose. I woke up with a tremendous jerk, sweating all over, within an inch of falling out of bed.” In the years since, the hotel has leaned into the reputation King bestowed upon it with ghost tours and a resident psychic.

Named after a shepherd who, along with his flock of 200 sheep, vanished without a trace in the forest, Hoia-Baciu hit it big in 1968 when a military technician photographed a supposed UFO hovering over the trees. Some believe it to be a portal capable of transporting visitors to places unknown. Those who pass through (and live to tell the tale) have reported rashes, nausea, and anxiety. The curved, spindly trees that make up the forest are particularly conducive to a twisted feeling, as is the location in Transylvania—a real nexus point of abnormal activity.

The St. Augustine Lighthouse is visited by over 200,000 people annually, though it's just as well-known for its otherworldly guests. Several tragic events that occurred at the now-historic site have contributed to the alleged paranormal activity. The ghost of a lighthouse keeper who fell to his death while painting the tower has been spotted watching over the grounds. Ever since the horrific death of three young girls, who drowned when the cart they were playing in broke and fell into the ocean, visitors have claimed to hear the sounds of children playing in and around the lighthouse.

Less than half a mile from the canals of Venice, Poveglia Island has served as a quarantine zone for bubonic plague victims, storage space for Napoleon’s weapons, and the site of an early 20th-century psychiatric hospital. The latter played host to horrific medical experiments and finally closed for good in 1968 after a doctor threw himself off the institution’s bell tower. Locals still claim to hear echoing chimes from the island—even though the bell was removed decades ago. Though it's illegal to visit Poveglia, you can see the island and decaying hospital at a safe distance from the beaches of nearby Lido or by hiring your own boat charter to pass a little closer (do not disembark onto the island).

Himeji Castle dates to 1333 and is regarded as one of the greatest remaining examples of Japanese castle architecture. It also has some rather eerie folklore associated with it—most notably the story of Okiku, a palace servant who was falsely accused of losing valuable dishes and thrown to her death in the castle’s well as punishment. Her ghost now sulks in the castle at night, counting dishes in a mournful tone; she reaches nine before shrieking and returning to the well’s depths. A visit to Himeji Castle is best done as a day trip from Osaka, about two hours away by train.

On the northern edge of Ireland's Wicklow Mountains, at the summit of Montpelier Hill, the ruins of a lone building remain. As many tales begin, the hill was originally site to an ancient grave, which wealthy Irishman William Conolly disregarded (even taking stones from) while building a hunting lodge in the 1720s. It's no surprise that terror ensued, and after Conolly's death, private club Hell Fire Club occupied the space, where they were said to engage in black masses, ritual murder, and other occultish happenings. At one such meeting, an unfamiliar guest with horse hooves as feet disappeared as mysteriously as they arrived. A curious farmer who had witnessed another night unfold was apparently left so terrified he no longer remembered his own name. Today, an enormous black cat with striking eyes is said to haunt Montpelier, which, beyond its murky past, offers forest trails and guided paths that make for an otherwise pleasant walk (before dusk).

Hidden among the canals of Xochimilco, Isla de las Muñecas (“Island of the Dolls”) is something of an internet legend and dark tourism mecca. The backstory centers on a man named Julian Santa Barrera, who reportedly encountered the body of a girl floating in the channels. Shortly thereafter, he found a discarded doll in the same canals, and he hung it from a tree on an artificial island in her honor—and to ward off evil spirits. So he continued, adding more and more dolls to appease the ghost of the young girl.

After Barrera passed away in 2001, his family opened the island to the public, and travelers have been seeking it out ever since. As if the mere idea of the island isn’t unnerving enough, there have also been reports of the dolls whispering to each other and moving their eyes.

Often considered the “king of Czech castles,” this early Gothic fortress in South Bohemia has undergone sieges and assaults from the 1400s onward, though, today, the source of its terrors is an impish creature called Rarášek, who is said to trip and poke at any unassuming visitor. A ghastly woman, known only as “the White Lady,” also resides here, while hellhounds allegedly guard a secret passage to the castle tombs.

Beyond the paranormal, visitors can enjoy self-guided tours through Zvíkov's cellars, courtyards, and rooms—be sure to stop and take a look at St. Wenceslas Chapel's frescoes.

The entire city of Savannah is essentially one giant ghost story, due in large part to the mysterious tunnels that run below the town’s streets. The underground structures play a major role in many of Savannah's most haunted locations, including Forsyth Park, the fountained green space you probably recognize from a postcard or two.

According to Savannah Magazine, doctors at the adjacent Candler Hospital (now the Savannah Law School) performed autopsies in the tunnels below. Maria Pinheiro, a historian and spokesperson with Ghost City Tours, says these below-the-surface rumblings make Forsyth Park particularly ripe for sightings of shadowy shapes that, even if unclear, it's certain they are not of this world.

#6303. Nomad Citizen: A New Social Safety Net for Entrepreneurs

If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health plan, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a corporate job. And you cannot use a country’s social safety net because, well, you’re not a citizen, right? You’re just roaming the world!

The travel insurance company Safety Wing is looking to change that. They have always wanted to create this all-in-one package for digital nomads that includes insurance, employee benefits, and a social safety net.

I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just launched what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.

Nomad Citizen is an annual membership that bundles health coverage, travel protection, income protection, and life insurance benefits into a single plan. It’s for location-independent entrepreneurs and business owners who spend more than half the year outside their home country and whose lives and income cross borders as a default.

Nomad Citizen covers you globally with no residency restrictions (except for Puerto Rico).

Nomad Citizen covers people under 56 and earning at least $4,000 USD per month. You sign up online, choose your start date, declare that you’re in good health, and confirm you’ll be outside your passport country for more than half the year. You can also add your partner and any children under 18.

But who should sign-up? This is an interesting product. I definitely think there’s a niche for it. After all, let’s say you’re an entrepreneur in Bali and don’t have access to any social safety net. What happens if you get sick or really hurt and you’re out of work? A friend of mine in Mexico was hit by a car and severely hospitalized and ate into his travel insurance limits really quickly. Afterwards, he couldn’t work for months while he was in rehab and started a GoFundMe for help. A product like Nomadic Citizen would have helped him. Or helped any of the other digital nomads who get injured on the road and have to raise funds.

I think this product is good for someone who is living in a country outside their own without access to social services and a robust social safety net. For example, if you live in Sweden and have access to all the benefits of the State, this product probably isn’t for you because they have tons of services but if you live in Thailand, Mexico, Indonesia, or France but don’t have access to benefits, or are just roaming the world, have a high income, work on your own, or have a family, then this product would be something to consider.

For those signing up on or after July 1, 2026, the Nomad Citizen membership costs $443 per month for those 18 to 39. If you’re 40 – 49, it’s $665 per month, and $875 per month for 50-55. Children cost $143 per month (couples on the plan can add their first child under 10 at no cost). You can pay monthly or annually.

A note about US coverage: Nomad Citizen is truly worldwide, including the US, although it should be noted that coverage limits were not designed for extensive use there…because well, the US health care system is just a mess.

Income protection: The income protection benefit is probably the single most compelling reason Nomad Citizen exists. Traditional income protection or disability insurance requires a fixed employer, a permanent address, and residency in a specific country. Freelancers and sole traders working across borders are essentially uninsurable for income loss through conventional schemes, such as government assistance.

If you’re a freelancer or remote worker and you lose your income (you’re laid off, your contracts dry up, or you can’t work due to a medical condition), Nomad Citizen pays you up to $4,000 per month for up to 3 or 6 months while you get back on your feet. That benefit doesn’t exist anywhere else!

Health insurance: Up to $1.5 million in annual coverage for inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, dental, vision, mental health, maternity, preventive care, wellness therapies, and more. This is just like health insurance where you live and covers everything you need. It is far more robust than regular travel insurance, which is only there for emergencies.

Travel coverage: Trip delays, cancellations, stolen electronics, lost luggage, evacuation, robbery, family visits during hospitalisation.

Parental leave: If you have a baby or become a legal guardian of a child, they pay US$4,000/month so you can take time off work without worrying about money. There is a waiting period of 3 years to access this benefit.

Long-term disability: If something really serious happens to you and you are permanently forced to stop working because, for instance,  you lose your eyesight, you’re diagnosed with cancer, you have a major stroke, or you can no longer do basic things like walk, dress yourself, or eat on your own, they pay you US$4,000/month up to age 75.

Visa assistance: Members can browse and apply for different governments’ versions of long-term visas designed for nomads (i.e. they can work on those visas) directly through our app interface without having to apply through the government websites. They handle all the direct communication with the government and quality check your application before submission to maximize the chances of approval.

Nomad Care Map: Find the best providers through their member-powered database of more than 4000 healthcare providers all over the world, with ratings for service and English level.

Payment cards: Use your SafetyWing card to pay for covered services up to $500. This auto-generates a claim that has already been paid so you do not have to wait for reimbursement. The SafetyWing card is a worldwide prepaid debit card that is sent to every Nomad Citizen member, which they can use to pay for doctor’s appointments or prescriptions without using their own money.

24/7 human support: You’ll have access to 24/7 live chat so you can get an answer from a real person within a few minutes.

Everything in one app: Claims, coverage details, customer care, provider search with Nomad Care Map, and visa assistance are all managed through a single app. There is no need to switch between a health insurer, a travel insurer, and a separate income protection provider (if one existed).

For health coverage, you either pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement or contact the 24/7 team to arrange direct payment with the provider. For travel claims, you collect documentation (police reports, carrier delay notices, receipts) and submit a claim. For income protection, you work with SafetyWing to verify the loss and provide evidence that you’re actively seeking new income. Everything is managed through one app and they make it really simple and easy to do.

I love SafetyWing’s mission and use their travel insurance on all my trips. This new Nomad Citizen product is perfect for people who are full-time digital nomads and want some sort of income protection as well as more robust health and travel coverage and the kind of social safety programs you would get if you lived in one place. After all, when you are a solopreneur, you do worry about what happens if you get injured, can’t work, or have a kid. It’s all on you, right? Nomad Citizen is the program that ensures that you won’t have to worry about this kind of stuff anymore.

#6302. Capital One Offers: How to earn cash back and rewards when you shop

If you have a Capital One credit card, you may be able to earn extra rewards on purchases through Capital One Offers.

Similar to Amex Offers and Chase Offers, the program gives eligible cardholders access to shopping deals that can help them save on purchases they were already planning to make.

Here's how Capital One Offers works, how to use it and what to know before shopping.

Capital One Offers is a shopping rewards platform that gives eligible Capital One customers access to special deals at participating merchants. Offers span categories such as clothing, electronics, home goods and travel.

The platform is available to eligible U.S. consumer Capital One credit card holders, including those with cards in the Venture, Savor and Quicksilver families. (Business credit cards are not eligible.)

You can access available offers through your online account or the Capital One mobile app. However, eligibility varies by account, so you'll need to sign in to see which offers are available to you.

Unlike the standard rewards you earn on everyday purchases, Capital One Offers requires you to select an eligible deal and follow its redemption instructions.

For example, if you find an offer for 5% back at a retailer, you could earn that reward on top of the points or miles you'd normally earn with your credit card, as long as your purchase meets the offer's terms.

Capital One Offers is different from Capital One Shopping. Capital One Offers provides deals through eligible Capital One accounts, while Capital One Shopping is a separate shopping tool that helps users find coupon codes, compare prices and track price drops.

Related: Everything you need to know about credit card merchant offers

The deals you'll find through Capital One Offers depend on what's available when you sign in. You might see discounts on clothing, electronics or hotel bookings, with participating merchants and reward rates varying.

Some offers apply to most purchases from a retailer, while others are limited to certain products or categories. Keep in mind that rewards may also exclude taxes, shipping and other fees.

You can find Capital One Offers through the issuer's website or mobile app:

From there, you can browse deals or search for a specific merchant.

How you redeem an offer depends on whether you're shopping online or in a physical store.

Keep in mind that for online offers, the link you use matters, as Capital One relies on tracking information to associate your purchase with the offer.

Be sure to confirm which locations, payment methods and purchases qualify. An online offer won't necessarily apply to an in-store transaction, or vice versa.

Related: How to maximize online shopping portals for your purchases

Capital One says rewards typically arrive in about 45 days, although some can take up to three billing cycles. Certain offers may take longer.

For hotel offers, payouts are issued after you complete your stay, and the reservation must be completed within one year of booking.

Related: The best credit cards for online shopping

There are a few things worth keeping in mind before taking advantage of an offer.

I've gotten into the habit of checking Capital One Offers whenever I'm shopping online with my Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card. Sometimes there's a deal worth using, but other times I'll find a better offer through another shopping portal.

That's why it's worth comparing your options before making a purchase. For example, an offer for 5% back through Capital One, for example, might not be as valuable as a higher reward rate elsewhere.

Just keep in mind that you generally can't stack Capital One Offers with other shopping portals or promotional codes. Using another portal or certain coupons could invalidate your reward, so you'll want to decide which offer to use before checking out.

For travel purchases, I'd also recommend comparing the total price and booking conditions rather than focusing solely on the advertised reward.

Each offer has its own terms, including potential spending requirements, expiration dates and usage limits. Some deals may exclude gift cards, certain products or other purchases, while others may be limited to a single transaction.

Look at the terms before shopping, particularly if you're making a large purchase or planning to use an offer more than once.

You can check the status of your Capital One Offers rewards by opening the menu on the right side of the Capital One Offers page and selecting "Shopping Trips." From there, you'll see a tracker showing the status of your purchases and rewards.

It's also worth saving your offer details and order confirmations, especially for purchases with longer payout timelines.

If your reward hasn't arrived when expected, double-check that you met the offer requirements before contacting Capital One.

Related: Capital One miles: How to earn, redeem and transfer rewards

Capital One Offers can be an easy way to earn extra rewards on purchases you're already planning to make.

Before shopping, check your account for available deals, compare your options and follow the offer's instructions to make sure your purchase qualifies.

Just remember that offers and eligibility can vary, so a deal available to one Capital One customer may not be available to another.

Related: Tips and tricks to get maximum value from your Capital One miles

#6301. American Airlines Pilots Told Not To Eat The Tiramisu, Now Union Says Never Mind

UPDATE: The Allied Pilots Association has withdrawn its warning about tiramisu served in American Airlines crew meals in Phoenix. Following an investigation involving American’s safety team, Phoenix inflight staff, and the caterer, the union now says it was a false alarm.

Yesterday, APA ​Aeromedical was advised by the ​PHX ​Flight ​Office that ​a dessert ​included ​with ​some crew meals may ​have contained ​alcohol.

Out of ​an abundance of ​caution, APA issued an immediate ​advisory recommending that crewmembers ​not ​consume the dessert, ​specifically ​the ​tiramisu, ​until ​additional information ​could be obtained. ​Following coordination ​with ​AA ​Corporate ​Safety, PHX Inflight, ​the catering ​provider, and ​other ​involved ​parties, APA has confirmed ​that ​the desserts ​in question ​are safe ​to ​consume ​and ​do not pose a ​risk to ​aviation safety.

We appreciate the ​PHX ​Flight ​Office ​for promptly ​raising the concern and ​working with ​both American Airlines ​and APA to investigate the potential ​issue. The ​initial ​advisory ​was ​issued ​based on the information available ​at ​the ​time ​and ​with crew ​and ​flight ​safety ​as ​the priority. ​We appreciate your patience ​while additional fact finding ​was ​conducted.

For those pilots ​involved ​in a HIMS ​program ​we ​would like to ​use ​this ​as an opportunity to ​remind you that ​consuming ​certain ​food additives ​and extracts in large quantities may pose a ​risk to ​abstinence ​monitoring. Please consult ​the APA ​HIMS Subcommittee ​for additional ​information.

As ​always, ​please reach out to APA ​Aeromedical ​with any ​questions or ​concerns.

APA explained that its initial warning was precautionary, based on information available at the time…though I’m wondering what information

American Airlines pilots have been warned to skip the tiramisu in some crew meals out of Phoenix because it contains alcohol. That is an awkward ingredient to find in a meal provided to people who are supposed to be flying airplanes…

JonNYC shared a warning attributed to the Allied Pilots Association’s Aeromedical–HIMS Committee concerning meals supplied by American’s contracted caterer in Phoenix:

“The contracted catering provider has included tiramisu containing alcohol on some crew meal trays. Because the dessert is not cooked after the alcohol is added, alcohol may remain in the finished product.

“We recommend that no crew member consume this dessert.

“APA cannot determine the amount of alcohol contained in an individual serving or what effect consumption could have if a crewmember were subsequently required to undergo DOT alcohol testing.”

"PHX Crew Meal Alert – Tiramisu Containing Alcohol

The APA Aeromedical–HIMS Committee has been made aware of an issue affecting crews based in or transiting PHX.

The contracted catering provider has included tiramisu containing alcohol on some crew meal trays.…

The notice says the committee is coordinating with the Phoenix Flight Office to have the dessert removed and replaced. In the meantime, crews are advised to accept an incomplete meal rather than eat it.

Pilots who have already consumed the tiramisu and have concerns about their fitness to fly are instructed to contact their union domicile representatives immediately. The warning expressly tells them not to let schedule pressure influence that decision.

The notice does not establish that a serving would cause impairment or a failed alcohol test. The committee says it does not know the alcohol content or the potential testing consequences. But crews should not have to evaluate that uncertainty while eating an airline-provided meal!

The FAA explains that a confirmed alcohol concentration of 0.02 to 0.039 requires temporary removal from safety-sensitive duties, even though that result is not itself a federal testing violation. A confirmed result of 0.04 or greater carries more serious consequences.

American’s Phoenix caterer apparently supplied an alcohol-containing dessert in crew meals, prompting a union warning to leave it untouched while a replacement is arranged. I like tiramisu, but this is one setting where the alcohol-free version is the obvious choice. Pilots have enough to think about without wondering whether their crew meal could complicate an alcohol test…

#6300. How Travel Can Be an Antidote to Optimization Culture

I’m seconds away from jumping into the Adriatic Sea from the platform of a 55-foot catamaran aptly named Slice of Heaven when one of my friends says she misses her routine Pilates classes. I try to bite my tongue—I don’t want to be rude!—but I can’t help myself. “Look around,” I say, exasperated. “This is your workout.”

I fling my hand toward the pebbly shore where our captain, Tony, has just dropped anchor in an idyllic bay somewhere between Stari Grad and Vis, along Croatia’s Dalmatian Coast. A forested hillside rises above the beach, and there’s not a single other boat in sight. Tony is busy launching the paddle board into the water, while our hostess, Matea, cooks up a surprise Croatian lunch. The cerulean water is so clear I can see all the way to the seafloor, where colorful fish glimmer in the light.

The author sailed from Split to Dubrovnik on a chartered catamaran dubbed Slice of Heaven.

By any measure, this is paradise, which is exactly why I’m baffled. Who could think about Pilates classes when this is right in front of you?

I love traveling with my friends, many of whom live all over the world—in Latin America, Europe, Africa, the US, and beyond—and this is one of the only ways we get to see each other. The Pilates comment doesn’t come out of nowhere, as we’re a group that keeps things balanced: Each trip usually contains equal parts revelry and cultural activities, loads of wine followed by electrolytes for recovery, and enough belly laughs and deep conversations to sustain us until we book the next getaway.

But recently, I’ve noticed a shift: our trips are becoming less of a break from normal life and moreso an extension of it. We spend more time stressing over holding onto the very routines we seek to escape than we do living in the moment. I understand the pressure to not only be healthy, but to look healthy, because it affects me, too. And now, with wearables like Whoop bands and Oura rings telling us how we feel, rather than the old-fashioned way—listening to our bodies to intuitively know how we feel—we can track our wellness progress. Or lack of it.

Sail Croatia operates the 55-foot catamaran Slice of Heaven for private charters of up to eight guests.

According to the Global Wellness Institute, the wellness economy reached $6.8 trillion in 2024 and is predicted to soar to $9.8 trillion by 2029, while wellness tourism alone reached $894 billion in 2024 and is on track to surpass $1.4 trillion by 2029. McKinsey’s Future of Wellness research even found that 84% of US consumers consider wellness a top priority in their everyday lives. It’s clear most people want to be well, and now more than ever, they’re refusing to leave their routines at home when they travel.

We’d been talking about this trip for months: an eight-day private catamaran tour with Sail Croatia that I intend to enjoy every minute of. I’m not immune to the pressure to be well and look well—especially when I’ll be in a swimsuit for eight days—so I’ve made the ocean my gym for the week, stand-up paddle boarding and swimming in the Adriatic. I know I’ll eat and drink more and sleep less over the next several days, but I also know I’ll swim and walk more and have memories that will last forever.

I take a deep breath and stretch before diving into the sea. When I surface, Tony throws me the paddle, and one of my friends joins me in my “workout.” We wobble around on the board until we successfully balance our weight, which proves even more interesting when Matea hands us two Aperol Spritzes.

I work up a sweat as I paddle us to the cliff walls, where we down our drinks before taking to the shore, acting like children as we take turns cannonballing into the water and climbing the rocks, looking for shells.

Perhaps I’m doing the same thing as my friend, but I’m more secretive about it—turning moments of this trip into an opportunity to stay fit—but for me, getting outside and into the landscape is what I call balance.

Mljet National Park's saltwater lakes are open to the public for swimming.

Over the next few days, we sail from Vis to Hvar, then on to Korčula and Mljet. Croatia exceeds all of my expectations. All I can think about is how blissful it feels to split a lavender cheesecake at San Marco restaurant above Hvar’s St. Stephen’s Square, the biggest in Dalmatia; how dizzying it is to climb the wooden ladder to Massimo in Korčula, a 15th-century tower that’s now a bar, where our cocktails arrive by pulley; and how freeing it feels to cycle the wide lanes beneath Mljet’s forested canopy, where the island’s saltwater lakes offer some of the most serene swimming of the trip.

But as we sail on, I start to notice just how intensely our routines follow us. In the galley next to the coffee maker, our collagen powders are in a neat row. We add some to our coffee every morning. All of us brought our favorite brand of electrolytes, the individual packs so many that they have their own shelf. My contribution is a basket holding as many NAD+ liposomal packs and sheet masks as my carry-on suitcase could fit. As I look at it all lined up, I start wondering where my limit is and whether bringing every protocol with me defeats the point of leaving home in the first place.

As soon as I notice it, I can’t unnotice it. Comments that would have usually blown over my head—or that I would have made myself—start stacking up like our supplements in the galley. Over lunch on the bow, someone mentions she’d kill for her protein smoothie instead of the fresh seafood pasta that Matea just made us. While strolling the limestone streets of Korčula, someone announces she’s in desperate need of a collagen sheet mask. On Mljet, while walking back from the lakes with our wet hair dripping down our backs, someone asks whether anyone has a hair mask, because the sea salt is wrecking hers and ruining her extensions.

Tracking technology isn’t inherently bad. In many cases, it’s helpful—but counting every minute of exercise or every calorie does give me pause. My friends are some of the sharpest, smartest, and most intuitive women I know, and we are all being sold the same promise—the same lie—that I am: That we no longer can gauge if we are well on our own, and that with the right protocol we can somehow outsmart aging, exhaustion, and the general chaos of being human. This is a seductive proposition, even for me.

I’m healthy; I’ve built an entire career writing about wellness and hospitality in all its forms. I die for a week at a medical spa in the mountains. I have an Oura ring I check religiously. I try to hit 10,000 steps a day. I have an unlimited membership to a Pilates studio. I take peptides, creatine, magnesium—the works; I do all of this because I want to feel my best. But when a trip full of paddle boarding, cycling, and hiking somehow isn’t enough—when the sea itself gets reframed as an interruption to a protocol—even I have to call it.

Dubrovnik's Old Town is a complex maze of staircases and alleyways.

This is where I realize I need to draw the line. For me, setting out on a trip has always been about discovery and connection. It’s a given that I’ll have unexpected moments of chaos while navigating an unfamiliar place, often in a language I don’t know, which makes it exhilarating. I find it kind of hilarious to sit down at a restaurant and order a meal and have it arrive nothing like I expected, and the most tremendous of honors to be invited into a home and eat a meal with strangers who quickly become friends. It’s this sense of spontaneity, of surrender, that makes travel worth it for me. Not whether or not these meals hit my macros.

That’s why, when we stop in Ston, known for its oysters and the Great Wall of Europe, and one of my friends comments that she’s finally getting her steps in as we climb the stone stairs and rattles off her Oura ring stats, I pretend not to hear. I’ve already made up my mind; I’ll no longer make my trip about this.

Instead, I choose to marvel at the ancient salt pans glittering below us and the farms scattered across Mali Ston Bay. I take even more joy in savoring freshly shucked oysters at the bayside Bota Šare restaurant.

Ston's Great Wall of Europe is a five-kilometer medieval stone wall with three forts.

On our last day of the trip, we arrive in Dubrovnik just before sunset. We go to one of the best restaurants in town, Gradska Kavana Arsenal, overlooking the Old Port, and for one night, it’s like all of our guards fall. We laugh uncontrollably as we enjoy rounds of champagne, two types of tartare, and a thick piece of chocolate cake. Back on the boat, we do what happens at the end of every trip. We stay up for hours in an attempt to squeeze out the last of our time together, all while lamenting that none of us want the trip to end. It’s been one of the most refreshing trips of my life, and I finally know why.

Aside from Croatia being downright gorgeous, the private catamaran experience felt freeing for a particular reason: It was the opposite of what so many hotels are becoming. It was inherently wellness-oriented without anyone handing us a biohacking menu; healthy meals were prepared for us daily without a detox protocol attached; and without a single workout class included. It was all salt water and sunshine, no supplement or gym equipment required.

Slide of Heaven's salon area hosts meals overlooking the Adriatic Sea

When I finally tuck myself into bed, I do the exact thing most wellness protocols would tell me not to do: I look at my phone. Immediately, I’m served a video from an influencer who has just completed our same itinerary through Croatia, sailing from Split to Dubrovnik.

What catches my attention isn’t her videos of the Dalmatian Coast, but her morning routine. It’s a montage of her waking up at 6 a.m., peeling off her mouth tape and collagen sheet mask, removing a weighted décolletage wrinkle pad, then launching into what seems like a 100-step beauty routine full of serums and LED masks. I don’t judge her for this. If anything, it makes me question if I’m doing enough.

I look through my own photos. Mine tell a different story: an impromptu dance party in Vis with a group of younger French men, grinning from ear to ear at a seaside tavern in Mljet, squid-ink risotto staining my entire smile. A selfie of the girls taken in Korčula during the hour I’d usually meditate but have one of the deepest conversations of our trip instead.

For some travelers, the influencer’s version of the trip isn’t so much a dream as it is a necessity to keep up with ever-evolving beauty standards. Even if I’m leaving the catamaran a little under-rested, sunburned, and salt-crusted—I’d choose our version of the trip every single time.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6299. What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

Dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

For businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

Build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

Even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

If an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

It makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to quickly reset and refresh before carrying on.

The first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

But I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

As I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

And this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

Now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

In response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

That’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

The big question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.

#6298. Holafly Plans: The Best eSIM Plan for Long Term Travelers

There are a lot of eSIM companies in the world. They all work a similar way: you download their app, pick your package, install the eSIM into your smartphone, and off you go. There’s many I like.

But one I like more than the rest is Holafly and I’ve been using their eSIMs for years. I find their app to be easy to use and their rates really competitive.

So when Holafly launched Holafly Plans, a single eSIM that works as an ongoing subscription across 160+ destinations, I was excited. It’s a great option for those who are looking for more data and flexibility than a traditional eSIM. (An eSIM is a digital SIM built directly into your phone’s hardware, so there’s no physical card to insert or swap. Instead of visiting a shop for a plastic SIM, you activate a plan by scanning a QR code or installing it through an app, and you’re connected within minutes. Because it’s software-based, a single phone can hold multiple eSIMs, letting you switch between a home number and a local or global travel plan without touching your device. I have like 10 installed. lol)

In this post, I’m going to explain what the product is, how it’s different than a traditional eSIM, and who I think this option is for!

Holafly Plans is a single global eSIM that covers more than 160 destinations on one ongoing subscription. You buy it once, install it once, and it just keeps working as you move from country to country. You don’t reswap SIMs, you don’t redownload anything, there’s no re-purchasing, and no hunting for a new QR code every time you land somewhere new.

It automatically reconnects you when you land in a new place. Think of it as like a traditional mobile carrier – but a lot cheaper.

You can buy it monthly or annually and it comes in two tiers: Light and Unlimited. There’s no annual contract and you can cancel any time.

The Unlimited Plan includes no data caps and an unlimited hotspot so you can tether your laptop on the go. If you’re a digital nomad uploading video, doing video calls, or just someone who doesn’t want to think about data ever again, this is a great add-on. This tier also comes with a local phone number from the US, UK, or Canada, which lets you receive SMS messages.

The Light Plan gives you 25GB of data a month, still includes a hotspot, and still covers the same 160+ destination coverage. For someone who mostly uses maps, messaging apps, and the occasional Instagram scroll, this package is probably the best option.

Additionally, with both Holafly Plans, once your plan is active, you get their “Always On” feature which is 1GB of backup data every month, automatically for life, even if you eventually cancel your subscription entirely.

Pricing varies a bit by region and currency and depending on how long you purchase, so check out their current rates on the Holafly Plans page. However, as an example, their unlimited plan is only $55 USD per month for 1 year, which is a lot cheaper than any US based carrier charges for their base option that includes unlimited 5G data overseas.  You can get monthly, quarterly, or yearly plans. Quarterly plans save approximately 10% while yearly plans save 15%.

Use the promo code NOMADICMATT at checkout to get 10% OFF Holafly Plans and 5% OFF all standard Holafly eSIMs.

Classic Holafly eSIMs are built for a single trip. You pick a country or region (there are 200+ available), choose how many days of data you need, and it covers just that trip. If you’re flying to Portugal for two weeks, a classic eSIM is still the simpler, cheaper option. It’s a one-and-done purchase. If you only take a couple trips per year then this is still the best option.

On the other hand, if you’re a digital nomad who is gone from your home country most of the year and moving between different countries all the time, then the Holafly Plans fly is the much better option. It’s a standing global subscription designed for people who are more or less always somewhere. Instead of buying a new eSIM every time your itinerary changes, you have one number, one connection, one bill that follows you across borders indefinitely. Plus, you can get a phone number, unlimited data, and a hotspot. In the US, if you were to get T-Mobile’s plan, which caps data and is the closest thing we have to “affordable” international plans, you’re going to spend over $100 USD a month (I know because I used to use this plan!). Holafly Plans costs less and gives you more.

Holafly also recently launched a new tier called The Ultra Plan by Holafly, and it’s a bit different from anything else in the eSIM world.

Basically, it takes everything in the Unlimited Plan (unlimited data, hotspot, phone number, 160+ destinations) and adds a a small travel insurance component that ib:

How much does it cost? Ultra is $90.95 a month if you pay monthly, $82.65 a month on the quarterly plan, or $73.41 a month if you pay yearly. For comparison, Unlimited is $64.90 monthly, $58.65 quarterly, or $52.41 yearly. Quarterly saves you about 10%, and yearly about 20%. (Use my code NOMADICMATT or MATTK gets you another 10% off on top of whichever plan you choose.)

So, is the upgrade worth it? Ultra costs about $26 a month more than Unlimited if you pay monthly, $24 more on quarterly, and $21 more on yearly. Here’s how I think about it: one lost bag gets you $150, which covers roughly six months of the difference, whichever way you pay. A single doctor visit abroad, or one session with a psychologist, nutritionist, or personal trainer, can easily cost more than that. And that’s before you even factor in the language barrier and the stress of figuring out where to go. With Ultra, you get unlimited access to all that support included in your plan.

If you’re heading out for a few months, quarterly is the sweet spot. You get the savings without committing to a full year. If you’re taking a two-week vacation, skip it and stick with a standard Holafly eSIM.

Just to be clear, this doesn’t replace travel insurance. It won’t cover hospital bills, theft, or emergency situations, so you’ll still need proper travel insurance for all of that but if you want small trip related coverage, this can be a cheaper option.

Getting set up takes a couple of minutes, not a couple of hours:

If anything goes sideways during setup, real people are on the other end of support 24/7.

Holafly Plans isn’t for everyone. If you’re taking a single two-week vacation, a classic destination eSIM will cost you less. However, if you’re a frequent traveler who is in and out of multiple countries within a given month or a digital nomad who needs reliable, ongoing connectivity for work, not just casual browsing, then get Holafly Plans. It’s easier and will save you money in the long run.

And, as someone who roams the world a lot and uses a lot of data, especially to stream video and use my phone as a hotspot, these plans save me a ton of money!

Is Holafly Plans different from a regular Holafly eSIM? Yes. Regular Holafly eSIMs are one-off purchases for a single trip or destination (200+ available). Holafly Plans is an ongoing global subscription for people who are more or less always traveling.

Does Always On cost extra? No. It’s included automatically with every Holafly Plans subscription and keeps giving you 1GB of backup data a month across 150+ destinations even after you cancel.

Can I switch between Light and Unlimited? You’d need to cancel your current plan and purchase the other tier — there’s no in-place upgrade yet.

London routinely ranks among the world’s most-visited cities. It is home to incredible museums, a fabulous theater scene, great restaurants, luxurious hotels and its main airport, Heathrow (LHR), is a hub for multiple airlines, making it a great stopping-over point on a larger trip.

That said, the British capital is well worth visiting on its own for anything from a few days to a few weeks, depending on how much of an Anglophile you are.

Despite the strong U.S. dollar, London is still an expensive destination, so if price points have been putting you off lately, here are some easy strategies to stretch your London trip budget even further using miles and points.

And if you have some strategies of your own to use airline miles, hotel points and credit card rewards to maximize a trip to London, please share those in the comments below!

Where you should stay in London depends on the purpose of your visit. If you are in town for business, you might want to stay near the City of London, while folks who want a quieter neighborhood might like Kensington or Notting Hill. Knightsbridge is best for those who want upscale shopping, while Mayfair has fantastic restaurants and boutiques.

London can get dreary and gray during the winter months and crowded during the summer, so your best bets are fall from September-November and spring from March-May when the temperatures tend to be mild and days will include a mix of sun and rain.

The number of miles you need to fly to London depends on which airline you take and which miles you redeem, as well as the time of year since some mileage programs require more miles during peak travel times. That said, you can find flights on some airlines, like Virgin Atlantic, by redeeming as few as 6,000 miles each way.

American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines all fly to London from various U.S. airports. You’ll also find plenty of flights from over a dozen U.S. cities from the U.K.’s two main carriers, British Airways and Virgin Atlantic.

The cost of a trip to London depends on when you visit, how long your trip is and where you want to stay. The city has options for travelers ranging from budget flights and accommodations to luxury hotels that can cost well over $500 a night. Luckily, many hotels are accessible using credit card rewards and hotel points.

Now that the FAQs are out of the way, here's what else you need to know to start planning your trip to London.

Virgin Atlantic flies to London Heathrow from 11 U.S. cities and using Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points can be a real bargain. Just beware of taxes and fees that can be several hundred dollars, even for economy tickets.

I like using the airline’s Reward Seat Checker tool to price out tickets between city pairs over a month at a time. You can often find economy tickets between the East Coast and London for as few as 6,000 miles each way. Yes, you read that correctly — you can cross the Atlantic for just 6,000 miles. Even better, premium economy starts at just 10,500 miles and Upper Class can require as few as 29,000 miles (though it’s often much higher).

Unfortunately, you’ll be on the hook for anywhere from $450-$1,700 in taxes and fees round-trip depending on your class of service. That’s a lot, but perhaps not so bad considering even some economy flights are costing upwards of $1,400 at the moment, saving a few hundred dollars by redeeming a few thousand miles can be well worth it.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is a 1:1 transfer partner of:

What’s more, some of these partners, including Amex and Bilt, offer limited-time transfer bonuses, so you can score even more of a deal on award tickets.

Related: The best ways to travel to London with points and miles

British Airways is one of the most generous airlines in the world when it comes to releasing award seats in its four classes of long-haul service: economy, premium economy, business class and first class.

The downside is the hefty fuel surcharges and taxes on the airline's flights to and from its London Heathrow hub. There are, however, some ways to mitigate those.

The key is to redeem points and miles from the right programs. The extra charges will still be relatively high, but you can end up saving hundreds of dollars per ticket — each way! To illustrate this most clearly, let's focus on British Airways business class.

While American Airlines AAdvantage would only require 57,500 miles each way in business class for British Airways flights between the U.S. and London, the taxes and fees can cost between $750-$1,000 each way. The same is true if you were to redeem 45,000-70,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points each way – with taxes and fees that can top $1,100.

Instead, you might want to consider redeeming Cathay Pacific Asia Miles. Flights from the East Coast start at 63,000 miles plus $200-$450 in each direction, while those from the West Coast incur the same taxes and fees, but require 93,000 miles.

For its part, British Airways Club would require 88,000-99,000 Avios in each direction depending on which city in the U.S. you’re flying from, plus taxes and fees closer to $400-$500. Yes, that is still a chunk of change, and it’s a lot more Avios or Asia Miles, but it can be well worth it to save close to a thousand dollars per person.

British Airways Club is a transfer partner of:

Cathay Pacific Asia Miles is a transfer partner of:

That means that although you’re spending more miles for a ticket than redeeming through AAdvantage or Atmos, you have a lot more transfer partner options to top up your British Airways or Cathay Pacific accounts.

Related: Great award availability but beware the taxes: British Airways business class review

Another way to save on taxes and fees on award tickets as well as sparing yourself a few miles is to redeem United MileagePlus miles for a ticket on United. Not only does United charge far lower taxes and fees than British Airways and Virgin Atlantic, but if you are either a United MileagePlus elite or carry a United cobranded card, you might be eligible for preferential redemption rates on award tickets booked through MileagePlus.

You’ll pay just $5.60 flying from the U.S. to London, in any class of service, and around $200-$400 on the return, depending on which cabin you’re in.

Plus, you can save on the mileage portion of your ticket if you’re an elite or a credit cardholder. Take these flights from London to Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD), for instance. Regular MileagePlus members would have to redeem 40,000 miles for coach, 50,000 for premium economy and 80,000 for United Polaris business class. But if you have access to preferential rates, you’ll save at least 10% of the miles and need just 36,000 for coach, 45,000 for premium economy and 72,000 for business class.

If you don’t currently carry a United credit card, consider the United℠ Explorer Card (see ) or the United Quest℠ Card (see ).

United is also a 1:1 transfer partner of Chase Ultimate Rewards if you carry one of the following cards:

Finally, don’t forget that United has a special partnership with Marriott. Normally, when you transfer 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy points to one of its airline partners, you end up with 20,000 airline miles plus a 5,000-mile bonus for 25,000 miles total.

With United, however, you get a 10,000-mile bonus, so 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy points convert to 30,000 United miles. That’s probably a special-circumstance use for most folks, but still something to consider if you’re swimming in Marriott points.

Related: The best times to apply for Chase’s United cards based on offer history

As you might expect, London is lousy with points hotels, and more are on the way. I’m most excited about the Waldorf Astoria London – Admiralty Arch and the St. Regis London, both of which should open in early 2027.

I’d suggest picking the area you want to stay in and then doing a search with your preferred hotel programs around there. In the meantime, here are some of my top picks with each program.

The swanky NoMad London opened in 2021 and immediately gained a following thanks to its maximalist decor and popular bars and restaurants, not to mention its central Covent Garden location. It’s now part of Hilton, so you can redeem points for stays. Nights start at $550 or 100,000 Hilton Honors points.

I also love the colorful BoTree Hotel, which is part of Hilton’s Curio Collection. It opened in a quiet pocket of Mayfair in 2023 and has bright but sophisticated rooms and is home to an outpost of the see-and-be-seen Italian eatery Lavo. Rates start at $400 or 108,000 Hilton Honors points per night.

I love Mayfair, so my top Hyatt pick for the city is Hyatt Regency London – The Churchill, which sits right on stately Portman Square and is turning 50 years old next year. The room decor is not exactly overawing, but the public spaces are grand indeed and the service is impeccable. Nights start at $440 or 25,000-55,000 World of Hyatt points per night.

TPG staffers also love the Great Scotland Yard Hotel, which is part of Hyatt’s Unbound Collection. Rooms are on the small side, but you can’t beat the history since it’s in a heritage-listed building that was once the Metropolitan Police headquarters. Rates start at $380 or 20,000-40,000 World of Hyatt points per night.

For something a bit hipper as well as budget-friendlier, try the Standard. It’s in a very busy area right near Kings Cross, but chic, 70s-inspired room decor and several buzzy bars and restaurants will make your time here feel like an upscale city experience. Rates start at $305 or 20,000-40,000 points per night.

Related: Which credit cards should you use for Hyatt stays?

Even among quirky Kimptons, the Kimpton Fitzroy is a standout thanks to the magnificent 1900 landmark building that houses it and its central Bloomsbury location. Rates start at $319 or 66,000 IHG One Rewards points per night.

The InterContinental London Park Lane has an utterly convenient location at Hyde Park Corner and features spacious rooms, specialty drinks inspired by the royal family at Arch Bar and an expansive spa and fitness center. Rates start at $433 or 83,000 points per night.

Related: Which credit card should you use for IHG stays?

It might occupy a heritage-listed building from 1910, but the London Edition feels utterly of the moment (even though it opened over 13 years ago). Rooms have Edition’s signature look of white textiles, wood paneling and minimalist bathrooms. It’s worth spending an evening admiring the sculpted ceiling at Berners Tavern while enjoying dishes from chef Jason Atherton’s menu. Rates start at $485 or 70,400 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

Formerly a Renaissance hotel, St. Pancras has since joined Marriott’s Autograph Collection and is a favorite among train enthusiasts thanks to its location in a landmark neo-Gothic edifice attached to the train station of the same name. Rooms feel opulent in a Victorian way, and its Moorish-inspired spa is a treat. Rates start at $280 or 52,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

While hotel points come in handy for saving bundles of money on otherwise expensive stays, if you are looking to splurge while in London, there are still ways to save on luxury hotels.

Travelers with either the American Express Platinum Card® or The Business Platinum Card® from American Express should check American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts, which sometimes has third- or fourth-night free packages at some of the city’s finest hotels. These bookings also come with perks like free daily breakfast for two, a $100 on-property credit, availability-based upgrades and guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout.

There are plenty to choose from, but my personal favorite London hotels that participate in Amex FHR include:

Remember, if you have the American Express Platinum Card or The Business Platinum Card from American Express you are also eligible for up to $300 in statement credits biannually for up to a total of $600 per year on prepaid Fine Hotels + Resorts, The Hotel Collection or Airbnb Luxe bookings (of two nights or more for THC and Airbnb) through American Express Travel® or the Amex Travel App™. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, those FHR bookings will require two nights or more to be eligible for this credit.

You might also consider booking a luxury hotel through the Capital One Premier Collection if you have the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card or the Capital One Venture X Business for valuable benefits like free daily breakfast for two, up to $100 in on-property experience credits and room upgrades (if available).

Likewise, if you have the Chase Sapphire Reserve or the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business you can book a hotel that is part of The Edit by Chase Travel℠. Cardholders are eligible for two statement credits of up to $250 each (for a total of $500) this calendar year to put toward stays of two nights or more booked through The Edit. During your stay, you are also eligible for availability-based upgrades, complimentary daily breakfast and a $100 on-property credit.

Related: Chase Sapphire Reserve’s The Edit credit: What to know

Although British food was long a punchline, the city has become one of the world’s premier dining destinations in the past two decades or so. These days, you can find everything from Sri Lankan hoppers and Scandinavian smoked fish to French haute cuisine and sustainable farm-to-table fare.

Prices are high, though, so it’s best to maximize rewards on your spending and any statement credits your credit cards might afford you.

Another favorite tip of mine: You can often find discounts of up to 50% at some restaurants by booking reservations via The Fork. Then, just show your reservation details at check in, enjoy your meal, and the savings will be automatically applied to your bill.

Related: The best credit cards for dining

Taxis and Ubers are easy to come by in London, though rides can be expensive. So if you do go this route, so to speak, make sure to use a card that earns bonus points on ride-hailing services.

It’s also easy to hop on the city’s Tube lines and buses, both of which are easy to navigate and affordable, by simply tapping on with your credit card. If you decide to do so, keep a card that earns bonus points on public transportation at the top of your wallet.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card (see ) earns 2 points per dollar on local transit and commuting, for example, and the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card earns 2 points per dollar on local transit purchases.

You might be able to use the Chase Sapphire Reserve’s $300 in annual travel statement credits toward transit purchases as well as taxis and Ubers since these charges often code as “travel.”

Related: The best credit cards for commuting expenses

No matter whether you spell it “theater” or “theatre,” no trip to London would be complete without seeing a production in one of the West End’s magnificent venues. Ticket prices tend to be more reasonable than in the U.S. but can still put a dent in your budget. Luckily, you can take advantage of the Chase Sapphire Reserve Stubhub credit to offset some of that cost.

Chase Sapphire Reserve cardholders receive up to $300 per year to use on purchases made through StubHub or its sister site, Viagogo. The credit is split into two biannual credits of up to $150 (activation required; through Dec. 31, 2027).

Among the productions currently available through Stubhub in London are “Paddington: The Musical” (just beware it’s mostly sold out except for last-minute tickets) and “Oh, Mary!”.

A few years ago, Capital One partnered with The Cultivist, a service that grants members free, priority access to dozens of museums around the world. Eligible Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card holders can register for half-price membership that costs $220 per year instead of $440. This auto-renews at the discounted rate for the second year and then is full price after that.

While $220 is a lot, if you visit museums frequently, you can end up saving far more than that on tickets since The Cultivist Enthusiast-level membership available with the Venture X includes priority admission for the cardholder plus a guest. In London, the participating museums include:

Finally, some credit cards levy foreign exchange fees on purchases you make outside the U.S. They tend to add 1-3% to your purchase price, which can add up quickly. Instead, use a credit card that waives foreign transaction fees, of which there are many to choose from.

If you travel abroad frequently, you might also want to consider the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card. In addition to waiving foreign transaction fees, the card actually earns 3 points per dollar on foreign transactions, in any category. It’s almost too good to be true, and that makes it one of the best credit cards for trips abroad.

Related: The best credit cards with no foreign transaction fees

#6296. Introducing “Delta Disruptive” Class For Flights Within Florida (Hilarious SNL Skit)

Forget Delta One. Saturday Night Live has imagined another cabin for Delta Air Lines it calls “Delta Disruptive Class,” and this one addresses a problem even a lie-flat seat cannot solve: the passenger who makes everyone else’s flight miserable.

In a spoof commercial from its October 31 episode, Saturday Night Live introduces “Delta Disruptive,” a separate section for passengers whose behavior makes them particularly unwelcome elsewhere on the aircraft.

The premise is simple: instead of letting these travelers ruin the flight for everyone, put them together behind a thick plexiglass partition.

— Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl), November 1, 2026

The fictional cabin accommodates everything from obnoxious personal habits to full-blown onboard meltdowns. There are passengers clipping toenails, fighting over seats, and shouting conspiracy theories. One customer offers a testimonial while duct-taped to her seat. A Tiffany Gomas character also makes an appearance..

Naturally, the airline presents all of this with the polished enthusiasm of a commercial announcing an exciting improvement to your travel experience.

“All Delta Disruptive flight attendants are the toughest, gayest, ex-Spirit Airlines employees who have seen much worse.”

I love how Kenan Thompson, who plays flight attendant “Kevin,” grabs an emotional support iguana and throws it off the plane. He also has a ring on every finger, lol.

The new cabin class is rolling out soon…on flights within Florida. Book now…

“Delta Disruptive” is a joke, but the desire to enjoy a flight without becoming an unwilling participant in someone else’s viral video is quite real. Part of me wishes that we could throw unruly passengers into padded part of the plane instead of diverting and costing everyone time and money.

As usual with SNL skits, the joke captures a frustrating truth about flying: as carefully as you may choose your airline seat, you cannot choose the person sitting nearby. One passenger can make an otherwise pleasant flight unbearable.

Join our mailing list for a daily summary of posts! We never sell your info.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Also funny that the Delta plane was a type Delta doesn’t yet have, the MAX, and the registration is an Alaska 737 Max9

That is so attentive! Classic MaxPower move, right there.

Why? It’s a satire program (and I assure you Lorne Michaels and the cast are politically correct). Don’t get all upset over nothing.

Gotta say, loved t he silver Delta livery!

I’m glad you told us it’s a “…fictional cabin…” and that “…Delta Disruptive is a joke…” I was thinking it was real until you clued me in.

You really had to put in those disclaimers?

It is not beyond our imagination that there is a so-called influencer who is making a video about being denied access to Delta’s Disruptive Class under the guise of wanting to “check it out.”

Always good to have a disclaimer, just in case.

Loved the comment that the flight attendants can handle this … they’re the meanest ex-Spirit FA’s who are used to handling much worse.

I was dying laughing one of SNL’s best skits in a long time.

I sure Delta loyalist wished they had used a different airline but I don’t think the skit and the joke would have landed like it did if they’d used a different airline.

Delta disruptive will have one of the best toilet to pax ratio. Might be worth considering

Next they need to introduce “Quarantine Class” for those that board while coughing up lung nuggets for their fellow passengers to enjoy.

I almost turned off the sound, thinking it was a commercial break.

Cute Skit but why pick on only Florida???
