#6295. The Best New Restaurants in NYC Come in All Cuisines and Sizes

New York City has a new restaurant flinging its doors open seemingly every hour—and that's on top of the time-worn institutions, from old-school steakhouses and delis to bagel shops run by the same family for decades.

When it comes to the new, we're spoiled for choice: One week, it's a fabulous Korean small-plates bar with a commendable natural wine list downtown; the next it's an imported taverna from Argentina in the Village where the steaks are juicy as hell and, well, there's even more great wine to work your way through. To help you parse through all the opening news and find the buzzy spots worth fighting for a reservation at, our editors are eating out night after night, trying new Mexican mariscos joints and modern Indian fine-dining spots, to report back on the ones that stand out.

This is our Fall 2026 status report on the best of the new—the places to try your luck walking into, or commit to a Friday night dinner at, whether you're a NYC local or a visitor in town for just the weekend. These are the best new restaurants in New York right now.

The best new restaurants in New York City stretch across Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island. Every business on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has personally tried the restaurant in question. When choosing new restaurants, our editors consider both high-end and affordable eateries that offer an authentic and insider experience of the city. We’re always looking for standout dishes, a great location, and warm service—as well as serious sustainability credentials. In terms of how we define ‘new,’ we've chosen to focus on restaurants that have opened within a year of the publish date. When you work your way through the list, check back in: We'll update this guide regularly as new restaurants open in New York City.

Read our complete New York City travel guide here, which includes:

This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

Neighborhood: Williamsburg, BrooklynGo for: Martini hour and Shrimp Voodoo

After around seven years of living in Williamsburg, I’ve finally found the moody, cozy refuge this pocket of the neighborhood was missing. Booth’s Extra Fine, which just opened on October 9, feels like a sexy little secret. Hidden behind discreet oxblood curtains, the space simulates a vintage 20th-century supper club with dark walnut, rich leather booths, and deep, amber, brain-massage-like lighting. The heart of the restaurant stems from chef Nick Pfannerstill’s grandfather, Booth—an effortlessly stylish Milwaukee car salesman whose 1920s-50s photos line the walls.

Lean into the nostalgia and splurge on the porterhouse steak for two (or three—it's massive), but don't skip the Caviar Royale or the chef’s-kiss Shrimp Voodoo appetizer, cooked and swimming in Creole garlic butter. Personally? I can't wait to return and try the dry-aged Extra Fine Burger and a nice martini. Speaking of martinis, look out for Booth's "martini hour" launching soon, putting $12 cocktails—gin or vodka—at your disposal. —Jessica Chapel, commerce writer

Neighborhood: Hudson Yards, ManhattanGo for: A standout egg curry

Indienne, a tasting-menu-driven Indian restaurant, comes from chef Sujan Sarkar, who has worked in kitchens across Mumbai, New York, and San Francisco and runs a Michelin-starred restaurant of the same name in Chicago. Sarkar’s shtick? In his words: he reimagines Indian cuisine by “blending classical Indian flavors with refined European technique.” Think: deconstructed and then reconstructed. It takes a couple of courses to get a feel for what Sarkar is doing. The dhokla, for instance, isn’t spongy; it’s cubed, dehydrated, crackly, and tinged with white chocolate. The zingy passionfruit pani puri arrives in the shape of an oyster shell over reindeer moss. But once you get past the initial surprises, things really pick up. The “egg curry”—a whole steamed egg sitting on top of curry foam encrusted with potato sev and topped with caviar, served with buttery babka pao and house-churned butter—is an absolute standout. Things get a little more traditional with the chicken makhani that my husband got: chicken, three ways (chicken breast topped with spiced chicken mince wrapped over malai mousseline), served with buttery dal and even butterier naan. I didn’t miss the meat for a second, being on the vegetarian tasting menu myself, because my celeriac kebab was smoky and melt-in-your-mouth. And then came another surprise: the ghewar, a traditional Indian sweet that arrived like a mini layer cake with edible gold leaf (there’s a lot of this) and a bouncy coconut foam. A Penicillin-adjacent drink made with apricot whisky, mead, and ginger kept me company along the way. As we left, we were shown Sarkar’s other venture in the same premises, the British-Indian chophouse Elder, that was busy on a Tuesday night. —Arati Menon, global digital director

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: ribeye among many other things

From the man (Pablo Rivero) behind one of Buenos Aires's most iconic steakhouses (Don Julio) comes Graciela—an Argentine tavern on a cozy corner in the West Village, where the wine list is long and commendable, the food is fire-cooked, and the room is star-studded in that quiet, in-the-know way. All the hype made me suspicious, but if you're expecting a Corner Store or Carbone experience, this is not that. It's just fantastic cooking that is elevated and pristinely executed enough to be covetable, with an experience that stays focused on the food. And the space, with dried herbs hanging from the ceiling and heavy wooden furniture and warm, low light, feels both moody and inviting; cool yet welcoming.

It's easy to rack up a major bill here, because every corner of the menu is worth exploring—from a red pepper dip with wood-fired oven-made bread, to the sliced bondiola coppa with lemon zest and olive oil (a very true must), to, of course, the salty, sizzling steaks. (The iconic whole tomato starter has been lost to the turning of the seasons, but I am certain something autumnal will replace it.) Some flavors are more complex, but much of what you'll find are crowd-pleasers, like the milanesa neapolitana which our serve aptly described as being "like a pizza milanesa" which is impossible to complain about. —Megan Spurrell, senior features editor

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: Roti, actually, to accompany the beef cheek panang curry

The preponderance of new restaurants in the West Village specifically should be studied—sometimes it feels like we could dedicate a whole list to that neighborhood alone. The best of them, like Hommali, take the cuisine of choice and present it in an eminently stylish, upscale dining room. Every time I asked general manager Kritayanee “Air” Promsarin where something—the stemware, any number of the vividly colorful paintings on the walls—had come from, the answer was JJ Market, or Chatuchak Weekend Market, in Bangkok. It just looks good in there, I can't stress it enough. And then there's the matter of the food, which is buoyant, delightful, and oftentimes a wonderful introduction to Thai flavors for many Americans. I'm talking about a cold tom yum seafood cocktail, a heavily-spiced beef tartare on tripe cracker, and tao jiew lon, a fermented soybean-coconut dip scooped up with fried veggies. The mains are enormous and well-priced, and the best bite of the evening was not the beef cheek panang curry (although that was great on its own), but rather the piece of delicate roti used to scrape up the last remnants of sauce. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: SoHo, ManhattanGo for: sashimi and sake pairing

For this toro-obsessed tuna lover, Noury’s torotaku tartare topped with uni was love at first bite. As I greedily piled the pale-pink tuna belly, pillowing orange uni, and pickled yellow daikon radish with a dash of sushi rice onto a sheet of toasted nori to make a DIY handroll, I knew at once that I had reached appetizer ambrosia. And the saké pairing? Divine nectar.

I had high expectations for chef-and-sommelier duo Alex Chang and Lina Goujjane, who opened Kiko together in 2024, which I believe remains one of the city’s most underrated restaurants simply because of its isolated locale in so-called Hudson Square. Now, with Noury the pair finally has an address to match their ambitions in prime Soho, on Sullivan Street between West Houston and Prince.

While Kiko is cozy and chic, Noury is stylish and sexy. The restaurant is modeled after a Japanese “izakaya,” relaxed dining establishments that serve shareable plates and drinkable tipples. As such, small bites, raw seafood, and saké are the star, but the vibe isn’t so puritan as an omakase counter. In addition to the daily changing sashimi and futomaki, there are also non-fish entrees like the steak haché (not my favorite bite, but a popular crowd pleaser) and pork and cheese mille feuille katsu; plus a surprisingly addictive chrysanthemum salad. To pull it all together, Chef Alex tapped Joji Miwa as Noury’s chef de cuisine, whose career spans award winning restaurants like Sushi Sanshin in Osaka and Sushi Noz in New York. That’s where he first met Lina, the mastermind behind the beverage program, which includes both extremely rare and accessible sakes and a selection of shochu cocktails and refined spirit-free options. Like at Kiko, the service at Noury is knowledgeable and their hospitality kind. Come. Eat. Drink. Be merry. —Hannah Towey, news editor

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: ox tongue

Somssi, like Arthur, is new but doesn't feel it. It's a West Village restaurant with no flash or bombast, just a short and clever menu that jumps off from operator Ahris Kim's Korean origins and a casual, dimly-lit couple of dining rooms with lace accoutrements and eclectic hanging art giving the most comfortable feeling that you're at a friend's supper club rather than a sterling food and beverage operation. There's the semi-viral "Potato, Potato, Potato and Caviar" croquette, which is what it sounds like and will appeal to all, but more fun is to be had with things like the Grilled Ox Tongue, which comes undisguised as such on the plate with its uneven triangular shape atop romesco. I only gagged once while eating it, when my teeth came too close to my own tongue and I thought too hard about what I was eating, but then quickly continued my feast for love of the novel and tender dish. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Nolita, ManhattanGo for: crudo spotted with stracciatella and a late night

It was fitting that I ended up at Tashca just a few days after returning from Portugal, because I could fully appreciate how plucked-from-Lisbon this special spot in the LES is. Open only on Thursdays (the space is available for private events on other nights), this breezy little restaurant feels like being at a friend’s slightly chaotic but very endearing dinner party. Your table may or may not be ready when it’s supposed to be (we were given sparkling wine when ours took 30 minutes longer than planned, which is a trade I would have willingly made), and on that note, all reservations are made by Instagram DM (and you will need one; I saw several walk-in hopefuls turned away). But when you do flit through the open doors into the dining room, you won’t want to leave. Candles burn low throughout the night, and flowers hang from light fixtures—and the food, most importantly, sings, toeing the line between beauty and comfort, with distinctly Portuguese dishes that feature great seafood, bright produce, and a long list of tasty wines to pair. On the night I visited, there was a $95 prix-fixe made in partnership with visiting chef Joao Magalhaes Correia (who is usually in the kitchen at his Lisbon spots like Bar Alimentar). It featured a couscous bathed in squid ink and topped with a perfectly charred skewer of grilled octopus; melon draped in presunto ham; and a crudo topped with globs of stracciatella that I never could have imagined would work as well as it did. Come early, and plan to stay late. —Megan Spurrell, senior features editor

Neighborhood: NoMad, ManhattanGo for: fried chicken, actually!

When the Jungsik team closed sleek offshoot Sea in NoMad in May, it wasn't to abandon ship. They worked with commendable quickness to open a new concept, Mūje, by July. Like Jungsik proper, Mūje serves a tasting menu. Unlike Jungsik proper, Mūje is casual and focused on Asian food more generally rather than Korean exclusively. It's also more affordable at $150 for eight courses (Jungsik will cost you $335 for 10). There's a lot of fun to be had here with such a premise, like the tender short rib that comes with four different wraps nodding to Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese approaches, respectively. The best bite by a mile is the chicken wing, which is insane. It comes deboned and stuffed with pork, a Chinese technique, but is fried with the Korean Prinkle seasoning (a combination of cheese and onion and other good stuff) to create something really special. You only get one, so savor it. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Greenpoint, BrooklynGo for: an immaculate and affordable champagne list, plus the half chicken of the moment

I loved being at Arthur. With its lively and long dining room, buoyant soundtrack of soul music, and warm service, it's a place that feels like it's been around for a long time despite having opened in April. Food and drink are reasons to visit, in equal measure. Charlotte Mirzoeff's wine list is extensive and counts the French along with the Corsican and Portuguese, with a Champagne list 30-plus bottles deep (Mirzoeff is obsessed with the stuff, wants us all to be drinking more of it, and has two options for less than $100 to help make that happen.) Kevin Finch's food is rustic and comforting, the type you want to eat on the regular, but never boring—escargot comes grilled on a skewer beneath a bed of chives so ample it looks like a wig, for example. Two favorites: the kohlrabi with anchovy, herbs aplenty, and hazelnut (sop up the sauce with the pillows of housemade brioche) and the sasso chicken, with its crispy skin served atop crispier rice. Burgerheads take note: they've got an excellent one, with dijon, blue cheese, caramelized shallots, and a thick brisket patty between a sesame seed bun, but it's only available on Wednesdays. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Dumbo, BrooklynGo for: oysters broiled with bone marrow butter

Mexican food is back in the former Gran Electrica space on Front Street, a stretch of Dumbo real estate bustling with tourists moving to and from the Brooklyn Bridge vantage point. This time, the operation is run by Alan Delgado, the chef behind Fort Greene burrito spot Los Burritos Juarez, with drinks from bartender Ivy Mix. The great backyard garden patio remains, although I enjoyed my meal in the front dining room, which manages a moody mise en scène with its terracotta walls and glowing light despite lovely, huge windows overlooking the street and its passersby. Mix's beverages are stellar and inventive, in particular the rotating micheladas and frozen beverages that are tart and perfect. On the food front, the must-order comes first in the oysters, which are broiled a delicious brown color in bone marrow, and arrive bubbling. It's the perfectly decadent start. People talk about the fish tacos in particular, but I preferred the suadero, a confit brisket with guac on a corn tortillas rather than the flour Delgado is known for (and which can be purchased plain on the side, something I recommend.) There are flashier entrees, but the Chile Colorado—a braised pork shoulder with pinto beans and pickled onions that takes on a stew-like consistency, is subtly smoky, extremely filling, and something I'll be returning for. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Williamsburg, BrooklynGo for: potato bread, celery salad, and a breezy dining room

In the location of the former Llama Inn, a beloved modern Peruvian eatery in Williamsburg, the new Cafe Bar J.F. has arrived. Despite a name that feels designed to be confused and/or forgotten (both of which I keep experiencing), the space inside—and the food they serve—is an honorable replacement for Llama Inn. The concept, which comes from the Llama Inn team and is spearheaded by chef Francisco Castillo, is a “South American Tavern”. To me? It feels like eating at one of the many breezy, design-eyed restaurants I love to splurge at in Lima or Buenos Aires, with dishes that build on beloved foundations like ceviche and asado. Madrid-based Plantea Estudio has elevated the room from the plant-filled corner it once was to a more demure combo of dark-wood and metal furniture (and while the rooftop remains open, the interior is so lovely I chose to stay indoors). The prices will get ya if you don’t pay attention, but certain items—the potato bread and the celery salad, two surprising ones—really lingered. Go for a date night, or a celebratory dinner with a friend, and take the excuse to work through the satisfying cocktail menu. —Megan Spurrell, senior features editor

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: Guinness, oysters, and whatever seafood special is on the chalkboard

My friend Sarah put it best. There we were—me leaning back in a booth, she perched on a stool—at Dean's, the lively new pub from King team leaders Jess Shadbolt and Annie Shi, the windows flung open in celebration of one of spring's first sunny days, and she says, “This feels like what the Hamptons is supposed to be like.” The parts that make it so: a location in the Village and the according clientele, nautical stylings (lots of dark wood and blues of the navy variety), abundant seafood done the British way. All to say that, somehow, we felt as though we'd stumbled into something of a seafood shack. The halcyon weather won't be a constant, of course, but the place will do just as well comforting the cold in winter with its pies and beers—the stargazy pie, a hopefully perennial special, is strikingly fish-forward when it appears on your plate, head and tail of a milky-eyed mackerel protruding. Whether or not you eat its eyeballs, the rest of the dish beneath the buttery crust is basically chowder, not at all intimidating but very much delicious. It's also rather heavy, so if you want to try as many dishes as possible while also downing excellent Guinness pour after excellent Guinness pour, perhaps stick to such happy hits as the oysters, fish and chips, and scallops in malt vinegar. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

#6294. New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a new card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To get your money back from such a fee, you’d need to take advantage of regular lounge access at airports, utilize your TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit, maximize every monthly dining or entertainment credit and sign up for every other fee credit, which often requires a purchase.

To quell this issue, the new card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t…

#6293. United Airlines Adds Five Routes From San Francisco, Including Four Surprising Transcons

United Airlines is adding five routes from San Francisco next spring, including four transcontinental flights to smaller East Coast markets. The latest additions, Richmond and Norfolk, are particularly interesting because both will operate just twice weekly. United is also taking on Breeze Airways directly in Richmond.

Across two rounds of announcements in late October, United unveiled new or returning service from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) to Charleston, Hartford, Oklahoma City, Richmond, and Norfolk.

I had not yet covered the earlier additions, so let’s look at all five together:

The new routes were flagged by Ishrion Aviation.

The first round of additions, from SFO to CHS, BDL, and OKC were loaded on October 22–23.

Charleston International Airport announced its seasonal San Francisco route on October 22, listing Boeing 737-800/MAX 8 aircraft. The airport emphasized both travel to the Bay Area and connections beyond United’s West Coast hub.

Bradley International Airport followed with its announcement of daily, year-round Hartford service. Unlike Charleston’s limited weekly schedule, this represents a daily commitment to the Connecticut market.

A Boeing 737 MAX 9 will be used for Hartford and a SkyWest-operated Embraer E175 for Oklahoma City. The OKC flight will operate daily.

The newer announcements extend that expansion into Virginia. Interestingly, none of these five new routes were formally announced by United.

Richmond International Airport announced its twice-weekly service on October 30. Meanwhile, Norfolk International Airport confirms its new San Francisco flights begin March 31.

The twist on the RIC and ORF flights are the frequencies. Twice-weekly service is familiar territory for leisure-focused airlines but rather atypical of the daily-or-better schedule many passengers associate with a United hub route or that of another network carrier. That certainly suggests United is approaching these markets differently from Hartford. A Richmond traveler can choose a Thursday departure and Sunday return for a long weekend. Someone needing to travel on other days will still need a connection or another option.

The Richmond addition also creates a direct competitive overlap with Breeze Airways, which already offers nonstop service between Richmond and San Francisco.

Breeze is an annoyance to United at SFO and while Breeze is smart enough not to full Independence Air (ramping up at a major United hub too much, too fast, then going bust), I would be incredulous if Breeze did not influence United’s decision to launch this route, particularly given the twice-weekly schedule.

The bigger question is whether both airlines can make the route work over time. More competition is useful when it lasts.

Both Hartford and Charleston’s airport announcements explicitly promote those onward connections…that’s true for all five routes. Ultimately, this is just United trying to grow its network and dominance at its primary West Coast hub.

United Airlines will add or restore five San Francisco routes in March 2027, with daily service to Hartford and Oklahoma City, four weekly flights to Charleston, and twice-weekly flights to Richmond and Norfolk. Richmond brings direct competition with Breeze, while the broader expansion strengthens United’s reach into smaller domestic markets. These are less glamorous additions than another international route announcement, but quite useful as United also continues to rebuild its domestic network.

#6292. 11 Gorgeous Mountain Cities in the US, Plus Where to Stay

Whether you're seeking snow that's smooth as butter or high altitudes that keep summer comfortably cool, there's nothing quite like America's mountain cities to scratch an itch for the outdoors. With over 100 distinct mountain ranges across the US, there are endless peaks to summit and après-ski offerings to enjoy. The possibilities range from astoundingly good omakase in Salt Lake City to heliskiing in Colorado's San Juan mountains.

Whatever your vibe is, there's something for you—it's not all log cabins and snow shoes in the country's best mountain cities. These are year-round destinations that offer world-class art, adrenaline-pumping slopes, and family-friendly activities. From Appalachia to the Rockies, these are the mountain cities to call home for your next adventure, plus our favorite, editor-approved places to stay.

Nestled in the foothills of the Rocky Mountains’ Ten Mile Range, Breckenridge is one of the country's most treasured ski towns, home to five peaks peppered with skiers of all abilities come winter. The once crown jewel of Summit County's mining towns, its lined streets are hugged by weathered saloons and colorful homes harking back to its boomtown days. Breck's—as regulars call it—real claim to fame though, is its nearly 3,000 acres of lift-served terrain. After you hit the slopes, there's plenty to love beyond the skiing, whether you're looking crawling through its craft beer and distillery scene or appraising the thriving arts district.

Stay here: A new kind of boutique hotel tailored to outdoor enthusiasts, the dog-friendly Gravity Haus Breckenridge draws out-of-towners with a wide variety of guest rooms (from bunk rooms to two-bedroom suites), a Japanese-inspired onsen, private ski lockers, and an in-house team to help you explore outside.

As Crested Butte lies just 24 miles from Aspen, the two are practically next-door neighbors, but you'd be remiss to skip this hidden gem because of that fact. There's something that feels more intimate about Crested Butte’s historic downtown, which looks like it was stolen out of a snow globe or used as the set of a holiday Hallmark movie, but it can keep up with the best of them. There's the world-class skiing and mountain biking with some memorable restaurants and watering holes to boot. In other words: all the beauty and nightlife, none of the pretense.

Stay here: If you want to stay an arm's length away from it all, check into Old Town Inn, which sits three miles away from Lake Grant and two miles away from Peanut Lake. The property also offers free shuttle service to Mount Crested Butte.

Mountain cities nearby a national park are automatic winners, but Whitefish somehow goes a step above the rest. Being steps away from Glacier National Park certainly helps as travelers gain access to some incredibly beautiful lakes and glaciers, but there's also the namesake ski resort in town that plus tons of summertime activities like hiking and zip-lining; and its mountain-backed, saloon-lined downtown has more than enough Old Western vibes to fill an entire vacation.

Stay here: Larch House is a new 39-key hotel is the first design-forward boutique hotel of its kind in Whitefish. It’s in the heart of downtown’s historic Railway District, a short walk away from all the town’s shops, restaurants, and bars.

Aspen, Colorado’s reputation precedes itself; it’s the quintessential mountain city that's been winning praise since 1879 (when it was originally founded as Ute City). Why? Its surroundings are simply awe-inspiring—snow-capped peaks in winter that turn into perfect hiking weather in summer—and its comfortably small footprint makes your whole itinerary easy to reach, from the famed slopes to downtown's designer boutiques and top-notch restaurants. Aspen has long been a hotspot for skiers searching for fresh powder and a lively après scene, but the town has been on a roll more recently with all types because of its worldly mix of cultures on display at institutions like the Aspen Art Museum. In addition to those seeking snow, Colorado's premier mountain city welcomes families, food lovers, and design seekers alike.

Stay here: There’s an inimitable charm to Aspen’s Hotel Jerome. From rustic to high fashion, the 135-year-old historical landmark sits in a perfect location for both rest and play. Offering both complementary hotel-to-hill transit and walkable proximity to designer shops, a stay at the Jerome is as convenient as it is decadent.

Two years after Hurricane Helene descended on Asheville, the creative spirit of the artsy Appalachian city is back and better than ever. With hundreds of artists bringing life to repurposed spaces, whether it's a glass studio, ceramics workshop, or open gallery, Asheville is abuzz again.it seems Asheville's pure energies are vibrating at a higher frequency than ever, even as it continues to rebuild. As Jeffrey Burroughs, a local jewelry designer shared with Condé Nast Traveler, “What music is to New Orleans art is to Asheville,” and visitors come here for much more than the bucolic scenery.

Stay here: Enfolded within the grounds of the opulent Biltmore Estate, the Inn uniquely summons what it was like to be a guest at the Vanderbilt family’s magnificent 19th-century mansion, but with 21st-century luxury and comfort.

Ouray calls itself the Outdoor Recreation Capital of Colorado, and it's an epithet well-earned. See why on the Perimeter Trail, a 6.5-mile loop that hugs the rugged mountain city. Set aside (at least) four hours for the full hike; shortly after your ascent, you'll be taken aback by views of the entire box canyon—a sight that continues along much of the journey. Among the trail’s highlights are the towering Cascade Falls, its Baby Bathtubs (smooth, carved rocks kids can play on), and the Box Canyon Falls high bridge. Because the Perimeter Trail is never more than a half mile from town, there are several points where hikers can cut the walk short and head back into Ouray.

Stay here: The adults-only Beaumont Hotel and Spa is made for those looking to rejuvenate their bodies after long days spent romping around Ouray's thrill-seeking offerings. Plan to spend a day soaking in the property's hot springs, which has been soothing visitors since 1886.

Salt Lake City is becoming something of a cultural haven in the Mountain West. Foodies flock to the city for its inventive dining—from speakeasy cocktails to picture-perfect omakase—while the mountains are never far for skiing or hiking—don’t miss out on the quirky annual events like Winter Roundup skijoring (skiers and snowboarders get towed by horses through the snowy streets) and the ultra-hip, indie-forward Kilby Block Party Music Festival. Boutique shopping and independent galleries are emerging alongside long-standing museums, lending downtown an even more vibrant, walkable energy. Between all the buzz, postcard mountain views, swanky bars, and hotels that balance history, style, and service, Salt Lake City has genuinely become a place you’ll want to return to—not just pass through.

Stay here: Downtown Hyatt Regency SLC is the city’s workhorse: spacious, modern rooms, consistent service, and direct access to the convention center and buzzy streets. It’s perfect for business travelers or anyone valuing convenience and reliable amenities.

The powder here is perfect, and so is the quirky, small-town vibe. But it’s when the mercury starts to rise that this historic mining community in the San Juan Mountains really shows off its shine: Warmer temperatures bring vibrant wildflower blooms, its famed film festival, and beloved bluegrass performances to Telluride. Come for the robust art scene where you’ll find a mix of creatives, outdoorspeople, blissful retirees, and the odd celebrity or two (Oprah Winfrey is among those who reportedly own a home here). Even with all the new hype, Telluride has gracefully managed to hang onto its authentic character and remains a favorite, down-to-Earth Colorado destination.

Stay here: The Madeline Hotel & Residences, Auberge Resorts Collection, located at the base of Telluride Ski Resort, is an ideal basecamp for your trip. This updated 83-room alpine retreat, which also features 71 residences, is surrounded on three sides by the San Juan Mountains and offers stunning views from its 4,000-square-foot outdoor terrace, complete with a heated pool, massive hot tubs, fire pits, and an al fresco lounge.

Jackson Hole is the epitome of why they call this region of the country big sky country. There are endless open spaces to admire the handsome soaring mountains, and it's no secret what makes so many first-time visitors never want to leave. The resort skiers and adventurous outdoorsy types have been coming for decades, and in recent years, the dining scene has only been getting better. All of which gives it an outsized place in the mind of travelers. Jackson Hole brings in a whopping 2.6 million visitors every year; the entire state of Wyoming has a population under 600,000. It’s a gateway to the National Parks, a winter wonderland, and an idyllic paradise year-round.

Stay here: Four Seasons Resort Jackson Hole, nestled at the base of Jackson Hole Mountain Resort in Teton Village, is the only ski-in/ski-out hotel in the village, and comes with unobstructed views of the Tetons, full-service alpine spa, an outdoor pool and jacuzzi (open year-round), ski concierge, and all the pampering you’d expect.

If the air feels lighter in Silverton, maybe because the landmarked former mining town rests at a cool 9,300 feet above sea level. The scene here feels closer to the industrial history than many of Colorado's other rehabbed mining outposts, with a good number of its colorfully painted storefronts catering to passengers from the out-and-back, steam-powered train from Durango. It's the perfect home base to spend a couple of days hiking and fishing in nearby San Juan National Forest. In the winter, this is one-horse town completely transforms into a mecca for serious backcountry skiers.

Stay here: For a real step back in time, step through the threshold of The Bent Elbow Hotel, whose façade nods to the Victorian architectural style that was rampant in Silverton's hey-day. Paired with the mountain-view balconies, you might just wonder which century you're in. But worry not about the loss of modern amenities, the rooms come equipped with special comforts from complimentary streaming services to white noise machines to complete your wind-down ritual.

Townsend is called the “peaceful side of the Smokies” for a reason. Instead of neon lights and chain brands, you'll find a small downtown area alongside the Little River with easy access to the national park. The eastern part of town is closest to the park’s most incredible waterfalls: Meigs Falls and Spruce Flats Falls. The Smokies lay claim to more than 700 fishable rivers, including the Little River, that can be visited with Townsend-based Little River Outfitters. In Townsend, Dancing Bear Appalachian Bistro is a local favorite, with seasonal Appalachian-inspired dishes like striped bass and sorghum glazed chicken on offer.

Stay here: Head to nearby Walland for Blackberry Farm, a Relais & Châteaux resort spread over 4,000 acres—and hands down the most notable stay in these parts. It has James Beard award-winning restaurants including The Barn (which accepts reservations from non-guests), known for its dishes crafted from seasonal and local ingredients.

#6291. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

#6290. Review: Emirates 777-300ER “Game Changer” First Class Dubai To Brussels

Seven years after my first flight in Emirates’ fully enclosed Boeing 777 first class suite, I returned to the same route and same flight, EK183, from Dubai to Brussels. The “Game Changer” suite remains extraordinary, but this flight demonstrated that even a superb seat cannot compensate for disappointing service, though perhaps my exceptions were too high? My latest review follows, with the original 2019 review preserved below for comparison.

I first reviewed this product in 2019 and came away impressed. Returning in 2026, I was curious whether it would feel quite as special after experiencing more of the world’s leading first class products. The suite certainly did. The experience around it was less consistent, especially compared with my excellent Emirates A380 flight from Mumbai to Dubai.

As I explained in the introduction to this trip report, I booked Mumbai–Dubai–Brussels for 102,000 Emirates Skywards miles and approximately $700 in taxes and fees. That included my A380 flight the day before and this flight to Brussels on a Boeing 777-300ER featuring Emirates’ “Game Changer” first class suites.

I took an Uber from my hotel to DXB. Emirates has a dedicated terminal for business and first class check-in and within area, there’s a posh first class check-in lobby.

However, with so many first class passengers, there is not the sort of personalized ground service you might experience with Air France or Lufthansa. After checking in, I was on my own to get through security, passport control, and to the lounge.

I visited both the Concourse A and Concourse B Emirates First Class lounges before my flight.

I reached the gate (further than I thought) about 30 minutes prior to scheduled departure and the flight had fully boarded, with a “final call” announcement from the gate agent and on the monitors.

I settled in onboard, noticing the cabin was booked full. What war?

The first class cabin has six suites in a 1-1-1 configuration with the middle suites having virtual windows (with a live feed of the world outside).

My suite, 1K, included a large table, screen, closet, cabinet for hand luggage, and an oversized, plush “dentist” chair. Sounds simple enough, but the accents were tremendous and I loved that Emirates’ first class cabin has ditched most (but not all) of the gold bling for a more refined look…it’s just so odd that after all these years Emirates has only retrofitted nine jets with this product.

There’s also a flip-up cabinet with a mirror that houses the amenity kit skin products and a cool souvenir notebook and pen.

The suite has universal A/C, USB-A, and USB-C power (plus HDMI for those still living in 2012).

There are also plenty of lighting options.

Within the suite, you can customize your experience not only via adjusting the seat from upright to reclined to fully-flat, but you can adjust the temperature and lighting (even the color of the lighting).

I didn’t need to sleep on this daytime flight to Brussels, but I ended up taking a 4-hour nap: the bedding is superb and the 79-inch bed very comfortable in 180º lie-flat mode.

In terms of the hard product alone, this seats beats out the JAL A350-1000 suite. But of course a flight is about more than the seat, especially in first class….

Emirates’ “ICE” entertainment system includes hundreds of movies, TV shows, live TV, music, and games…more than enough for a journey around the sun, let alone a quick trip to Europe.

Noise cancelling headphones are from Bowers & Wilkins.

While this flight did not have Starlink Wi-Fi, the OnAir internet was complimentary and worked reasonably well, even if it felt more like dial-up than high speed.

It was also a lovely day just to look out the window, especially as we neared Brussels.

Upon boarding, I was offered a refreshing glass of Champagne and chose Dom Rosé 2010.

Menus were distributed prior to pushback, with a la carte breakfast and lunch choices available throughout the flight. along with an exceptional collection of wine and spirits plus a “movie snack bar” menu.

I thought the breakfast choices were limited. My omelet was fine, but I’ve had much better omelets on other carriers and even had a better one out of Mumbai on Emirates the day before.

Service began with fresh fruit, a cappuccino, orange juice (with ice cubes?), rhubarb yogurt, and delicious bakery items like a cinnamon bun and almond croissant.

The omelet had beans, potatoes, and cooked spinach with it…utterly forgettable.

After waking up from extended nap, it was time for the main feast. While my meal was being prepared, I was offered mix nuts and hydrated with some sparkling water.

The caviar course was excellent and I had more Dom Pérignon Rosé with it.

Next came fabulous Arabic mezze with humus, grape leaves, tabbouleh, falafel, kibbeh, and fattoush salad..everything was great.

With time running out, I skipped the soup and went right for my main course: pan-fried lamb loin and cutlet, served with olive caramel sauce, tomato fondue, beetroot jus, potato pavé with pistachio dukkah-crusted kale, and blanched sugar snap peas.

Sadly, it was so overdone that I did not finish it. However, I did enjoy some excellent garlic bread and red wine (a Bibi Graetz Colore 2015 from Tuscany) with it.

Lunch ended with a cheese course and chocolate truffle cake (with roasted hazelnuts and pistachios). The cheese included:

The “new” 777 has two lavatories in the front of the cabin, shared by crew. They are spacious, though not like upstairs on the A380:

I was never proactively offered an amenity kit. When we landed, I asked about it and was told, “They are on request only.” So be aware of that…

Slippers and pajamas (what Emirates class loungewear) was proactively offered. I took size medium, which fit me (I’m 6’1″) and was very comfortable.

As I mentioned above, skin products from Byredo were present in the suite.

I’ll repeat what I wrote in my first impressions of this flight.

After breakfast, my dishes sat for over 20 minute untouched. Not the service I was expecting.

I woke up a couple hours before landing for the meal and was totally ignored for almost 30 minutes (and my suite door was open). I realize that I could have just pressed the call button (and eventually did), but I don’t think that should be necessary in first class…I think that the FAs should have been far more proactive in monitoring the cabins.

When I did call the FAs to begin meal service, there was 90 minutes left in the flight, which in theory should have been time for everything. I provided the full order and the caviar came quick, but once again the crew was not attentive. I finished the caviar and waited. Finally, the mezze came and I finished it…and waited. I waited and waited for the main course and it came (having been left in the oven far too long).

I waited again. The captain announced our descent into Brussels. My glass was empty, my plate was pushed way, but no one was coming.

Do I really have to push the call button after I finish each course? That’s not the kind of first class service I like.

With 40 minutes left in the flight, I finally flagged a FA down and asked her to bring the cheese and dessert at once. She seemed very agitated, not in the hostile sense, but because she was so stressed…because it wasn’t only me trying to finish my lunch, but the other four in the cabin (it was booked 5/6).

She brought over the cheese and dessert and I ate it…it was fine…but I felt too guilty ordering coffee with so little time left…again, not a feeling I should have in first class. Drink refills were not offered.

The pre-arrival service could have been so much better executed. The service flow was so perfect on my A380 flight because the flight attendants took charge and proactively executed service. Not so on this flight and it wasn’t because the FAs were too busy: they were chatting in the galley.

So was it was the best flight ever? Nope. The A380 flight the day before was perfect…this one was not.

I think it’s always appropriate to mention here that I am incredibly grateful to fly first class on Emirates and this sort of “first world problem” is not meant to condemn Emirates or gripe so much as it is to offer an honest comparison between this and other premium cabin products. Comparatively speaking, Emirates fell short here.

Despite the questionable service, what a pleasure it was to fly on this product and enjoy the beautiful suite and multi-course meals. I look forward to doing this again. Next time, though, I think I’ll skip breakfast and just have one meal in the middle of the flight.

The review below was originally published on June 7, 2019, and covers my earlier flight from Dubai to Brussels.

I booked my ticket from Dubai to Brussels a couple night before the trip using Emirates Skywards. The points transfer on a 1:1 basis from American Express Membership Rewards and the trip cost 85,000 miles and about $420 in taxes/fees. The same trip would have been 75,000 miles with Qantas, which has now been added as an American Express transfer partner.

I began the day with a 4:00 A.M. cab ride to Dubai International Airport from the Park Hyatt. Although I tired to sleep, I was too excited for the upcoming journey. Pulling up to the Emirates premium class check-in area Dubai, a line of uniformed staff were waiting to assist with luggage, but today I was traveling only with hand baggage.

Inside, I  found myself the only passenger in a huge terminal…it felt a bit surreal. After checking in, I proceeded down a long hallway toward the security checkpoint and passport control.

After a couple hours in the first class lounge, I headed to the gate for boarding, which began ahead of schedule about an hour prior to takeoff.

B1 is used for aircraft departing from remote stands and passengers were being funneled down a single escalator and onto a waiting bus. I tried to board but was told to wait and that first class boarding would begin “soon”. So I waited. And waited. And waited. 25 minutes passed. I was getting antsy. So were the three other first class passengers. We were the only ones left in the gate area.

Finally, we were invited to head downstairs where our “first class” bus was awaiting. I don’t know if “first class” was the right word, but the bus was very comfortable. We soon began what turned out to be a 15-minute bus ride to the aircraft…which seemed to be parked in Abu Dhabi (I jest…). Upon reaching the aircraft, we were invited to carry our own bags up the fairly steep air stairs onto the 777-300ER that would shortly be departing for Brussels.

Onboard, three FAs were waiting at the door. After a warm welcome, one escorted me to my suite.

I was grinning ear-to-ear as I stepped into the beautiful six-seat cabin. Wow, this was spacious! The cabin is arranged in a 1-1-1 configuration with four window/aisle suites and two suites in the middle, one with an entrance on aisle one and the other with an entrance on aisle two.

My suite, 2K, included a large table, screen, closet, cabinet for hand luggage, and an oversized, plush chair. Sounds simple enough, but the accents were tremendous and I loved that Emirates’ latest first class cabin has ditched most (but not all) of the gold bling for a more refined look.

What I appreciated most about this new cabin was the attention to detail Emirates placed in making it practical. For example, my rollerboard carry-on fit perfectly in the cabinet, which was so much more convenient and aesthetically pleasing than having to leave it under the ottoman (like in Singapore or Etihad First Class) or store it in a closet (Lufthansa First Class) or overhead bin (Air France First Class).

There was also a closet that easily accommodated my garment bag and clothes on a hangar and smaller storage cabinets along the window.

A power port and USB charger was conveniently located within arm’s reach, as was a USB-C charger (which my laptop has…).

Adjacent to my seat was a touch panel that allowed for control of the lighting (including customizable mood lighting) and the temperature of the suite. The armrest also had a four-button seat control.

In addition the drink cabinet, there was a basket with snacks sitting on the table along with beautiful orchids:

But the attention to detail went even further. The careful stitching on the seat and embroidered Ghaf (prosopis cineraria) tree above the window further showed how much thought Emirates put into this cabin. And the overhead lights were shaped like diamonds.

Each suite had binoculars to look out. These were not souvenirs; FAs collected them as we approached Brussels.

The suite across the aisle from me stayed vacant, so I had a chance to check out the “fake” windows”. Kudos to Emirates for trying, but I was not impressed.

I structured the flight around a nap…not because I wanted to sleep through a pricey flight, but because I slept poorly the previous two nights and wanted to try out the bed and bedding.

Thus, shortly after my post-takeoff breakfast flight attendants prepared the bed for me while I changed into my pajamas. The bedding is simply tremendous, with a satin-like finish that was soft and so comfortable.

Window shades lower by button (sheer blinds and blackout) but Emirates also added real curtains. While I figured these were purely for aesthetic reasons, light seeped through one of my three windows so it turns out the curtains were quite practical.

The only annoying thing was that I could not figure out how to shut off the small band of blue light overhead:

I slept for about 3.5 hours, asking the FAs to shake me awake with about two hours to go until landing.

Prior to pushback, I was offered a drink of choice and chose orange juice, which was freshly-squeezed. Later on in the boarding process, I was also offered Arabic coffee and a choice of dates.

After takeoff, I examined the menu for today’s flight:

Having had steak for “breakfast” I was actually in the mood for some eggs, but only a light continental breakfast was offered. No problem…I wasn’t all that hungry. The purser, Ashwin, came by to introduce himself and took my breakfast order. I just wanted some fruit and yogurt along with a cappuccino. Almost immediately, my table was prepared by Tetiana and I was offered more orange juice along with a basket of warmed breakfast breads.

The table folds out from the console in front:

Mixed nuts were also offered and I enjoyed a glass of Dom Pérignon 2008 Champagne.

I do try to stay away from these fatty carbs, but the croissants smelled so good I ended up eating two of them…and some danish. So much for my light breakfast…

The fruit, yogurt, and cappuccino (notice the chocolate powder stencil art is the Emirates logo?) were all tasty and the whole breakfast service took only about 20 minutes. I still had plenty of time for sleep and a big feast prior to landing.

I was presented with a hot towel after my breakfast dishes were cleared.

After my nap, Tetiana again set up my tray table for lunch.

Hot bread from the oven and my favorite Isigny Sainte-Mère butter from France were offered.

I started the meal off with some more Dom, though this time some Dom Pérignon Rose 2006. It was served at the perfect temperature and was a spectacular accompaniment to the meal which would follow.

I began with caviar, admittedly more so for the trip report than because I felt like it. Still, I ate it and enjoyed it. I appreciated that Emirates warmed the blinis.

While I was eating my soup, Maria brought over my next course, a green salad with French dressing.

For my main course, I ordered a beef filet with asparagus and boiled potatoes. The dish was beautifully presented and the asparagus with truffle hollandaise sauce was spectacular…even better than Lufthansa First Class.

But the beef filet? Not so much…it was served beyond well-done and I ended up only nibbling at it. Such a shame that it was served overcooked. Tetiana was concerned that I did not eat and offered to bring me something else, but by this point I was already full and there were still two courses left.

As you can read in the menu above, the cheese course was quite extensive. I had a sample of each piece, but could not finish it.

Finally, I completed my meal with warm chocolate cake with raspberry sauce and another cappuccino.

Kudos to Emirates for an excellent dining experience in first class.

Emirates does not offer amenity kits on daytime flights. That said, there were several toiletries available in the lavatory and a box at each seat contained Byredo (Swedish) amenities like eye cream and skin toner. The amenities were “hidden” away in a cabinet along the table that folded up to reveal a mirror with lights. A leather-bound notebook and writing pen were also present.

Pajamas were available by request. Emirates uses “breathing” pajamas that are supposed to help the body stay ventilated. While that may just be a gimmick , I loved the soft pajamas and they have become my new favorite airline pajamas…my old favorites were also from Emirates.

Finally, the slippers were also quite comfortable and also large enough for my feet.

Ok, this is what surprised me the most. I knew the flight would have wireless internet, but like all (and I do mean ALL) my previous Emirates flights, I just assumed it would not work. Boy was I wrong. Not only was the internet functional and free (as a Skywards member), it was FAST!

Make sure your Skywards number is associated with your reservation in order to take advantage of the complimentary wi-fi.

On the other hand, the IFE was no surprise. I knew Emirates would offer a comprehensive library of movies, TV shows, live TV, games, and music and of course it did. There were even two cameras to allow for live views from outside.

What did impress me, however, was the wireless remote in the suite and the detachable tablet that served as a secondary IFE device, especially suited for games and music. When detached, it was totally wireless and also controlled the seat, could summon FAs via video conference for service, and easily controlled my customized soundtracks.

Newspapers were offered prior to takeoff.

Lastly, the Bowers & Wilkins noise-cancelling headphones were comfortable and worked very well.

Two first class lavatories were compact, but kept very clean and offered towels, Buglari toiletries, and other amenities like toothbrushes and combs. There were even little bars of soap like airlines used to offer decades ago.

Tetiana, Maria, and Ashwin provided excellent service from start to finish. Tetiana and Maria primarily took care of me and were not only lovely and charming, but highly polished. I appreciated how precisely the table was set, drinks were poured, and food served. I never had to wait long between courses and plates and utensils were always promptly cleared. Throughout the flight, I was addressed by last name.

Upon landing in Brussels I requested a picture of the flight crew and they happily obliged:

The only problem with this flight was that it ended so quickly. 6.5 hours was not enough time to fully enjoy the wonderful hard and soft product onboard. I was simply ecstatic throughout the flight…Emirates takes first class to a whole new level.

Was this my best first class flight ever? I don’t know if I’d go that far, but it was absolutely the best first class hard product (suite) I have ever experienced. While the old Emirates suite is still very nice, the new suite is even more spacious, even more comfortable, and even more cutting-edge.

Emirates has room for improvement with its first class ground product, but its in-air product is top-notch.

#6289. Where to Eat, Stay, and Play on Easter Island, the Wild, Remote Island in the Pacific

At 1,292 miles from its closest inhabited neighbor, Pitcairn Island, and 2,200 miles from continental Chile, Rapa Nui (Easter Island) takes isolation to the extreme. Here, at the lonely eastern edge of Polynesia, the empty horizon seems to curve with the Earth itself. It’s an extraordinary setting for one of archaeology’s enduring mysteries: Why did a group of Polynesians carve nearly 1,000 monolithic human figures (known as moai), haul them across the island to distant ceremonial platforms over the course of centuries, and then topple them all to the ground? There are plenty of theories, and fewer answers. It adds an element of mystery to an already dramatic landscape, and one that has proven to be timelessly alluring.

Today, this Chilean territory is essentially an open-air archaeological museum, with many of its enigmatic moai (representations of Polynesian ancestors) returned to their upright positions following seven decades of restoration. Of course to see Rapa Nui only through its superhuman past is to miss much of the story: The island’s distinct Polynesian culture remains a vital presence, particularly in its sole town, Hanga Roa, where nights come alive with cheerful ukulele music and hip-swirling dances. There’s also a vast, vibrant sea, windswept volcanic plains, and a food culture that draws on the island’s rich heritage and maritime setting.

As a repeat visitor to the island, this is my guide to Rapa Nui.

There are thousands of stone moai—representations of Polynesian ancestors—on Rapa Nui.

Unless you sail over on one of the dozen or so annual cruise ships that dock here, including National Geographic Resolution and Silversea’s Silver Cloud, you’ll likely arrive via air at the world’s most remote commercial airport, Mataveri International. LATAM is the only carrier serving Rapa Nui with at least one daily flight from Santiago, 5.5 hours (and two time zones) away. Once on island, visitors typically sleep in the town of Hanga Roa and organize day trips to the archeological sites, which are never more than a half-hour drive from each other.

The Chilean Government officially transferred administration of Rapa Nui National Park in 2017 to the Ma'u Henua Indigenous Community, an organization run by elected members of the Rapa Nui community. Recently, they’ve increased entrance fees (currently CH$95,000, or about $100 USD) to stave off overtourism, while establishing initiatives encouraging longer stays, deeper cultural connections, and stronger protections for the fragile moai. Chief among the changes is a requirement to visit all archeological sites beyond Hanga Roa with a certified guide. Consequently, it’s become less common these days for visitors to rent a car (or bike) and explore on their own.

Head to La Kaleta for lunch along the rugged coastline.

La Kaleta's ceviche is served within view of working fisherfolk.

Seafood is a highlight of the Rapa Nui dining scene where the tuna is so fresh, you’ll invariably want to eat it raw in a ceviche, carpaccio, or tiradito (thinly sliced in a spicy citrus sauce). Te Moai Sunset makes a particularly painterly version of the latter. Paired with a pisco sour and views over the modern Moai de la Paz (“Peace Moai”), it’s the most idyllic place to wind down during—you guessed it—sunset. Similarly, the mahi-mahi is sublime over roasted Rapa Nui sweet potatoes at the tiki-style Te Moana, while the dockside ceviche lunches at La Kaleta let you watch the fisherfolk in action.

Kotaro has long been Hanga Roa’s hidden treasure: a small, quirky Japanese restaurant with an impeccable tasting menu and strict dining rules outlined on the website (no kids or chitchatting with the chef, for example). Neptuno Sunset is another off-piste favorite thanks to its seafront location near the end of the airstrip, slightly removed from the action. Bountiful seafood pastas are the specialty, but do save some space here or elsewhere for a dessert of po’e, a sweet, dense sponge cake made from mashed ripe bananas.

The wide open spaces are less jungly than most expect from Polynesia, but gorgeous nonetheless.

Many assume that Rapa Nui will have the jungle-clad hills of other Polynesian destinations like Hawaii or Tahiti. Instead, it’s covered mostly in grassy plains and looks more like Ireland. While there are two fine beaches on the northern coast at Ovahe and Anakena (which is apt for swimming), this is not your standard resort island, and sunbathing is secondary to the mystique of the moai.

Rapa Nui National Park has two chief archeological sites from the moai-building era: Rano Raraku and Ahu Tongariki. The latter is the island’s largest ahu (moai platform) with 15 statues often viewed in silhouette at sunrise. The former is a volcanic crater and quarry site where the ancient Rapa Nui designed some 95% of the island’s sculptures; about 400 remain in situ in various states of construction. There are dozens more ahu sites (many with restored maoi) spread throughout the island. The other major historical attraction is Orongo, a stone village perched on the rim of the Rano Kau volcano, which served as the ceremonial center for religious festivals dedicated to the creator god Makemake.

Just offshore from Orongo are Los Motu, small islets that were central to the annual Tangata Manu “Birdman” competition from the 17th to 19th centuries, which involved a death-defying race down Rano Kau, into the Pacific, and up sea cliffs to secure the unbroken egg of a sooty tern. Today, Los Motu is a popular snorkeling site where you can ply the gin-clear waters in search of vibrant corals and 142 marine species found nowhere else on earth, including the rare Easter Island butterflyfish. Mike Rapu Diving Center is one of Rapa Nui’s longest-running and most respected operators for snorkeling and scuba diving. Back on land, there are excellent hikes to be had up Terevaka, the highest point on the island at 1,675 feet, or around the barren Poike Peninsula, which holds several little-explored archeological sites, including petroglyphs and an enormous rock carved in the shape of a human face.

Modern Polynesian culture is alive and well on this island of 7,750 people. Though there are many souvenir shops with kitschy moai and colorful shell necklaces, for top local craftsmanship, seek out the paintings, woodcarvings, and jewelry at Mana Gallery, on the north end of Hanga Roa. The music school Toki Rapa Nui, co-founded by classical pianist Mahani Teave, offers occasional concerts and guided visits of its sustainable Earthship building, which is shaped like an eight-petal flower. More popular are the evening Polynesian dance shows from groups like Kari Kari and Te Ra’ai, the latter of which comes with a traditional (if highly theatrical) umu feast cooked in an underground earth oven with hot stones. For something less overtly touristy, check out the contemporary Polynesian music at Iti Lafken.

Explora Rapa Nui offers all-inclusive stays with daily adventures led by local guides.

For an all-inclusive stay with daily adventures led by local guides, book at Explora Rapa Nui, an architecturally striking hotel about 15 minutes outside Hanga Roa. Of all the Explora properties, this one has the finest food and shrewdest guides. Right on the edge of town, the Leading Hotels of the World property Nayara Hangaroa gives you a bit more flexibility to book things à la carte. It boasts an oceanfront pool, three unique dining concepts, and oval-shaped rooms styled after homes in the nearby Orongo ceremonial village.

More affordable options include the centrally-located (and playfully designed) Hare Nua Hotel Boutique, or the lush garden rooms of Pikera Uri Eco Lodge, from which you can explore the island on horseback. In general, prices are significantly higher here than in mainland Chile due to the remote location and lack of local resources.

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.
