#6278. We've Tested Dozens of Toiletry Bags—These Are Our Top Picks

If there's one travel truth I live by—and hold dear to my heart—it’s that a dream vacation deserves a dream toiletry bag. After all, what’s a perfectly packed carry-on without a designated home for your favorite lipstick, beloved serums, sunscreen, and all those little beauty essentials that somehow multiply before every trip? The best toiletry bags make room for the whole glam squad, without adding any more suitcase chaos to the packing equation.

On all of our worldly journeys, Condé Nast Traveler editors (myself included) have tested dozens of travel toiletry bags to find the ones worth your precious packing space, from streamlined makeup pouches for the less-is-more crowd to roomy, cleverly compartmentalized cases for those who believe in a 10-step skincare routine. It's no easy job finding the best ones: Some tear after just a few months of use, others have awkwardly sized compartments. Many are too big for a standard carry-on, while others have proven too small to fit the simplest of our travel necessities.

With wipe-clean linings and durable construction, plus smart pockets and ultra chic designs, the carefully selected, editor-tested toiletry bags that earned a spot on this list are the crème de la crème. Read on for our recommendations to keep your essentials organized and your travel beauty routine in check.

Tested by: Jessica Sulima, commerce writer

How long have you been using it? About a year now, and despite how much it’s melded to different parts of my suitcase, the leather has stayed nicely intact.

What is it best for? It's best for longer trips, when you need to carry full-size toiletries. That being said, it also works if you don’t have that much to pack, because the leather folds down however you’d like. I like that the products stay upright for the most part, so you don’t have to worry about bottles squeezing open. The shape makes it so that you can rifle through your things comfortably without dumping everything out.

How much does it hold? My entire skincare routine—cleanser, toner, moisturizer, sunscreen—plus my daily makeup. There’s even room for my vitamins too.

Tested by: Madison Flager, commerce director

How long have you been using it? I've been using this Peak Design toiletry bag for five or six years.

What is it best for? If you're in search of a toiletry bag to keep up with an extended itinerary, this is your solution: It's ideal for longer trips of five days and more. Sometimes I pack it on weekend trips too, but it's a bit bulky, so I find it better suited to checked luggage, or trips where I'll need a good amount of product.

How much does it hold? This is one of the toiletry bag's best features—it truly holds so much. Everything in my routine fits like a glove, each with a dedicated space. I usually bring along shampoo, conditioner, body wash, face wash, moisturizer, eye cream, contact solution, a toothbrush, toothpaste, and floss, plus smaller items like tweezers and nail cutters. There's an exterior pocket sized for a toothbrush, and one inside with a magnetic snap where I store a razor. Plus, there’s a hook on the outside, so you can hang it up in the bathroom.

Tested by: Jessica Chapel, commerce writer

How long have you been using it? This gem is a newer addition to my travel rotation. I've traveled with it for around two months now—and knew it had to be mine when I saw it came in a glazed dark cherry colorway. (That's now sold out, but there are loads of other fun colors to choose from in the same style.)

What is it best for? Given its spacious yet puffy, cloud-like design, the Luka bag is ideal for any trip where you have some extra room in your carry-on, or are bringing a checked bag. It's a bit bulky for a weekender or duffel bag, though I'd try to squeeze it in if I was packing light. For any of these trips, you can use the hanging clip for easy access.

How much does it hold? It's a bit deceiving just how much this toiletry bag holds—which is much more than it gives off at first glance! I bring all of my beauty products in here, from foundations to lipsticks and moisturizer galore. And though he packs way lighter than me, it can fit my partner's personal care items, too: a face buzzer, hair gel, a toothbrush, and so on. As well as the main pocket with a zippered enclosure, it has two convenient, grab-and-go side pockets as well as an enclosed compartment on the back.

Tested by: Hannah Chubb, senior commerce editor How long have you been using it? I’ve had Away's large toiletry bag for just over two years now, and have been obsessed with it ever since.

What is it best for? This is my travel companion for holding my go-to skincare products and toiletries, and it comes with me on every trip. I do also keep all my everyday products in there at home, so it's proven to be always at my ready. It's so chic—especially because it has my initials embroidered on the front—and keeps everything contained. I love that it has so many interior compartments, both zippered and clear, to keep small objects like hair ties, jewelry, and Band-Aids separated from my bigger tubes and bottles.

How much does it hold? Full disclosure: I don’t travel light. But this bag truly holds so much. It fits my entire skincare routine, toothbrush case, deodorant, hair products, body wash, razor, and beyond with ease. The two halves make it easy to find a place for everything.

Tested by: Bridget Knowles, associate social media manager

How long have you been using it? Elizabeth Scarlett’s eponymous label is a London-based luxury accessories brand I discovered during a bout of retail therapy in East London eight years ago. I’ve never looked back since—it’s an unspoken “it-girl” possession.

What is it best for? For longer trips, the Wash Bag is really great to keep everything organized. It has a wipe-clean lining fit for all lotions and potions, and you can personalize it with monograms too, which makes for a great gift. For shorter trips and everyday use, I use the Everyday Pouch—which I strongly suggest adding to your cart. (It’s my life companion in many ways.)

How much does it hold? I put everything in the Wash Bag: daytime makeup, going out makeup (you get me), my nighttime routine, and my morning routine. It’s lined with pockets so you can easily organize brushes, and—I mean—my electric toothbrush even fits in it. That’s how good it is.

Tested by: Meaghan Kenny, commerce editor

How long have you been using it? I've been using—and in love with—this toiletry bag for around two years now.

What is it best for? I promise, my adoration of this bag comes from more than just its good looks. I've been reaching for it nonstop to carry my very extensive skincare routine with me wherever I go—and it's made packing easier than ever. I think I've finally cracked the code to keeping my toiletries organized and ready to go whenever I am. The extra roomy toiletry bag is designed to be packed in your checked luggage, where you have more suitcase space and no restrictions on the amount of liquids you can have inside.

How much does it hold? I used to keep all of my reusable toiletry bottles and miscellaneous minis in a small storage bin underneath my bed. And when it was time to pack for a trip, I'd sift through it and decide what I needed for a particular trip. I decided to put all of my go-to toiletries inside The Kit, including cleanser, body wash, moisturizer, shampoo and conditioner, dry shampoo, tooth paste, floss, and even contact lenses. Now when it's time to travel I can easily grab the pre-packed kit and throw it right into my personal item. I don't even open it anymore to see what I need—it's already stocked up and ready to go.

Read a full review of the toiletry bag here.

How long have you been using it? I ordered this Calpak train case in unison with the aforementioned Luka toiletry bag—so around two months now.

What is it best for? With its boxy, clear, and haute look, the train case is best for extended trips where a checked bag is obvious. Otherwise, it's a superb makeup bag at home for those who don't love too many compartments, and like to have their ready products in view: The transparent panels let you quickly locate what you need without digging. (Not to mention, it looks super cute with the Luka, given the matching colorways. I'm obsessed!)

How much does it hold? When this bad boy arrived at my apartment, it was (luckily) bigger than I expected. It's tall, so it can easily hold my toner bottles, makeup brushes, and blending sponges.

At home, not only does it store my everyday beauty products, but a stock of my next-on-the-lists and just-in-cases—it's where my unopened moisturizers, different lip shades, and nail care products go. My favorite part? There's a hidden, dedicated interior organization pocket attached to the top compartment, which holds the products I wish to keep separate.

#6277. Breeze Airways Launches Nonstop Flights To 6 New Destinations: See Map Now

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Breeze Airways continues to develop its niche network of point-to-point flights between secondary airports or unserved markets. The airline will add services to six new destinations in the coming months, with the airline replacing Spirit on a number of routes, while also adding new international destinations in Jamaica and the Dominican Republic.

Utah-based Breeze Airways is another airline developed by aviation entrepreneur David Neeleman, who also supported the establishment of Azul Linhas Aereas, JetBlue, and WestJet. Breeze operates a fleet of 66 Airbus A220-300 aircraft.

As US ultra-low-cost carrier Spirit Airlines collapsed earlier this year, a number of popular leisure routes were left unserved. While some airlines, like JetBlue, were able to establish an extensive network in Fort Lauderdale after Spirit's exit, other carriers have been slowly picking up the pieces left behind by the Florida-based budget airline.

A major gap was left at Myrtle Beach International Airport (MYR). Breeze has been one airline stepping up here, and is now one of the largest carriers at the airport by destinations served. This coming February, Breeze will reconnect the South Carolina tourist hotspot of Myrtle Beach and Latrobe (LBE) and Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) with regular nonstop flights.

Adding to the airline's network will be a nonstop flight from Latrobe to Orlando International Airport (MCO). The airline's reintroduction of flights to Latrobe reestablishes commercial air service at the Pennsylvania airport that otherwise was left abandoned by Spirit.

Montego Bay (MBJ) and Santo Domingo (SDQ) will become the airline's latest international destinations when the airline adds services to these popular vacation hotspots. Breeze will add the nonstop flight from Tampa to Montego Bay in December, followed by Santo Domingo the following June.

These routes from Tampa join the airline's growing international network from the airport, which will see Cancun International Airport (CUN) also join the list this December 18 (not counted in this analysis). A full breakdown of Breeze's international services from Tampa can be seen in the table below.

From December 18 - Previously announced and not counted in this analysis

A notable mention is Breeze's upcoming new service that will connect Tampa to St. Thomas (STT) in the US Virgin Islands. This is not classed as an international flight. Travelers between these two cities can travel without a passport. Breeze will add the new flights to St. Thomas on December 16.

Four cities will join Breeze's network, including another international destination. Find out more here!

Buffalo Niagara International Airport (BUF) is set to gain three new Breeze Airways routes next June/July, as the airline connects the upstate New York city to Charleston (CHS), Myrtle Beach and Raleigh–Durham International Airport (RDU). All services will begin in time for the peak of summer.

Of these new services from Buffalo, just one will face direct competition. Denver-based Frontier Airlines maintains a seasonal service from Buffalo to Raleigh.

#6276. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

Good thing you did the Edit deal as the Thompson doesn’t honor Hyatt Globalist benefits. So, no upgrade and no breakfast for Globalists.

Not true (unless something changed) stayed here in May 2023 and got Globalist benefits

Am I the only one finding Edit hotels are north of $1000 a night? Whatever the credit Chase is giving is for staying at an Edit property isn’t enough to offset the exceptionally high rate.

I’ve stayed at that Thompson many times and been upgraded to suites and the Upper Stories. The previous poster is empirically wrong.

doesn’t Edit usually require a two night minimum? How did you get the benefits for only a one night stay?

#6275. My Favorite Airbnb: A Dreamy Thatched Cottage Tucked Away in the Cotswolds

Choosing the perfect place to hole up for a weekend getaway is not always straightforward. But this spring, the decisions seemed to make themselves. After a relentlessly busy start to the year, I was looking for a place to escape. And the place needed to fit certain criteria: Somewhere my partner and I wouldn't have to speak to anyone but each other; somewhere we could sleep for 12 hours a night and take the days slow and easy without guilt; somewhere within a couple of hours’ drive from our home in northwest London; somewhere rural, where I wouldn’t be woken up by the neighbors’ bathroom light or the sound of the tube; and somewhere we could have the place to ourselves, but still be close to some nice pubs or restaurants, so we wouldn't have to hunt and gather our own dinners, God forbid.

An Airbnb in the Cotswolds was the obvious choice. Luckily, I remembered I’d saved a cozy-looking cottage on Instagram a few months prior to feeling the sudden urge to get away. I revisited my staycation wishlist and found Strawtop Cottages: two 16th-century thatched-roof cottages that sit side by side on a quiet street in the quaint little village of Adderbury. I booked one of them, Strawtop Two, for a long weekend in April.

We checked into Strawtop Two after a speedy drive from London on a Friday night. As we unlocked the front door, we found switched-on lamps casting a cozy glow across the beamed living room; kindling ready to be lit in the wood-burning fire. In the egg-yolk yellow kitchen, a fresh loaf of sourdough was sitting pretty on the chopping board for us; organic eggs and marmalade on the counter; Daylesford butter, bacon, and rosé in the fridge. My partner prepared a simple supper while I nosed around the rest of the cottage, discovering a sweet dining room with floor-to-ceiling windows and an enormous bunch of fresh flowers around the back, as well as a boot room with Barbour jackets, Wellies for stomps across the fields, and umbrellas (likely a requirement, considering we were visiting in April).

I learned that the sister properties are owned by local content creator Josie Irons (@Josieldn on Instagram) and her husband Charlie Irons (who manages the properties), who have been custodians here for just a small part of the cottages’ centuries-long history. Their meticulous renovations have restored the spaces beautifully, preserving all the Grade II-listed original features that make staying here feel like a journey back to a simpler, more peaceful time, while adding plush finishing touches that feel every bit as cosseting as those of the area’s top-of-class hotels.

I originally saved this cottage because of the kitchen, drawn in by sunshiny pictures and clips of its buttery-hued walls, vintage copper pans, and an old-school kettle whistling on the Aga stove. But as I nipped between the two bedrooms—one on the first floor with minty green walls, one folded into the eaves on the top floor with tongue-and-groove woodwork—I found there’s a lot more to love here, like the Bamford pillow mist left next to the beds, and the blackout blinds creating one of the darkest and quietest bedrooms I’ve ever drifted off in. Wrapped up in the bed linens, I snoozed more peacefully than I’d managed to in months.

After homemade coffee sipped while listening to the Roberts Radio on Saturday morning, we headed a few minutes up the road to The Yurt at Nicholsons restaurant. This was one of a handful of recommendations that Charlie had sent us ahead of time. Normally, I’m a stickler for doing my own research (read: a snob and a control freak), but in the name of keeping things as relaxed as possible, I decided to put my faith in his suggestions. I shouldn’t have hesitated: a gooey camembert croissant, cut through with umami bacon, and a full English breakfast with melty pork belly chop and smoky baked beans hit the spot.

Our supper, also recommended (and booked for us) by Charlie, at The Norman Knight was every bit as impressive. I ordered perfectly blushing steak frites and felt smugly like I’d uncovered a hidden gem. Our Sunday lunch at The Duke of Cumberland’s Head, where we shared bowls of cauliflower cheese and crispy potatoes, was one of the tastiest roasts I’ve had in a while. Trust me, having Charlie as a de facto concierge is one of the biggest unsung perks of booking a stay here.

Back at the house, we hibernated on the sofa, reading the paper and watching Netflix in the dinky living room. I took mental notes of my favorite design details: the antique coffee table laden with magazines, the books plopped into recesses in the stone chimney, the deep-green rainfall shower stocked with Bamford products, the Steamery steamer and Dyson hairdryer in the bedroom vanity, and the Soho Home robes. If I could make my London flat one-tenth as comfortable as this little countryside cottage, I’d be thrilled. For now, I’ll bookmark the cottage next door for my next escape.

#6274. My Favorite Airbnb: A Dreamy Cabin on a Vineyard Just 2 Hours From London

I'm always on the hunt for a new cabin stay in the British countryside. Having visited at least two a year since 2020, I'd now dub myself something of an expert. Living in East London, sometimes all I crave is solitude, and I find that a slightly rustic spot, kitted out with all the necessary amenities, can be more restorative than a jam-packed, buzzy hotel stay.

I don't drive (hey, I'm a Londoner), which can be a rather large obstacle when planning cabin stays. But Liba Vineyard, a luxury glamping site made up of three pod-style homes in Porton, just a 15-minute taxi ride from Salisbury station, presents no such problem. The pods are all bookable on Airbnb, and I scooped up the Hawthorn Pod for a stay this autumn, eager to hunker down and work on writing my upcoming book. Door-to-door from London, I managed to reach it in two hours, armed with enough books and food to last two nights.

Once I'd settled into the Hawthorn Pod, I realized the Wi-Fi was excellent, and I wouldn't need to leave at all during my stay. The pods are dotted along winding wood-chip paths, which branch off towards the three cabins: Hawthorn, Beech, and Elder. All sleep four people and have a wood-fired hot tub, although Hawthorn is slightly more snug than the other two and better suited to solo visitors and couples. Beech is best for anyone traveling with children, while for larger groups, renting all three would be a fun way to celebrate a birthday. It's a spot that can be both solitary and social, depending on what you're after.

Inside, the pods are neutral, bright, and cozy. Draped curtains add a sense of grandeur to the French doors, while the bathroom—the biggest test of any cabin—was a welcome sight. A flushing toilet and strong water pressure are unsung luxuries, and things I'm always relieved to find in a cabin. The kitchen has everything you'd need, but there's also an outdoor barbecue firepit, making cooking here a genuine joy.

Nearby, there are plenty of sightseeing opportunities, pubs, day trips, and activities: UNESCO World Heritage Site Stonehenge is just a 15-minute drive away, while Cranborne Chase National Landscape and the New Forest are both under a half-hour drive. The property itself is full of life as well, with alpacas grazing, chickens clucking, and a muster of peacocks running between hedgerows. On Mondays and Wednesdays, you can join a yoga class in a studio above the winemaking barn.

Each morning, I'd wake to the sound of peacocks, open the drapes to soft golden light trickling in, and breathe in the fresh air before lighting a fire to get breakfast started. Since returning home, I've longed for the calm of those mornings and the methodical mindfulness of cooking over a flame.

The owners have big plans in the works. Soon, wine will be available from the vineyard, which is expected to produce up to 10,000 bottles a year over the next few years. Chris Reynolds, who owns the land with his wife, Louise Marshall, gives every pod guest a tour, something that will become an even bigger selling point once wine is available to taste. Ahead of this, visitors can sponsor a vine through a subscription model in exchange for wine, pod stays, and events such as harvest parties. Liba is already certified organic and is working towards biodynamic certification within the next nine months.

Next summer, the 10-acre farm will be bookable for weddings, while early discussions are underway about an on-site café and additional activities to complement the existing yoga studio.

Delta Air Lines is adding another route from its fastest-growing “focus city.”

Over the weekend, the Atlanta-based carrier filed plans to launch nonstop service from Austin Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) to Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) outside Bentonville.

Flights will begin in March 2027, with Delta offering service on board a Delta Connection regional jet.

The service will give the Texas capital a nonstop link to northwest Arkansas — not to mention parts of Oklahoma, Missouri and Kansas, which are all a relatively short drive from XNA.

SkyMiles news: Delta announces Medallion qualification requirements for 2027

The airport is also the closest option for travelers heading to the University of Arkansas.

For Delta, it’s the latest in a series of expansions in Austin.

The carrier has grown its flight offerings at AUS at a fast pace over the last couple of years, targeting the airport as one of its top non-hub “focus cities.”

That growth included the airline’s first nonstop service from Austin to Europe, which Delta revealed in August. Those flights to Paris will begin in April.

That’s on top of new routes to major tech hubs like San Jose in California's Silicon Valley and popular leisure destinations like Bozeman, Montana, and Cancun in Mexico.

All told, the airline plans to operate up to 70 daily departures by March, Delta chief commercial officer Joe Esposito told me this summer.

In 2019, it had 28 peak daily departures from AUS.

“The boom is incredible,” Esposito told me in August, noting that a growing number of Delta flyers will also start seeing itineraries with connections in the Lone Star State. That said, Delta has stopped short of saying it will ever make Austin a hub.

“We want to be the business carrier of Austin — we’re quickly moving in on the leading corporate carrier for Austin,” he said. “Then you wind up connecting people.”

It's likely no coincidence, then, that Delta would be interested in service to Bentonville: the region is home to Walmart's corporate headquarters.

As for this latest route, Delta’s service from AUS to Northwest Arkansas will launch on March 7.

It’ll be a late-night departure, with flights taking off just before 9 p.m. The return flight from XNA to AUS will launch the next morning, on March 8.

The service will be on board an Embraer 175 regional jet operated by regional partner SkyWest.

“This new direct route is another example of Delta’s continued investment in Austin and our commitment to making it easier for Austinites to get where they want to go as we continue growing alongside this important community,” Luis Guitart, Delta’s Austin-based regional sales manager, said in a statement to TPG Monday.

While Delta has grown its flight offerings in Austin rapidly over the past couple of years, Southwest Airlines remains the market leader at the airport.

Southwest, like Delta, plans to offer its biggest schedule ever from AUS in 2027.

The airport will also be home to one of its inaugural airport lounges.

Delta, for its part, is planning a second — larger — Sky Club at AUS for the coming years.

By the way, Delta's new route to Northwest Arkansas will add to a strong run of air service growth for that region, too.

This year, the airport will see 28% more total flights than it did just two years ago, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

Beyond its future route to Austin, Delta serves Bentonville from five other airports — all hubs: Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis, Salt Lake City and New York's LaGuardia Airport (LGA).

#6272. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6271. United Airlines CEO Insists He Runs The “World’s Best” Airline. Does That Title Even Matter?

Scott Kirby believes United Airlines is the best airline in the world (he has for quite some time). I understand his argument, and there are aspects of United that compare favorably with just about any competitor. But the claim raises a more interesting question: what actually makes an airline the best? The answer depends on much more than the seat or the route map or any other single quality…and maybe that’s asking the wrong question anyway.

In his recent Cheeky Pint interview with John Collison and Ben Thompson, Kirby made a case for United that deserves more than an eye roll.

His argument is not that United serves the best food or offers the most luxurious seats. He acknowledges that Asian and Middle Eastern competitors do better on the physical product and probably service. He also identifies schedule as the primary reason people choose an airline. But he believes United’s technology changes the overall assessment:

“I say schedule is the number one reason people pick an airline. But, everything else matters for brand-loyal customers. It’s service, product, reliability, and technology. The Asian and Middle East carriers do better than the US airlines on product for sure, and probably service too. I think we do a really good job, but they have different cultures for service, so they do better on that. But I think technology is the differentiator.

“United, that’s why I now believe that United in totality is the best airline in the world, and it’s because of technology. It’s exponentially getting better. Things like being able to do this for customers when there’s a delay and tell them what’s going on. We started it this summer. AI allows us to institutionalize this. But if you’re going to have a delay, like sending customers weather radar maps. In Chicago, there was a day where the weather was over the horizon, but you had to fly. It was sunny at the airport, but you had to fly through this line of thunderstorms, and so the routes were closed. You couldn’t—

“We sent half the people the normal weather delay, which they think you’re lying… Because it’s sunny outside. You must be lying to me. We sent half a picture with the radar map, and you have to fly through this line of thunderstorms, and the routes are closed because of outside. The people with a 1-hour delay, I think the numbers were negative 60 NPS on the normal way of sending it, plus 60 when we send a picture of the map. A 120-point difference.”

His case for United rests on technology: better tools for managing travel, clearer communication during disruptions, and connectivity that makes time onboard more useful. For example, he describes sending passengers radar maps to explain why distant thunderstorms were delaying flights even though the weather at their airport looked fine. His point is that passengers respond much better when they understand what is happening.

Thus, Kirby is acknowledging that competitors outperform it in some traditional measures of onboard quality, but arguing that United’s technological advantages outweigh those shortcomings.

I think he is right that these things matter. I am less convinced that they settle the question.

Start with the most obvious consideration: an airline is not particularly useful if it cannot conveniently take you where you need to go. I love trying new products and will sometimes take an absurd routing to do so. Most travelers understandably do not approach their trips that way.

A nonstop flight at a convenient time can be more valuable than a better seat reached through a connection. Frequency matters too. An airline with several flights a day gives you more options, particularly when something goes wrong.

This is a substantial part of United’s appeal. Its network gives me reasons to fly it that have nothing to do with whether another airline serves better Champagne.

But the best network for me may be largely irrelevant to someone living elsewhere. A traveler in Taipei and a traveler in Chicago are starting with very different choices. There is no universal route map that works best for everyone.

Emirates is a good example of why an airline’s reputation may need to be separated from the particular experience you are buying.

Mention Emirates and many people think of luxury (massive first class suites, showers, and bars onboard with beautiful flight attendants serving you extensive food and beverage offerings). That “halo effect” reputation is understandable.

But someone booking business class on an older Boeing 777 may encounter a product that falls well short of that image. The retrofitted 777s improve the situation with a 1-2-1 layout and direct aisle access, but I would not put that seat ahead of the leading business class products elsewhere.

Singapore Airlines illustrates this as well. Its reputation for service, built in part around the Singapore Girl branding, is extraordinary. Yet some travelers strongly dislike its longhaul business class seats, particularly their sleeping position.

A beautifully presented meal and gracious service cannot entirely compensate for a bed in which you struggle to get comfortable. Singapore’s new cabin reveal on Friday, November 6, will be particularly interesting for that reason.

My recent Emirates 777 first class flight demonstrated the reverse problem: a superb suite paired with service that did not live up to it. I loved the space, but the experience still fell short.

So what about Kirby’s argument that technology is most important?

We sometimes talk about technology as if it is separate from the passenger experience. But an app that lets you solve a problem without standing in line is providing service. A clear explanation of a delay is providing service. Working internet can determine whether a long daytime flight is productive or frustrating.

US airlines deserve credit here. Their digital tools can be excellent, and United’s app is absolutely the best in the business, no question about it. But even the Alaska, American, and Delta apps are–comparatively speaking–much better than their non-US peers.

To be clear, that does not mean every American airline leads every foreign airline or that an attractive app excuses indifferent employees. It does mean that evaluating service solely by how someone pours your wine misses a large part of what an airline does for its customers.

Connectivity is especially important to me. Extra legroom and a better meal are welcome, but painfully slow or non-functioning Wi-Fi can materially change how I feel about a flight. For someone hoping to disconnect and sleep, it may barely register. The features can be measured. The importance each passenger assigns to them cannot be universal.

I also recognize the limitations of my own perspective. Much of my coverage focuses on premium cabins, and those experiences influence my preferences. But what does the airline offer someone in economy?

Some Asian carriers offer a more appealing combination of legroom, meals, and attentive service than their US counterparts. That deserves weight, even if the business class cabin lacks the latest suite.

At the same time, the aircraft still matters. So do the fare restrictions, baggage allowance, and cost of choosing a seat. A generous meal does not tell us whether the ticket represents good value.

For a family paying for several tickets, the best airline may be the one offering a tolerable nonstop journey at an affordable total price. For a tall passenger, a little more legroom may matter far more than the entertainment selection.

An airline cannot claim superiority for everyone based on what it provides a small number of passengers at the front of the aircraft.

A great airline should operate reliably and treat passengers well when it fails.

Those are related, but separate, expectations. I want to arrive on time. When that is impossible, I want an honest explanation and practical assistance.

No airline can prevent every weather delay or mechanical problem. But how it prepares, communicates, and recovers tells me much more than a polished promotional video.

American Airlines is a useful example from my own flying. I would argue that some of my recent meals on American have been the best among the US network carriers. Its free Wi-Fi has also tends to work very well for me. Those are real strengths.

Nevertheless, my experiences with inconsistent service and operational problems place American well below Delta and United in my overall assessment. That is not a claim that every American flight is bad or every Delta flight is good. It is the cumulative effect of repeated experiences. A carrier earns my confidence over time, and it can lose it the same way.

The loyalty program belongs in this discussion too.

Award availability, redemption prices, and the usefulness of elite benefits all affect how much value I receive from an airline. A good program can persuade me to choose one carrier when the alternatives are otherwise similar.

But I try to separate the airline I enjoy most from the program in which I find the most value.

An excellent redemption does not make an uncomfortable seat comfortable. Status does not make a canceled flight depart. Conversely, a wonderful airline can have a loyalty program that gives me little reason to engage with it. Ideally, the program reinforces a relationship the airline has already earned through its service.

Qatar Airways and STARLUX are among my favorites because I have found their overall experiences so compelling. The appeal extends beyond a seat or a meal: I look forward to flying them because of the reliable Wi-Fi, excellent service, and quality in everything.

Air France has also come such a long way. Its newer business class seat is excellent, and the addition of Starlink on equipped aircraft addresses something that matters greatly to me. Combined with the food and service I enjoy, that makes it an increasingly attractive choice.

Yet I still have many reasons to fly United. Its network and technology have practical value in my life that an exceptional flight on another carrier cannot always replace.

That is why my favorite airline and the airline I choose for a particular trip need not be the same…maybe the point is that talking about which carrier is “best” is ultimately futile and our focus instead should be rewarding carriers who do things well and not patronizing those that continually disappoint.

Kirby’s claim is worth discussing because he recognizes that being the best involves more than having the fanciest cabin. Technology and network utility deserve more credit than they sometimes receive.

But I would not crown United the best airline in the world on that basis alone. The seat still matters. So does the person serving you, the reliability of the operation, and what happens when your plans unravel.

For me, the best airlines are the ones that bring those elements together consistently, but at the same time I realize how arbitrary my own evaluation can be. Thus, I tend to think asking “who is best” is the wrong question versus asking “who does X,Y, and Z well?”

What makes an airline the best for you—and which airline comes closest?

#6270. 55 Thoughtful Gifts for Men Who Love to Travel

The holiday season will be here before we know it, which means it’s time to start thinking about gifts for the ones you love. When you’re shopping for a special guy in your life this year, skip the things he doesn’t actually need and go straight for the ones that count: thoughtful pieces he’ll put to good use on his next trip, upgrades to his everyday essentials, and a few small luxuries that make being on the road that much better. The best gifts for men, after all, aren’t necessarily the flashiest—they’re the ones that become part of his routine, whether that means packing them in a carry-on or enjoying them on a quiet Sunday morning at home.

I’ve hand-selected over 50 gift ideas for men who love to travel, featuring many talked-about favorites with a few less expected additions too. From a timeless leather weekender that’s perfect for a quick getaway to at-home accessories that will enrich any guy’s space, I've got you covered with plenty of options he’ll love. Read on for all of the best travel gifts for men or jump straight to the section you think will interest him most.

At Condé Nast Traveler, editors spend a lot of time debating, researching, testing, and re-testing all things travel accessories and luggage. If you’re looking for the best suitcase to buy your guy this holiday season, look here. But if you want something a little unique that will absolutely rock his travel routine for years to come, check out some of the gift ideas below. To make his next long-haul flight more comfortable, consider gifting him a comfy neck pillow, sleep mask, or a pair of compression socks. A ludicrously capacious leather weekender or a luxurious Italian notebook are smart upgrades he’ll cherish forever. And in case of emergencies, a good ol' fashioned flask will more than do the trick.

Here’s the thing about men: There’s a part of us that will always relish having a new toy to play with. This category is for those who will appreciate a wild card gift and savor the element of surprise. A perfect pair of travel-sized binoculars made from the best optical-grade crystal in the world? Jackpot! The latest generation of AirPods with top-notch noise-canceling technology? Bingo! A smart watch that can track his steps on the go? Perfect!

Clothes are a tough gift for the holidays. Everybody is different, every body is different, and a lot of guys are just downright picky when it comes to what they get dressed in everyday. That being said, there are a few tricks of the trade to consider here—when gifting clothes, don’t go too big, too outré, or too outlandish. The secret is to select timeless, quintessential pieces that travel well, age well, and can be styled into any wardrobe: a Barbour jacket, a crisp white shirt, or a navy suit that packs nicely into a suitcase. When in doubt, a pair of high-quality sunglasses in a classic silhouette is generally a win too.

Lovers of the great outdoors are a funny bunch to shop for. They typically have all of their most treasured gear ready to go already, so this is a demographic for whom you need to be on your A-game. Gifts for outdoorsy types need to be the newest of the new with smart details, category-leading engineering, and unassailable durability. Think a lightweight Norwegian cooler that keeps drinks cold without any ice (that’s right—no ice), or a comfortable running shoe that can handle endless wear and tear. Outdoorsy folks will say that they can never have too many puffy layer-type things—so go ahead and consider a thick blanket or the iconic Arc’teryx Atom insulated hoodie. And if all else fails you can get them a beautiful Stanley bottle to keep their favorite soups and beverages warm in even the most wintry conditions.

I hate to stereotype the genders—but a lot of self-care products out there are marketed more heavily toward women, leaving the average guy in the lurch. He may not know the benefits of investing in a Dr. Barbara Sturm skincare regimen, or how an Omnilux LED mask can help slow visible signs of aging. There’s a whole world of self-care products out there! Here, I’ve gathered some of the best items to kick-start his journey—sometimes all it takes is Dr. Dennis Gross’ miracle-working peel pads.

Food is one of my favorite ways to experience travel. If you’re not quite ready to gift someone a trip to sample authentic panettone straight from the oven in Italy, the good news is that the marvels of modern packing and shipping have made some of the world’s tastiest foods closer than ever. A sampler of high-quality spices will upgrade his at-home cooking. A $60 bag of beans is the perfectly fun gift for a coffee snob who might not buy it for himself. And a perfectly unassailable upgrade to his go-to sauté pan (if he even has one), or the investment of a proper stand mixer, are foolproof.

No matter what the recipient’s sense of style is, there are certain upgrades that are likely to fit into most any home. Beautiful linen sheets are always welcome, as is a great bathrobe or pair of slippers to remind him of a luxury hotel. When in doubt, the flourish of a Flamingo Estate candle hits just the right notes.

#6269. JetBlue Cancels 13 International Nonstop Routes: See Full List Now

JetBlue continues to change as the carrier confronts many ongoing challenges. As part of this, and influenced by the exit of the now-defunct Spirit Airlines, it has really focused on growing at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL). Significantly, JetBlue now has more flights from the Florida airport than it does from New York JFK or Boston.

The airline's network has seen many changes recently. For example, so far this year, JetBlue has ceased 13 international routes. All are to the Caribbean, Mexico, or Central America, although there are big questions about whether another European route will end.

The following list does not include New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Ponce, in Puerto Rico, as that country is a US territory and the route was domestic. Flights ended in January this year after being served for 21 years. As JFK remains JetBlue's leading international gateway, particularly for short-haul operations, nearly half of the eliminated markets (six) are from the Big Apple's busiest airport.

End Month (No Flights Scheduled Past Then)

JFK to Bonaire (Bonaire fully removed from network)

JFK to Tulum (Tulum fully removed from network)

JFK to Belize City (Belize City fully removed from network)

JFK to Antigua (Antigua fully removed from network)

Perhaps unsurprisingly, most of the links only launched fairly recently. Nine were inaugurated between 2020 and 2025, including all but one from JFK and all but one from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR). JetBlue grew significantly at EWR during the COVID-19 pandemic. Freed-up aircraft enabled the carrier to test out things that it might not have ever done.

Cirium Diio data shows that JetBlue had an average of 44 daily departures from EWR in 2021 (domestic and international), which has fallen to about 15 for 2026. Total international activity from the New Jersey airport has fallen by 90% in the same period. Only one international route remains (Santiago, in the Dominican Republic). The airline has moved away from EWR to where it believes it can win.

Once renowned as the world's most dangerous city, with 20+ murders a day, San Pedro Sula is located not far from the northern coast of Honduras. It is the second most populous city in the Central American nation.

The US Department of State recommends passengers 'reconsider travel' to Honduras due to the overall rate of crime, gang activity, and violence. Of course, most passengers are Honduran Americans or the Honduran diaspora. When all airlines are included, booking data suggests that more than 1.6 million people flew between the US and Honduras in the 12 months to May 2026 (4,300+ daily).

JetBlue's debuted in Honduras in June 2025, initially with only one route: JFK to San Pedro Sula's Ramón Villeda Morales International Airport (SAP). The carrier flew daily on the A320, with an overnight flight back to the Big Apple. It was, at the time, one of two airlines on the airport pair, coexisting with Avianca, but that carrier pulled out in January 2026. United Airlines continues to operate between EWR and SAP.

JetBlue served JFK-SAP between June 2025 and May 2026. The US Department of Transportation shows that the airline carried 70,070 round-trip passengers, but only filled 68.1% of the available seats. Only four months had a load factor that exceeded 70.0%. While fare and yield information is unavailable, it is no wonder the route was cut. JetBlue still operates between FLL and SAP.

JetBlue has dropped four international destinations in 2026 while expanding elsewhere and making Fort Lauderdale its busiest airport.

Focusing on November 2026 shows that the airline has an average of 91 daily departures beyond the US border, which has fallen by 10% compared to the same month last year. And it is 17% lower than the record for November, which was set in 2024 (110 daily).

JetBlue's international services are from JFK (an average of 38 daily departures this month), followed by FLL (27), Boston Logan International Airport (BOS; 12), Orlando (six), San Juan (in the US territory of Puerto Rico; six), EWR (one) and Tampa (one). Compared to November 2025, JFK's international activity has reduced by a quarter, while FLL is up by 63% to the highest level in seven years.

#6268. Cruising to Alaska? Check if Your Next Port, Bus, or Lodge is Indigenous-Owned

The Huna Totem Corporation was featured on Condé Nast Traveler's Bright Ideas in Travel 2026. Read the full list of winners here.

From April to October, cruise ships tower over downtown Juneau’s Marine Way, a coastal path that connects the port zone to downtown. Should a traveler pause for a moment between ship and souvenir store, they’ll notice Kaagwaantaan Kootéeyaa, a tall, intricately carved pole rising against a backdrop of forest and mountains. At its base, a panel explains that the cedar pole depicts five of the Kaagwaantaan Tlingit clan’s crests: a hat, person, orca, eagle and bear. It is an arresting introduction to the long-overlooked human history of this place.

Since 2023, totem poles have adorned this highly trafficked shoreline, part of Kootéeyaa Deiyí (“Totem Pole Trail”)—a city-wide project led by the Sealaska Heritage Institute (SHI) that represents the cultures of the Tlingit people who have inhabited Juneau for at least 10,000 years, as well as the Haida and Tsimshian who arrived a few hundred years ago. Visible evidence of the region’s Indigenous communities was previously limited, says SHI’s Ricardo Worl (Tlingit), who sees the trail as “an opportunity to reestablish our presence on our ancestral lands.” Noting that more than a million cruise ship passengers land in Juneau each year, Worl hopes the trail “is the beginning of their education about our culture.”

Alaska’s cruise industry has long invited travelers to experience the “Last Frontier” while relegating Indigenous peoples to the margins of the tourism economy. Now, a shift is occurring—one that goes beyond simply incorporating Indigenous culture into the cruise experience. Across Alaska, Native corporations are increasingly owning and shaping the tourism infrastructure itself, from cruise docks and terminals to ground transportation, giving them a greater stake in how destinations develop, and how visitors experience them.

I came to Alaska to see how Indigenous ownership is changing the experience on the ground, following a route that took me from whale watching at cruise ports on the coast to bear and moose spotting at a lodge deep in the Interior. At each stop, I saw how Alaska Native corporations are shaping the places that travelers pass through.

Created following passage of the 1971 Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, Alaska Native corporations are for-profit companies run by and for Alaska Native shareholders. For Huna Totem, a Tlingit village corporation representing shareholders with ties to Hoonah and Glacier Bay, tourism is an important part of its economic development strategy. Its best-known development, Icy Strait Point in Hoonah, is Alaska’s first private cruise destination and has become a model for Alaska Native-owned tourism—creating local jobs, keeping economic benefits within the community and making Tlingit culture part of the visitor experience.

When Icy Strait Point opened in 2004, Huna Totem leadership was focused on “providing economic stability for generations, so the culture can be perpetuated,” says Ruth Banaszak, director of marketing and communications. Icy Strait Point has two cruise ship piers located about a half-mile apart and activity areas for 30 different excursions to distribute visitor flow around the site so that it never becomes overwhelming. To get around the vast site, I made use of the forested walking trails and two gondola systems, one of which took me to the summit of Hoonah Mountain, which I quickly and thrillingly descended via the ZipRider, a six-cable zipline. Walking around the museum exhibits housed inside a 1912 salmon cannery that closed when the fishing industry declined, I could connect tourism's present and future with its economic history. The cannery was once a symbol of loss; now it provides new economic opportunities. “We hire around 350 people for the season,” says Banaszak. “So, in a town of 950, anybody who wants to have a job in the community has one.” The model has also allowed local residents to build businesses of their own, including boat tours to Point Adolphus where, in just two hours, I spotted dozens of orcas, a few humpback whales and uncountable numbers of sea lions and sea otters. In each place, instead of being whisked onto an excursion operated by an outside company, I was experiencing a destination that had been shaped by the community whose ancestral home I was visiting.

“We’ve done this for our own community in Hoonah,” says Banaszak, “so now [we’re asking] how can we take what we’ve learned here and help other rural communities do the same thing?”

That thinking has led Huna Totem around Southeast Alaska and beyond. In Whittier, the corporation opened Glacier Gateway cruise terminal in 2024. Huna Totem and Doyon, Limited, another Alaska Native corporation, have also acquired Portage Glacier Cruises and Alaska Coach Tours, creating Native-owned touchpoints that extend from ship to shore and beyond. In Klawock, on Prince of Wales Island, Huna Totem partnered with Doyon and the local Alaska Native village corporation Klawock Heenya to develop a new cruise port in 2024. The destination uses a single-ship model, with development focused on Tlingit culture, local involvement and community values.

Back in downtown Juneau, Huna Totem is developing Áak’w Landing, a cruise dock and waterfront development targeting its first full season in 2028. The project is designed to improve how cruise visitors move through the city—including eliminating the need for tender boats at the site—rather than simply bringing in more ships. Reflecting its approach of being “culturally driven, community-centric, [and] business-focused,” says Banaszak, Huna Totem sees the project as both infrastructure enhancement and an opportunity to incorporate Alaska Native culture into the visitor experience—two poles from SHI’s Kootéeyaa Deiyí will be raised at the site.

The broader ambition is to create a network of Native-owned tourism businesses across Alaska. “So that Alaska Native tourism grows: culturally-led tourism as it should be done, people telling their own story themselves,” Banaszak says.

The cruise industry may seem an odd venture for Doyon, Limited, which is based in Fairbanks and represents the largely Dene people of the Interior, but, says Jordan Sanford, president of Doyon Tourism, “more than 60% of visitors come to Alaska by cruise, so [we realized] if we wanted to grow, we needed to be involved.”

Deep in Denali National Park, Doyon has operated Kantishna Roadhouse, the park’s only Indigenous-owned lodge, for 30 years. Arriving via a small plane from the park entrance—road access, closed for five years due to a landslide, will return in 2027—I spent blissful days backcountry hiking free from cell service. Evenings were spent listening to presentations by staff, such as an introduction to Dene beadwork and regalia; spotting wildlife including grizzly bears, moose, and caribou, then watching the setting sun light up the slopes of mighty Denali. Since 2004, in partnership with Aramark, Doyon has also operated bus tours, transit services, and campgrounds in the park. The partnership with Huna Totem gives Doyon an opportunity to diversify and grow, while responding to a recent shift in cruise passengers’ expectations: “They’re looking for more authentic experiences,” she explains. “We see that as our advantage. We put shareholders to work, and they share their culture,” she says. “There's a lot of businesses here that have been sharing the culture for so long, but from non-Alaska Natives,” she adds.

Next up is the restoration of the 1925 Chatanika Gold Camp near Fairbanks, which is scheduled to open in 2027 as a northern lights experience center, filling a critical infrastructure gap. Aurora viewing in Alaska today typically means pulling off the side of the road and drinking a hot chocolate, says Sanford. With Chatanika, “we're creating a space [with] cultural programming to make it more of an experience.”

It’s another link in an emerging network of Native-owned businesses across the state. The ultimate goal is “an Alaska Native-owned corridor, where [travelers] are visiting Alaska Native-owned businesses along the way,” says Sanford. For cruise passengers, that means more opportunities to encounter Indigenous culture, while knowing that Indigenous people are benefiting from the industry. And it means that your next Alaska cruise itinerary might begin at a Native-owned port, continue aboard a Native-owned bus, lead to a Native-owned excursion, and end at a Native-owned lodge.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

Sometimes, simplicity is king. And that's certainly the case with the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card.

The Venture Rewards is a card I frequently recommend to beginners who want to earn rewards they can maximize for travel.

Why? Because for a reasonable $95 annual fee, the card earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase, making it easy to build a rewards balance without keeping track of bonus categories. Plus, it offers valuable travel perks and flexible redemption options, whether you want to keep things simple or explore more advanced strategies.

Whether you're new to earning travel rewards or recently picked up the card yourself, here are six beginner-friendly ways to make the most of the Venture Rewards.

Earning a welcome bonus is one of the easiest ways for beginners to kick-start their points and miles journey.

Currently, new Venture Rewards cardholders can earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, they'll also receive a $300 credit for Capital One Travel hotel and vacation rentals upon account opening.

According to TPG's October 2026 valuations, Capital One miles are worth 1.85 cents per mile. When including the credit, the total value of this welcome offer comes to $1,688. That makes this offer the most valuable we've seen in over two years.

Those 75,000 Capital One miles can be a great starting point for anyone new to maximizing points and miles.

And as for the $300 Capital One Travel credit, it's a great way to dip your toe into the world of travel portals. You could use it to cover a weekend hotel stay, save on a vacation rental or offset the cost of a more expensive trip.

Just remember that the credit must be used toward eligible hotel or vacation rental bookings through Capital One Travel within your first cardholder year.

Related: Credit cards 101: The beginner’s guide

One of the Venture Rewards' best perks is that it earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase.

With some travel rewards cards, you earn more points when spending in certain everyday categories. But with the Venture Rewards, you'll earn 2 miles per dollar whether you're filling up your tank, furnishing your apartment or stocking your fridge.

The card also earns 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel.

TPG lead writer Katie Genter has held the Venture Rewards for more than a decade and still finds it useful for everyday purchases: "I like the Venture's straightforward earning structure and the fact that it earns versatile yet valuable Capital One miles."

She often uses her Venture Rewards for purchases that would earn just 1 point or mile per dollar with another rewards card.

If you're new to the world of points and miles, the Venture Rewards can be a great place to start, given how simple it is to earn rewards that can then be used for travel, which we'll cover below.

Related: The best credit cards for everyday spending

Another way to maximize your Venture Rewards as a beginner is to book eligible travel through Capital One Travel, the issuer's online travel booking platform.

As mentioned above, Venture Rewards cardholders earn 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through the portal, compared to the standard 2 miles per dollar on other purchases.

For example, booking a $1,000 hotel stay through Capital One Travel would earn you 5,000 miles (compared to 2,000 miles if you booked directly with the hotel). That's an additional 3,000 miles, worth approximately $56 according to TPG's valuations.

Plus, Venture Rewards cardholders can access Capital One's Lifestyle Collection, which offers benefits such as a $50 experience credit for each eligible hotel stay and potential room upgrades (when available).

However, I don't recommend using the portal as your default method of booking travel. You usually won't earn hotel loyalty points or receive elite status benefits when booking through a third party, so it's worth comparing prices and benefits before making a reservation.

Still, for beginners looking to earn more miles without changing their spending habits, Capital One Travel can be a useful tool.

Related: Should I book flights through a travel portal?

Beyond earning miles, the Venture Rewards comes with several travel perks that can help you save money and make your trips a little easier.

One of the most useful is a statement credit of up to $120 (every four years) for a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fee. All you need to do is pay the application fee with your card, and you'll receive a statement credit for the eligible charge.

Both programs can help you save time at the airport, but Global Entry also includes TSA PreCheck benefits, so I recommend it for international travelers.

Another perk for international travelers is that the Venture Rewards charges no foreign transaction fees. This means you can use your card abroad without worrying about the additional fees some credit cards charge on international purchases.

The card also offers several travel protections, including an auto rental collision damage waiver and travel accident insurance, which can provide some added peace of mind when you're away from home.

You can also enroll in complimentary Hertz Five Star status, which comes with benefits like a wider selection of rental vehicles and the ability to skip the rental counter (at certain locations).

For a card with a $95 annual fee, these perks can offer strong ongoing value, especially if you travel a few times a year.

Related: 7 of the best starter travel credit cards

If you aren't ready to transfer your miles to travel partners but still want to redeem your rewards for travel, another option is to use your miles to cover eligible travel purchases.

Rather than searching for award availability or navigating airline loyalty programs, you can book an eligible travel purchase with your card and redeem miles to offset the charge within 90 days of the purchase.

When you redeem miles this way, each mile is worth 1 cent. That's less than TPG's valuation of Capital One miles at 1.85 cents per mile, but it offers a straightforward way to use your rewards.

For example, if you book a $300 flight with your Venture Rewards, you can redeem 30,000 miles to cover the purchase. You can also use this feature for other eligible travel expenses, including hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars.

TPG director of site strategy Carly Helfand has relied on this method before, redeeming 100,000 Capital One miles to cover a last-minute Airbnb purchase.

While transferring miles to travel partners can yield higher redemption values, covering travel purchases is a useful alternative when you want to book directly or can't find award availability that works for your dates.

For potentially higher-value redemptions, consider transferring your Capital One miles to the issuer's airline and hotel partners.

If you're new to the world of travel rewards, transferring miles simply means moving your Capital One miles into another travel loyalty program, where you can then redeem them for flights or hotel stays.

Capital One has more than 15 travel partners, including Air France-KLM Flying Blue, British Airways Club and Wyndham Rewards.

Most of Capital One's airline partners offer a 1:1 transfer ratio, meaning 1,000 Capital One miles become 1,000 miles in the partner program. However, some partners have different ratios, so be sure to check before transferring.

Personally, I love transferring my Capital One miles to airline partners to book flights to and around Europe.

For example, I recently transferred about 6,000 Capital One miles to Air France-KLM Flying Blue to book a Scandinavian Airlines flight from Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) to Stockholm Arlanda Airport (ARN). I paid just $11 in taxes and fees for a flight that would have otherwise cost about $450 in cash, giving me 7.3 cents per mile in value — well above TPG's valuation of 1.85 cents per mile.

If you're just getting started, don't feel like you need to master transfer partners right away. You can begin by redeeming miles for travel purchases and explore transfers as you become more comfortable.

Related: How to transfer Capital One miles to airline and hotel partners

The Capital One Venture Rewards stands out as a beginner-friendly travel rewards card thanks to its simple earning structure, valuable travel perks and flexible redemption options.

If you're new to the world of points and miles, start by using the card for everyday spending and exploring simple travel redemptions. As you become more comfortable, you can transfer miles to travel partners to unlock even greater value.

And even as you become more experienced with points and miles, the Venture Rewards' simplicity and flexibility make it a card worth keeping in your wallet long term.

For more details, read our full review of the Capital One Venture Rewards.

#6266. Aman At Sea: Amangati “Superyacht” Sets Sail Spring 2027, From $6K+ Per Night

Aman at Sea voyages are best booked through travel advisors, who can get you the best price possible, while adding extra perks. Ford and his team are happy to help with any requests, and can be reached at [email protected].

In 2027, we’re going to see the launch of a new ultra-luxury cruise line, as hotel group Aman is getting into the cruising industry, with the Aman at Sea concept, and its Amangati “superyacht,” as it’s called.

I’d like to provide an update about this concept, as sailings are now bookable well into 2028, so we have a sense of both the summer sailings in Europe and winter sailings in the Caribbean. If you think the recent entrants into the market are expensive, wait until you learn the details of this one.

It’s interesting to see the increasing trend of luxury hotel groups launching cruise lines, or perhaps more accurately, licensing out their names to partner on new cruising concepts. For example, in 2022 we saw the launch of Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, and in 2026, we’ve seen the launch of Four Seasons Yachts and Orient Express Sailing Yachts.

Amangati (“peaceful motion” in Sanskrit) is expected to set sail in the spring of 2027, as Aman’s first superyacht. Yes, this marks the Aman brand getting into the luxury cruising industry, on a ship that’s being described as a “floating sanctuary.”

The 600-foot ship will be around 23,000 gross tons, and will have a hybrid propulsion system, using battery power to reduce emissions and improve efficiency. It’s currently being built in Italy’s T. Mariotti shipyard, and it will be delivered to Neptune Co., which is a joint venture between hotel group Aman and Cruise Saudi.

The ship is expected to feature a total of 47 suites, each with a balcony and floor-to-ceiling windows. The suites will be among the largest at sea.

When it comes to amenities, the ship will have four restaurants, a jazz club, a 52-foot pool, a beach club and marina, a spa with a Japanese garden, two helipads, and much more. Sinot Yacht Architecture & Design is behind the design, and the intent is to take cues from traditional ryokan architecture.

For those not familiar, Cruise Saudi is owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, and is intended to promote the cruise and tourism industry in Saudi Arabia. However, it doesn’t appear that the plan is actually for the ship to cruise in Saudi Arabia, at least for the foreseeable future. So it seems to primarily be part of the country’s larger investment in the cruising industry.

Here’s how Aman CEO Vlad Doronin describes the idea behind the ship:

Aman has published the inaugural voyages for Amangati, for sailings between May 7, 2027, and March 31, 2028. Unsurprisingly, the ship will spend summers in Europe and winters in the Caribbean, with transatlantic sailings in November and March.

In both summer in Europe and winter in the Caribbean, sailings will be five to eight nights each, and they’re roughly what you’d expect in terms of itineraries. You can either book directly through Aman at Sea, or through a travel advisor.

An eligible travel advisor will be able to add a minimum of a $500 shipboard credit, while paying the standard rate. You can generally expect pricing parity between all booking sources, so you won’t find discounted sailing prices anywhere. Ford and his team are happy to help with these requests, and can be reached at [email protected].

Before we talk about the pricing for Aman at Sea, what’s included with journeys? It’s an interesting topic, because historically ultra luxury cruises have been all-inclusive. However, Four Seasons Yachts is countering that trend, by not including lunch, dinner, or alcoholic drinks.

With that in mind, Aman at Sea will include the following with the cost of sailings:

As you can see, Aman is sort of taking a middle ground approach here. Alcohol aside from beer isn’t included, and neither is dining at the specialty restaurants.

How much are Aman at Sea rates? Pricing is per suite rather than per guest. As it currently stands, I see five-night journeys starting at $32,500, while I see seven-night journeys priced as high as $54,600. So we’re looking at somewhere around $6,000-8,000 per night for an entry level suite. You’ll generally find that Caribbean sailings are a little cheaper than European sailings.

Admittedly these suites are massive by ship standards, but that’s definitely on the very high end of the market, and easily 50%+ more than Four Seasons Yachts is charging (though with some more inclusions).

Prior to 2026, I hadn’t taken a cruise since I was a kid. However, this year I’ve given all three of the luxury cruise lines associated with hotels a try, and I’ve shared my thoughts on Four Seasons Yachts, Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection. I’ve even done a direct comparison of the three concepts, based on my firsthand experience.

Let me of course acknowledge that these cruise lines are all at the very top end of the market, so I’m not claiming or suggesting that they’re the best value options out there. Instead, I’ve taken such an interest in them because I find the crossover between hotels and cruise lines to be so interesting, and also find it noteworthy how these are all cruise lines targeted at people who historically haven’t considered cruising.

With that in mind, here’s how I’d broadly sum up the experiences offered by the three existing players:

In general, I’d expect Aman at Sea will probably be closest to Orient-Express Sailing Yachts in terms of exclusivity, while probably being more like Four Seasons Yachts in terms of design (since it’s not a sailboat). I will say, given the price point, I do find the lack of inclusions to be a bit frustrating. Then again, the standard suites will be absolutely massive.

The concept of luxury cruising is nothing new. However, there’s no denying that the industry is evolving a bit:

Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection is the only one of the concepts that has now been in service for some time, and based on what we know, the financial performance has left a bit to be desired. And that was before the cruise line expanded to three ships, and it’s before three competitors entered the industry.

Ultimately the success of these ventures comes down to whether they can convince people that cruising is “cool.” I don’t think these cruise lines will be cannibalizing brands like Silversea, but instead, I think they’re going after those who would otherwise vacation on land.

The other thing worth keeping in mind is that at some point, these cruise lines are competing with the concept of just chartering a yacht, which is a concept that will have more appeal for many people.

Obviously $6K+ per night is a massive amount to spend on a cruise. But the reality is that people easily pay that kind of money for peak season rooms in place like Saint-Tropez. Can these hotel-branded cruise lines convince people who want to “see and be seen” that it’s as cool to be on a ship as it is to be in the South of France? It seems like a tall order, but I guess time will tell.

Ironically, I think the volume of new entrants into the market is actually quite helpful in building demand, since cruises are finally being talked about more among non-cruisers. While they’re all competing for the same types of guests, I know a fair number of people have tried one of these cruise lines, then rebooked on another cruise line, etc.

Aman will be getting into the luxury cruising space in the spring of 2027, with the launch of its 600-foot Amangati superyacht. The ship looks incredible, and it seems like we’re seeing the luxury hotel groups all one-up each other.

The pricing is at the very top end of the market, which doesn’t come as much of a surprise. Will there be enough people willing to pay $6K+ per night for Aman’s cruising concept to keep these ships full, especially without most alcohol included? Only time will tell.

What do you make of Aman getting into the luxury cruise industry?
