#6260. How I earned over 3,800 points and miles buying $180 worth of sports tickets with my Freedom Flex

Beyond welcome bonuses, points and miles aren't always the easiest to earn. That's why I advocate for stacking your card's earning rates with shopping portal bonuses and other promotions whenever you can.

That's exactly what I did recently when I purchased three tickets for my parents and me to see the Portland Timbers while they were visiting. The total charge was about $180; if I'd paid with a card earning just 1 point per dollar spent and skipped the other offers, I'd have earned only 180 points.

But by paying close attention to my Chase Freedom Flex®'s (see rates and fees) quarterly categories and promotions offered by Rove and Paze, I was able to walk away with just shy of 4,000 points (or over $75 in value back). Here's exactly how my earnings break down.

For Q3 2026, the Freedom Flex offered select live entertainment as one of its rotating 5% quarterly bonus categories (activation required; on up to $1,500 in combined quarterly category spending per quarter).

Despite being marketed as a cash-back card, the Freedom Flex actually earns Ultimate Rewards points. That means my earning rate for live entertainment purchases in Q3 was effectively 5 points per dollar spent, since I have an eligible card that allows me to convert my Freedom Flex rewards into fully transferable points.

On its own, this category earned me about 900 points, a solid haul considering I'd earn only 180 points during quarters when live entertainment isn't offered. Still, while planning my purchase, I knew I could do better.

I've been a big fan of Rove over the past several months, using it for a variety of events and travel bookings. Rove offers members the opportunity to earn Rove miles, which are transferable to over 20 airline and hotel partners. This includes partners that aren't offered by any credit card loyalty programs, such as Frontier Miles and Lufthansa Miles & More.

It's free to join. Rove has its own travel booking portal, but for this particular purchase, I focused solely on its shopping portal. At the time, Rove offered 6.5 miles per dollar spent on StubHub purchases.

By booking my tickets through StubHub, I earned over 1,100 Rove miles. An unfortunate downside to shopping through Rove is that your miles often take an extended amount of time to post, which isn't uncommon with shopping portals. I'm still waiting for my miles to land in my account, which Rove indicates could take until early December.

Don't forget to start your purchase in the Rove app, on Rove's website or via its browser extension. If you're using the browser extension or accessing Rove via desktop, make sure all other shopping portal browser extensions are disabled.

With my decision to book through StubHub, there was one more way I could make my purchase work for me: Paze.

Currently, eligible Chase cardholders can earn 10 additional Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent when checking out with Paze at select merchants (through Dec. 31). StubHub is among those eligible for this promotion, meaning I could triple-dip on my purchase.

Checking out with Paze instead of the standard StubHub checkout process earned me roughly 1,800 additional points.

Using Paze at checkout is easy. You should be able to select it as a payment method on your eligible merchant's checkout screen, just as you would with a digital wallet or credit card.

One technical snag to note: I wasn't able to get Paze to work on mobile, but it worked on the first try on desktop. My transaction didn't say anything about Paze, so don't fret if the same is true for you. My points posted with no problem after a few days, but I recommend screen recording your purchase as proof if you're worried.

To summarize, here's how my earnings and their value broke down in the end:

*Valuations are according to TPG's November 2026 valuations and are not provided by credit card or program issuers.

My Freedom Flex is one of my oldest cards, but I still pull it out regularly, thanks in large part to strategies like this. While Chase's Paze promotion isn't limited to this card, the Freedom Flex is the only Chase card currently open to applicants that offers rotating 5% quarterly bonus categories.

Live entertainment reliably appears as a quarterly category every year, so I expect I'll be able to replicate this strategy (or a similar one) in 2027.

The more credit cards you open, the harder it becomes to find new welcome bonuses to earn. With welcome offers being the main way to earn heaps of rewards at once, it's important to have other ways to earn points and miles when that well starts to dry up.

Knowing how to maximize your purchases, especially larger ones or those you're splitting with friends or family, will help you maintain a large rewards balance even when you're not actively applying for new credit cards.

If you're currently not a Freedom Flex cardholder, you can apply and, upon approval, have the chance to earn $250 cash back (or 25,000 bonus points) after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months of account opening. That's one of the easiest welcome bonuses to earn right now, but this offer ends soon.

If you hold an eligible Ultimate Rewards card, such as the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees), you can transfer the points you earn with your Freedom Flex to Chase's 14 transfer partners.

The Timbers weren't able to walk away with the win, but the more than 3,800 points and miles I earned from the tickets I purchased helped ease the sting of that loss.

You can create a strategy like this with virtually any card in your wallet. Consider the offers, limited-time earning rates and promotions that are available for your specific card; take a look at shopping portals like Rakuten and Rove to see what they offer; and use sites like Cashback Monitor to make sure you're getting the best deal.

Effectively maximizing your card's earning potential means thoroughly understanding which offers and deals are available to you and knowing how to combine them. It requires a little extra work on your part, but that effort will be worth it when those extra rewards help take you on your next dream trip.

To learn more, check out our full review of the Chase Freedom Flex.

#6259. How To Redeem Alaska Atmos Rewards Points: Rules, Fees, & Sweet Spots

Alaska Atmos Rewards (formerly Alaska Mileage Plan) has long been a favorite points currency among miles & points geeks, given the carrier’s unique array of airline partners, generous stopover policy, and attractive redemption rates.

In this post, I’d like to take an in-depth look at how to redeem Atmos Rewards points. How do you earn Atmos Rewards points, what are the rules around redeeming them, and what are the best uses?

There are several different ways to go about earning Alaska Atmos Rewards points, from credit cards, to outright buying points, to transferring them from other cards.

The Atmos Rewards program has three co-branded credit cards, issued by Bank of America, and they all have excellent welcome bonuses with limited eligibility restrictions:

What’s so great is that you can potentially qualify for all of these cards, so that’s an opportunity to earn lots of points. For example, I picked up both the Atmos Rewards Summit Card and Atmos Rewards Business Card on the same day.

The Atmos Rewards program is transfer partners with Bilt Rewards, so you can transfer Bilt Points to Atmos Rewards at a 1:1 ratio. This could be a great reason to pick up one of Bilt’s credit cards, with options including the Bilt Blue Card (learn more), Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

You can even pay rent with an Atmos Rewards card and earn 3x points while paying a 3% fee, which could be a useful deal, especially if you’re pursuing elite status.

The program also partners with Marriott Bonvoy®, so you can transfer over Marriott points. The ratio is that 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy® Points convert into 25,000 Atmos Rewards points (if you convert in different increments, it’s a 3:1 ratio).

This can be a solid value, and there are lots of credit cards that can earn you Bonvoy points, including the Marriott Bonvoy Business® American Express® Card (learn more), Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card (learn more), and Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more).

The Atmos Rewards program is pretty aggressive about selling points, and the program seems to offer promotions on purchased points every couple of months. When we see these offers, you can expect bonuses in the range of 90-110%. This is often an opportunity to acquire Atmos Rewards points for under two cents each.

It doesn’t cost anything to join the Atmos Rewards program, so I generally recommend signing up ahead of time — you have to be a member for at least 10 days in order to take advantage of one of these promotions.

Not only are there great ways to earn Atmos Rewards points either through credit cards or by buying them outright, but Atmos Rewards is also a good program to credit flights to.

For one, Atmos Rewards is the last major US frequent flyer program to give members the option to earn points based on distance flown rather than dollars spent. Atmos Rewards allows mileage earning on a variety of airline partners, ranging from Condor to Cathay Pacific. Atmos Rewards lets you earn points for travel on the following airline partners:

The one thing worth mentioning is that you can only earn Atmos Rewards points on Korean Air, Philippine Airlines, and Starlux Airlines, if you book through Alaska, rather than through one of the partners.

Alaska Atmos Rewards has some great redemption opportunities, though there are also quite a few rules to be aware of. Let’s cover some of those basics.

Alaska Airlines belongs to the oneworld alliance, though the airline has an array of partners beyond oneworld. It’s possible to redeem Atmos Rewards points for travel on the following airlines:

All Atmos Rewards award redemption partners can be booked online at alaskaair.com. If you have a complicated itinerary or are having issues with the website, you’ll want to call the Atmos Rewards partner award desk, which can be reached at 800-252-7522.

When it comes to redeeming points, Atmos Rewards has three simple award charts that are a combination of zone and distance based.

There’s the Americas award chart, which covers any travel from the United States to anywhere in the Americas, including North America and South America.

Then there’s the Europe, Middle East, and Africa award chart, which includes travel from the United States to Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, and travel within Europe, the Middle East, and Africa.

Lastly, there’s the Asia-Pacific award chart, which includes travel from the United States to Asia-Pacific, within Asia-Pacific, and between Asia-Pacific and Europe, the Middle East, and Africa.

The most significant thing to understand here is that the “starting at” prices are actually what you’re going to pay if there’s saver level award availability. All partners have the same award pricing assuming there’s saver award availability.

There are a few other important things to mention:

The Atmos Rewards program awards status points for award travel booked through the program. This applies for travel on Alaska, Hawaiian, and all other partner airlines.

Just book using Atmos Rewards points and have your Atmos Rewards number on the reservation, and you’ll earn one status point per mile flown, regardless of the class of service (this assumes you select to earn Atmos Rewards points based on distance flown).

This is a massive point of differentiation for the program, and if you ask me, it’s a contributing reason that many American loyalists might want to consider Atmos Rewards.

One of my favorite things about the Atmos Rewards program is that you are allowed a stopover on a one-way award ticket when traveling between regions. This is possible regardless of which partner you redeem with.

So if you book a roundtrip as two one-ways, this means you can potentially get two stopovers on a roundtrip ticket. To book a ticket online with a stopover, just use the multi-city function, and you can search each portion of the ticket individually.

Now, admittedly with the program being distance based, you are in some cases potentially paying more for itineraries with stopovers, but it’s still a useful feature.

On the surface, Atmos Rewards should have access to the same award availability as other partner airlines do, though in some cases Atmos Rewards inexplicably doesn’t have access to the same space. Most commonly:

This won’t be consistent, but it is something to be aware of, and it sure can be frustrating. There’s generally not any way to get around this.

When searching award availability on some partner airlines, you may see award pricing that’s way above what the chart suggests. This includes for some flights on Aer Lingus, Icelandair, Qatar Airways, and Starlux Airlines. In those situations, what’s happening is that there’s no saver level award availability, but Atmos Rewards has negotiated to have more award availability at a higher cost.

I know this kind of pricing frustrates some people and makes them think the program doesn’t offer good value. However, in these situations, other partner airlines simply wouldn’t have access to the award space. So I wouldn’t view it as a negative, but rather just as an opportunity you probably don’t want to take advantage of.

Atmos Rewards blocks many many partner awards within 72 hours of departure. I’ve been told that this policy won’t stick around, though I don’t have a timeline for when it will change, and it continues to be live. It’s certainly something to be aware of when it comes to last minute redemption opportunities.

Furthermore, Atmos Rewards doesn’t have access to any nonstop domestic American awards at the saver level within six days of departure. Don’t expect this to change, as it’s presumably a commercial decision on American’s part.

There are a couple of fees associated with redeeming Atmos Rewards points:

Atmos Rewards no longer has any change or cancelation fees for award tickets, which gives you lots of flexibility to speculatively lock in awards, or even change them if a better routing opens up. The only exception is that the $20 partner award booking fee can’t be refunded.

Atmos Rewards passes on carrier imposed surcharges (often referred to as fuel surcharges) for travel on some partner airlines. Specifically, these apply for travel on British Airways, Hainan Airlines, and Icelandair. Fortunately they don’t apply for travel on other partner airlines.

Atmos Rewards doesn’t allow award tickets to be placed on hold. To book an Atmos Rewards award ticket you need to have sufficient points in your account, though you can always cancel it for free.

Atmos Rewards points don’t expire. However, if you don’t have any account activity for over two years, your account may be locked for security reasons, and your points may be accessed by contacting Atmos Rewards and verifying personal details.

We all have different travel goals, so there’s never going to be a one size fits all answer as to what the best use of points is. Broadly speaking, my favorite way to redeem points is for aspirational redemptions in first and business class, since that’s where you’ll get the most outsized value.

However, nowadays I’d argue that the redemption sweet spot with Atmos Rewards is largely for shorter awards, given the distance based pricing. In some way, the Atmos Rewards award charts are almost a competitor to British Airways Club, in terms of the great value of short haul redemptions. Since you can redeem Atmos Rewards points for flights globally, I figured the best way to share some sweet spots would just be to take a look at each award chart individually.

Before I do, let me acknowledge a new reality of the miles & points hobby. The reality is that airlines are getting savvier when it comes to how they release award space, and in many cases, they open fewer award seats to members of partner frequent flyer programs. This is beyond any carrier’s control, but it does limit the arbitrage opportunities by using great frequent flyer programs.

Below is the Atmos Rewards award chart for the Americas, which applies exclusively if traveling within the Americas (including North and South America).

Here are some of the sweet spots, as I see it:

Honestly, I think this is the chart with the most consistently good pricing, whether traveling short haul or long haul. So if you can find award availability within the Americas, you should be pretty happy with the pricing. I redeem Atmos Rewards points constantly for travel on American, as it’s a way to get a good deal on domestic flights, especially in a premium cabin. It might not be the most aspirational thing on earth, but it sure is practical.

Below is the Atmos Rewards award chart for Europe, Middle East, and Africa, which applies if traveling within or between any of those regions, and also applies if traveling between the Americas and any of those regions.

Here are some of the sweet spots, as I see it:

Below is the Atmos Rewards award chart for Asia-Pacific, which applies if traveling within Asia-Pacific, and between Asia-Pacific and any other regions. Note that Asia includes the Indian subcontinent, since some other award charts put that in the same region as the Middle East.

Here are some of the sweet spots, as I see it:

Alaska Atmos Rewards is one of the most useful programs for redeeming points. Given the zone and distance based award chart, you’ll generally find the best value with the program for shorter distance itineraries, where pricing can be very attractive.

I’d say Atmos Rewards is a program that has become practical more than aspirational, and that’s something that I don’t mind, at least at this point in history. It’s not like there are many Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines, or Qantas, ultra long haul first class awards to snag, so we’re not missing out on that much.

Atmos Rewards is my go-to program for most awards covering a distance of up to 1,500 miles, give or take.

What’s your favorite use of Alaska Atmos Rewards points?

#6258. Livery of the Week: Aer Lingus

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Aer Lingus’ standard livery is centered on the shamrock, a symbol that has represented the Irish carrier for more than 80 years. Although the airline has changed its aircraft appearance several times, the three-leaf emblem remains the most recognizable feature of its fleet.

The current design was unveiled on Jan. 17, 2019, during a ceremony at Dublin Airport. It marked Aer Lingus’ first major aircraft rebranding in more than two decades, replacing the predominantly green-and-white scheme introduced in the 1990s.

The redesign retained the shamrock but introduced a revised version with a slight tilt and more pronounced heart-shaped leaves. According to Aer Lingus, the changes were intended to represent movement and the airline’s Irish heritage while giving the logo a more contemporary appearance.

The most noticeable change was the shift away from the green upper fuselage used on the previous livery. The updated scheme features a predominantly white aircraft with a teal vertical stabilizer and engines. Large teal “Aer Lingus” titles appear along the forward fuselage.

The shamrock appears in several locations beyond the tail. Aer Lingus incorporated the emblem into the airline’s wordmark, near the aircraft’s boarding door and on the wingtips. The airline specifically positioned the wingtip design to make it visible to passengers looking out from the cabin.

The aircraft’s lower fuselage also received a teal treatment, making the color visible from below. The combination of white and teal replaced the darker green that had dominated much of the airline’s branding for decades.

Aer Lingus worked with global design consultancy Lippincott on the rebranding. The airline considered more than 50 shamrock designs before selecting the final version. The updated identity also included a new typeface, redesigned digital platforms and changes to other customer-facing materials.

Two aircraft were presented in the new colors during the January 2019 unveiling: an Airbus A330-300 named St Munchin and an A320 named St Schira. The A330 made its first scheduled flight in the updated livery the following day, operating from Dublin to New York.

Aer Lingus has also retained several connections to its earlier aircraft designs. Its 1960s-inspired retro livery, introduced in 2011 to celebrate the airline’s 75th anniversary, featured a darker green-and-white appearance that contrasted with the newer scheme.

More than seven years after its introduction, the 2019 design remains the standard appearance of Aer Lingus aircraft. The colors and placement of the branding have changed, but the shamrock continues to link the carrier’s modern fleet with its earlier history.

#6257. 11 Best Airbnbs Near SoFi Stadium to Make the Most of Your Super Bowl Weekend

With its translucent roof, cutting-edge technology, and $5.5 billion price tag, SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles ranks among the most ambitious sports venues in the world. Since opening in 2020, it has made headlines for its indoor-outdoor design and massive dual-sided video board suspended above the field. It's played host to some spectacular events, from Super Bowl LVI in 2022, when the Los Angeles Rams won on their home turf, to FIFA World Cup matches in 2026. As the official host of the Super Bowl LXI in 2027, SoFi continues to attract fans from around the world. But getting there—and finding the right Airbnb to stay at nearby—can be quite the challenge.

LA traffic is notorious for turning a short trip into an hours-long commute, especially during a big event like the Super Bowl. Add expensive rideshares and post-event congestion, and transportation to SoFi Stadium can quickly become a headache. The solution? The Airbnbs below, which let you stay closer to the action to make the most of your trip.

Every property on this list is less than a 25-minute drive from the stadium (sans traffic), and some are just steps away, so you can skip the transportation stress and spend more time enjoying the big game. Read on for the best Airbnbs near SoFi Stadium, whether you’re headed there for the Super Bowl, the next buzzy concert, or to take a behind-the-scenes stadium tour.

#6256. Air Canada Cancels All Flights To This Long-Haul Destination: See Map Now

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Air Canada will not resume its service from Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ) to Mumbai Airport (BOM) next year, as the airline restructures its Indian operations. The Star Alliance carrier has historically maintained the service to Mumbai with a stop en route at London Heathrow Airport (LHR).

Data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company, shows that the service to Mumbai has been operated with a mix of both the airline's Boeing 787-8 and 787-9 aircraft. It was last served in March 2026.

The service cancellation comes as Air Canada opts out, while Air India will step in. The Indian flag carrier will serve the route instead, with Air Canada deploying its aircraft elsewhere. Air Canada's service to Mumbai, as previously mentioned, operated as a one-stop service via London, providing an extension to the airline's existing robust network of flights through the British capital.

Flights from Toronto operated to London, and then, as a fifth-freedom service, onward to Mumbai. They departed from Toronto in the evening for an overnight service to London, before departing from the UK at midday for an early morning arrival into Mumbai the following morning.

Return flights departed from Mumbai at the eye-watering time of 4:00 AM (standard for India to Europe departures), with a mid-morning arrival into London. Onward flights to Toronto departed after lunch, for a later afternoon arrival back in Toronto. The full schedule for the service is detailed in the table above.

As Air Canada terminates its Mumbai service, the route will be picked up by Air India, which will operate the service with a stopover in Rome Fiumicino Airport (FCO) on the India to Canada leg. Return flights are expected to operate nonstop.

This will see Air Canada's Indian destinations drop to just one, Delhi Indira Gandhi International Airport (DEL). The Star Alliance carrier operates to Delhi with nonstop flights from Toronto year-round, while seasonal flights are added from Montréal-Trudeau International Airport (YUL).

As these schedule changes come into effect, Air Canada is also planning its service resumption to Tel Aviv (TLV) and Dubai International Airport (DXB) this coming March, subject to the ongoing geopolitical tension in the Middle East. A snapshot of the airline's Middle East plans for later this year, and the beginning of 2027, can be seen in the table above.

The route was initially scheduled to operate nonstop flights both ways but it will now include one stop on the westbound journey.

Air Canada maintains flights to India due to strong family, cultural, and trade ties between the two countries. There is a large Indian diaspora in Canada, and there are an estimated 800,000 people with Indian heritage who reside in the Greater Toronto area, according to the website Indians In Canada. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is also set to visit Toronto in December.

Strong trade ties fuel a large part of the airline's demand to serve India, and with ongoing restrictions on Russian airspace access, this has forced the airline to reroute service, such as through London Heathrow for its Mumbai link. Air Canada has had a long history of serving India, having served the country on and off again for many decades. Its latest modern nonstop service began in 2015, when the airline began its service from Toronto to Delhi.

#6255. How a United credit card can save you hundreds of thousands of miles on flights

What if I told you that having a United credit card could mean the difference between paying 295,000 miles or just 72,000 miles for the exact same international business-class flight?

That's not a rare or theoretical example. It's a real award flight that a friend of mine was trying to book recently.

And while United's credit cards are currently offering welcome bonuses of up to 100,000 miles, there's another benefit that can be even more valuable long-term: Access to expanded saver award availability and dramatically lower award prices for eligible cardholders.

In fact, on some flights, the savings can quite literally be hundreds of thousands of miles per ticket.

Here's how it works — and why having a United credit card can make such a huge difference when it's time to redeem your miles.

Apply here for a limited-time offer on the United Club℠ Card — Earn up to 100,000 bonus miles: Earn 90,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn an additional 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening (see rates and fees)

A friend of mine was recently searching for business-class award flights from Geneva Airport (GVA) to Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) for a trip next month. He knew United cardholders could access lower award prices, but he didn't have a United card, so he asked me to compare what we were seeing before deciding whether to apply.

As a non-cardholder, he was seeing business-class prices of 295,000 United miles per person, plus taxes and fees for the one-way trip from Geneva to Newark. That's a lot of miles when multiplied out for a family.

As a cardholder, I checked the same flights and saw a much lower price.

For the same business-class flights, my price was just 68,000 miles per person, plus taxes and fees.

That's 77% fewer miles for the same lie-flat seat on the same plane.

Now, I have United elite status in addition to a United credit card, which brings my award price down a little further. But even without elite status, someone with an eligible United credit card could book that flight for just 72,000 miles. That's a savings of 223,000 miles on a single one-way ticket.

Here's why the difference is so dramatic: The savings aren't simply the result of a 10% cardholder discount. Eligible United cardholders can also access expanded saver award availability, which can unlock significantly lower award prices on certain flights.

And this isn't just one route or one date.

I also searched for business-class award flights from my home airport of George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston to Sydney Airport (SYD) and quickly found a flight priced at 400,000 miles for someone without a United card.

The cardmember-only price? Just 85,000 miles, plus taxes and fees. That's a savings of 315,000 miles — or nearly 79% — on a single award ticket. Multiply it out by a family, and it gets even more incredible in a hurry.

Related: What it's like in United's new elevated business class

While lots of United award flights have really big savings like the examples above, not every flight will offer discounts that dramatic.

You'll always save at least 10% off qualifying United-operated award flights just by having a United card. That number jumps to at least 15% if you also have United elite status.

So, to give another real-world example, my family flies several times a year between George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston and Orlando International Airport (MCO).

On this example date, one-way flights were priced at either 15,000 or 21,000 United miles, depending on which flight I selected.

However, because I have the United card, those flights were priced at 12,700 miles instead of 15,000 miles, or 17,800 miles instead of 21,000 miles.

Those savings aren't as headline-grabbing as the first example, but for a family of four booking round-trip flights at those rates, the savings could add up to roughly 18,000 to 26,000 miles, depending on the flights selected.

Related: United's big mileage changes are now in effect

One thing I really love about this is that you don't need a premium United card with a high annual fee to unlock these award savings.

You can get the $0 annual fee United Gateway℠ Card (see rates and fees) and get savings, too.

If you have the United MileagePlus® Debit Rewards card or the $0 annual fee United credit card, you do have to spend $10,000 in eligible purchases on those cards in a calendar year to unlock the award discount.

For travelers who can meet that threshold through purchases they'd make anyway, the Gateway could provide a way to access lower award prices without paying an annual fee.

Another option is the United℠ Explorer Card (see rates and fees), which actually has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150 annually. Eligible Explorer cardholders can access the award discounts without meeting the Gateway's $10,000 spending requirement.

The information for the United MileagePlus Debit Rewards has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Related: 8 reasons to upgrade from the United Explorer Card to the United Quest Card

Beyond the ongoing award-booking savings, United's credit cards currently offer increased welcome bonuses, including some of the highest offers we've seen on these cards.

The information for the United Club Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

United credit cards can offer more than bonus miles and travel perks. For eligible cardholders, access to expanded saver award availability and discounts on qualifying award flights can translate into substantial savings when redeeming MileagePlus miles.

Being able to save airline miles with a co-branded airline credit card isn't unique to United, as several airlines offer this valuable perk to their cardholders. However, the mileage savings you get with most cards and airlines are often capped at around 15%.

As the Geneva–Newark and Houston–Sydney examples show, the difference can sometimes amount to hundreds of thousands of miles on a single ticket. However, savings vary by flight, and not every cardholder automatically qualifies for these benefits.

Being able to take a lie-flat seat across the globe and make it cost in the neighborhood of 70,000-85,000 miles instead of 300,000-400,000 miles, just by having a credit card is exactly the kind of tip that brings award travel out of just the hands of a small few and puts it into the hands of many of us.

For travelers who regularly redeem United miles, these award-booking advantages could be among the most valuable reasons to carry an eligible United card.

#6254. Singapore Airlines’ New First & Business Class Cabins Will Be Unveiled This Week

In November 2024, Singapore Airlines announced a huge investment into its premium passenger experience, which will see the introduction of all-new cabin products, plus the expansion of first class. These cabins will be retrofitted on dozens of Airbus A350s, and will also be available on newly delivered Boeing 777-9s in the future.

The product was initially supposed to roll out as of the spring of 2026, though as is all too common nowadays, the project was delayed due to supply chain constraints, etc. The good news is that the wait is almost over — the new product will be unveiled on Friday, November 6, 2026, with an entry into service planned for the first quarter of 2027. Let’s recap all the details we know as of now.

Singapore Airlines will be investing 1.1 billion SGD (~835 million USD) to update the interiors of its entire long haul Airbus A350-900 fleet. This consists of a total of 41 jets, and includes the carrier’s seven A350-900ULRs, with the “ULR” standing for “ultra long range,” as these planes operate the world’s longest flights.

The only A350-900s that won’t be reconfigured are the ones that are specifically designed for regional flights, featuring the same cabin products you’ll find onboard Boeing 787-10s.

With this project, we can expect changes across cabins. We’ll see first class added to the carrier’s ultra long range A350s, an all-new business class product, refreshes to premium economy and economy, plus an updated inflight entertainment system and the installation of Starlink Wi-Fi.

How will the layouts of these jets change, once reconfigured? Singapore Airlines’ standard long haul A350-900s:

Singapore Airlines’ ultra long range A350-900s:

Singapore Airlines will be introducing new first and business class products. This isn’t just some new interim product, but rather this is intended to be the carrier’s new premium product in the long run. The same seats that are being installed on the Airbus A350-900s will also be installed on the carrier’s Boeing 777-9s, so these are very much “flagship” cabins.

Singapore Airlines initially intended to debut new premium cabins on its 777-9s, which were first supposed to be delivered in 2020. However, those have now been pushed back to late 2027 at the earliest. So clearly Singapore Airlines decided that it’s finally time to introduce new cabins, even if the 777-9 keeps getting delayed.

Singapore Airlines will introduce a new first class product on its subfleet of A350-900ULRs, which operate the world’s longest flights. This same product will be available on 777-9s in the future, but won’t be available on standard A350-900s. Furthermore, there are no plans to retrofit existing 777s with this product. A350s will have four of these seats, while 777s will have six of these seats.

Below is the first teaser picture of Singapore Airlines’ new first class.

Currently Singapore Airlines only has first class on its A380s and 777-300ERs, so it’s cool to see this product expand.

Official details about the new first class are limited, other than that it’s “designed with increasingly discerning travellers in mind,” and that the first class seats “promise to deliver an unparalleled in-flight experience.”

We have reason to believe that the new cabin will be in a 1-2-1 layout. Why? Well, Singapore Airlines filed a patent some time back, clearly for the carrier’s new first class product. The patent is for the 777-9, where the airline will have a first class cabin with six seats.

The plan seems to be to have individual suites along the windows, plus a double suite in the center. However, the center suite can be used by either one or two people, so if people are traveling separately, there’s a partition that can go up.

As you can see, there’s a bit of staggering with the cabin, to maximize the width of the suite, as the aisle curves a bit.

This looks like a very nice product, though to be perfectly honest, it doesn’t look like anything revolutionary. Nowadays some of the top first class products are in a 1-1-1 configuration, like what you’ll find on Japan Airlines and Emirates. Admittedly the flexibility of the double suite in the middle is great for those traveling with someone, since that’s not something that was really considered with the new Japan Airlines and Emirates products.

For that matter, we have reason to believe that Cathay Pacific may offer the world’s best first class on its 777-9s, as it could very well be in a 1-1 configuration.

This is super exciting. Singapore Airlines is one of the best airlines in the world, with incredible service, food, drinks, and more. However, at this point the carrier’s business class hard product isn’t really cutting edge anymore.

With details being so limited, all we can do is speculate as of now. So I have a few thoughts:

In late 2024, when this project was first announced, Singapore Airlines shared the following timeline for debuting the new first and business class seats:

Unfortunately that timeline didn’t stick. Several months ago we learned how the first retrofitted aircraft wouldn’t enter service until the first quarter of 2027, best case scenario, with the expectation being that some long range A350s would be reconfigured before the first ultra long range A350 gets a makeover.

The revised timeline reflects industry-wide supply chain constraints, as well as delays in the certification of one of the new seats (a common industry problem). The aircraft will be retrofitted by SIA Engineering Company in Singapore.

So, is that still the timeline we’re looking at? It would appear so. Singapore Airlines has confirmed on social media that it will unveiling its all new products on Friday, November 6, 2026.

From the first sketch to the final detail, discover how the new Singapore Airlines travel experience comes together across every cabin class and every part of the journey.Unveiling on 6 November 2026. pic.twitter.com/dTML7QmOXe

This announcement is actually being marketed as being about more than just seats, as it’s described as “the new Singapore Airlines travel experience,” and we’ll learn how it “comes together across every class and every part of the journey.” We’ve already seen the airline tease details of a new dining concept as well as new amenities across cabins, so presumably this will all come together to form the new experience.

Which routes are likely to get the new cabins first? While we’ll see how this plays out, based on historical precedent, it’s likely that Sydney (SYD) and London (LHR) will be the first two destinations, since those are the first destinations where the airline has sent all of its new long haul products.

Singapore Airlines plans to introduce all-new cabins on its Airbus A350-900s, which will also eventually be installed on Boeing 777-9s. Most exciting is an improved new business class product, which is long overdue. Singapore Airlines will also be adding first class to its subfleet of A350-900ULRs, with a boutique cabin having just four seats.

While this product was supposed to enter service as of the second quarter of 2026, the timeline has been pushed back to the first quarter of 2027, due to supply chain constraints and certification issues… a familiar story! The expectation is that the new cabins will be unveiled this week, on November 6, 2026. I’m mighty curious to learn the details, so I’m happy that the wait is finally (almost) over.

What do you make of Singapore Airlines’ plans to introduce new long haul cabins?

#6253. Buy Finnair Plus Avios For 50% Off (1.06 Cents Each): Best-Ever Price Worth It?

The Finnair Plus program has just launched its newest promotion on purchased Avios, offering up to a 50% discount, which is an opportunity to acquire Avios for as little as 1.06 cents each. This is the best offer from the program of the year, and you can use this to acquire any “flavor” of Avios at an advantageous rate.

Strategically buying points for premium travel can be a great value, especially with a specific use in mind, so this is an offer I’d seriously consider.

Between 12:01AM EET on November 2 and 11:59PM EET on November 16, 2026, Finnair Plus is offering a limited time promotion on purchased Avios. If you purchase Finnair Plus Avios, you can receive the following deal:

Beyond the discount, you can also receive tier points toward status equivalent to 10% of the Avios purchased. This is of course useful if you’re going for elite status with Finnair, but otherwise, is of limited value.

Now, here’s where it gets interesting — Finnair lets you select the currency in which you want to buy Avios (you can find the option to switch currencies at the top of the screen), and the price differs:

So based on current exchange rates, you’re best off paying in JPY, followed by USD, followed by EUR. If you maxed out the promotion with a 50% bonus and paid in JPY, the best deal you could get would be to pay $2,110 for 200,000 Avios, which comes out to 1.06 cents per Avios (in USD), inclusive of all taxes and fees.

Note that this offer is only available to Finnair Plus members who joined the program before October 30, 2026, and have a minimum balance of 50 Avios in their account (though those Avios can be transferred from another “flavor” of the currency).

When Finnair Plus offers a promotion on purchased Avios, it’s common to see either a 50% bonus or a 40-50% discount. The 50% discount gives you the absolute best price, so this is definitely the time to buy Avios, if interested.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Finnair Plus Avios purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

Since the purchase of Finnair Avios can potentially be billed in a foreign currency, there is one other great option. The Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more) offers 3x points on foreign purchases, so that’s a fantastic card for this kind of purchase.

What should you expect from Finnair Plus award pricing, and the best ways to redeem to Finnair Plus Avios?

Below you can find the one-way Finnair Plus award redemptions rates for travel on Finnair.

Awards also have surcharges, though they’re at least mild. If you have a connecting itinerary, you’ll only be charged the surcharge correlated to the most expensive segment flown.

When your award booking includes a connecting flight, Avios are charged separately for each flight, except for flights within Finland and Northern Europe. For example, a Frankfurt to Helsinki to New York business class award would cost you 82,500 Avios (20,000 Avios plus 62,500 Avios). One awesome thing is that Finnair Plus has an award seat guarantee, meaning there’s pretty consistently award availability when booking far in advance.

Finnair Plus also allows redemptions on partner airlines, though the pricing isn’t particularly attractive, for the most part. The more important thing to keep in mind is that it’s possible to transfer Avios between the various “flavors” of the currency.

Therefore this promotion is also an opportunity to earn Avios that you can transfer 1:1 to programs like Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club, Iberia Club, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, etc. That opens up more redemption opportunities.

Finnair Plus has launched a promotion on purchased Avios. This is the best price of the year from Finnair Plus on purchasing Avios (and the best price for purchasing any current of Avios this year, for that matter).

There’s absolutely value to be had here, especially since this is an opportunity to earn any “flavor” of Avios, thanks to the 1:1 transfer options.

#6252. In Luxor, Ancient Egypt feels newly alive

The water is cold and clear. Half-hidden amid the palm-tufted grounds of the Mortuary Temple of Seti I, this sacred sunken lake on Luxor's west bank was once the domain of ancient Egyptian priests. More than 3,000 years later, women from nearby villages still come, hoping its waters will serve as a fertility aid or a balm for their sick children, says my guide Ahmed Hassan, who was born and raised on this side of the Nile. It's one of the area's many miracles, he adds: No one knows where the water comes from, but it hasn't run dry since those priests of antiquity first bathed here. Hedging my bets, I submerge my hands.

It can be difficult to know what to believe in this transcendent stretch of Upper Egypt, 410 miles south of Cairo, where the Nile exudes a life force of its own; the mountains cradle secret treasures; and the light, particularly at golden hour, plays tricks, almost convincing you that you have traveled back in time. The line between the real and the mystical feels flimsy, whether you are considering the scale of the approximately 1,000-ton, 65-foot-tall colossus of Ramses II, inexplicably carved from a single piece of granite and lying prostrate at the king's statuesque funerary temple, the Ramesseum; or observing the unnerving precision of the hieroglyphs in the tomb of Ramses V and VI, in the Valley of the Kings, that has proved immune to the ravages of time.

Formerly ancient Thebes, Luxor—whose name comes from the Arabic Al-Uqsur (The Palaces)—served as Egypt's capital during the New Kingdom, from circa 1550 BCE to 1070 BCE. On the west bank of the Nile, sugarcane and banana plantations lead to a limestone canyon topped by Al-Qurn, or The Horn, a natural peak shaped like a pyramid. The rulers of the New Kingdom decided that this would be the ideal spot to protect their richly decorated tombs from grave robbers—a failed exercise, since every tomb in the Valley of the Kings was looted in antiquity, bar that of now legendary boy king Tutankhamen.

“There are many sites that have an impressive amount of ‘stuff,’ but what you have in Luxor is truly monumental,” Mennat-Allah El Dorry, from the American University in Cairo's department of sociology, Egyptology, and anthropology, tells me. “You have Karnak and Luxor temples on the east bank, and the mortuary temples on the west, as well as Valley of the Kings. It is such a dense area.”

I take her recommendations, balancing the quiet of the lesser-visited, only partially restored Mortuary Temple of Seti I and the Ramesseum with the many-splendored tombs at the Valley of the Kings, where voyeuristic crowds swell to see the diminutive mummy of Tutankhamen languishing 26 feet below ground. By contrast, the tomb of Ramses V and VI close by is deserted. A toothless, djellaba-wearing guard smiles conspiratorially before letting me behind the barrier. He takes my phone and assumes the practiced ease of a fashion photographer directing his next magazine cover: “Come closer; go there; look over your shoulder.”

Much of Luxor feels like it hasn't changed in centuries. At sunset the sails of felucca boats trace a timeless scene on the Nile's surface. Amid the clip-clop of horse-drawn carriages, the call to prayer tumbles from minarets and the sky settles into strips of apricot and lavender.

Matching the restraint of Arax is the stripped-back Marsam Hotel and discreet yet stately Habu Hotel, the latter just feet away from the Medinet Habu Temple. But Hotel Al Moudira sits at the opposite end of the spectrum. Founded by Italian Lebanese artist Zeina Aboukheir in 2001, and originally designed by famed Egyptian architect Olivier Sednaoui, the hotel revels in its maximalism: a whimsical interplay of domes and arches embellished with terra-cotta plaster, frescoes, and antiques. In 2022, Aboukheir sold the hotel to its new owner, Florian Amereller, but she still guides its creative direction, most recently in the design of six new villas. I stay in one of the five rooms in the salmon pink Villa Casbah, where hand-painted silhouettes of gazelles trip skittishly across the walls.

Chef Gioconda Scott at The Moudira Farm Kitchen

Under its new ownership the now five-star Al Moudira has expanded to include a huge swath of surrounding farmland. It's here, in an open kitchen engulfed in greenery, that I find British Spanish chef Gioconda Scott in the midst of a busy lunch service. In 2025 she launched The Moudira Farm Kitchen, where she transforms the fresh produce grown on-site into an unfussy, seasonal menu inspired by the Mediterranean. “This is simple cooking,” says Scott, who populates her kitchen with young chefs from the local tourism college. “Every element has to be good. If you don't have a good olive oil or a good tomato, there's no hiding.”

The restaurant itself is filled with products made by artisans on the farm. Crockery, rendered in a range of earthy tones, was crafted by potters whom guests can join for classes. I can hear the distant clack of the loom that wove the jaunty turquoise tablecloth, while, in other corners, artisans carve alabaster, blow glass, and upholster furniture.

The same crafts inhabit the decks of Al Moudira's new, 180-foot Nile Canopus, a nostalgia-infused nod to historic travel along this evocative waterway. Open-air decks with safari-tent-style coverings, a cozy library, and rooms fitted with brass beds and bespoke teak and rattan furniture are designed to evoke the age of Amelia Edwards, author of the seminal 1877 travelogue A Thousand Miles Up the Nile.

There has been a proliferation of new dahabeahs on the Nile, which offer more intimate, personalized experiences than do the hulking, 50-cabin motorboats that also ply these waters. Laden with modern conveniences, today's dahabeahs are admittedly no longer sprightly enough to be harried along by wind and sail; instead they are pushed and pulled by dinky-looking tugboats. On the inside they are increasingly elaborate. Karine Hassoun called on Egyptian painters, professors, and artisans for her eight-cabin dahabeah, Nile Divine, a celebration of contemporary Egyptian craft. In the nine-cabin Oro, a dark wood exterior pays tribute to the dahabeahs of old but with a dramatic brass wall in the reception area, a plunge pool extending out over the deck, a full-fledged bar up top, and suites with private terraces and hot tubs. Oberoi Hotels and Resorts will join the fray later this year with two seven-suite dahabeahs featuring interiors by Karim Mekhtigian, founder of Alchemy Design Studio, while Waldorf Astoria Hotels and Resorts' new, 29-suite Nile cruiser will bring to the water all the elements of its land-based hotels, including its Peacock Alley brasserie.

Change is underway on land too. I see the cranes hovering over the east bank, pinpointing where a Four Seasons Hotel, due to open in 2027, is rapidly taking shape. The much-loved Winter Palace—archaeologist Howard Carter's base during his 1922 Tutankhamen tomb discovery and where Agatha Christie was inspired to write parts of Death on the Nile—recently closed for a renovation and will reopen as a Mandarin Oriental in July 2027, exactly 120 years after its official inauguration, hopefully with original features and charm fully intact.

That's only weeks before next year's solar eclipse: On August 2, Luxor will witness the moon masking the sun for its maximum duration, a total of 6 minutes and 22 seconds. Just enough time for that line between the real and the mystical to grow even flimsier.

A few feet from Habu Temple, recommended for its deeply etched hieroglyphs and particularly well-preserved colors, is a property with its own historic pedigree: the unassuming, 17-room Habu Hotel was one of the first hotels to open on Luxor’s West Bank in the 1920s. It has been given a smart revamp, its public areas now filled with antiques, including stately granite busts and wooden statues from the 1800s. Sundowners on the hotel’s charming rooftop terrace bring you close enough to the temple’s chiseled interior that you can admire its exterior engravings from the comfort of your lounge chair.

A day spent tirelessly exploring Luxor’s sites is best ended in the spa at Hilton Luxor Resort and Spa, where treatment rooms look directly over the Nile and the infinity pool is one of the best spots in the city to catch Luxor’s famous sunsets. This is an ultra-convenient base if you want easy access to the historic sites on Luxor’s East Bank—Karnak Temple, in particular, is within walking distance. A private breakfast on a felucca offers a fresh perspective of the Nile, especially if you time it to coincide with hot-air balloons rising majestically over the Valley of the Kings.

For a stripped-back stay that’ll make you feel like an Egyptologist of old, head to Marsam Hotel, which started life as the excavation house for the University of Chicago, before being converted into a hotel in 1939. There’s (very intentionally) no swimming pool or TVs; the 29 pared-back rooms and five suites are designed for guests who are serious about exploring the many sites that surround this historic hotel. Whether or not you spend the night, make time for lunch at Marsam’s farm-to-table restaurant, where the menu changes daily and you’ll be serenaded by the resident donkeys, camels and horses.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

As High As 300,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

World of Hyatt is my favorite hotel loyalty program, and I've loved redeeming my World of Hyatt points over the years on everything from cheap and cheerful Category 1 airport hotels to luxurious bespoke properties on idyllic Greek islands.

I knew that the program had expanded the ways to redeem points beyond hotel stays to experiences via its Find experiences platform. But I've never given it much thought, assuming the value (or the experiences themselves) wouldn't be that great.

So, when Hyatt recently invited me to an event that it sponsors, the Laver Cup tournament at London's The O2 arena, I jumped at the chance to go as a tennis enthusiast. I'd been to The O2 countless times for concerts and thought I knew the venue pretty well. But Hyatt was auctioning off a luxury experience in the ultra-VIP Legends Club, a space I didn't even know existed that turned out to be on a completely different level of luxury, in part due to its courtside seats for watching the action.

Seeing how few Hyatt points the winning bids went for, especially given this impressive level of premium hospitality and access, I came to the realization that this might just be the most valuable way to redeem World of Hyatt points.

Related: This is how you do a luxury all-inclusive: Zoetry Mallorca, bookable with Hyatt points

Find is World of Hyatt's experiences platform, where members can book everything from fitness workshops and chef's table dinners to Broadway tickets, paying with either cash or World of Hyatt points. You don't need to stay at a Hyatt hotel to take part, though some experiences include accommodations.

Most Find experiences are advertised with a fixed price — and that's where you might struggle to get outsize value. When TPG travel writer Rachel Craft tested a fixed-price Find dining package in Denver, it delivered less value than TPG's valuation of World of Hyatt points at the time, and she concluded that members would probably get more value redeeming their points for hotel stays.

Auctions work differently. A small number of limited-time experiences, often tied to Hyatt's sports sponsorships, go to the highest bidder, with members bidding in points rather than paying a set price.

Before you bid, it's worth knowing the rules:

Auctions are usually only a small portion of the Find options available at any one time, so here's how you can find them:

The Laver Cup packages were a savvy example of just how much value a Find auction can deliver.

Each of the three packages Hyatt auctioned included:

Starting with priority, fast-track entry to the venue, the Legends Club was a significant step up in luxury from anything else I've seen at The O2. It even surpassed my impression of the Virgin Red Room, a corporate suite at The O2 that can be booked with Virgin Red points.

The two-level hospitality suite (usually hidden behind the stage at traditional concerts) was huge and opened onto the arena, with a perfect view down the baseline.

Before the play started, there was even a Q&A with tennis legend Andy Murray, which isn't something you get with a regular ticket.

Premium food and drinks were included from 90 minutes before the session until the final ball, and the Champagne kept flowing the entire time.

When it was time for the tennis, I headed down to my own courtside seat in the second row. I was so close to the current No. 3 player in the world, Carlos Alcaraz, that I could almost have reached out and touched him.

I didn't stay at the Park Hyatt this time, but having toured the hotel, I can see why it would make the package even more appealing, with spacious rooms, marble bathrooms, views over the Thames and a 65-foot indoor pool.

Published all-in prices for a single Legends Club ticket ranged from $1,329 to $2,652 for Friday night and from $1,461 to $2,916 for either Saturday session, depending on the seat.

Standard rooms started at $633 per night when TPG reviewed the Park Hyatt, and the hotel's 60-minute "Back to Brilliance" massage cost $279 per person. Add the two-night stay and hotel credit, and I estimate each package was worth between $5,000 and $8,000 before assigning any value to the transfers.

A search engine index of Hyatt’s official Find homepage shows Hyatt auctioned off three Laver Cup packages with Legends Club single-session tickets and Park Hyatt accommodations (plus the above-mentioned inclusions) with winning bids of 81,583, 120,560 and 160,000 points, although the closed listings are no longer visible on the live page.

TPG's October 2026 valuations assign a value of 1.65 cents to every World of Hyatt point. By that valuation, the winning bids were worth about $1,346, $1,989 and $2,640, respectively. Even using the low end of my estimated package value, those redemptions delivered about 6.1, 4.1 and 3.1 cents per point, respectively, or roughly 1.9 to 3.7 times TPG's valuation, a spectacular result.

Put another way, the Category 8 Park Hyatt London River Thames costs 35,000 to 75,000 World of Hyatt points per night for a standard room, so two nights can cost 70,000 to 150,000 points. The two lower bids were below the 150,000-point threshold required for two standard award nights on top-priced dates, while the highest bid was only 10,000 points higher.

Of course, not every auction will deliver this much value. Popular experiences, such as Formula One races, can attract plenty of competition, and you have no control over where the bidding ends. However, you can decide up front what an experience is worth to you and stop bidding if the price goes past that amount.

World of Hyatt members earn points on eligible Hyatt stays and Find bookings paid for with cash, but a credit card can be the quickest way to build your balance for an auction.

You can choose between two cobranded cards:

Or, you can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to World of Hyatt from the following cards:

Chase Ultimate Rewards points held in Chase Sapphire Reserve and Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business accounts transfer to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio.

Points held in Chase Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred accounts transfer at a 4:3 ratio, meaning 1,000 Ultimate Rewards points become 750 World of Hyatt points.

Bilt Points currently transfer to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio through Dec. 31, 2026. The ratio will drop to 4:3 on Jan. 1, 2027.

Related: How many Hyatt points do you need to transfer before the Sapphire Reserve beats the Sapphire Preferred?

Fixed-price Find experiences still would not usually tempt me away from a hotel redemption, but auctions are a different story.

This was easily the most luxurious sporting experience I have ever attended, from the VIP entry to the spectacular views and the hospitality of the Legends Club, which offered everything I could imagine, including proximity to some of the world's best tennis players.

Factor in the accommodations, transfers, food-and-beverage credits and other perks, and it's clear this is an exceptional way to redeem World of Hyatt points. You'll potentially considerably exceed our valuation of these excellent hotel points by redeeming them this way.

The 2027 Laver Cup will be played at the Intuit Dome near Los Angeles from Sept. 24 to 26, 2027. As the official hotel partner, look out for Hyatt Find experiences and auctions for next year's tournament.

#6250. Save On Air France-KLM Flights With Amex Offers (Targeted)

The Amex Offers program has just rolled out a great new targeted offer for the purchase of Air France-KLM flights, which could be worth considering for anyone planning travel. We’ve seen this offer in the past, and I’m happy to see it return, as I always get significant value from it. However, this offer isn’t quite as lucrative as past ones.

With a new targeted Amex Offers deal, you can earn a $250 statement credit when you spend $2,500 or more with Air France-KLM by December 15, 2026. (Enrollment required)

It’s possible that there’s also a version of the offer for 25,000 bonus points rather than a $250 statement credit, and if so, I’d consider that to be more valuable. That’s because based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, so I’d value the 25,000 points at $425.

For what it’s worth, in the past when I’ve purchased sustainable aviation fuel with Air France in order to earn XP (the metric by which you qualify for status), that triggered an Amex Offers deal. So at least anecdotally, that seems to work. Furthermore, taxes and carrier imposed surcharges on award tickets also seem to qualify.

I’m always happy to see this offer available, though let me note that this isn’t as lucrative as in the past. In past situations we’ve seen a $200 statement credit or 20,000 bonus points after spending $1,000+, so as a percentage return, this definitely isn’t as good.

This Amex Offers deal is targeted, though it’s possible you’ll see it on multiple of your cards. If so, I’d highly recommend registering your American Express Platinum Card® for this offer. That’s because the Amex Platinum offers 5x points on airfare purchased directly with airlines on up to $500,000 per calendar year and then 1x.

Based on my valuation of 1.7 cents per Membership Rewards point, the 5x points offers an incremental 8.5% return on spending. On top of that, the Amex Platinum offers valuable travel protection, should you experience irregular operations.

In other words, if you took advantage of this offer with the Amex Platinum for a $2,500 ticket, you’d receive a $250 statement credit plus 12,500 points. By my valuation, that’s a return of $462.50 on $2,500 of spending, which comes out to an 18.5% return.

There’s a new targeted Amex Offers deal for a $250 statement credit when you spend $2,500+ on an Air France-KLM ticket. If you’re planning travel on Air France or KLM, this has the potential to be a solid deal. Ideally you’ll see this offer on the Amex Platinum, so that you can really maximize your points.

Were you targeted for this Amex Offers deal, and if so, do you plan on taking advantage of it?
