#6249. 15 of the Coolest Marathon Courses Around the Globe, From the Arctic Circle to the Great Wall of China

The TCS New York City Marathon is consistently one of the best days of the year in the city—it's emotional, it's inspiring, and it shows off the best of humanity. If you're a runner or a spectator who got the itch for more this past weekend, you're in luck: There are tons of incredible courses around the world, and while they may not traverse NYC's five boroughs, they will take you to world wonders, through safari lands, and across borders.

As someone who regularly travels for halfs, I spend a lot of my time researching and bookmarking races. For me, running through a new place one of the best ways to get to know a destination—you get the lay of the land, see what the community is like, and notice things you might not see from a car or public transportation. And as destination races grow in popularity, the courses offered are getting even more spectacular. The races on this list—halfs, fulls, 10Ks, and more—prove it. Below, I’ve rounded up 15 of the most spectacular races happening in the next year or so, all of which are well worth traveling for.

Date: March 13, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half marathon, 10K, 3.5K

What to know: If you haven't run a Rock ‘n’ Roll marathon yet, you're missing out on a good time. As the name suggests, these music-centric runs make for an extremely lively course—bands and DJs fill the roads and the after party. Locations change each year, and in 2027, the series is going to Taitung on Taiwan's east coast; runners will move between the mountains and the Pacific Ocean on a flat, smooth route. After the race, be sure to check out the area's night markets, hot springs, and endless good eats.

Where to stay: Luxury hotels near the starting line include the Sheraton Taitung Hotel, which has an outdoor swimming pool, and Formosan Naruwan Hotel, with a spa and saltwater pool.

Date: April 25, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, 21-miler, 11-miler, 12K, 5K

What to know: With a cliffside, oceanview course running from Big Sur to Carmel along California’s iconic Highway 1, it doesn’t get much more scenic than this. It’s a Boston qualifier race and has a six-hour time limit, along with several course length options, making it a good one to run with a group, even if your ideal mileage differs.

Where to stay: Room blocks are available at a few different properties in Monterey, closer to the finish line. Of course, there is no shortage of luxury hotels in the area—Alila Ventana Big Sur, Post Ranch Inn, and Carmel Beach Hotel are a few Traveler favorites.

Date: April 4, 2027Registration: The 2027 lottery entry has taken place; check back in May for the 2028 race; charity bibs are still availableDistances included: Half-marathon

What to know: As the name suggests, the course runs past several London landmarks, including Big Ben, the Tower of London, the London Eye, and Somerset House. It’s a lively course—musical performances, DJs, dancers, and themed cheer stations can be expected—and even better, it's a flat one, with 238 feet of total elevation gain.

Where to stay: In 2026, Blue Orchid Hospitality and the Clermont Hotel Group offered discounts for race weekend stays at properties like The Wellington Hotel, The Tower Hotel, and Thistle Trafalgar. We’ll update that list once 2027 partners are announced. For luxury stays near the starting line, consider Raffles London at the OWO or the Corinthia London.

Date: April 04, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half marathon, 10K

What to know: Okay, I'll get the cons over with first (for most, I'd presume): This is a cold and snowy course. Once you've got that fact out of the way, you can weigh the very unique pros. This Finnish Lapland course kicks off in Santa Claus Village square (!) in Rovaniemi, starting exactly on the line of the Arctic Circle. It's put together as part of a five-day running program with log cabin lodging, each with a private sauna, as well as activities like husky sledding, Northern Lights excursions, and an Ice Pool Experience. It all wraps up at a trophy dinner with—wait for it—Santa Claus himself. This is peak whimsy, friends.

Where to stay: Lodging is included in the tour package.

Date: May 15, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half-marathon, 8.5K

What to know: This race lets you run along one of the seven wonders of the world. It’s a strenuous, hilly course, but if the views alone don’t keep you going, the residents in local villages cheering you on along the route just might.

Of note, to register, you must sign up for a tour package; the starting price is $790 and includes race entry plus two nights of accommodations. It’s sponsored by Albatross Adventure Marathons, which also puts on The Big Five Marathon (more details below) and the Iceland Volcano Marathon, among other adventurous runs.

Where to stay: Hotels must be booked along with the packages. For a relaxing post-race stay, check into the Mandarin Oriental Qianmen, Beijing, with its award-winning spa (after a massage, consider the tea meditation too) and standout dining options, from Italian to dim sum.

Date: May 16, 2027Registration: Open now and quite affordable—the most expensive distance is €39 ($44)Distances included: Half-marathon, 10K, 5K (paved course); 17K, 8K (trail)

What to know: Set in Tossa de Mar, a beautiful, historic seaside town on Spain’s Costa Brava, these runs are all about the coastal views. Of course, that does mean a challenging, hilly course for all but the 5K, which boasts a flat route in the town’s center. Of note, the maximum time is on the shorter end: 2 hours 35 minutes for the half, 1 hour 15 for the 10K, and 45 minutes for the 5K.

Where to stay: Zel Costa Brava, about a 10-minute drive from the starting line, was mentioned in our list of the Best Places to Go in Spain and Portugal in 2026. It has a funicular to take guests down to the beach, a huge pool with plenty of lounge chairs to kick back on, and a spa with a thermal circuit, ideal for soothing sore legs.

Date: June 11-12, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half marathon, 5K

What to know: Running around America's first national park, near sites like the Grand Prismatic Spring, is bound to be a highlight for any outdoor-loving runner. While not inside the bounds of the park, the views from the Custer Gallatin National Forest and the Hebgen Lake Ranger District are still impressive. The half marathon starts bright and early at 6 a.m. and has a four-hour course limit. There are five aid stations along the way, and 552 feet of elevation (of note, there are some technical, rocky sections to contend with).

Where to stay: The Lazy Duck Inn is the most convenient choice, given it's location near the start and finish line. To pad out the rest of your trip, check out our guide to where to stay in and near Yellowstone.

Date: June 19, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Full marathon, half-marathon

What to know: The name says it all: You might just see the big five while you run! The course takes runners through the South African Savannah on the Entabeni Game Reserve. It is a smaller race, with a maximum of 300 participants, in a moderate climate (expected to be in the 60s to 70s this year) along a sand and gravel trail. Past participants rave about this one, calling it “The ONLY marathon I have wanted to run twice!” and “the best adventure ever.” Like the Great Wall course, registration requires selecting a tour package, starting at $3,560 for the seven-day package, which includes accommodation, meals, game drives, bush walks, and more.

Where to stay: At the end of any package, you’ll be transferred to Johannesburg International Airport. Give yourself a night to decompress at the Park Hyatt Johannesburg, where peacocks roam the grounds, rooms overlook serene gardens, and Sunday brunch comes with a side of live music.

Date: June 19, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half-marathon, 10K, 5K, kids race

What to know: The Tromsø, Norway, race begins at 8:30 p.m.—but thanks to the midnight sun the event is named after, it’s still light out. One of the northernmost races in the world, with a course surrounded by mountains and fjords, it boasted 9,000 runners from an impressive 88 countries last year. Of note, the maximum time limit is 5 hours and 30 minutes for the marathon and 3 hours and 30 minutes for the half.

Where to stay: Right in Tromsø, St. Elisabeth makes for a lovely stay, especially if you take advantage of the spa’s thermal bath, pool, and saunas. A bit further out (45 minutes or so), the Yggdrasiltunet Farm Hotel offers an even more blissful setting for a post-race escape with its wood-fired barrel sauna, guided ice bathing, hot tub overlooking the sea, and yoga classes.

Date: June 20, 2027Registration: Open now (half marathon is already sold out; sign up for 2028 notifications on the website)Distances included: Half marathon, 10K

What to know: The race website dubs this “the most beautiful run on the planet,” and honestly, that might not be so hyperbolic. Running through Canada's first national park sounds like a dream, especially when the course passes by the Vermilion Lakes, Legacy Trail, and Bow Valley Parkway, with wildlife likely to be spotted along the way. It's not a particularly hilly course, with a total elevation gain of 418 feet, but do note the elevation, which maxes out at 4,620 feet.

Where to stay: The official host partner is Banff Lodging Company, which operates 16 hotels across Banff, Canmore, and Lake Louise, including Hotel Canoe & Suites and Otter Hotel. Guests can receive a 15% discount on these rates. Afterward, consider a wellness-centric stay at the stunning Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise.

Date: July 03, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Full marathon, half-marathon, 10.55k

What to know: Designed for adventure-seekers, this Northern Iceland race explores one of Earth's geological hot spots—you’ll run along the rim of two volcanic craters and over black lava rock, with steaming geysers taking your mind off the miles ahead.

Unless you’re an Icelandic resident, you’ll need to book the six-day tour package, which is around $3,100 and includes accommodation, transportation, meals, a celebratory post-race dinner, and some activities, with add-ons like whale-watching and waterfall chasing available too. Of note, race entrance is not included in that fee ($350 for the half and full, and $223 for the quarter marathon).

Where to stay: Our resident Iceland expert and contributing writer Erika Owen highly recommends one of the tour lodging options, Fosshotel Glacier Lagoon, saying that it “embodies the best of Iceland: seclusion, surrounding nature, and beds topped with Icelandic wool blankets.” On your way out of town, consider a stay at The Retreat at Blue Lagoon; beyond the must-dip-in thermal baths, the tasting menu at Michelin-starred Moss is well worth a splurge.

Date: July 18, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half-marathon, 5K, The Pairing (both!)

What to know: A 13.1-mile route through Napa and Sonoma’s wine country, this course is surrounded by farms, vineyards, and ranches—yes, there are gently rolling hills, but it’s not an overly challenging course. The real prize for the 3,000-ish participants is at the finish line: At the post-race wine festival, top local vineyards reward you with wine tastings, and your goodie bag includes a commemorative wine glass.

Where to stay: Several hotels partner with the race to offer discounted stays, including the Westin Verasa Napa Hotel, notable for its Hyperice Recover & Recharge Kit available at the front desk. (Heads up for other future runs: Hyperice and Normatec products can be found at most Westins across the US! I swear by the Normatecs and Hypervolt for post-race recovery.) Just across the street from the starting line sits Carneros Resort and Spa, a seven-time Readers’ Choice Award winner; down the street is Stanly Ranch, Auberge Collection, a resort with a gorgeous outdoor pool that’s exactly where I’d want to park myself post-race.

Date: October 15–17, 2027Registration: Opens January 1, 2027Distances included: Marathon, marathon relay, half-marathon, 5K, one miler, kids races

What to know: This is one course that’s absolutely on my running bucket list, and one I hope to tackle in 2027 (which happens to be the event's 50th anniversary!). It’s the only US race I’ve found that crosses borders: After starting in downtown Detroit, runners cross over the Ambassador Bridge into Windsor, Ontario, before returning to the US through the Detroit-Windsor Tunnel (yep, an underwater mile!). Uniquely, this means you will have to carry your passport during the marathon and international half.

Where to stay: The AC Hotel Detroit at the Bonstelle is minutes from the start line, and well-situated to other places of interest (Little Caesar’s Arena, Fox Theater, the Detroit Institute of Arts). For a post-race treat, stop by Warda Pâtisserie. JW Marriott Detroit Water Square, opening in February 2027 near the Riverwalk, is sure to be a lovely place to stay too.

Date: November 2027Registration: Not yet openDistances included: Marathon, 10K, 5K

What to know: History buffs will love this course in Greece, which, according to legend, follows the original marathon route Pheidippides ran way back in 490 B.C. when he brought news of victory from the battlefield of Marathon (it’s also the course used in the 2004 Olympics). The marathon course stays open for eight hours and passes by landmarks like the Athens Concert Hall, Eleftherias Park, the Presidential Palace, and the National Garden. There are packages available if you want transportation, accommodations, and tour options baked into your visit; they’re not required for entry, but individual registration tends to sell out first, so plan accordingly.

Where to stay: The race starts in the town of Marathon, northeast of central Athens. For a stay close to the finish line with an excellent spa and both indoor and outdoor swimming pools, consider Hotel Grande Bretagne, a Luxury Collection Hotel. A bit further south, the seaside One&Only Aesthesis offers a touch of coastal glamour, plus a Guerlain spa.

Date: November 2027Registration: Not yet openDistances included: Marathon, marathon relay, half-marathon, 5K, one miler

What to know: The course begins in downtown Tulsa, weaving through neighborhoods and the University of Tulsa campus. Along the way, you'll encounter lots of support from the community, with block parties hosted along the course to cheer runners on. Of note, this is a Boston Qualifier, and race day temperatures tend to sit around the 50s.

Where to stay: Room blocks are available at several partner hotels, including Brut Hotel, a charming boutique hotel a short drive from the start line with an outdoor pool, rooftop bar, and spa. I’m eyeing the Olympian Massage, designed to “relieve tension and restore mobility by utilizing deep tissue and sports massage techniques.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6248. Save On Etihad Flights With Amex Offers (Targeted)

The Amex Offers program has just rolled out a great new targeted offer for the purchase of Etihad Airways flights, which could be worth considering for anyone planning travel (that’s not to say you should or shouldn’t plan travel on Etihad, for a variety of reasons — I’m just sharing a deal!).

To my knowledge, this is the first time that we’ve seen an Amex Offers deal for Etihad purchases, so it’s nice to see another airline join the Amex Offers “circuit.”

With a new targeted Amex Offers deal, you can earn a $200 statement credit when you spend $1,000+ or more with Etihad Airways by December 31, 2026. (Enrollment required)

It’s possible that there’s also a version of the offer for 20,000 bonus points rather than a $200 statement credit, and if so, I’d consider that to be more valuable. That’s because based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, so I’d value the 20,000 points at $340.

Let me emphasize that while the terms suggest that you need to book an Etihad flight through the US website that originates in the US, I’ve had similar Amex Offers triggered in the past for flights that didn’t originate in the US, so it’s anyone’s guess how that’s actually enforced here.

This Amex Offers deal is targeted, though it’s possible you’ll see it on multiple of your cards. If so, I’d highly recommend registering your American Express Platinum Card® for this offer. That’s because the Amex Platinum offers 5x points on airfare purchased directly with airlines.

Based on my valuation of 1.7 cents per Membership Rewards point, the 5x points offers an incremental 8.5% return on spending. On top of that, the Amex Platinum offers valuable travel protection, should you experience irregular operations.

In other words, if you took advantage of this offer with the Amex Platinum for a $1,000 ticket, you’d receive a $200 statement credit plus 5,000 points. By my valuation, that’s a return of $285 on $1,000 of spending, which comes out to a 28.5% return.

There’s a new targeted Amex Offers deal for a $200 statement credit when you spend $1,000+ on an Etihad ticket. If you’re planning travel on Etihad, this has the potential to be a solid deal. Ideally you’ll see this offer on the Amex Platinum, so that you can really maximize your points.

Were you targeted for this Amex Offers deal, and if so, do you plan on taking advantage of it?

#6247. Air Fares Still ‘Quite Low,’ A4A CEO Says

Air fares have risen about 22% year-over-year, largely due to the surge in jet fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

But considering the very low-cost environment that prevailed prior to 2026, tickets are still relatively inexpensive, Airlines For America CEO Chris Sununu said this week.

“Airline costs are actually quite low,” Sununu told CBS’ The Takeout. “They’ve risen 22 percent in the last year because of the Iran war, but from all-time lows. So no, overall, flying in the United States is still incredibly affordable.”

“If you want that premium seat, that first class seat, obviously you pay a little more for that,” he continued. “That economy seat is still very affordable.”

Airline ticket prices have risen since February, when the conflict began. The collapse of ultra-low-cost Spirit Airlines in May and major carriers’ shift toward premiumization could also be playing a role.

When pressed by host Major Garrett on reports that U.S. airlines are letting seats go empty instead of lowering prices to effectively discipline the market, Sununu said that was “100 percent” false.

“If a flight is not making money, believe me, it’s been pulled off because jet fuel is so high,” he said. “Instead of three flights a day from Wichita to Green Bay, there’s two flights. So, no, when you get on a flight now, it’s going to be more often than not very very crowded.”

Asked about the FAA’s sweeping air traffic control modernization effort, Sununu was positive and credited Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford with launching the first serious system-wide upgrade in decades.

“For forty years they’ve done nothing,” he said. “And they’ve done more in the last twelve months than they have in the previous forty years. And that is coming as a cynic of Washington, who has seen the political landscape littered with failed infrastructure projects.”

The main benefit for customers, Sununu added, will be efficiency.

“It’s always going to be safe,” he said. “But over the past few years they’ve had to slow the system down, because it is so antiquated, to ensure the safety. But now we get that efficiency back.”

#6246. United Airlines Launches 11 New International Routes This Winter: See Full List Now

United Airlines is the second-largest international operator from the US, behind American Airlines. Of course, United's strength is long-haul, for which it is comfortably number one. In fact, the Star Alliance member is the world's second-largest long-haul carrier, after Emirates.

On Sunday, October 25, United (like other Northern Hemisphere airlines) switched to winter schedules based on IATA slot seasons. This will be maintained until Saturday, March 27, 2027. In this period, Cirium Diio data shows that United will have an average of 350 daily international departures, up by 2% compared to last winter. 11 additional routes help.

Schedule analysis shows that United will introduce, or resume, the following routes beyond the US border during the cold season. They are from five hubs. As they have all been announced, this article simply summarizes them and provides some context and information.

The October 31 launch of United's first service from Newark to St. Croix is not included. That is because the Caribbean destination is in the US Virgin Islands and is, therefore, considered domestic. United's three flights from Las Vegas to Tokyo Narita in January 2027 for the Consumer Electronics Show are also not featured.

Washington Dulles to Los Cabos (above photo is of the relaunch)

Houston Intercontinental to Tuxtla Gutiérrez (the following photo is from the relaunch)

Daily 737 MAX 9 (only until January 4, 2027)

Houston Intercontinental to Santo Domingo

3 weekly 737 MAX 8 (only until January 3, 2027)

No, it's a brand-new market for United; it'll coexist with Japan Airlines

* October 25, 2026, to March 27, 2027, only

When all airlines and US airports are considered, Cirium shows that United is the second-largest operator from the US to Mexico, behind American. United serves the transborder country from eight hubs and other airports. On a typical day, it has 86 daily departures to Mexico. For very obvious reasons, most of them — 46 daily and 53% of the total — are from Houston George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH).

After a 13-year absence, flights from IAH to Tuxtla Gutiérrez have resumed. As such, United now serves 25 destinations in Mexico from the Texas hub. They include Tulum, to which various US airlines have stopped flying. United will join them, as it is pulling out in January 2027. Service to Chihuahua returns at the start of the summer 2027 season.

16 of the 25 airports see the regional jets of United Express. Ten markets are exclusively in the hands of such equipment, whether on the E175 operated by Mesa or SkyWest, the CRJ550 with GoJet, or the ERJ145 with CommutAir. The 50-seat CRJ550 is on one route: Monterrey (from February 11, 2027). The ERJ145 also has only one market: Puebla, 669 nautical miles (1,237 km) away. Six routes see both RJs and non-RJ narrowbodies, while nine do not see RJs at all.

Only one of the transcontinental services have seen United before. Find out more here!

Starting on December 11, flights from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) to Sapporo will, of course, be a proper winter service. That's because the Japanese city is famous for being the gateway to skiing and other sporting activities and broader winter fun.

The other two upcoming long-haul routes — Los Angeles to Osaka and SFO to Okinawa — almost did not make the list. That's because the first departure from California will be on March 27, which is the final day of the northern aviation winter based on IATA slot seasons. The first service from Asia will be on March 28, the first day of the northern summer season. Okinawa will be a seasonal route, while Osaka will be flown year-round.

#6245. Ouch: Flying Blue Makes Earning XPs Through SAF 50% More Expensive

The Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has just rolled out a quiet devaluation, and it’s one that many savvy Flying Blue members won’t be happy about. The airline group has increased the cost to contribute toward sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), and in turn, has reduced the ability to earn elite status through this method. And we’re not talking about a minor price increase either…

Personally I consider Air France-KLM Flying Blue elite status to be valuable, not just for the SkyTeam Elite Plus perks, but also for the more Air France- KLM specific benefits, like access to more award availability.

Earning Flying Blue elite status is based on the concept of XPs (“experience points”), and how many of those you rack up. One really innovative thing that Flying Blue has done is that it has been possible to earn XPs through environmental contributions:

As I see it, this is a win-win — this program can genuinely help you earn status, while doing something that’s good for the environment, and also contributing to Air France-KLM’s long term environmental goals.

Well, seemingly overnight, Flying Blue has increased the cost to purchase SAF, and in turn, earn XPs. With these changes, you earn one XP for every €15 contributed toward SAF, compared to the previous amount of €10.

A 50% overnight increase is rough. It gets even worse than that, though. There’s no longer any “rounding” with this, so for short haul economy flights you might find that you’re not offered any XPs if the contribution amount is €14, and you’re offered one XP if the amount is €28.

The past year or so has definitely been rough for the overall value of the Flying Blue program, including for elite members:

This is of course all frustrating, though I guess the other side of the equation is that Flying Blue Platinum status has become more valuable over time, but primarily through punitive measures:

How do we make sense of increasing the cost to contribute to SAF, and in turn, earn XPs? I wonder if Flying Blue management thinks that people will still buy SAF at the same rate as before? I know I certainly won’t, though maybe I’m in the minority (I’ll instead increasingly earn XPs through Flying Blue’s co-branded credit card in the US, since that opportunity was recently improved).

For that matter, I’m curious to what extent the number of people buying SAF matters to Air France-KLM? Does this materially contribute to any environmental initiatives, or is it not a priority?

I still get value from my Flying Blue Platinum status, and don’t have plans to change my strategy. Honestly, that partly comes down to how hard it has become to find award availability in business class on long haul flights through other programs.

But I’m definitely slowly becoming less enthused by the program. Then again, I guess that sums up the reality of miles & points more broadly — this isn’t what it once was, and it’s getting harder and harder to make the case for being loyal. It’s no different than World of Hyatt, where they’re clearly trying to cash in. I guess that is the goal of any for-profit business, eh?

Flying Blue has just devalued the rate at which you earn XPs for SAF contributions. You used to earn one XP for every €10 contributed, while you now earn one XP for every €15 contributed. A 50% increase in cost overnight is huge.

I always thought this was a unique aspect of the Flying Blue program, since it’s a win-win for consumers, the airline group, and the environment. Obviously they’ve decided on a different equation now, and for us members, this isn’t good news.

What do you make of this change to Flying Blue when it comes to earning XPs for SAF?

#6244. Getting to Know New York Through Its Sandwiches

“By the end of our time together, I will be asking you again: ‘So, what is a sandwich?’”

An expert-led tour that starts by questioning its own object of inquiry is unconventional. But then, so is our guide. Ben Gollan, known to his Instagram followers as A Man and His Sandwich, has spent the last nine years reviewing sandwiches across New York City. Gollan moved here from Australia in 2016, after nearly a decade as a government lawyer. For about as long, he has run an Airbnb Experience that turns a food crawl into a two-hour pilgrimage to the city’s best sandwich slingers.

It was a pastrami sandwich at Harry & Ida’s, a former deli in the East Village, that turned Gollan into a professional sandwich hound. “It was a fourth-generation Jewish deli that broke every rule of pastrami sandwiches: it was thick-cut and fabulous,” he says as we dash across Bowery. We’re scuttling over from a coffee shop in Cooper Square that served as our meeting point and into the East Village—a neighborhood of contrasts that still manages to connect New York's past and present. There are 12 of us in total, mostly locals, a couple of newer transplants, and just one traveler. “It’s usually mostly visitors, so this is different,” he says.

It’s a great introduction to the city. After all, New York runs on sandwiches, and there’s no shortage of great ones, whether it’s a classic Italian deli sub you’re after or a grab-and-go banh mi. They’re economical, versatile, delicious and, as is the point of Gollan’s tour, telegraph the city’s greatest personality trait—its diversity. So is there such a thing as a New York sandwich? “Not really,” he says, "but the chopped cheese, born in East Harlem, might come closest.”

The Bono at Via Della Scrofa, a small family-owned joint that wouldn't look out of place on the streets of Rome

“We start here because it’s closest to what we think of as a traditional sandwich,” says Gollan, before filling us in on the origins of what is the modern-day sandwich. It involves John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, who, in the 18th century, gave his title to the now-ubiquitous food. Gollan loves to talk and think about sandwiches as much as he eats them. “Although I've learned never to trust history, especially when rendered by colonizers,” he muses. “Do we really think it took us till the 1700s to invent the sandwich?”

Named after a Roman street, Via Della Scrofa is the kind of bottega or alimentari you might find in Rome, with a tiny counter selling tiny espressos and focaccia, as well as imported groceries from Italy. “It's small family-owned joints like this that make New York what it is,” says Gollan. While the rest of the group gets to try the Porcodeddena panini (made with porchetta), I’m getting a Bono: grilled eggplants sweetened with sun-dried tomatoes, with arugula and buffalo mozzarella, in a warm roll that’s toasty on the outside and soft and warm on the inside. The bread is perfect—it’s a rosetta (or michetta), a traditional Roman bread roll. I wash it down with a Crodino, a popular non-alcoholic bitter aperitif from Italy.

Around us, the Lower East Side Arts & Culture Open House, an annual event, had taken over the street, adding personality to our time with its bands, pop-up stalls, and lively crowds. Gollan regales us with stories of owner Giovanni Bartocci, describing him as a real character with “a man bun, suspenders, tattoos, and naturally, a Harley," and I look around hoping he'll show up. I ask Gollan why he isn’t eating with us. “I never want to tire of these sandwiches, and if I keep eating them, I will.” The wind picks up and blows over the canvases at an art stall, but the band is undeterred, playing “New York, New York.”

A spicy Pakistani rendition of the chopped cheese at Nishaan

The writer and her chopped cheese sandwich, the chapli kebab replaced with Impossible Meat.

Order: A chopped cheese, but make it desi

An 11-minute walk up 1st Avenue and a few blocks later, we spot our next sandwich spot. A cobalt-blue sign reads Nishaan; bags of rice are piled high along its exterior; and a long line snakes out of what I can only assume is a tiny space inside. Nishaan began as a pop-up at the weekly open-air food festival Smorgasburg and went on to win season 18 of The Great Food Truck Race. While there are other dishes on the menu (elote chaat, mango lassi), it’s Nishaan’s twist on that great New York City bodega staple, the chopped cheese, that many are after: a spice-laden chapli kebab, chopped up on a griddle with peppers and onions, then enhanced with a zingy cilantro sauce and tamarind chutney. When it opened in August 2025, it was one of the most talked-about new restaurants in New York City, which has emerged as a hub for a new generation of Pakistani eateries. “New York belongs to everyone, and so does the sandwich,” proclaims Gollan.

In a city that runs on pastrami, vegetarians like me don’t faze Gollan; he orders me a version with Impossible Meat. We tuck ourselves out of the wind and into an alley and dig in. I can’t stop eating, making a mess as I go along. “Half the fun of a sandwich is the experience of eating it,” Gollan adds.

Regulars love the pho sandwiches at Sunny and Annie’s—sandwiches stuffed to the brim with pho ingredients, minus the broth.

Sunny and Annie’s is a 24/7, 365-day-a-year kind of neighborhood classic with 92 items on its sandwich menu.

“We’re taking a detour,” says Gollan, frantically looking around him. It’s the day of the Tompkins Square Halloween Dog Parade, and the crowds around us are building, as are the dogs in costume—cheese boards, UPS drivers, and, suitably for the occasion, hot dogs. We ditch the idea of cutting through the park and work our way around the revelers.

Our destination? Sunny and Annie’s, a 24/7, 365-days-a-year kind of neighborhood classic that has been open since 1997. There’s no front door here, because there’s always someone around. Inside, past the candy, chips, and dish detergent, we’re greeted by what must be the most extensive sandwich menu I’ve ever encountered, all written out on brightly colored sheets of paper stuck to the glass counter. There are 92 handheld options in total, some named after politicians and celebrities, like the Jackie Chan—bulgogi, cilantro, avocado, lettuce, jalapeños, and onions, served on a roll or hero. There’s also a chicken cutlet sandwich called the Australian. It’s not named after Gollan.

This is not a place to linger, so we keep it moving. Outside, the crowds have thickened, and Gollan instructs us to head to a neighborhood bar called ABC Beer Co., which often features at the end of his tours. As someone who has spent many a night in an East Village bar, I’m disappointed I’ve never been here before. It’s spacious, has a backyard, and is equally welcoming to couples on dates and families with little ones.

The writer's sandwich tour ended at ABC Beer Co, a hybrid beer bar and store with a particular focus on NYC breweries.

Gollan appears with our pho sandwiches, wrapped in spinach tortillas. They smell like pho, taste like pho; only the avocado throws me off.

Some of us get ciders and wine, and the conversation winds back to where we started: So, what really is a sandwich? “I want this to get contentious: bang the tables, let’s have a food fight," Gollan says, egging us on. Hot dogs? Quesadillas? What about a hamburger? A pizza folded in half? Does it have to have a carb? What about a lettuce wrap instead of bread? Gollan briefs us on a famous 2006 Massachusetts lawsuit—White City Shopping Center vs. Panera Bread—which legally answered an age-old culinary debate: Is a burrito a sandwich? The judge ruled that a burrito is, in fact, not a sandwich, clearing the way for the Mexican fast-casual joint to open in the vicinity of Panera Bread. “A sandwich court case is my Roman Empire," he says. “When this question goes to the Supreme Court, I will be there.”

The point of this tour—and the posed question—Gollan says, was never to walk away with an answer, but to open our minds and palates. So, what are Ben Gollan’s own rules for a sandwich, I have to ask. He lists the following:

And then he adds: “Take those rules and throw them in the bin.” And with that, class is dismissed.

The NYC Sandwich Tour can be booked directly on the A Man and His Sandwich website, as well as on Airbnb. Tours run every day of the week, with the exception of Tuesdays and Wednesdays. Ben Gollan, who proudly calls himself the Chief Sandwich Officer, often leads the experiences himself, but he also has co-hosts to help guide fellow sandwich enthusiasts on these two-hour outings. Along the way, guests sample three standout sandwiches—from the classic to the “slightly unhinged”—before finishing up at a bar to settle the debate over what really counts as a sandwich. While my tour focused on the East Village, Gollan also leads sandwich tours around Williamsburg. And word on the street is that he has his eye on opening a sandwich shop of his own one day.

#6243. Report: Alaska to Lay Off 200 Employees

Alaska Air Group, the parent company of Alaska Airlines, Hawaiian Airlines, and Horizon Air, will lay off about 200 workers as financial losses tied to the higher price of jet fuel grow.

The Honolulu Star-Advertiser obtained an email sent to employees Friday morning acknowledging the cuts.

“Despite having the right strategy and strong momentum, fuel prices and geopolitical challenges are putting significant financial pressure on our business,” CEO Ben Minicucci wrote. “If current conditions persist, we could lose as much as $700 million this year, which would be our first adjusted pretax loss outside of the pandemic since 2003.”

According to the Star-Advertiser, 125 workers in Washington state will be laid off, and 48 in Hawaii.

The affected employees will be out of a job Nov. 13, but will continue to receive pay through the end of the year.

Alaska’s leadership said no front-line, non-management positions have been affected, suggesting the eliminated jobs are management-related.

Separately, Hawaiian Airlines CEO Diana Birkett Rakow said in an email to staff that, of the 48 affected positions at Hawaiian, 40 roles will be eliminated entirely, and eight people will be be offered other jobs within the airline.

Birkett Rakow also said that two senior leaders – Jim Landers, head of Hawaii operations, and Shelly Parker, head of guest operations – will retire at the end of the year. Both of their positions will be eliminated following their departure.

#6242. Belavia Can Once Again Do Business With Boeing, As US Lifts Sanctions On Belarus

Belarusian national carrier Belavia has faced sanctions from the United States and European Union for quite some time, due to a combination of the “hijacking” of a Ryanair flight, along with the country’s support for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Well, if Belarusian media is to be believed, these sanctions are now being lifted, so the country’s airline can once again buy planes from Boeing…

Belarusian state owned national news agency BelTA is reporting that the United States Department of Commerce has granted Boeing a license to resume full cooperation with Belavia. This was announced by Valentin Rybakov, the Belarusian representative to the United Nations. If true, this means that Belavia can once again purchase planes and parts directly from Boeing.

This all seems to be related to a visit to Belarus by an American delegation in September, where the country’s president, Alexander Lukashenko, met with US Special Envoy John Cole. This meeting included a larger lifting of sanctions. It also comes at a time when we’re seeing the Trump administration increasingly lifting sanctions on Russia in relation to the invasion of Ukraine.

In 2021, the United States imposed sanctions on Belarus, after the country engaged in what was referred to as a state sponsored hijacking. A Ryanair Boeing 737 was flying between Greece and Lithuania, and as the plane approached Belarusian airspace, an air traffic controller claimed there was a bomb onboard, and that the plane needed to divert to Belarus.

As it turned out, an opponent of the Belarusian government was onboard, so the real motive with this was to have him arrested. Obviously this violates all sorts of international laws and aviation treaties, which is why action was taken against the country. Then in 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, additional sanctions were imposed against Belarus, given its support for Russia.

Obviously having sanctions imposed on you by both the United States and European Union makes it challenging to buy new aircraft, given the aircraft manufacturing duopoly we have (unless you consider the aircraft manufacturers in China and Russia to be competitors).

So most of Belavia’s aircraft acquisitions in recent times have been smuggled into the country using shady middlemen. For example, in 2025, Belavia acquired Airbus A330s through an imaginary Gambian airline, as one does.

Belavia can reportedly once again buy aircraft and parts from Boeing, after the United States lifted sanctions that were imposed around five years ago, when the country hijacked a Ryanair plane. This easing of sanctions comes as part of a larger reversal by the Trump administration, as it takes less of a stance against Russia and Belarus.

It’ll be interesting to see what comes of this, and if Belarus places some big Boeing aircraft order in the near future…

What do you make of the US lifting sanctions on Belarus on the airline front?

#6241. There's a New Luxury Sleeper Train Route Coming to the French Riviera Next Spring

As someone who travels a lot for work, I would give anything to swap a flight for a train—even if that means spending eight hours on the rails.

Thankfully, it's easy to travel Europe by train at nearly any price point. And although I am a big fan of modern high-speed routes, the most romantic way to see the continent is certainly aboard one of Belmond's gorgeous luxury trains, which travel to destinations such as the British countryside, the Amalfi Coast, and the Scottish Highlands.

But in 2027, my bucket-list Belmond journey is a glamorous new addition to its already impressive collection of itineraries: the French Riviera.

The Venice Simplon-Orient-Express offers three cabin types: Historic Cabins, Suites, and Grand Suites.

On May 10, 2027, the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express is launching a new route from Paris to Monaco, traveling to Monte Carlo for the first time in its history.

The journey, which will become a regular addition to the train's annual schedule, will take passengers through some of the most spectacular scenery along the French Riviera before arriving in the glamorous principality.

The new route will take travelers to Monte Carlo for the first time in the train's history.

The experience begins in Paris, where passengers will board the train's distinctive midnight blue carriages before settling into their accommodation for the night. There are several options to choose from, including the classic Historic Cabins, Suites, and Grand Suites, each drawing inspiration from the train's Art Deco heritage.

For those looking to really splash out, there's also L'Observatoire, an exclusive carriage created in collaboration with French artist JR. Designed as a private sanctuary on the rails, it comes complete with a bedroom, an en-suite bathroom featuring a freestanding bathtub, a spacious living area, a library, and even a secret tearoom.

As evening approaches, guests can enjoy dinner in one of the train's two restaurant cars, Étoile du Nord and L'Oriental, before heading to the famous Bar Car 3674 for cocktails and live piano music.

But perhaps the most exciting part of the new journey comes the following morning. After waking up to breakfast served in their cabins, passengers will be treated to sweeping views of the Mediterranean as the train makes its way along the Côte d'Azur. The route passes the red cliffs of the Massif de l'Estérel and travels through Saint-Raphaël towards Cannes and Nice. The train will then continue towards Monaco before arriving at Monaco-Monte-Carlo station.

Breakfast served aboard the Venice-Simplon Orient Express.

Monte Carlo also has a surprising connection to the train's history. In 1977, two original train carriages were purchased at an auction in the principality, helping set in motion the project that would eventually become the luxury train we know today.

“Introducing the destination feels like a natural continuation for the Venice-Simplon Orient Express, bringing the romance of luxury rail travel to a locale that has always understood the art of arrival,” says Pascal Deyrolle, Belmond's Europe area managing director for trains. “There's also something rather special about coming back to Monte Carlo, given the role it played in the train's history.”

The new journey is part of Belmond's expanding collection of European rail experiences, alongside the second year of its “Villeggiatura by Train” itinerary, which connects the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express with Belmond hotels in Italy.

Of course, a journey this luxurious comes with a price tag to match. Tickets for the new Paris-to-Monte-Carlo route start from €4,870 (approximately $5,450) per person, based on two people sharing a Historic Cabin. The fare includes the overnight journey, all meals with sommelier-selected wines, unlimited soft drinks, transfers, and 24-hour steward service.

#6240. Transfer Amex Points To Virgin Atlantic Flying Club With 30% Bonus: Worth It?

The Amex Membership Rewards program has just launched a new 30% transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. While Flying Club is in some ways a niche program, this is a deal that has the potential to offer outsized value, and I’m sure it will interest many people. I’d probably speculatively take advantage of this, except for the fact that I moved a bunch of points last year when there was a 40% transfer bonus.

Between November 2 and November 30, 2026, the American Express Membership Rewards program in the United States is offering a 30% bonus on points transfers to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,300 Flying Club points for every 1,000 Membership Rewards points transferred. Transfers are generally instant.

For context, Amex seems to offer a transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club once or twice per year. The last promotion we saw was over the summer, and this is the second offer so far in 2026. When we do see these offers, they’re typically in the range of 30-40%, so this is on the low side of that range, but could still represent a great deal.

Virgin Atlantic is definitely a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic, there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta.

In late 2024 we saw Flying Club introduce dynamic award pricing for travel on Virgin Atlantic. While the changes are a mixed bag, what’s exciting is that on the low end, redemptions are cheaper than ever before. It’s now possible to fly one-way Virgin Atlantic Upper Class between the United States and the UK for under 30,000 points, and that’s before a transfer bonus.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 45,000-47,500 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with. Then when you consider the 30% transfer bonus, that means you could be paying significantly fewer Amex points. First class can also be a good deal.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Through November 30, 2026, Amex is offering a 30% bonus when you transfer points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. This is definitely more of a niche program, but with a specific use in mind, there’s a lot of value to be had.

With the 30% bonus, award travel on Virgin Atlantic will be an even better value. There’s also lots of value to booking on partners, ranging from SkyTeam airlines, to Air New Zealand, to All Nippon Airways.

#6239. American Resumes Service to Haiti After Two-Year Pause

American Airlines on Sunday restarted service to Haiti after a nearly two-year hiatus brought on by gang violence in and around Port-au-Prince.

The carrier is now operating daily nonstop flights between Miami and Cap-Haitien, using Boeing 737 aircraft.

The inaugural flight on Sunday was staffed by an all-Haitian, Creole-speaking crew, the airline said.

“The connection between the United States and Haiti is incredibly meaningful, which is especially true in South Florida,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “We know the critical role air service plays in linking countries and communities, so we’re beyond proud to reinstate such a consequential connection for so many.”

U.S. airlines suspended service to and from Haiti in 2024 amid a rise in gang violence. Toussaint Louverture International Airport in Port-au-Prince was temporarily closed after bullets struck aircraft taxiing on the tarmac.

So far, American is the only U.S.-based carrier to have resumed service to the country.

#6238. It's Official: Lufthansa Signs $1.2 Billion Deal To Purchase 44.9% Of TAP Air Portugal

Lufthansa Group and the Portuguese government have officially signed an agreement for the German aviation giant to acquire a 44.9% stake in TAP Air Portugal for €1.025 billion (approximately $1.2 billion). The signing took place in Lisbon earlier today, nearly three weeks after Portugal selected Lufthansa ahead of rival Air France-KLM. The transaction remains subject to regulatory approval.

The agreement represents another milestone in Lufthansa's European airline consolidation strategy. It could add Lisbon as the group's seventh hub while significantly strengthening its position in Latin America. However, the deal also raises two important questions: how did Lufthansa beat Air France-KLM, the airline group that many experts favored, and can it replicate IAG's success with Iberia?

The agreement was officially signed at Lisbon Airport (LIS), with Lufthansa funding the acquisition entirely from existing liquidity. Euronews reports that the group could increase its holding to 49.9% by purchasing shares initially reserved for TAP employees, potentially lifting total consideration to €1.2 billion. Portugal will initially retain majority ownership, while European Commission approval is still required before completion.

Lufthansa CEO Carsten Spohr emphasized that the airlines' networks are complementary, particularly in South America and Brazil. Lisbon will become Lufthansa Group's seventh hub, with further growth planned across Portuguese-speaking Africa and North America. The group also expects up to €450 million in synergies, with most potentially achievable before acquiring majority ownership.

“Together with TAP's employees, we want to continue the airline's success story, preserve its Portuguese identity, and develop Lisbon into a Lufthansa Group hub.”

Lufthansa has also welcomed the possibility of TAP's full privatization, while its commitments include maintaining the airline's Portuguese identity, strengthening regional connectivity, and expanding investment in Portugal. The government has outlined potential fleet growth to 130 aircraft, while Lufthansa Technik's new facility near Porto should help increase the group's Portuguese workforce to more than 1,000 by 2030.

Air France-KLM initially appeared to be the more attractive buyer. While Lufthansa enjoys an existing relationship with TAP through Star Alliance, potentially simplifying commercial cooperation, the Franco-Dutch group seemed the more complementary partner with its hubs at Paris and Amsterdam. Most crucially, Air France-KLM wasn't already entangled with the integration of a prior acquisition, as Lufthansa is with ITA Airways.

But ultimately, the financial offer proved decisive. Portugal revealed that Lufthansa's proposal was up to 16% higher than Air France-KLM's, with less uncertainty. Both bidders had improved their proposals during final negotiations, and their strategic commitments had become broadly comparable. Prime Minister Luís Montenegro described Lufthansa as "the choice that best protected Portugal's national interests."

Lufthansa's experience integrating SWISS, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, and ITA Airways provides another potential advantage. Its multi-brand model allows carriers to retain their identities while sharing commercial and operational resources. However, TAP's minority ownership structure presents challenges: Lufthansa must deliver substantial synergies without initially enjoying the control associated with its other acquisitions.

The $1.2 billion investment is more than three times what it paid for 41% of ITA back in 2025. So why is it splurging on a smaller European carrier? Brazil provides the answer. The group estimates its share of Europe–Latin America traffic at approximately 9%, rising to a calculated 20% when TAP is included. More specifically, Lisbon's established connections to Brazil offer access to markets where Lufthansa's existing network is comparatively limited, helping it compete more effectively with IAG and Air France-KLM.

The obvious comparison is the creation of IAG and the transformation of Iberia following its 2011 merger with British Airways. After restructuring, Iberia developed into one of Europe's most profitable airlines, recording a 16.2% operating margin and €1.31 billion in operating profit in 2025. Its Europe–Latin America and Caribbean capacity reached a record 5.5 million seats, demonstrating the financial potential of a strong transatlantic network.

Lufthansa hopes to replicate that success through coordinated schedules, purchasing, distribution, and stronger connecting traffic. However, Iberia's turnaround occurred under IAG's full ownership, whereas Lufthansa must initially work alongside the Portuguese government. With TAP also facing profitability pressures, the €1 billion investment is a significant bet that its valuable Brazilian network can deliver an Iberia-style transformation.

#6237. On Location: How Coastal Newfoundland Set the Scene for Netflix's No. 1 Series ‘Below’

A mysterious sea creature is captivating audiences on Netflix as the Josh Hartnett-led series Below remains the No. 1 show in Netflix’s global rankings. The six-episode thriller paints an eerie image of small-town life in Newfoundland, and viewers are intrigued by the mystique of the striking Canadian backdrop.

Despite the fictional giant squid terrorizing Snook’s Arm, the show pulls on elements of reality, from climate change affecting the Atlantic Canadian sea life to the government-run resettling of remote fishing towns, which started in 1954 and continues to this day. It’s that history that drew production designer Emmanuel Fréchette into the project.

“When I found out that more than 300 towns in Newfoundland had been resettled, I was amazed,” he tells Traveler. “The script is very interesting, mixing that reality with the mundane life in Newfoundland—and this creature!” After all, creator Jesse McKeown (The Umbrella Academy) had frequented the region for years, inspired to bring an authentic depiction of its culture to the screen.

That started behind the scenes as the cast and crew engaged in Newfoundland and Labrador’s most famous tradition. Visitors, who they called CFAs (or Come from Aways—this is also where Broadway hit musical draws its name), get “screeched in” by kissing a cod to become honorary citizens. So they all went to St. John’s Christian’s Pub to pucker up. “The guy there is such a great character, and he has a routine and speech that’s very entertaining," Fréchette says.

When it came to filming locations, the remote regions posed practical challenges, so the majority of the sets were built by production, a joy for Fréchette, who was trained as an architect. “I was stunned by the humble architecture, built by boat owners and builders,” he says of the homes’ low ceilings. “The structures are very endearing and make you think of a boat, so I wanted to follow that thread.”

That’s also what helped root the fantastical storyline into reality. “This was vernacular architecture—architecture without architects—just following the needs of the people out of survival, and I found that so beautiful,” he says. “So I really tried to mimic what I was seeing all around me that survived the decades.”

And it’s clearly had an effect on audiences. According to data provided by Booking.com, not only have searches for the province’s capital of St. John’s risen 16.9% by Americans on the platform compared to last year, but the coastal town of Twillingate, home to the floating icebergs, has skyrocketed 123.7%.

Here, Fréchette shares the filming locations from the popular Netflix series Below.

The show is set in the actual resettled town of Snook’s Arm, which had a population of 10 when it was approved for resettlement in 2017, according to the CBC. But its remote location would have been difficult to film in with such a big crew, so Brigus South—a town with a population of about 700 at last count in 2021—stood in.

“We picked that place because it had a connection with the water,” Fréchette says of the inlet going deep into the land. “Lots of the characters are dragged into the water, so it was great to have this presence for the eeriness.”

But to get the cozy town ready for its close-up took work, as the crew designed and built about 80% of what appears in the series, including the fish plant, Fishermen’s Hall, and wharf. The Penneys home was an existing home they covered, and the church was also a house that they retrofitted, adding the bell tower.

When Fréchette was scouting locations, he stayed in a hostel by the sea in Twillingate, about 275 miles northwest of the capital. “We’d be having a coffee with the window open, and suddenly we were freezing,” he recalls of a sudden drop in temperature from 68 degrees Fahrenheit to 50 degrees Fahrenheit. That’s when they’d look up and see an iceberg floating their way. “It lowers the temperature all around the bay—it’s such an amazing phenomenon.”

As it turns out, the Atlantic town sits along Iceberg Alley, where from late April through July, the remnants of broken glaciers glide down the coast. Many of the shots of Calvin (Hartnett) harvesting icebergs were actual footage from these massive blocks of ice naturally floating along.

The capital served as the home base for the cast and crew, who were spread out across hotels and home rentals during filming. But its Ocean Sciences Centre, about 30 minutes north of downtown, found the spotlight as one of the most striking structures in the series, the marine research center where Dr. Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis) worked.

While Fréchette admits it took some work to convince the operating facility to shoot there, he’s excited it worked out because “it really adds production value and is a great location.” After all, the circular wooden structure reflects that government building architect of the 1960s and early 1970s, “at a time we were dreaming and imagining things beyond what was possible to build today.” Reminiscent of designs by Canadian architects like Arthur Erikson, he adds that “it was ambitious, but it had a vision—and is fantastic!”

About 20 miles north of St. John’s at the top of the Avalon Peninsula sits Pouch Cove, a town of about 2,000 residents. The art director told Fréchette about the Pouch Cove Heritage Society, a historical building that was closed since they were fundraising to preserve it, so one weekend, they went up to visit. “The floor was sunken in and it was structurally unsafe,” he says.

The show’s head carpenter and engineer got to work, fixing it up, temporarily transforming it into the interior of Below’s Fisherman’s Hall, while permanently restoring it for the community. “It was a win-win because they were happy to get the money from the location, but also the work we did on it was helpful for them.”

When Calvin returns to his abandoned childhood town of Little Pot Rock, that dilapidated setting was an actual resettled town, about a 30-minute drive down from Pouch Cove on a dirt road that the production had to grade in order to shoot there.

“It was quite tricky, but just stunning—really wild and rugged,” Fréchette says, calling it “the most amazing location.” All that was there was one tiny house, about 12 by 20 feet, but it never showed up on camera. Instead, the production custom built all of the Budgell family’s dwellings. But the area can be visited as part of a 4.3-mile hike along the East Coast Trail.

The fishing village of Bay Bulls is home to North America’s largest Atlantic puffin colony, as well as a prime whale watching destination. But for Below, it was all about the functional purpose of its Pennecon Marine Base. Though it never shows up on screen, its industrial harbor was essential in order to dock the boat used as the research vessel since it had a draft (depth) of nearly 10 feet, and they needed an appropriate spot that the cast and crew could board. Also shot here were the exterior scenes of the submersible, which was hung from the boat by a crane and lifted onto the dock.

Pittman’s fish farm played an integral part of the plot, as Calvin confirmed that the sea creature was real—but it turns out the location was landlocked. “It was very complicated to do this on the sea because we’d have to deal with tides and storms, so we decided to cheat it on a lake in Brigus,” he says of the town that’s actually about 60 miles northwest from Brigus South. There was no actual fish farm there, so they custom-built the floating dock and cabin.

While the outside of Linda’s Bar was filmed using a retrofitted Brigus South home, the interior was actually the Rising Tide Convenience shop in the town of Harbour Main, about 33 miles southwest of St. John’s. The local business, best known for its homemade ice cream, “looked great inside, so we dressed it up,” Fréchette says, taking extra care to ensure the exterior entrance they built flowed seamlessly between cuts. As for Noah (Kaleb Horn)’s on-screen screech-in? That was a prop, but an actual frozen fish to ensure the fish kiss was genuine.

#6236. Are Authorized Users Eligible For Credit Card Bonuses?

Here’s a topic that seems to cause confusion among some people. If you’re an authorized user on someone else’s credit card, are you eligible for the bonus on that card if you apply outright? The answer is actually pretty straightforward, so let me explain…

Credit cards frequently offer huge upfront welcome offers, whereby you can earn a lot of bonus points for spending a certain amount within a limited timeframe. While there are different credit card application rules for each bank, there are generally restrictions whereby an existing cardmember can’t apply for a card they already have, while also receiving the bonus.

How does that work in the context of authorized users? If you’re the authorized user on someone else’s credit card, can you apply for the card as the primary cardmember and earn the bonus? The answer is universally yes — being an authorized user on someone else’s credit card doesn’t preclude you from applying for that card yourself, and earning the bonus.

When welcome bonus rules talk about existing cardmembers, they’re specifically talking about primary cardmembers, and not authorized users.

You don’t even need to cancel your authorized user card to be able to do this. For example, say you’re an authorized user on your spouse’s Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more), or Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more), or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more). You could remain an authorized user, and still apply outright and earn the welcome bonus on the card.

For those in relationships, it can sometimes be difficult to decide under which circumstances it makes sense to apply for a card outright, rather than being an authorized user on a spouse’s card (and vice versa). There are pros and cons to each.

The advantage of adding someone as an authorized user is that it minimizes annual fees, since many cards have lower (or no) annual fees for authorized users, compared to the primary cardmembers. Meanwhile the advantages of having both people in a relationship apply for a card outright is that many cards have big welcome bonuses, and on top of that some cards pay for themselves on an ongoing basis.

For more on this topic, see my post on the best credit card strategy for families.

Many credit cards have amazing welcome bonuses, though you’re generally only eligible for them if you don’t already have that card. The good news is that across the board, being an authorized user on someone else’s card still makes you eligible to apply for that card outright and receive the bonus (assuming you’re otherwise eligible for the card).

Therefore this really comes down to deciding for each card whether the economics of applying outright make sense.

Have you ever applied for a credit card on which you’re already an authorized user?

What if your an authorized user on a card, but you want to now get that card as a primary cardmember with the welcome bonus, but you also want to retain the account history/account age with your authorized user card on your credit score (and are looking to close the authorized user card)? If they get their own Platinum, we will cancel the AU card (because we don't want to pay an extra AF for that card). Is it possible for them to get all three? How would you go about this?

If you are a frequent American Airlines flyer, you have plenty of credit card options to help you earn additional miles and make the most of every American Airlines flight.

For a limited time, new Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® (see rates and fees) cardholders can earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first five months from account opening. This matches the highest offer we've seen on the card.

There have also been some recent changes to Citi's American Airlines credit card lineup. The premium Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® (see rates and fees) recently added a new dining credit. Plus, Citi and American Airlines have also announced upcoming changes to two other cobranded cards.

Here’s a rundown of the top Citi / AAdvantage credit cards and their current offers. Holding one of these cards could be a straightforward way to score a business-class ticket on American or one of its Oneworld partners.

*The offer value is based on TPG's November 2026 valuations.

**Annual fee will increase from $99 to $150 starting Jan. 24, 2027

The information for the Citi / AAdvantage MileUp card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The Citi / AA Executive is American’s top-tier personal card.

Best for: Those who want Admirals Club access

Welcome bonus: Earn 80,000 bonus miles after spending $8,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

According to TPG's valuations, the welcome bonus is worth $1,160. We recommend waiting until at least 100,000 miles are on offer.

This card is best suited to frequent American Airlines flyers who can take advantage of its Admirals Club membership, statement credits and elite-status benefits.

At $695, the Citi / AAdvantage Executive has a much higher annual fee than other options but comes with a notable benefit for frequent flyers: Admirals Club access for you and up to two guests traveling with you (when you have a same-day boarding pass for an eligible flight).

†A qualifying stay is one of two or more consecutive nights booked directly through Omni Hotels & Resorts on omnihotels.com. Enrollment in the Champion Status benefit is required.

The card also offers travel protections and the ability to earn up to 40,000 bonus Loyalty Points per elite qualification period, making it particularly useful for those pursuing American elite status.

To learn more, read our full review of the Citi / AA Executive.

Apply here: Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Legend Mastercard

The Citi / AA Business is Citi’s business card for American Airlines loyalists.

Welcome bonus: For a limited time, earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first five months from account opening.

According to TPG’s valuations, the welcome bonus is worth $1,088. This matches the highest offer we've seen in the card's history, so now is a great time to apply if you are interested.

Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first 12 months, then $150 thereafter (increases from $99 on Jan. 24, 2027)

With this card, you (and up to four companions) get a free first checked bag when flying a domestic American Airlines itinerary on the same reservation.

If you spend $30,000 with the card in a cardholder year and renew your card, you’ll earn a companion certificate, which allows you to take a companion on a flight for $99 (plus taxes and fees).

The certificate can only be used for a round-trip, domestic itinerary (i.e., one to and from the 48 contiguous states, unless you live in Alaska or Hawaii) in the Main Cabin. The certificate is granted upon account renewal, and the account must remain open for a full billing cycle after the anniversary date.

To learn more, read our full review of the Citi / AA Business Mastercard.

Apply here: Citi / AAdvantage Business World Elite Mastercard

The Citi / AA Globe is best suited for those who fly often but not enough to justify having the premium card.

Best for: Semifrequent American Airlines flyers

Welcome bonus: Earn 60,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

According to TPG’s valuations, the welcome bonus is worth $870. This is the standard offer on the card, so we recommend waiting to apply.

The Globe's standout perks include four Admirals Club passes each calendar year and a 5,000 "Flight Streak" Loyalty Point boost after four eligible American Airlines flights. You can do this up to three times per year for a total of 15,000 Loyalty Points.

The card also provides an annual companion certificate each cardholder year (starting in your second cardholder year), allowing you to pay $99 (plus taxes and fees) for a round-trip domestic Main Cabin ticket each year. Plus, you'll receive the first checked bag free (for the cardholder and up to eight companions on the same reservation; on domestic flights), preferred boarding and a Splurge credit.

It's a decent option for those who can take advantage of the card's companion certificate, lounge access and AAdvantage-related perks in exchange for a more modest $350 annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the Citi / AA Globe.

Apply here: Citi / AAdvantage Globe Mastercard

The Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select is a solid option for American Airlines flyers who want basic airline perks without paying for a more premium card.

Best for: Casual American Airlines flyers

Welcome bonus: Earn 50,000 bonus miles after spending $2,500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

According to TPG’s valuations, the welcome bonus is worth $725. This is the card's standard offer, so we'd recommend waiting for a better bonus if you're not in a rush to apply.

Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first 12 months, then $150 thereafter (increases from $99 on Jan. 24, 2027)

*Earning rate for these purchases starting Jan. 24, 2027

If you fly American Airlines often enough to want an upgraded flight experience but aren't interested in Admirals Club access, this is a solid card option. It’s affordable and easy to keep in your wallet.

You’ll receive benefits like preferred boarding, a free first checked bag (for you and up to four companions on domestic American Airlines itineraries), and discounts on inflight snacks and beverage purchases.

As a cardholder, you’ll also earn 1 Loyalty Point for every eligible AAdvantage mile earned from purchases, and this card charges no foreign transaction fees.

Another great benefit of this card is the ability to earn a $150 American Airlines flight discount (after spending $20,000 or more on purchases during your card membership year and renewing your card; increasing from $125 starting Jan. 24, 2027).

To learn more, read our full review of the Citi / AA Platinum Select.

Apply here: Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select World Elite Mastercard

The Citi / AA MileUp is Citi’s entry-level American Airlines product.

Best for: Beginners looking to earn American Airlines miles

Welcome bonus: Earn 15,000 bonus miles and a $100 statement credit after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

According to TPG’s valuations, this welcome bonus is worth $318 (including the statement credit). The statement credit is a sweetener on top of the standard amount of miles, making now a good time to apply.

If you’re a beginner looking for an inexpensive way to earn American miles, this could be a good entry point into the Citi AAdvantage credit card lineup.

As a no-annual-fee card, it offers few perks, but you will get 25% savings on inflight drinks and snacks.

However, anyone taking more than a couple of American Airlines flights per year will likely be better off with an American Airlines card that charges an annual fee, since those cards offer higher earning rates (in select categories) and more valuable perks.

To learn more, read our full review of the Citi / AA MileUp.

Related: My beginner's blueprint to find the flight awards you want

Citi doesn’t limit the total number of credit cards you can hold, but it does cap your overall credit line across accounts.

You can only apply for one card every eight days, no more than two cards in 65 days and just one business card every 90 days.

Finally, Citi’s 48-month rule means you can’t earn a welcome bonus on the same AAdvantage card if you’ve received that bonus within the past four years.

Whether you’re after entry-level earning, mid-tier perks or premium Admirals Club access, there’s a Citi / AAdvantage card for a range of American Airlines flyers.
