#6215. WestJet Vs. Porter Airlines: Which Carrier Is More Premium In 2026?

Canadian air travel has long been defined by a strict dual-class hierarchy, with flag carriers drawing a hard line between elite business class amenities and standard main cabin seating. However, as Porter Airlines aggressively expands its fleet of Embraer E195-E2 jets from coast to coast, the definition of a premium domestic flight has undergone a dramatic transformation. WestJet counters by refining its Boeing 787-9business class and rolling out high-speed Starlink WiFi across its narrowbody fleet, so now, Canadian travelers face two fundamentally different visions of luxury.

Deciding which airline holds the true premium crown depends entirely on whether a passenger values front-of-cabin hard product hardware or an upgraded baseline economy experience. As both carriers vie for market share across transcontinental and transborder routes, comparing their cabin products, seat pitches, and inflight services is more important than ever before booking.

WestJet offers the superior high-end premium product, while Porter Airlines delivers a far more upscale everyday experience for the average passenger. WestJet’s top-tier product is its business class cabin on the 787-9, which features fully lie-flat seats, direct aisle access, premium dining, and dedicated lounge access on long-haul routes. Conversely, Porter does not fly widebody aircraft or offer lie-flat seats, instead focusing on what it markets as an elevated economy experience across its entire fleet.

The fundamental difference lies in how each airline treats the main cabin. As per Seat Maps, Porter’s E195-E2 jets feature a two-by-two seating configuration with no middle seats, complimentary beer and wine served in real glassware, premium Canadian snacks, and fast, free WiFi for every passenger. WestJet’s narrowbody Boeing 737 fleet sticks to a traditional three-by-three layout in economy, where middle seats remain standard and buy-on-board food and drink policies apply.

Ultimately, WestJet wins for long-haul luxury and dedicated premium seating upfront, whereas Porter wins for overall comfort and inflight amenities in the main cabin. For anyone seeking true intercontinental luxury, complete with fully lie-flat suites, direct aisle access, multi-course dining, and dedicated airport lounge access, WestJet’s 787-9 fleet provides a full-service hard product that Porter cannot match. However, for standard domestic economy travel, Porter completely reshapes expectations by removing the dreaded middle seat across its entire E195-E2 fleet.

On narrowbody routes, WestJet’s premium product is WestJet Premium, situated in the forward rows of its 737s. This dedicated cabin features much wider recliner seats in a two-by-two layout, 37 inches to 38 inches (94 centimeters to 97 centimeters) of seat pitch, hot meal choices, and complimentary alcoholic drinks served on multi-hour flights.

Porter takes a different hardware approach with its top fare, PorterReserve. Rather than installing wider business-class seats, PorterReserve utilizes the same two-by-two seat frame found throughout the E195-E2 cabin, but expands seat pitch substantially to 36 inches (91 centimeters) across the first four rows. Instead of a wider chair, PorterReserve is a fully bundled, all-inclusive fare tier that includes fresh meals, pre-mixed cocktails, dedicated airport check-in, priority security screening, early boarding, two free checked bags, and fee-free flight changes.

On shorter domestic hops, PorterReserve frequently delivers comparable legroom and superior soft-product perks at a fraction of the cost of traditional business class. However, on transcontinental flights exceeding four hours, flyers seeking a true widebody recliner or lie-flat bed will find WestJet’s hardware significantly more comfortable.

They are from four Canadian airports. Discover them all here!

Aviation analysts and industry reviewers frequently frame PorterReserve not as a traditional business class, but as an enhanced, all-inclusive economy product. A September 2026 review by Frugal Flyer noted that even though PorterReserve falls short of international long-haul business class standards, citing cold meals served in cardboard packaging and standard seat padding, its price-to-value ratio directly challenges Air Canada’s domestic business class and WestJet Premium. The reviewer concluded that Porter is best understood as an upgraded, hassle-free way to fly economy without surprise add-on fees.

Porter’s strategy of democratizing cabin comfort has earned substantial industry accolades. Passengers voted Porter an APEX Four Star Major Airline, while the carrier also earned USA Today’s Readers’ Choice award for Best Economy Class and was named Skytrax’s Best Regional Airline in North America.

Meanwhile, WestJet continues to defend its premium positioning by expanding its long-haul Dreamliner network across Europe and Asia, operating non-stop routes as long as Calgary International Airport (YYC) to Rome Fiumicino Airport (FCO). WestJet executives emphasize that their two-tier strategy, combining international widebody luxury with a high-density regional fleet, provides the full-service flexibility that global business travelers demand, as reported by AvioRadar.

When compared with Canada's flag carrier, Air Canada, both WestJet and Porter fill distinct operational niches in the domestic and transborder markets. Air Canada’s Signature Class on Boeing 787, 777, and Airbus A330 aircraft remains the traditional benchmark for long-haul business class in North America, featuring private executive pods and extensive Maple Leaf Lounge networks. However, on domestic and transborder narrowbody routes, Air Canada’s standard economy cabin features the same three-by-three seating grid and buy-on-board food service found across WestJet’s 737 fleet.

Against low-cost alternatives like Flair Airlines, Porter and WestJet sit in a completely different tier of reliability and service. Ultra-low-cost carriers strip away all passenger amenities to offer bare-bones transport, whereas Porter elevates the baseline flight experience without charging flag-carrier premium prices. Meanwhile, WestJet approaches its own soft product differentiation by offering a spectrum of products ranging from ultra-basic economy up to widebody transcontinental business suites.

This positioning explains why customer choice varies so much by market segment. For price-sensitive travelers wanting an uncompromised economy flight, Porter beats both Air Canada and WestJet on value. However, for corporate travelers who rely on alliance connections, global lounge access, or international lie-flat seats, traditional network carriers like Air Canada and WestJet are still considered the necessary choice.

Montreal's new $450 million airport, YHU, aims to avoid Mirabel's pitfalls by focusing on domestic convenience rather than international prestige.

It is clear that Porter’s product highlights are compelling, but there are very real and impactful trade-offs that exist, trade-offs that travelers really need to evaluate carefully before booking. Network scale and schedule redundancy are the major factors to keep a close eye on as Porter’s jet fleet and route map, though expanding rapidly across North America, is a fraction of the size of Canada's traditional market leaders. If an aircraft suffers a mechanical delay or severe weather cancellation, WestJet’s broader fleet and dense flight schedules offer far more daily rebooking options to help stranded travelers recover. Passengers on thin Porter routes may face significantly longer wait times for the next available seat during irregular operations.

Rapid network expansion also introduces operational strain that directly impacts schedule reliability. Industry tracking data from Cirium records Porter’s on-time arrival rate trailing competitors at 71.9%, compared to WestJet’s 73.6% on-time performance. In real-world terms, this gap means a higher likelihood of flight delays for passengers working around tight connection windows or strict business itineraries. Combined with Porter’s leaner fleet infrastructure, a single delayed turnaround can trigger compounding schedule slippage throughout the day, whereas WestJet's operational scale lets it manage aircraft swaps and delay buffers more effectively across its main hub channels.

None (Embraer E195-E2 / Dash 8-Q400 only)

2-2 across entire jet fleet (zero middle seats)

Passengers that are accustomed to traditional business-class perks should note that PorterReserve does not grant access to third-party airport lounges. Those seeking quiet terminal spaces or complimentary meals before departure must rely on independent credit card lounge passes or opt for WestJet Premium and Business fares. Additionally, dual-airport cities present routing traps, as Porter operates out of both Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ) and Billy Bishop Toronto City Centre Airport (YTZ), meaning travelers need to double-check departure locations to avoid costly airport mix-ups.

The rivalry between WestJet and Porter Airlines in 2026 shows a clear division of passenger priorities across North American skies. If your primary goal is securing a true lie-flat suite on an international flight, or sitting in a wide, dedicated recliner seat with lounge access on a long transcontinental route, WestJet offers the superior hardware product.

However, for short-haul regional routes and transcontinental travel in standard economy, Porter delivers an unmatched base experience. With zero middle seats, free fast Wi-Fi, and an amazing drinks service included for every single passenger, Porter has successfully raised the bar for everyday domestic air travel.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

When choosing between the two Canadian carriers, the best way to make the right choice is to take a closer look at specific aircraft types and total route duration. For quick two-to-three-hour hops, Porter’s standard cabin or PorterReserve fare offers extraordinary overall value. For long-haul intercontinental journeys where seat width and flat-bed rest are paramount, WestJet’s premium cabins will be the definitive choice.

#6214. Southwest’s New Credit Card Bonuses Offer Up To 90,000 Points Toward Companion Pass—Last Chance Before Rules Change

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Southwest’s Companion Pass lets someone fly with you for just taxes and fees, even when you redeem points for your own ticket. For someone who flies Southwest with a partner a few times a year, it’s the single best deal in domestic air travel. And the easiest way to earn it is about to disappear.

There’s still a final window to use an 80,000- or 90,000-point credit card initial bonus toward a pass valid through December 31, 2027. You need to apply by December 2, 2026 and get approved. Neither bonus gets you all the way there on its own, but both give you a huge head start.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. It has a $229 annual fee. This is the premium Southwest co-brand card, really designed for folks who fly the airline. It makes those trips better, and spending helps earn both elite status and Companion Pass®. The travel benefits cover the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation: First checked bag free. Preferred or Standard seat selection at booking, at no additional charge, when available. Extra Legroom seat upgrades within 48 hours of departure, at no additional charge, when available. Boarding with Group 5 or earlier if another benefit qualifies you for a better group. You earn 4 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, including flights, inflight purchases and Southwest gift cards; 2 points per dollar at gas stations and restaurants; and 1 point per dollar on other purchases. There are also 7,500 anniversary points each year. The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. Its annual fee is $99. That’s a much lower spending requirement for a bonus that’s only 10,000 points smaller. First checked bag free for the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation. Standard seat selection within 48 hours of departure, when available, for the same group of travelers. Group 5 boarding or earlier if you otherwise qualify. 3,000 anniversary points each year, plus a 10% anniversary flight discount code that excludes Basic fares. The Plus card earns 2 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, and 2 points per dollar at gas stations and grocery stores on the first $5,000 in combined purchases per anniversary year. Other purchases earn 1 point per dollar. I’d choose Plus for the lower cost of getting the bonus. Priority costs $130 more per year, but gives you better seat benefits, 4,500 more anniversary points and a larger initial bonus. For a family that flies Southwest regularly, those seating benefits can easily be worth the difference. How Close These Bonuses Get You To Companion Pass Under the 2026 rules, earning 135,000 Companion Pass qualifying points in a calendar year gets you the pass for the rest of that year and the following year. Southwest credit card customers receive a 10,000-point qualifying boost, so they effectively need 125,000 more. Priority: 90,000 bonus points plus the 10,000-point boost gets you to 100,000. You need another 35,000 qualifying points. Plus: 80,000 bonus points plus the 10,000-point boost gets you to 90,000. You need another 45,000 qualifying points. The purchases you make to earn the bonus also earn points. Assuming those purchase points post in 2026, spending the minimum at 1 point per dollar reduces the remaining gap to 32,000 points with Priority or 44,000 with Plus. Bonus category spending and qualifying points you’ve already earned reduce it further. Qualifying flights and eligible partner activity can help fill the gap, too. Check your Companion Pass progress in your account. Once you have the pass, book your own Southwest flight with cash or points and add your designated companion, as long as there’s an available seat. Their taxes and fees start at $5.60 one-way. You can use the benefit repeatedly and change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. How Optimal Timing Of The Companion Pass Has Changed As I covered in Southwest’s 2027 Rapid Rewards overhaul, unlimited Companion Pass becomes a benefit of the new Platinum elite tier next year. Initial bonuses generally stop helping you qualify. Anniversary points, referral bonuses and extra points from card bonus categories stop counting, too. Southwest’s transition exception preserves the initial bonus for customers who apply by December 2, 2026, are approved, and meet the offer’s requirements. Even if you finish the required spending in early 2027, the bonus can count toward 2026 qualification for a pass ending December 31, 2027. So the old strategy of waiting until January to earn nearly two years of Companion Pass doesn’t work here. A bonus earned under this exception won’t get you a pass through the end of 2028. And Chase’s terms distinguish the initial bonus from ordinary purchase points. Those purchase points must post to your Rapid Rewards account in 2026 to count toward this pass. Spending after your December statement closes generally posts in January. You also want the 10,000-point qualifying boost credited in 2026; Southwest allows up to 30 days after account opening for it to arrive. You still have to meet the initial bonus spending requirement within the first 3 months from account opening. The transition rule doesn’t extend that deadline. I’m a former Companion Pass holder, and a promotional Companion Pass holder.Southwest still represents about 40% of the seats out of my home airport in Austin. Even with all the changes they’ve made, being able to bring someone along on those flights for just the taxes is huge. Before applying, you can’t currently hold a Southwest personal credit card, and you can’t have received an initial bonus on any Southwest personal card in the past 24 months. Southwest business and employee cards are excluded from that restriction. Chase’s usual 5/24 rule also applies: generally, you need fewer than 5 new credit card accounts on your credit report in the past 24 months. If you’re eligible, can handle the required spending, and have a path to the remaining qualifying points, I’d take advantage of this before December 2. #6213. Southwest Premier Business Card Review: Is The $149 Annual Fee Worth It?

The Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Premier Business Credit Card is the more basic of the two Southwest business cards. This card has a $149 annual fee, and gets you a handful of valuable benefits when you fly Southwest, including complimentary upgrades to Preferred seating within 48 hours of departure and a free checked bag, among other things.

If you fly Southwest at least a few times a year and you qualify for a small business credit card, the Southwest Premier Business Card is worth considering. It’s worth an extra close look right now, because now is your last chance to earn a Southwest credit card welcome bonus that counts toward the airline’s valuable Companion Pass benefit. I’ll get into all that and more below in my comprehensive Southwest Premier Business Card review.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Premier Business Credit Card

Before getting into the Southwest Premier Business Card in detail, let’s take a broader look at the card’s main features:

I also put together my pros and cons for the Southwest Premier Business Card:

The Southwest Premier Business Card is Southwest’s entry-level business credit card. Let’s take a look at the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and annual fee, given that these are factors that many people consider when applying for a card.

The Southwest Premier Business Card currently has a welcome bonus where you can earn 60,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 within the first three months.

Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each, as that’s roughly the rate at which you can redeem points toward flights. So by my valuation, 60,000 Rapid Rewards points are worth ~$720.

While this is a decent welcome offer, let me note that we’ve seen bigger limited time welcome offers in the past. So if you’re primarily after the best welcome offer, it could make sense to wait to apply.

The welcome bonus on the Southwest Premier Business Card isn’t available to those who currently have this card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on this card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible for this card (including the welcome bonus) if you have the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more), or any personal Southwest credit card.

Also remember Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, apply. With the 5/24 rule, you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the last 24 months. However, business credit cards aren’t always included on your credit report, so they often don’t count toward 5/24.

The Southwest Premier Business Card has a $149 annual fee. There’s no cost to add additional users to the card. You can set individual spending limits for additional cards, and you can earn points on their spending.

The Southwest Premier Business Card doesn’t charge any foreign transaction fees, so you can use it abroad without worrying about racking up extra charges.

Obviously the rewards structure is an important factor to consider when applying for a credit card. So how does the Southwest Premier Business Card do on that front? In addition to offering bonus points in select spending categories, the card also offers the ability to earn status through spending, so let’s cover those details.

As far as the rewards structure goes, the Southwest Premier Business Card offers:

While these are some good bonus categories, I wouldn’t consider this to be an industry-leading rewards structure — there are better cards for airfare spending, and better cards for everyday spending.

Based on my valuation of Southwest points at 1.2 cents each, using the Southwest Premier Business Card to book Southwest flights gets you a 3.6% return on spending, while the 2x and 1x categories get you 2.4% and 1.2% returns on spending, respectively.

Spending on the Southwest Premier Business Card can count toward A-List elite status. Specifically, through the end of 2026 you can earn 2,000 Tier Qualifying Points (TQPs) toward A-List for every $5,000 you spend on the card. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on the card will earn one TQP.

A-List status ordinarily requires 35,000 TQPs per year, and offers perks like priority boarding, a 25% points bonus, same-day standby, priority check-in and security lane access, and a dedicated phone number.

However, Southwest has announced some big changes to its loyalty program, including new status level names and the introduction of a third tier called Platinum. Starting in 2027, A-List status will become Silver status. Earning it will require 35,000 TQPs (unchanged) or 25 qualifying flights (up from 20 today).

Personally I probably wouldn’t spend that much money on a credit card to earn A-List status, but for some people this could prove to be worthwhile, especially if you’re close to earning A-List status otherwise.

One of the very best values in travel is the Southwest Airlines Companion Pass. With Southwest Companion Pass, you can have someone travel with you for the entire year (whether on a cash ticket or award ticket), and just pay taxes and fees for them. This is such an incredible deal, and basically doubles the value you can get from flying Southwest. The pass is valid for the rest of the calendar year in which you earn it plus the following full year, so the earlier in the year you earn it, the more it’s worth.

Historically, you’ve been able to get the Companion Pass by earning 135,000 Rapid Rewards points in a calendar year — and Southwest credit card welcome bonuses counted toward this, along with referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending on the card, and more. Starting January 1, 2027, though, this will no longer be the case.

Southwest is updating its elite status program to have three tiers, the highest of which is called Platinum and gets you unlimited Companion Pass trips. At that time, credit card welcome bonuses and all the other points earning mentioned above will no longer count toward qualifying for the Companion Pass (or any level of status).

To earn Platinum, and therefore the Companion Pass, you’ll instead need to earn 140,000 TQPs or take 100 qualifying flights. This change isn’t specific to the Southwest Premier Business Card; it applies to welcome bonuses across all Southwest credit cards. But the good news is that points from the current welcome bonus offer do count toward Companion Pass qualification for the rest of 2026 and through 2027, per Chase’s offer details, so now is your last chance to take advantage before this opportunity is closed.

I have an entire post on how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but I’ll briefly cover how redemptions work and how to get the most value out of your points here.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, which means that the value you’ll get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. That said, there are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, with Basic awards usually offering the highest redemption value.

In my experience, the best-value Southwest point redemptions are usually for international routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. Southwest also flies to Hawaii, which can be a good use of points, but I’ve found that the redemption value is often a bit lower on these in-demand routes. And of course, if you have the Companion Pass your points become twice as valuable because a friend can travel for free minus taxes and fees.

There are no change or cancellation fees on Southwest award bookings, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d want to cancel and rebook rather than change your existing itinerary.

The Southwest Premier Business Card has a solid welcome bonus that’s especially valuable now that it’s your last chance to earn it and have it count toward the Companion Pass, but that’s not the only reason to consider this card. There are also several ongoing perks that can make your experience flying Southwest a little more comfortable.

One major ongoing perk of the Southwest Premier Business Card is that you earn 6,000 Rapid Rewards bonus points on your account anniversary every year. As mentioned above, I value Rapid Rewards points at around 1.2 cents each, so to me, that’s like $72 worth of value annually.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers a free first checked bag for you and up to eight additional passengers on your same reservation.

If you usually check bags on Southwest — especially if you don’t have Southwest status, which gets you a free first checked bag — this benefit alone can help you recoup the annual fee. For non-elite Southwest travelers, a checked bag costs $45 one-way, so you could save $90 on a roundtrip flight. With two roundtrip flights with checked bags in a year, that already cancels out the $149 annual fee.

As a Southwest Premier Business cardholder, you can select a Preferred or Standard seat within 48 hours prior to departure, if they’re available. This benefit also extends to eight travelers on your same reservation. The cost for a Preferred seat can vary from $28 to nearly $50 depending on the flight.

The Southwest Premier Business Card also gets you a 15% promo code each year on your account anniversary. You can use this to score a 15% discount on a Southwest flight, excluding Basic fares. This perk is another nice way the card can save you money when flying Southwest, especially if you book cash tickets in addition to award flights at least once a year.

Southwest Premier Business cardholders can board with Group 5, or earlier if they have status or a fare that entitles them to a higher boarding group. This perk extends to eight additional travelers on the same reservation.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers 25% savings on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases on Southwest. Just charge your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for 25% of the purchase total, which should appear within two billing cycles.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers a great welcome bonus, and the $149 annual fee can be largely offset by the 6,000 anniversary bonus points and other benefits. The welcome bonus can also go a long way toward earning the Companion Pass, which is all the more reason to get the card now before this opportunity ends.

That said, I don’t necessarily think the Southwest Premier Business Card is a great pick for everyone. If you’re not loyal to Southwest or you split flying across multiple airlines, it’s probably not the best card for you. And if you want flexible points that you can redeem with a variety of airlines and hotels, it could also be best to skip this card.

First, let me compare it to the more premium Southwest Performance Business Card, then I’ll share the points currency I recommend earning instead if you’re mainly concerned with booking award flights on Southwest, not extra perks with the airline.

The Southwest Performance Business Card (learn more) is the more premium sibling of the Southwest Premier Business Card. Overall it comes with more benefits — and in some cases enhanced versions of the same perks on the Southwest Premier Business Card.

Here’s a quick overview of how the Southwest business credit cards compare:

The extra 3,000 anniversary points are worth $36 by my valuation, so you’d need roughly $9,500 in Southwest spending for the extra point per dollar to cover the rest of the $150 fee difference, before counting the seating and Global Entry perks.

If you fly Southwest several times a year and you want as many perks and points as possible, the Southwest Performance Business Card could be worth the higher annual fee.

If your goal is to earn Southwest Rapid Rewards points, but you don’t actually plan on earning the Companion Pass or Southwest status, there’s a much faster way to earn those points.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. You can earn points at a much faster rate with the following business cards:

The Southwest Premier Business Card is a good entry-level Southwest Airlines business credit card with a nice welcome bonus. The current bonus can earn you a lot of travel on Southwest, and can even help you earn Companion Pass — but only if you earn the bonus under the current offer, before the 2027 program changes take effect.

This card is definitely worth considering, though the only other consideration is that I think it could be worth paying the premium for the Southwest Performance Business Card, which has better ongoing perks. And earning Ultimate Rewards points with a Chase credit card could also make more sense unless you really value the Southwest-specific benefits.

Which Southwest business credit card do you prefer?

Gone are the days of the “sure thing” complimentary upgrade. But, for those who find themselves on the road more than once a month, top-tier elite status can mean the difference between being there for that special family event or a disappointing night in an airport hotel.

Due to a ton of work travel, I currently hold top-tier status in the Big Three US airline elite programs. As a Northern Virginia resident, United is my primary airline, and I earned its invitation-only Global Services status again this year. As I was trying to figure out which of these three status levels was the most rewarding, I realized I may not even have the best elite status in North America.

No, I’m not talking about Southwest Airlines A-List Preferred status. I think there’s a reasonable argument for looking north.

Air Canada Aeroplan Super Elite status may actually be better for many frequent travelers, even if it seems complicated as a U.S. resident.

Here are a few reasons to consider earning Super Elite status.

One area where Aeroplan really shines is lounge access — a perk that even top-tier elites at most U.S. airlines can't count on when flying domestically.

Super Elite members can bring immediate family into any Maple Leaf Lounge as well as an additional guest. Delta Diamond, United 1K and American Executive Platinum members get no complimentary lounge access as a benefit of their status.

While Aeroplan doesn’t grant access to their Signature Suites lounges, Super Elites can enjoy lounge access with partner airlines such as Emirates and Virgin Australia. They also have access to an arrivals lounge at London Heathrow.

Arguably one of the most valuable benefits of Super Elite status is Priority Rewards. With few exceptions, a Priority Reward can be redeemed for a 50% discount on a one-way or round-trip flight, including on partner airlines (and Air Canada has a lot of partners).

Aeroplan members can earn these rewards multiple times each year as part of Milestone Benefits.

If you hold 25K status, your Priority Rewards are valid on economy flights in Canada and the United States (including Hawaii). However, Super Elites can redeem them for all cabins up to and including business class, including on partner airlines.

When you consider the pricing of international business class award flights, it’s not hard to imagine saving 100,000 Aeroplan points or more when redeeming a Priority Reward on a round-trip ticket.

You can book a flight for someone else, even if they’re not immediate family, so long as you use your Aeroplan points.

If you travel as much as I do, you might consider the Air Canada Concierge Service to rival Priority Rewards in value. Super Elite members get access to a personalized concierge service.

Reports from Super Elite members indicate that Air Canada concierges have a healthy amount of autonomy to fix problems while you’re traveling, including moving you to other airlines to get you to your destination as quickly as possible. In many major airports, Air Canada has local concierges, so the support is right where you need it.

This level of service used to be commonplace with the U.S. carriers. While invitation-only levels such as United Global Services offer more flexible rules during irregular operations, my personal experience over the past few years is that many tools that used to be available to those agents have been restricted or removed.

How does a U.S. resident earn Super Elite status? It’s a bit complicated, but you have options. Cabotage restrictions prevent an airline like Air Canada from flying you between New York and Los Angeles, even if you connect in a Canadian gateway.

However, if you travel internationally, especially in a premium cabin, Air Canada is well situated to get you to many places in Europe and Asia. With hubs in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver, AIr Canada can connect you to Europe and Asia. It may be easy to forget Toronto as an option if you live in Ohio or Indiana and need to fly to France.

The Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card (see ) is also a great way to accelerate your quest for Super Elite status. Just holding the card gives you 5,000 Status Qualifying Credits each calendar year and entry-level 25K elite status. Spending on the card can earn another 20,000 Status Qualifying Credits. That means the credit card alone can get you 20% of the way to Super Elite.

Top-tier elite status is largely similar among American, Delta and United. While Air Canada shares many of the same benefits with them, Aeroplan has a few key benefits that set Super Elite status apart.

Priority Rewards allow your mileage balance to punch above its weight. Lounge access and a dedicated concierge service can make travel much smoother, even on the toughest days. And a few business class tickets to Europe can quickly put you in the range of Aeroplan Super Elite status.

#6211. Hyatt Dining & Spa Awards: Are They Worth Redeeming Points For?

While the most popular way to redeem World of Hyatt points is for free night award redemptions, there are some lesser known ways to redeem Hyatt points. One of those is the ability to use points for Dining & Spa awards, which can be a surprisingly good deal.

This doesn’t get a lot of attention, and it’s particularly useful if you want to minimize your out-of-pocket when staying at a Hyatt property, while still indulging in on-property experiences.

Most people don’t realize that you can redeem World of Hyatt points toward the cost of on-property dining and spa experiences, and the value proposition can be surprisingly good. Specifically, you can redeem a certain number of points for a certain amount of credit to use toward on-property spending, even if you’re not staying at a Hyatt property. Let’s take a closer look at how this works.

Below is a chart showing the various redemption opportunities available with Hyatt’s Dining & Spa awards, along with how much value you can potentially get per point:

As you can see, you can redeem anywhere from 1,000 points for a $10 credit, to 65,000 points for a $1,000 credit. The value per point ranges anywhere from 1.0 cents per point, to 1.54 cents per point.

1.54 cents per World of Hyatt point sounds like a solid deal. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, World of Hyatt points are worth 1.4 cents each, so this actually offers solid value, at least on the surface. Is there a catch, though?

The exact redemptions that are allowed vary by hotel, but generally you can expect that these awards can be used for food and beverage purchases, spa and salon services, and spa and salon retail items.

On top of that, when charged to a member’s guest room, the following charges may be eligible:

laundry, dry cleaning, telephone charges, pay-per-view movies, parking, gift/retail shop, service charges, taxes (not including room taxes) and gratuities

Meanwhile the following charges are expressly prohibited from being eligible:

room rates, room taxes, alcoholic beverages (in certain jurisdictions), catering or banquet charges, and casino charges

If you’re staying at a Hyatt then you should be able to redeem these awards for cumulative charges over the course of your stay. However, I’d recommend confirming this with the front desk at check-in, including which outlets would be eligible for these redemptions, since individual hotels could have different policies.

Not all Hyatt hotels participate in this program. Miraval, Unscripted by Hyatt, Hyatt Select, Destination by Hyatt, Hyatt Vacation Club properties, Hyatt Vivid, Bahia Principe, Impression by Secrets, Secrets, Dreams, Breathless, Zoëtry, Alua, Sunscape, and other Legacy AMR Collection resorts, as well as some Dream properties, do not participate. Furthermore, redemption of these certificates is limited to registered guests at Hyatt Zilara, Hyatt Ziva, and Hyatt Studios properties.

To be positive, you can search participating properties at this page.

You don’t need to redeem for these certificates in advance, but rather the World of Hyatt member should just inform the Hyatt employee at the eligible outlet that they’d like to redeem points toward their purchase at the outset. You’ll need to have your membership information, and should then be asked how many points you want to redeem.

If you’re a registered guest at a hotel then you can apply one of these at check-out toward multiple purchases over the course of a stay. If you’re not a registered guest then you’ll have to settle your folio at the particular outlet you’re at.

There are a few other things to potentially be aware of:

On the surface, being able to redeem World of Hyatt points for up to ~1.54 cents toward the cost of a purchase is a solid deal. Is it exceptional? No. But as a way of essentially “cashing out” your points to offset cash costs I think it’s very good.

I do think it’s important to create a more realistic valuation of these redemptions, though. When you redeem these awards you’re forgoing the opportunity to earn points on these purchases:

As a Globalist member I earn 10.5x points per dollar spent, which I value at a return of ~15% (1.4 cents per point). That’s an opportunity cost that’s worth factoring in, so in reality, I’d adjust the maximum value from 1.54 cents to ~1.3 cents.

Personally, this isn’t how I’d redeem my World of Hyatt points, though I do think many people could find this to be worthwhile for a splurge:

World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, allowing members to redeem points for dining and spa experiences at most Hyatt properties. This has the potential to be a solid deal, as getting 1.54 cents per Hyatt point toward the cost of a purchase is a good redemption. However, do factor in the points you’re forgoing, which brings down the redemption value a bit.

While I wouldn’t say this is the best way to redeem Hyatt points, this could be worth it to lower how much cash you’ll pay for a Hyatt stay, especially at a secluded resort where you’re likely to spend most time on-property.

What do you make of Hyatt’s Dining & Spa awards? Could you see yourself redeeming points for them?

#6209. 59-Room Andaz Turks & Caicos At Grace Bay Opening April 2027, Now Bookable

The much delayed Andaz Turks & Caicos is getting closer to opening. The hotel has now moved forward the date as of which it’s accepting reservations, and we’ve also learned more details about the on-property amenities. Let’s cover all the details, as we’re potentially under five months from the opening…

The Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. This will mark Hyatt’s first hotel in Turks & Caicos, and the first Andaz property in the Caribbean. For that matter, it’s one of the only Andaz properties that’s currently in the pipeline outside of Asia, as the brand has really lost steam.

The 5.5-acre resort will offer four restaurants and bars, three outdoor pools, a spa, a kids club, a fitness center, tennis and pickleball courts, and more. The Andaz will be comprised of 59 rooms and 73 branded residences, so at least the hotel portion of the property will be boutique. It’ll be located directly on Grace Bay, known for offering one of the most beautiful stretches of beach in the Caribbean.

As far as the culinary concepts go, the Andaz Turks & Caicos will feature the following:

Runa Spa & Wellness, the spa at the Andaz, will be around 7,000 square feet. It will have five treatment rooms, along with a sauna, cold plunge, relaxation area, and more.

The opening of this resort has been majorly delayed. It was initially announced in 2018 with a 2021 opening, but the timeline slipped by six years, presumably due to a combination of the pandemic, plus… well, how hotel construction projects often work out. Hopefully there are no additional delays beyond the current planned spring 2027 opening.

With the Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay bookable, what are rates like? For those redeeming points, this is a Category 8 World of Hyatt property, meaning a free night redemption in a standard room costs 35,000-75,000 points per night.

World of Hyatt’s new award chart sure makes top end redemptions expensive, unfortunately! As of now the hotel is primarily bookable between April and November of 2027, so this doesn’t really cover peak season. For most dates, I currently see rates of either 35,000 points, 45,000 points, or 55,000 points per night. So value here is highly dependent on which of those rates you can find.

When it comes to cash rates, those currently start at around $900-1,300 per night, and that depends on when you’re staying. That’s inclusive of the service charge, but exclusive of the taxes.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, complimentary breakfast, and a hotel credit.

I suppose good options on Grace Bay are limited, and this hotel is boutique. But at these rates, they better offer something significantly better than the typical Andaz experience, in my opinion.

Turks & Caicos is absolutely beautiful, and it’s an easy getaway from the United States, given how close it is to Florida. Historically, the country hasn’t had that many points hotels, though that’s slowly starting to change.

Several years back, we saw the opening of the Ritz-Carlton Turks & Caicos. It has an amazing location on Grace Bay and the grounds of the property are beautiful, but it otherwise doesn’t feel very luxurious, and lacks personality.

So it’ll be nice to have another points property, and I look forward to learning more about the Andaz. Maybe I’m overly optimistic, but I think the Andaz might just end up offering a better experience than the Ritz-Carlton, at least based on the design renderings, and also the more boutique scale of the property. Andaz really is quite an inconsistent brand.

I of course should acknowledge that many people are understandably frustrated by the way that Grace Bay has developed over the years, given all the huge concrete towers that have taken shape along the beach. It has definitely lost its charm a bit, though the beach is still gorgeous.

Even beyond Grace Bay, we’re seeing some other great new options in Turks & Caicos. In 2025, we saw the opening of Salterra Turks & Caicos, a Marriott Luxury Collection property. This is great for those who want a bit more secluded of a trip, since South Caicos Island is a bit less crowded than the area around Providenciales. This is also where Sailrock Resort is located, which is an independent hotel affiliated with Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH).

There’s also a Waldorf Astoria Turks & Caicos planned for a 2028 opening, located on Dellis Cay, a nearby island that’s not as developed, which can be reached by a 25-minute boat transfer from Providenciales. That should also be a great option, especially with how the Waldorf Astoria portfolio is developing. However, don’t count on that timeline sticking either.

The Andaz Turks & Caicos is accepting reservations for stays as of April 2027, and it will be located on the famous Grace Bay. The property will have just 59 hotel rooms, in addition to residences, so I like how it’s on a smaller scale than some other properties.

This should be a very nice addition to the Caribbean points hotel market. Hopefully we don’t see any additional delays with the opening…

What do you make of the upcoming Andaz Turks & Caicos?

Grace Bay is the right spot for it. Snorkel Bight Reef right off the beach, then the Thursday Fish Fry at Bight Park is the local night out. Da Conch Shack in Blue Hills is worth the short drive for cracked conch with your feet in the sand. Chalk Sound is the place for a calm turquoise kayak. FWIW a free planner like Wanderlog makes it easy to pin all of that around the hotel. I’d wait a month or two after opening unless you’re fine with soft-opening hiccups

Andaz is such a crappy, limited-service brand with an inflated price tag. Grace Bay is also wildly overbuilt. Much better off at COMO Parrot Cay. Amanyara is the worst Aman at which I have stayed.

Burning Hyatt points on this is probably better value than $1,500+ at Amanyara… (or what are they going to call it if the dispute with the owner isn’t resolved? New Janu nearby, etc.)

#6208. Use Lyft For Work? How To Get 6%–8% Back, Plus Extra Airline Or Hotel Points

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

I have a personal preference for Lyft, as regular readers know. One of the things that I really like is that they have the best rewards in rideshare. But I didn’t realize things get even more lucrative for business travelers using a Lyft business profile. They have benefits, like:

keeping all of your regular rewards to use on personal or business rides. earning with Lyft’s airline or hotel partners goes up significantly for eligible business travelers. and pocketing 6% – 8% back in Lyft Credits on business profile rides, to use on your own rides later. That’s why it makes sense to sign up for a business account. Bonus, it lets you separate personal and business rides, which makes expense management easier (and you won’t mistakenly apply personal credits to reimbursable trips as I sometimes do by accident). Earn Lyft Credits On Top of Travel Rewards The original idea of a frequent flyer program was that you’d earn rewards on business travel. Your employer pays for a ticket, you benefit personally with your miles. That kept you loyal. This is really the same idea that the airlines pioneered about 45 years ago. When you ride for work, you can get Lyft Credits to use on your own trips later – 6% for standard rides taken with your business profile and 8% for premium, airport, and scheduled business profile rides. And you can do this even while earning with your preferred travel partner, and you earn those points or miles faster than you do with a personal account (where I’ve already been happy with the points-earning). How To Join I already use Lyft for business travel, so enrolling is a no-brainer since it’s fast and free and you accelerate your earnings. This also lets you bill a business card or directly to your employer and it integrates with popular expense tools. Lyft estimates that over half of business travelers forget to take advantage of automatic company expensing, leading to missed rewards and lack of visibility for organizations. Can We Just Appreciate Rideshare For A Moment? For most of my life there was no such thing as rideshare. For a brief time in Austin where I live, the city government chased it away, and I actually had to re-learn how to get to the airport. Now I pull up my Lyft app and I’m frustrated if I see that my driver is six minutes away. Six minutes. That’s my complaint. A stranger is coming to my exact location, in their personal car, because I touched glass. That’s sorcery with seatbelts. It used to be that you had to stand on the curb with your arm out like the Statue of Liberty, just waving at traffic. “Please! Someone! I have money and a destination!” And the taxis would just drive by. Sometimes they’d slow down just enough to let you experience hope before crushing it. You’d make eye contact with the driver. He’d look at you, look through you, and drive right past. And if it rained? You were done. Some cab would blast through a puddle and soak you like you’re Carrie Bradshaw in Sex and the City. Now you press a button and a tiny map shows you a little car cartoon coming toward you. You get in, you get out. Start to finish, it’s frictionless. And to top it off, you even get rewarded for it. Just by using a business profile, you can earn Lyft Credits and extra travel points or miles on rides your company is already paying for. George Clooney said it best in Up In The Air, “I don’t spend a nickel if I can help it unless it somehow benefits my mileage account.” Your company is spending the nickel. You might as well get the miles. #6206. How Perth Easily Became Australia's Gateway To Europe

Australian travelers bound for Europe have always had to face a two-stage journey, with a domestic transcontinental flight to an east-coast hub, followed by a long-haul connection through the Middle East or Southeast Asia. There is one location that bucks this trend, that being Perth. Sitting nearly 2,000 miles (3,218 km) closer to London than Sydney, quietly positioned Western Australia as the nation's natural international springboard, the Western Australian city has become the main entry point for non-stop flights to continental Europe.

That transformation did not happen by accident; it came as a result of a fundamental realignment of airline fleet strategies, airport infrastructure investments, and international route rights. Using advanced long-range twin-engine aircraft, Qantas turned Perth International Airport (PER) into a high-yield international hub. But as airspace disruptions and competing long-haul technologies emerge, how long can Western Australia maintain its exclusive hold as Australia's direct bridge to Europe?

Perth became Australia’s gateway to Europe due to its location, as the vast distance between the southern continent and European airspace is within the maximum range limits of modern twin-engine airliners. In March 2018, Qantas launched its historic 9,010-mile (14,499 km) Perth to London Heathrow Airport(LHR) route using a 236-seat Boeing 787-9, as covered by Fortune. Flying directly out of Western Australia cuts three to four hours off the total travel time compared to departing from Sydney or Melbourne Airport(MEL), which therefore removes the traditional intermediate stopover in Singapore Changi Airport (SIN), Dubai International Airport(DXB), or Doha Hamad International Airport(DOH).

According to reporting from The Points Guy, that single route showed that non-stop ultra-long-haul flights between Australia and Europe were not only technically feasible, but exceptionally profitable. The success of the London service encouraged Qantas and local state planners to expand the Perth hub, eventually leading to the launch of Perth– Rome Fiumicino Airport(FCO) in June 2022, the first direct flight connecting Australia with continental Europe, and a subsequent seasonal non-stop service to Paris Charles De Gaulle Airport(CDG).

As highlighted in Travel Weekly, Qantas confirmed that 2026 would be its biggest year yet for Western Australia, adding nearly 300,000 seats between Perth and London, Paris, and Rome. In fact, the Perth–Rome route alone gained 44 extra flights and close to 10,000 more inbound seats between May and October 2026, as per the Government Of Western Australia. This massive expansion reinforced Western Australia's unique status as the only Australian state offering direct, non-stop passenger services into the European continent.

Supporting high-yield international transit traffic meant Perth Airport and Qantas had to overcome the separation between domestic and international terminals. Traditionally, passengers connecting from Melbourne, Sydney, or Brisbane had to land at the domestic terminal precinct and transfer across the airfield to the international terminal, creating a friction-filled connection experience. To resolve this, Qantas negotiated a custom arrangement to process international customs and immigration directly within its domestic Terminal 3 and 4 wing, as reported by MTA Travel.

The temporary operational fix laid the groundwork for Perth Airport’s massive "One Airport" consolidation program. According to an official media statement from the Government of Western Australia, WA Premier Roger Cook stated that these expanded international connections "cement WA's status as the gateway to Australia from Europe", noting that over 20 non-stop international routes now operate out of Perth. This multi-billion-dollar infrastructure effort aims to consolidate all domestic and international flights into a unified central terminal precinct, drastically reducing transfer friction for connecting passengers.

As well as the European routes, Qantas expanded Perth's network horizon even further by adding non-stop flights from Perth to Johannesburg Airport(JNB) and Auckland Airport(AKL) starting in December 2025. Connecting trans-Tasman, African, and European corridors through a single hub meant that Perth Airport could change its identity from a regional destination into a major global transit nexus. However, just as Perth was solidifying its status as an unshakeable aviation crossroads, major geopolitical shifts halfway across the globe put its route network to a tough operational test.

A closer look at why Qantas made adjustment to one of the world's longest non-stop flights

Geopolitical conflicts across the Middle East have caused major challenges for global air corridors, forcing international airlines to navigate closed or restricted airspace over Iran, Iraq, and the Levant region. For traditional Gulf mega-carriers operating out of hubs like Dubai, Doha, and Abu Dhabi, flight paths faced rerouting or temporary operational halts. As reported by Aerospace Global News, this systemic disruption created an unprecedented surge in demand for alternative routes linking Australia directly to Europe. Travelers who previously opted for a Middle East transfer sought out Qantas's direct services out of Western Australia to avoid the volatile airspace altogether.

However, the unforgiving flight-planning realities of ultra-long-haul aviation meant that Qantas faced its own operational complications. As highlighted in coverage by Simple Flying, westbound headwinds combined with strict airspace avoidance protocols forced Qantas to adjust its flagship outbound flights. Outbound services from Perth to London and Sydney to Paris via Perth were rerouted through Singapore Changi for technical refueling stops, though the inbound flights from London and Paris back to Perth continued to operate non-stop.

During these operational changes, Perth–Rome stood out as a critical non-stop survivor. In order to capture redirected European demand, Qantas boosted Perth–Rome services from four weekly flights to daily operations, adding over 1,400 seats per week to the continent during peak seasons. Such tactical network shifts brought to center stage both the strategic resilience and the delicate operational vulnerability of running ultra-long-haul corridors out of Western Australia.

Operating commercial non-stop sectors exceeding 8,000 miles (12,874 km) is exactly where operational factors need to be monitored closely. Payload capacity, fuel burn, and takeoff weight limits massively affect the viability of the flight, and so a balance needs to be achieved. The 787-9 aircraft assigned to Qantas’s long-haul Perth operations feature a custom passenger configuration of just 236 seats, significantly lower than the standard high-density layouts deployed by international competitors. Restricting cabin capacity reduces total payload weight, allowing the twin-engine widebody to carry the massive fuel load required for a 17-hour block time.

Every additional seat, cargo pallet, or gallon of jet fuel alters the aircraft's takeoff performance, particularly during warm Australian summer months. When strong winter jet streams push against westbound aircraft over the Indian Ocean, flight planning managers rigorously weigh passenger counts against fuel reserves. If headwind components exceed baseline estimates, the aircraft risks exceeding its Maximum Takeoff Weight (MTOW) or infringing strict Extended-range Twin-engine Operational Performance Standards (ETOPS) margins.

The constraints here explain why Qantas relies on premium-heavy cabin configurations and elevated ticket yields to make these non-stop routes viable. Despite this, as airframe technologies advance, Perth's hard-won geographic monopoly faces a threat from within Qantas’s own future fleet commitments.

Qantas shakes up its international network to offer more flights to Europe via Singapore.

The long-term outlook for Perth as Australia's main European gateway faces a major test from Qantas's flagship ultra-long-haul initiative, Project Sunrise. Designed to connect Sydney and Melbourne directly to London Heathrow and New York non-stop using ultra-long-range Airbus A350-1000ULR aircraft, Project Sunrise will completely remove the need for an intermediate domestic transit stop in Western Australia.

Once direct non-stop flights from the East Coast launch, a significant portion of high-yield corporate travelers who currently route through Perth will opt for point-to-point non-stop services from Sydney or Melbourne. According to reporting by The Points Guy, Project Sunrise specifically targets high-yield travelers on Australia's busiest transcontinental corridors, potentially diverting transit traffic away from Western Australia’s hub.

Replacing Perth is not quite the plan, as Qantas plans to position the two operations as complementary long-haul networks. While Project Sunrise caters to premium demand from Australia's largest financial centers on the east coast, Perth will continue serving as a regional springboard, capturing origin-and-destination demand across Western Australia, trans-Tasman feeder traffic, and routes to Southern Africa.

Perth's transformation into Australia's primary direct gateway to Europe is really something special, something that quite often gets overlooked in the global aviation world. Non-stop ultra-long-haul routes could succeed using fuel-efficient twin-engine widebodies, so Qantas and Perth Airport were able to jointly morph international travel patterns across the Southern Hemisphere.

The long-term test for Western Australia will be maintaining its route volume as Project Sunrise aircraft enter service and direct east-coast routes come online. Continued investment in terminal consolidation under Perth Airport’s "One Airport" masterplan, combined with scheduled route restorations, including Qantas returning the Perth–London sector to a full non-stop rotation, are really what will determine whether Perth retains its dominance as a transit hub.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Airspace restrictions and jet fuel economics are still highly volatile, but Western Australia's geographic location is an unshakable natural asset. Perth was able to make direct connections from Australia to the other side of the world possible, so even if Project Sunrise takes away its lead, we still have Perth to thank for opening up one of the longest direct route selections in the world.

Online shopping portals can help you save money on everyday purchases, and some let you earn rewards on top of the points or cash back you already get from your credit card.

Capital One Shopping takes a slightly different approach: It combines shopping rewards with coupon codes, price comparisons and deal alerts.

You don't need a Capital One credit card or bank account to use Capital One Shopping. The free service is available through its website, browser extension and mobile app, and you can redeem eligible Shopping Rewards for gift cards rather than cash or travel points.

Here's how Capital One Shopping works, how to earn and redeem rewards, and what to know before using it.

Capital One Shopping is a free online shopping tool that helps you find lower prices, apply available coupon codes and earn rewards at participating retailers. It can also compare prices across merchants and alert you to potential savings.

Unlike a traditional airline or hotel shopping portal, Capital One Shopping doesn't directly award airline miles or hotel points. Instead, eligible purchases and promotions earn Capital One Shopping Rewards, which can be redeemed for select retailers' electronic gift cards.

Capital One Shopping is separate from Capital One Offers, which provides shopping promotions to eligible Capital One cardholders.

You can shop through the Capital One Shopping website, install its browser extension or use its mobile app.

Keep in mind that rewards aren't necessarily credited immediately. Capital One Shopping says eligible rewards typically post within 30 to 90 days after making a qualifying purchase or completing a promotion's requirements, although some may take longer.

Returns, cancellations and other exclusions can affect reward eligibility. Using another shopping portal or applying an unlisted coupon code may also interfere with tracking, so be sure to review the offer's terms before completing your purchase.

The Capital One Shopping browser extension can help you find savings without having to manually check the portal before every purchase.

Once you've installed the extension and signed in, you can shop at participating websites as usual. Depending on the retailer, the extension can alert you to available Shopping Rewards, search for coupon codes and compare prices.

I keep the Capital One Shopping extension installed on my browser, so whenever I'm shopping online, I can easily see if any rewards are available. Even if an offer isn't always available, it's nice to know when I might be able to earn something extra on a purchase I was already planning to make.

Before checking out, review the terms of any available offers, including minimum spending requirements and product exclusions. It's also worth comparing the final price after discounts and shipping rather than choosing a retailer based solely on its advertised rewards rate.

Capital One Shopping also offers price-drop notifications for eligible products, which can be useful if you're planning a larger purchase and have some flexibility about when to buy.

Unlike traditional cash-back shopping portals such as Rakuten and TopCashback, Capital One Shopping lets you redeem your rewards for electronic gift cards at participating retailers rather than cash.

When you're ready to redeem your rewards, sign in to your Capital One Shopping account and navigate to the "My Rewards & Savings" section. From there, select "Redeem Now" to browse available gift cards and complete your redemption.

Available retailers and redemption amounts may vary, so check your account for current options.

Keep in mind that Shopping Rewards aren't the same as cash. If you'd prefer rewards that can be deposited into your bank account, a traditional cash-back shopping portal may be a better fit.

You don't need a Capital One credit card to use Capital One Shopping, so consider using a card that earns a strong rewards rate on everyday purchases or online shopping.

You can generally earn credit card rewards on eligible purchases in addition to Capital One Shopping Rewards, allowing you to earn rewards through both programs on the same purchase.

Personally, I like using my Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card for online purchases. While it doesn't offer bonus rewards specifically for online shopping, it earns at least 2 miles per dollar on purchases, so I know I'm getting a solid return on my spending.

For example, if I make a $200 purchase through Capital One Shopping using my Venture X, I'll earn 400 Capital One miles in addition to any eligible Shopping Rewards.

Related: The best credit cards for online shopping

Capital One Shopping is a free tool for finding online discounts, comparing prices and earning rewards that can be redeemed for gift cards.

You don't need a Capital One credit card to use it, and eligible purchases can earn Shopping Rewards on top of your usual credit card rewards.

If you regularly shop online and don't mind redeeming rewards for gift cards rather than cash or travel points, Capital One Shopping is worth trying out. Just be sure to compare prices and review offer terms before making a purchase.

#6203. JetBlue Leads The Industry In Raising Checked Bag Fees… Again!

For whatever reason, JetBlue tends to be the industry leader when it comes to raising checked bag fees, and competitors tend to follow. Earlier this year, JetBlue was the first major US carrier to raise checked bag fees, and now the airline is raising checked bag fees again…

Effective immediately (for tickets purchased as of November 3, 2026), JetBlue has increased checked bag fees. JetBlue has a rather complicated fee structure for checked bags, with both off-peak and peak pricing, plus different pricing based on whether you pay for the bag 24 hours or more in advance.

Below is a chart with JetBlue’s new checked bag fees.

As you can see, an off-peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $50-60 (depending on whether you pay in advance), while a peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $55-70 (depending on whether you pay in advance). For context, below are the dates that are considered peak for the purposes of bag fees.

It goes without saying that paying $50-70 for a first checked bag is a pretty substantial cost, especially when you consider how little checked bags used to cost. On a one-way, you’re looking at $100-140. For a family of four, you’d be looking at $400-560.

When JetBlue raised checked bag fees earlier this year, the airline released a statement claiming it was increasing checked bag fees to be “more competitive,” and that “while we recognize that fee increases are never ideal, we take careful consideration to ensure these changes are implemented only when necessary.” I imagine this time around, the logic is much of the same.

The simple reality is that oil prices are way up. Airlines have actually done a solid job of being able to make fare increases stick. But that’s not enough to fully offset the increase in the cost of jet fuel.

JetBlue is in a rough financial spot, and it hasn’t turned a profit since before the pandemic. The airline is hoping to turn an operating profit in 2027, though that strikes me as being particularly optimistic. So the logic for raising checked bags is threefold:

JetBlue has just increased checked bag fees once again, and you’ll now pay $50-70 for a first checked bag on a domestic flight. This is JetBlue’s second price increase on checked bags so far this year. When airlines are trying to increase revenue, checked bag fees are often low hanging fruit.

When competitors match, it also becomes something that’s unavoidable for consumers, other than getting a credit card… which also has upside for the airline! I’d be shocked if other airlines don’t match this move from JetBlue.

What do you make of JetBlue increasing checked bag fees?

#6201. Marriott Earnings Call: New Upgrade List Encourages Elites To Pay For Better Rooms—But Puts Its Credit Card Cash Cow At Risk

Marriott earned $794 million in the third quarter, up from $728 million a year ago. They’re doing well. At the same time, I’ve been covering reports of layoffs in the customer service teams guests turn to when hotels won’t honor benefits. And on their earnings call, Marriott explained that its new elite upgrade list is being designed to preserve owners’ ability to sell upgrades. The company is getting better at monetizing Bonvoy. More than half its fee growth came from credit cards. But they’re spending down the trust that makes the program worth something in the first place. The hotel business has been good, outside of pockets like the Mideast. Marriott’s revenue per available room rose 6.5%. Adjusted earnings per share rose from $2.47 to $3.02, beating the $2.84 analysts expected. Marriott’s quarterly filing identifies $68 million in additional credit card fees compared with the same quarter last year. More than half of the increase in franchise fees comes from cards. Third Quarter Fee Growth   Increase   Share From Higher Card Fees Franchise fees   $131 million   52% Total gross fees   $184 million   37% I’ve covered owners’ unhappiness with these economics. Fifty-one owners representing about 1,000 hotels demanded better compensation for award stays. They’re supplying the rooms, Marriott sells them at a discount to Chase and American Express customers. The basic hotel loyalty bargain is a loop. Hotels pay into a program that rewards guests for stays. Those guests redeem points for more stays. Owners supply discounted award nights in exchange for a program that encourages customers to choose their hotels. A vacant room is cheap to give away. When an award guest doesn’t displace a paying customer, the hotel’s cost is mostly cleaning, utilities and whatever benefits it provides. Deep discounts make sense. But Marriott selling the points through Chase and American Express, using access to those discounted nights to monetize the owners’ inventory, infuriates some of them. As I’ve explained about bank payments for rewards, Marriott’s reported card fees aren’t everything the banks pay. Some money funds points and benefits. Some pays Marriott for licensing its brand and customer access. On the earnings call, Marriott pointed to the ways they’re appeasing owners: lower fees for Bonvoy higher reimbursement on high-demand award nights more flexible renovation requirements (letting owners allow the product to slip) a guest recommendation incentive. Marriott discussed its new upgrade lists. I covered the beta last month. Members can see their place in line and an estimate of upgrades matching their reservation. CEO Anthony Capuano told investors the feature would provide that visibility “while still preserving premium room upsell opportunities for our owners.” Showing you a position on a list doesn’t commit a room to you. A hotel can keep selling premium rooms while guests wait for complimentary upgrades. The later it commits the room, the longer it has to find someone willing to pay. Marriott hasn’t explained the beta’s inventory or clearance rules. They’re promising more visibility, but they aren’t saying hotels will release more rooms or confirm upgrades earlier. People who are lower on the list – and therefore less likely to get a free upgrade – become motivated to buy the upsell. Which, in turn, means fewer upgrade rooms available even at the top of the list. I’ve already described where Marriott’s technology investment is headed: selling room attributes and extras that guests used to receive as part of their stay or status. Better views, room locations and upgrades are going to become new opportunities for revenue generation. Selling a premium room is perfectly reasonable. But Bonvoy also encourages guests to concentrate their stays and spending to earn upgrades. And they’ll sell those same upgrades back to lower-tier elites for tens of dollars – prioritizing minor ducats over long-term value. Meanwhile, Capuano trumpeted 309 million Bonvoy members. I’m amazed anyone keeps repeating these enrollment numbers seriously. It means a guest signed up to get a lower (member) room rate. That tells us they wanted to pay less for the reservation they were already making. It says nothing about interest in Bonvoy or continued engagement. And the numbers are large because Marriott has a lot of hotels and rooms. I’ve reported on employees signing guests up who don’t even know about it, alongside hotel incentives worth as much as $10,000 a month for enrollment performance. Marriott intentionally does not share active members When I wrote about Chris Buckner taking over Bonvoy, I argued that his biggest opportunity was getting hotels to deliver the benefits members had already earned. Marriott’s business depends on guests starting their hotel search with Marriott. The brand is supposed to stand for a consistent product, and Bonvoy is supposed to make the brand sticky. That’s what lets Marriott deliver customers to owners as “leads” and charge for access to them. The reservation system doesn’t have value to sell to owners if guests stop trusting the hotels it displays. An individual owner can save money by denying breakfast or an upgrade. The damage gets spread across the whole portfolio. That hotel benefits from shirking on the program, while the program loses value. That’s why Marriott is supposed to enforce its promises. Yet they rarely seem to! I covered a breakfast dispute where the hotel closed the guest’s case seven times before finally paying the $100 benefit guarantee the guest was clearly due. In Marriott’s system, the hotel becomes the judge of complaints against it. . I may be one of the most infrequent travelers, but I still remember the moments I signed on encouraged by desk staff to SPG when staying at the Sheraton Boston. I was immediately upgraded to a mini suite and got take out from the Kon TIki off the lobby and enjoyed every minute of my stay. I used to play a game called Roller Coaster Tycoon. One time I built an amusement park, where nobody could leave. At first it worked great. Then the customers became more and more unhappy, and no new people came to my amusement park.

More seriously, goodwill is an asset. Over the short run, you can increase profits by monetizing assets. However, over the long run, that will cause the goodwill to depreciate significantly. Famous brands that have no value any more are everywhere.

I am lifetime Platinum (Titanium currently). However, Marriott’s tricky app (in terms of pricing and cancellation date) (as I commented previously), removal of the ability to add guests, and other unfriendly acts are causing me to book elsewhere often.

For example, I am planning to meet my girlfriend near LAX. The LAX Marriott would normally be a good choice. However, we are flying in on different itineraries. If my plane is delayed, she won’t be able to check in. Going to book elsewhere.

As a Starwood transfer and current Marriott Lifetime Titanium (1700+ nights) I’m very disappointed with Marriott/Bonvoy. I actually just reread Gary’s “Marriott Names A New Bonvoy Boss From JetBlue And The Points Guy—Will He Make Hotels Honor Your Benefits?” that he linked to above. It was a pretty good read. I am at the point where I do not expect any of the benefits to be honored. Enough said.

The whole craziness with Marriott and its ongoing process of nickel and diming its customers who buy into its “loyalty” program (Bonvoy) reminds me quite a bit of the “Master of the House” scene in the musical “Les Miserables” in which the innkeeper continually gouges and shortchanges his guests (with unexpected extra charges for everything) … and publicly brags about it. What Marriott does (and increasingly other so-called hospitality companies do) is at best shameful. Marriott and the others are selling you are for the most part illusions and wishful thinking for your blind “loyalty.”

The visible list mostly tells lower tier elites their odds. That’s exactly the moment the upsell starts to look tempting. Paying makes sense when the trip really needs the bigger room, a family stay or an anniversary, or when the paid upgrade is a small add on to the standard rate. If it’s just nice to have, Platinum and above can still sit on the list and see what clears.

The hotel’s own site or Google Hotels will show what that suite category costs booked outright for the same dates. FWIW that same Marriott can also price diff depending on which country you search from, since inventory and rates vary by market. Free tools like Arbitrica check it from around 195 countries and find kind of the lowest price in the world, which tells you fast whether the upsell is a deal. Then decide whether to pay now or gamble on the list

Marriott now views engaged loyalty members as suckers and adversaries. I’m lifetime platinum but generally tend to avoid their hotels.
