#6199. Limited Time: Citi AAdvantage Business Card 75K Bonus Miles Offer (Double Dip Loyalty Points!)

The Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® is American’s primary co-branded business credit card. We’ve just seen an excellent new limited time welcome offer rolled out on the card, which is in line with the highest ever offer that we’ve seen on the card.

That makes this the ideal time to apply. Not only that, but this is a card that many people will want, given that it’s my favorite American card for earning AAdvantage elite status, since you can basically double dip Loyalty Points.

Link: Learn more about the Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard®

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card currently has a limited time welcome offer of 75,000 AAdvantage bonus miles after spending $5,000 within the first five months. This is a highest-ever offer, in line with the best bonuses I recall seeing on the card.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I value AAdvantage miles at 1.5 cents each, so to me the bonus is worth $1,125. There are some incredible uses of American AAdvantage miles, including for travel on some world class partner airlines.

Also keep in mind that credit card spending will qualify for Loyalty Points (helping you earn elite status, including Gold, Platinum, Platinum Pro, or Executive Platinum), though the welcome bonus as such won’t. Upon completing minimum spending, you’d earn a minimum of 5,000 Loyalty Points. As I’ll explain below, you can even double dip the Loyalty Points you earn.

If you’re interested in applying for the Citi AAdvantage Business Card, the typical Citi credit card application restrictions apply, including that you can be approved for at most one Citi card every eight days, and at most two Citi cards every 65 days.

On top of that, the bonus isn’t available to those who have received a new account bonus on this exact card in the past 48 months. Eligibility is unrelated to having any other American Airlines credit cards.

If you’re concerned about Chase’s 5/24 rule, note that applying for a Citi business card generally won’t count toward that limit. I should also mention that at least anecdotally, this card seems to be quite easy to get approved for.

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card has an annual fee that’s waived for the first year, so you can “try” the card before you have to pay a fee. While the fee after that is technically still $99, it’s increasing to $150 as of January 24, 2027, so that’s what you’d pay on account renewal.

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card offers a variety of valuable perks, including:

Above I mentioned how the Citi AAdvantage Business Card is the best card for earning AAdvantage elite status. The reason is because through December 31, 2028, the card essentially lets you double dip Loyalty Points. If you add an authorized user, their spending will earn 1x Loyalty Points per dollar spent for both their own account, and for the primary cardmember’s account. So this is a way to essentially get two-for-one elite status qualification, which is awesome.

With the annual fee increasing as of January 2027, the card will also pick up several valuable new perks, including the following:

Read a detailed review of the Citi AAdvantage Business Card.

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus of 75,000 AAdvantage bonus miles after spending $5,000 within the first five months. This is a great offer on a valuable card that even has its annual fee waived for the first year.

This is also my favorite card for earning AAdvantage elite status, since you can essentially earn Loyalty Points for two members at once. Authorized user spending earns Loyalty Points for the authorized user’s AAdvantage account, and also for the primary cardmember’s AAdvantage account.

Anyone plan to pick up the Citi AAdvantage Business Card with 75K miles?

#6198. The Two Promised Lands

#6197. Oneworld Explains The Money Behind Your Lounge Access—And Why Credit Cards Help Decide Where Airlines Fly

Historically, if I used Royal Jordanian status to enter an American Airlines lounge while flying American, Royal Jordanian didn’t get a bill. American was carrying me and bore the lounge cost. In a new interview, oneworld’s commercial chief describes a payment model that sounds like that arrangement may still apply, despite reporting that says the rules changed. Who pays for your lounge visit helps explain why airline alliances are so difficult to run. The airline that gives you status, the one selling you a ticket, and the one providing your benefits can all be different. Each wants the customer and the revenue, and they have to agree on who picks up the costs. Roger Blackburn, oneworld’s Vice President of Commercial and Loyalty, and Gilbert Ott, its Director of Loyalty (and former blogger of God Save the Points), talk about how this works in an unusually candid interview. It’s essentially herding cats, with airlines that compete for the same customers promising to take care of each other’s passengers. Blackburn explains that a lounge hosting another airline’s passenger gets paid by: …the airline who’s … lifting that customer out of the station. At least that’s how our model works. One Mile at a Time has said its understanding is that this changed, and that the program providing status now pays when status is the reason someone gets in. This affects the economics of status matches, for instance. An airline offering status to someone who mostly flies its partners has a very different cost calculation if it’s getting a bill for every lounge visit. The lack of billing was also a limiting factor on offering status matches (confined to a formula relative to the total size of the elite pool). Blackburn describes the lounge operator as delighted to have another airline’s passenger because they’re getting paid. That true when there are empty seats. When the lounge is full, another paid visit can make the experience worse for the airline’s own customers. I’ve written about American’s lounge visits growing several times as fast as its passenger traffic. Better lounges encourage more people to use them, and to stay longer. Improving the product creates demand for more space. That’s also why Blackburn’s explanation of where oneworld builds its own lounges is helpful. They want airports served by enough member airlines to keep a lounge busy across the day. One airline might struggle to justify the rent and staffing for a single daily departure. Several airlines with departures at different times can share a better facility. Delhi and Mumbai come up in the conversation, and Blackburn hopes to have more lounge news “fairly soon.” The banks competing for that space also help pay for the airlines’ products. Ott argues that credit card and loyalty revenue supports better lounges, seats, food and inflight connectivity. He’s largely right, and the case goes further: credit cards support more flights. An airline becomes more attractive to cardmembers when it flies where they need to go. It also needs destinations they want to redeem their miles for. Delta has explicitly connected its growth in Austin and Raleigh with acquiring American Express card customers. A flight that looks weak based only on ticket revenue might make sense once you count the card spending it helps generate. As I discussed in my recent piece on Scott Kirby and credit card economics, a customer might choose an airline’s card because its Chicago schedule works for their business travel, then redeem the miles for Hawaii. Assign all the card revenue to Hawaii and you can end up cutting the flights that made someone want your card in the first place. A better seat and lounge help sell that relationship, too. And an alliance makes the card more useful by offering places to spend miles that the airline doesn’t fly to itself. Of course airlines can manage this badly. Sell more miles while planes are full, without making enough desirable award seats available, and customers wind up with growing balances they struggle to use. Sell more lounge access without adding enough capacity and the customer gets a line at the door. The alliance has to get its members to participate in making those benefits valuable. Asked whether oneworld should set minimum protections around changes to earning, status qualification and award availability, Ott describes the programs as largely sovereign and emphasizes a spirit of cooperation. Asked how much say the alliance has over the number of award seats a member releases, he calls it a collaborative process. I’d put it a different way: an alliance trying to influence airlines is pushing on a string. It’s the problem I’ve written about with airlines holding back their best awards from partners. They want to offer their members access to everyone else’s seats. But making their own best seats available can benefit another airline’s credit card business, while keeping those seats for their own members can help sell their own miles. Ott makes the case that a redemption can introduce someone to an airline and turn them into a valuable customer. That’s true as far as it goes, but those seats have an opportunity cost and getting the airline with the seat to value that speculative future business enough to release it (for a foreign customer who might not travel with them often and probably won’t take their credit card) can be a challenge. So can getting the partner buying the award seat to pay enough to make that worthwhile. Blackburn says oneworld is improving how quickly miles reach accounts following a flight across the alliance, with everyone expected on a new standard by the end of the year. He also says oneworld’s earlier artificial intelligence round the world booking assistant is gone, despite earlier claims of a fivefold increase in booking conversions. The interview returns to the oneworld Loyalty Summit in September, where I spoke about how artificial intelligence gives customers better tools to choose rewards programs. (The summit photo below is courtesy of oneworld.) Ott mentions verifying elite status without relying on screenshots that someone can easily manipulate. I saw a presentation at the summit for a product that was basically Plaid for airline status: the customer logged into their existing airline account to demonstrate their status to another company. I questioned whether airlines would allow that access to their systems. Gary, will you keep your Royal Jordanian Golden Sparrow, or shoot for Platinum Hawk next time?

American Airlines Flagship Lounges are worth it. The ones in JFK, MIA, and ORD are worth it–fast-flowing French champagne and self-serve liquor bar. I think that there are a couple others. Easy to get in with OWE status on a foreign carrier, even though the JFK have door attendants snootier than the Amtrak lounge door attendant in Washington, DC.

I haven’t tried the credit card access angle, yet. I should try it.

Which JFK lounge is considered the Flagship? Hadn’t heard this previously.

there is of course no longer a jfk flagship lounge, the american lounges there are joint with BA. the old flagship lounge is now greenwich (business class lounge). there’s also soho (the oneworld emerald lounge) and chelsea (concorde room, effectively)

If Gib Ott says the sun rises in the east, verify it. This is the guy who anointed himself as the best travel blogger in the world. I questioned him in the comments about that and he blocked me for doing so. His response on collaborating on award seats is ridiculous.

#6196. Air Tahiti Nui Will Offer Free Starlink Wi-Fi On Its Boeing 787s As Of 2027

Air Tahiti Nui has just announced a massive upgrade to its inflight connectivity, as the airline will be rolling out free Starlink Wi-Fi across its (small) fleet in 2027.

Air Tahiti Nui has revealed that it plans to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its entire fleet, which consists of four Boeing 787-9s. The airline plans to offer this service for free to passengers in all travel classes.

Starlink will be introduced in 2027, though no timeline beyond that is known yet, so it could be early or late in the year. Presumably once installation starts, it’ll be completed very quickly — four planes could easily be fitted with Starlink in a single week.

Air Tahiti Nui operates some very long flights — including from Papeete (PPT) to Paris (CDG) via Los Angeles (LAX) so having fast and free connectivity is super valuable. While so many airlines market their Wi-Fi as being high speed, Starlink is the only product currently in service where you can consistently stream videos, etc.

Currently, Air Tahiti Nui’s Dreamliners are equipped with Panasonic Wi-Fi, which actually has relatively decent speeds. The catch is that Air Tahiti Nui chooses to have insanely high pricing based primarily on data usage, rather than just offering a full flight pass for a fixed amount.

Below is Air Tahiti Nui’s current pricing chart for Wi-Fi… could they make this any more complicated? $28 for 100 MB of data is absurd, and $98 for unlimited data is even more ridiculous.

This kind of pricing just strikes me as being so stupid. All you end up doing is frustrating passengers, and I also have to imagine this isn’t actually the system that maximizes usage. It’s weird to have a provider with speeds that are actually semi-usable (Panasonic is better than OnAir), and to then do this with it.

So anyway, Starlink will simply be a massive upgrade for Air Tahiti Nui in every way. Speaking of which, I’d sure love to return to French Polynesia at some point (and fly that all-business class Air Tahiti turboprop, while I’m at it).

In 2027, Air Tahiti Nui intends to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its fleet of four Dreamliners. It remains to be seen exactly when in 2027 it’ll happen, but this represents a huge upgrade to the passenger experience. The airline currently offers Panasonic Wi-Fi with awful data-based pricing (or an unlimited package that will run you close to $100).

What do you make of Air Tahiti Nui introducing Starlink?

#6195. American Airlines Passenger Stuck Overnight Couldn’t Get A Hotel Voucher—They Got A Credit Card Pitch Instead

An American Airlines passenger says they couldn’t get a hotel voucher during a flight delay. The chat agent did, however, have something else ready: a pitch to open a Citi credit card, spend $2,500, and earn 50,000 miles. That’s not even as good as the standard offer! American’s stated purpose is “To Care for People on Life’s Journey.” That journey includes a sales presentation while you’re trying to figure out where to sleep. The passenger shared a screenshot of the exchange. It begins with the agent asking, “Does any of that work for you?” Then comes a lengthy offer for the Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select Mastercard: the initial bonus, free checked bags, double miles at restaurants and gas stations, and a request for permission to send a one-time email with more information. American Airlines offered me a credit card deal during a conversation about a delayed flight and their inability to provide a hotel voucher from mildlyinfuriating Always be selling! Always be closing! It’s Glengarry Glen Ross, and the passenger asking for help is the lead. American Pays Agents To Make These Pitches In May 2023, I reported that American’s reservations agents would switch from pitching Avis rental cars to Citi credit cards. At the time, I argued that agents should judge whether the conversation had gone well enough for a customer to be receptive. American’s AAdvantage Cash support materials explain why an agent might make the ask either way: Contact center and Premium Guest Services representatives earn at least $50 for each approved application carrying their referral code. That rises to $100 as they move through annual sales tiers. There are also $100, $300, and $500 bonuses for reaching Gold, Platinum, and Diamond. They earn elite status like we do. There’s also a separate guide to pitching cards during chats, complete with prescribed transitions from talking about travel benefits to offering the card. American Already Knows When To Stop Selling I’ve written for years about credit card announcements that interrupt sleep on early morning flights. As Kevin Williamson once put it, [T]here is the Clockwork Orange sensation of being literally strapped into a seat while someone screams corporate banalities at you on a loudspeaker fifteen inches from your head… It is a “limited-time” offer in the sense that the sun eventually will run out of gas and become a dying star, first engulfing the Earth in fire and then leaving the wreck of the solar system a sterile plane of interstellar cold and utter silence, which will be interrupted only by some addled flight attendant screeching about the limited-time Barclays card offer. The airline’s guidelines at least suggest: Use the approved script, which should take about a minute. Make the announcement only once per flight segment, at cruise before descent, between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. Skip late night and redeye flights. Refrain from offering the card or making announcements during delays, cancellations, diversions, and other events affecting the customer experience. Meanwhile, the pressure to sell keeps growing. On October 15, the flight attendants union objected to American inserting a 15-minute card-sales module into mandatory fourth quarter training. Selling remains voluntary, but management made the training required and offered a $25 qualification reward. They Have A Sales Script For Your Bag Fee, Too American’s airport agent talking points for “Real Time Benefits” identify two moments to pitch: when a customer is about to pay a checked bag fee, and when they’re worried there won’t be overhead bin space for their carry-on. For most instantly approved applicants, the card’s first checked bag benefit and Group 5 boarding can apply to the trip a passenger is already taking. The airline says the boarding group can take roughly seven minutes to update on a digital boarding pass. If the customer has already prepaid for bags, agents are told to shift the pitch to the miles, boarding, and free bags on a future eligible trip. I’ve even proposed plastering aircraft lavatories with credit card ads if attaching revenue to that space would persuade American to give us larger bathrooms since the space becomes monetized rather than deadweight loss. The inflight sales operation has instructions for distributing the commissions fairly among participating flight attendants. Brochures are prefilled with employee numbers, then stacked in a 1–2–3–3–2–1 sequence when three crew members participate. They’ve worked out whose referral code the next passenger gets. A Few Applications Don’t Prove This Is A Good Idea Maybe the number of applications generated from unhappy customers isn’t zero. The agent already has their attention, the sales text is ready to paste, and a small number of approvals can produce real money. But a positive response rate doesn’t establish that the pitch was worth making. You have to count the customers you make angrier, the business they take elsewhere, and whether someone who applies will actually keep and use the card. As I covered in looking at American’s Citi economics, their ambitions depend on acquiring customers, retaining them, and getting their spending. American’s deal announcement projected annual payments approaching $10 billion. They’ve finally come to realize that it matters whether customers like the airline enough to carry it in their wallet. In August, I covered their push for friendlier inflight service to increase card applications. Taking care of passengers makes them more receptive to the pitch. A customer service chat that hasn’t resolved the passenger’s hotel problem starts with.. not that. In August, I covered their push for friendlier inflight service to increase card applications. Taking care of passengers makes them more receptive to the pitch. A customer service chat that hasn’t resolved the passenger’s hotel problem starts with.. not that. In May 2023, I reported that American’s reservations agents would switch from pitching Avis rental cars to Citi credit cards. At the time, I argued that agents should judge whether the conversation had gone well enough for a customer to be receptive.

American’s AAdvantage Cash support materials explain why an agent might make the ask either way: Contact center and Premium Guest Services representatives earn at least $50 for each approved application carrying their referral code. That rises to $100 as they move through annual sales tiers. There are also $100, $300, and $500 bonuses for reaching Gold, Platinum, and Diamond. They earn elite status like we do.

There’s also a separate guide to pitching cards during chats, complete with prescribed transitions from talking about travel benefits to offering the card.

I’ve written for years about credit card announcements that interrupt sleep on early morning flights. As Kevin Williamson once put it, [T]here is the Clockwork Orange sensation of being literally strapped into a seat while someone screams corporate banalities at you on a loudspeaker fifteen inches from your head… It is a “limited-time” offer in the sense that the sun eventually will run out of gas and become a dying star, first engulfing the Earth in fire and then leaving the wreck of the solar system a sterile plane of interstellar cold and utter silence, which will be interrupted only by some addled flight attendant screeching about the limited-time Barclays card offer.

The airline’s guidelines at least suggest:

Meanwhile, the pressure to sell keeps growing. On October 15, the flight attendants union objected to American inserting a 15-minute card-sales module into mandatory fourth quarter training. Selling remains voluntary, but management made the training required and offered a $25 qualification reward.

American’s airport agent talking points for “Real Time Benefits” identify two moments to pitch: when a customer is about to pay a checked bag fee, and when they’re worried there won’t be overhead bin space for their carry-on. For most instantly approved applicants, the card’s first checked bag benefit and Group 5 boarding can apply to the trip a passenger is already taking. The airline says the boarding group can take roughly seven minutes to update on a digital boarding pass. If the customer has already prepaid for bags, agents are told to shift the pitch to the miles, boarding, and free bags on a future eligible trip. I’ve even proposed plastering aircraft lavatories with credit card ads if attaching revenue to that space would persuade American to give us larger bathrooms since the space becomes monetized rather than deadweight loss. The inflight sales operation has instructions for distributing the commissions fairly among participating flight attendants. Brochures are prefilled with employee numbers, then stacked in a 1–2–3–3–2–1 sequence when three crew members participate. They’ve worked out whose referral code the next passenger gets. A Few Applications Don’t Prove This Is A Good Idea Maybe the number of applications generated from unhappy customers isn’t zero. The agent already has their attention, the sales text is ready to paste, and a small number of approvals can produce real money. But a positive response rate doesn’t establish that the pitch was worth making. You have to count the customers you make angrier, the business they take elsewhere, and whether someone who applies will actually keep and use the card. #6192. Crumbling Europe and the Lessons for U.S.

Here in the U.S. there's been much debate over how much government should give to its citizens. One of Europe's proudest achievements has long been generous cradle-to-grave welfare. But today, it's cracking under the weight of high debt and massive immigration. There's simply not enough money to fund all the benefits. In France, when the government announced freezes on public pay, pensions, and budgets- it sparked weeks of protests that turned violent. In Spain, net migration has hit records. In Britain, welfare now costs more than income tax. Today: how far can the Welfare State stretch?

Earlier this year, JetBlue raised its checked bag fees and kicked off a wave of fee hikes across the industry. United followed. Then Delta, American and Southwest.

Seven months later, JetBlue is leading the fee-hiking charge again.

The carrier on Tuesday raised its bag fees for the second time in 2026.

Going forward, customers will pay at least $50 per bag. That’s a 28% jump from the lowest fee the airline previously charged its customers.

Passengers who don’t pre-pay for their bag will pay $60 for their first piece of checked luggage.

And because JetBlue uses a dynamic baggage-pricing system, flyers will pay even more for their checked baggage on peak travel days.

In a statement about the airline's second bag-fee hike this year, the carrier pointed to rising fuel and operating costs.

“This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one,” a spokesperson said.

Here’s how JetBlue’s bag fees will shake out, going forward.

These fees will apply to flights booked starting Nov. 3.

So if you had already purchased a JetBlue flight prior to Nov. 3 — including trips for the holidays — the previous fees would apply to your trip.

As noted above, JetBlue also raised the fees customers will pay for their second checked bag, too.

Here are the days where JetBlue's "peak" baggage fees will apply, through October 2027.

JetBlue does continue to offer free baggage perks as a benefit of certain cobranded credit cards. Plus, its Mosaic elite status members each get at least one free bag.

Customers flying in JetBlue’s premium Mint cabin are still entitled to their first bag free. The same goes for flyers who book the carrier’s new domestic first-class (BlueFirst) seats, which are set to debut on some flights next month.

As JetBlue raises its baggage fees, the biggest question for consumers is how the rest of the airline industry respond.

If history is any indication, we’re about to see another wave of fee hikes across the industry.

After JetBlue raised its bag fees in late March, it took only weeks for nearly every major U.S. carrier to follow with their own fee hikes.

This would be the latest case of sticker shock for travelers, who are simultaneously battling surging fares.

Even budget airline Frontier last week reported customers had paid 71% more in fares over the prior quarter.

All of this comes as airlines have had to contend with sky-high jet fuel costs in 2026 — which they’ve aggressively passed onto customers.

But while jet fuel costs may eventually fall, it’s unlikely flyers will see any future relief when it comes to baggage fees — typically, once those go up, they don’t come back down.

While JetBlue has raised its baggage fees, it is worth noting that passengers do have freedom to bring a full-size carry-on bag on JetBlue flights, regardless of the fare type. The airline no longer bars its Blue Basic (basic economy) passengers from using the overhead bins.

Of course, the belongings packed in any carry-on bag must meet the Transportation Security Administration's 3-1-1 liquids policy.

#6190. Are Mount Everest climbers dreamers, or just cultists?

In the title of his 1997 bestselling adventure tale, “Into Thin Air,” mountaineer and writer Jon Krakauer employs a double entendre so clever that its effect is extraordinary. Throughout the book, Krakauer recounts his attempt to summit Mount Everest the year earlier in what would become, at the time, the mountain’s deadliest season. I’ve been momentarily halted by that title each time I’ve picked up my tattered $5 thrift-store copy over the last few weeks. It’s witty, but not grim; accurate but also imaginative. In three words, “Into Thin Air” conveys not only the literal effect of Everest’s high altitude and how quickly the mountain can take a life, but also the ardent, almost fatuous confidence of those who choose to climb it.

The dissonance between reason and ambition is what makes “Into Thin Air” such a compelling read. For someone like myself, who knows next to nothing about climbing, Krakauer powerfully elucidates the pull of a mountain like Everest and the trance-like state in which it ensnares its adversaries. Unlike some climbers, Krakauer can wax poetic while staying honest about the stakes. He writes about mountaineering as a spiritual practice, good for the mind and body alike, while questioning why some find that clarity only by staring death in the face. In that respect, extreme climbing is an incredibly selfish endeavor. Before he begins his push for the summit, Krakauer remembers his wife, Linda, telling him before he left for Nepal: “If you get killed, it’s not just you who will pay the price. I’ll have to pay, too. For the rest of my life.”

That sentiment echoed in my mind throughout “Everest: The Other Side,” the remarkable new documentary from National Geographic, helmed by “Free Solo” and “Nyad” co-directors Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin. The film is brutally honest in its depictions of cold human narcissism and the relentless pursuit of glory in the name of nebulous spiritual fulfillment. Yet it’s just as candid about humanity’s collective desire for all those things in one form or another.

Such a wanton, helpless display of pride makes for a character study as gripping as it is frustrating. From that disharmony, “Everest: The Other Side” forges a uniquely human story of actualization at all costs, revealing the true price of a life spent looking up and not around.”

We are an arrogant species, frustrated by our humble place in this ecosystem. And yet, we feel everything intensely. When we love, we want to take that love to the ends of the Earth. We want physical proof of emotions we cannot put into words. Maybe then all of this will mean something.

As “Everest: The Other Side” asserts, nothing in this already mystifying life is ever so simple. The film’s subjects, mountaineer Jim Morrison and his partner Hilaree Nelson, found love at the edge of the world and made a life together, with Morrison becoming co-parent to Nelson’s two young sons. But their shared lust for adventure created a prickly tension within their family unit, a strain between their passion and parentage that sits at the documentary’s emotional center.

Like those pulled by devout religion or extreme acts of faith, Morrison and Nelson are powerless before their distinct higher calling — especially with the literal highest calling of all, Everest, in their sights. They don’t just want to summit the mountain from its treacherous north face; they want to be the first people ever to ski down it. In their quest, personal glory and public vanity are forever at odds. Such a wanton, helpless display of pride makes for a character study as gripping as it is frustrating. From that disharmony, “Everest: The Other Side” forges a uniquely human story of actualization at all costs, revealing the true price of a life spent looking up and not around.

Because this is National Geographic, the film is only partially concerned with relaying that price. This documentary is made for IMAX-loving, secondhand adventure seekers. Those who want sweeping shots of impossible sights won’t be disappointed.

But while “Everest: The Other Side” includes countless breathtaking sequences of Earth’s tallest mountain and plenty of nail-biting anxiety in the eventual summit push and ski attempt, those moments are merely the film’s selling points. The crux of this story is on Nelson and Morrison’s shoulders, and their sincerity flies in the face of good judgment and self-editing, giving viewers a palpable sense of their egos. This isn’t to say that either of them is a raging narcissist who cares only about themselves, but there’s no doubt that their sport’s seismic, life-altering dangers are on full display, warts and all.

Early in the film, Nelson tries to communicate the draw of climbing, and how fundamentally at odds it is with her role as a mother. “People ask me, ‘How do you find balance?’” she says. “There isn’t. It’s just chaos. You’re just hanging on. You want to be with your family, but you have a passion, and you want to work, and you need to make money. You’re all over the map.”

It would be easy to dismiss Nelson as selfish, or, at the worst and most damning, a bad parent. How can someone have young children and decide to part with them for two months for a climb that is about, at face value, little more than bragging rights? How can a parent let their children spend two months wondering if their mother is dead or alive?

These are easy questions to ask from the comfort of a living room or the cushion of a theater seat, but much harder to answer when you’re living the life. It’s important to remember that, in life, most of us have desires that would yank us in severe directions. It reminds me that cult experts will tell you that any of us could fall into the clutches of a cult, and those of us who argue otherwise are likely among the most vulnerable. Anyone who insists they are too self-aware to be pulled into something that goes against their own interests is admitting that they don’t know themselves or humanity very well. That’s one of life’s great mysteries: Why do we do things that we know are wrong, or bad for us? Death and taxes might be certain, but so are mistakes and regret, no matter how much we’d like to believe that we’re big enough to let go.

Conflict is ever-present in Morrison, who chooses to climb Everest despite its perils. For him, the adventure is about more than pride or titles; it’s about honor and love. The journey is intended both to strengthen his bond with Nelson and honor the memory of his late wife and their two children, who died in a horrific commuter plane crash in 2011, a decade before he and Nelson decide to attempt Everest. Recalling the aftermath, Morrison tells how climbing brought him clarity. Unable to move from the edge of his driveway, consumed by grief, he eventually found the strength to simply walk up the slight incline and into his home — a microscopic example of the human spirit’s extraordinary tenacity he hopes to commemorate in the Everest climb.

We are an arrogant species, frustrated by our humble place in this ecosystem. And yet, we feel everything intensely. When we love, we want to take that love to the ends of the Earth. We want physical proof of emotions we cannot put into words. Maybe then all of this will mean something.

But more tests lie ahead. The route to Everest proves demanding in heart and health. And while training together for the big summit push by climbing a lower peak in Nepal in 2022, Nelson loses her footing in an avalanche the size of a small snow drift. On a ski slope, the drift would be minor. But on a mountain, every movement is measured. Nelson is swept away and under the snow, toward a cliff. We see it happen in real time, captured on a helmet GoPro. The moment is almost unassuming in its speed, but it permanently shapes everything that follows. Nelson is lost amid a series of avalanches, and the clock starts ticking.

Counting the seconds seems futile. But climbing is futile, too. For Morrison, left to search for his partner amid the snow, hazardous ridges and cliffs, it all seems like a waste. More pain, more trauma, more memories that are left for only one person to hold onto. I was immediately reminded of what Krakauer’s wife told him by satellite phone before he began his push from Everest’s base camp. “Saying goodbye to you was one of the saddest things I’ve ever done,” he remembers her saying. “I guess I knew on some level that you might not be coming back, and it seemed like such a waste. It seemed so f**king stupid and pointless.”

Want more from culture than just the latest trend? The Swell highlights art made to last. Sign up here

It’s hard not to dwell on that sentiment, already knowing what and who Nelson would leave behind if disaster struck. On some level, and to some people, it is all stupid and pointless. But that split second fortifies Morrison, confirming that his quest to Everest is for everyone that he’s lost, and every heartstopping moment along the way. It’s a spiritual pursuit, the kind that we make when we travel to a family member or friend’s favorite place to scatter their ashes; the kind that we make when we give eulogies, or just sit in the grass, staring into space, thinking about everything and nothing, everyone and no one.

Some may be driven to climb Everest just to say that they did it, while others are looking for something else, something with no name. They want to pierce the heavens and reach through the atmosphere to grasp the indescribable truth that unites us all. And if they don’t make it back down to share that peace with the rest of us, it might be enough to experience it just once.

Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian has sharply criticized plans to separate the carrier from its joint venture partner Virgin Atlantic at London Heathrow Airport. In a LinkedIn post, Bastian described the proposals as "short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers."

Delta CEO Ed Bastian has publicly attacked Heathrow's plan to move Delta from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4 in 2028, calling it "short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers" in a LinkedIn post and saying Delta will "pursue all available remedies to correct this decision." The move, part of Heathrow's once-in-a-decade Terminal Occupancy Review, would end Delta's co-located operation with joint venture partner Virgin Atlantic, which stays in Terminal 3. Four other carriers — Finnair, Japan Airlines, Latam, and China Southern — would also switch terminals, while British Airways keeps its existing arrangements at Terminal 5. Heathrow says the changes free up capacity, reduce congestion, and improve resilience, and airport insiders cited by Sky News said airlines representing around 81% of Heathrow passengers backed the final proposal — a figure weighted by British Airways, which carries roughly half of Heathrow's traffic. Virgin Atlantic CEO Corneel Koster told The Sunday Times minimum connecting times between the two airlines could rise from 60 to 90 minutes, and said there is still time to reverse the decision before 2028. North America is Heathrow's largest market after the EU, with 1.86 million passengers in September 2026, or 25.9% of traffic.

#6186. The power of Latinas’ Trump regret could swing this election

RIO GRANDE CITY, Texas â When Cynthia Villareal voted for President Donald Trump in 2024, she did so trusting his campaign promises of lower gas prices, border security and âassistance for the people â for the middle class.â

The 43-year-old mother of four turned out for Trump alongside a sizable majority of voters in heavily Latino Starr County, which hugs the border with Mexico and had reliably turned out for Democratic candidates for five generations.

Less than two years later, Villareal said the promise of her vote never materialized. âHe said gas prices were gonna go down. They havenât â they havenât at all,â said Villareal, who drives around the Rio Grande Valley for her job supervising home health aides and feels every little surge. Villareal manages workers in a shortstaffed, tough profession where wages have simply not kept up with the cost of living. Many of her best workers, she said, are immigrants without permanent legal status experiencing the brunt of Trumpâs immigration agenda.Â

âI mean, he didnât mention that these ICE agents were just going to be picking up all of these hardworking employees, you know, that have no backgrounds,â Villareal said, referring to immigrants without a criminal record. âTheyâre leaving people without their family, basically, and then some of the people are even dying in there,â she said of immigration detention. âLike, who knows what theyâre doing to these poor people?â

For Villareal, life is more expensive, and her job harder. âItâs just too much.âÂ

Latina votersâ rightward shift was a crucial part of Trumpâs reelection in 2024, and while more Latino men backed the president, Latinas actually made larger strides to the right in the last four presidential cycles.Â

Ahead of the midterms, Latinas are also registering higher levels of regret when thinking about their support for Trump, a dynamic that may decide the outcome of competitive races from Texas to Florida and beyond.Â

Voters like Villareal shed light on how Trump regret among this swingy and powerful group of voters âÂ Latinas vote at higher rates than Latino men â may be the swell that breaks into a blue wave for Democrats this November.Â

âI do think the narrative of this election could be that Latina women, in particular, help decide who is in control of the House of Representatives and the balance of government. And I say that because of the shifts weâve seen over time and the shifts back that we are seeing now among Latina women in particular,â said Stephanie Valencia, who studies Latino voters at Equis Research.

Latinosâ political power this cycle is spread across the midterms map. Latinos make up at least 15 percent of the population in six of the 17 most competitive congressional districts, as well as in 29 other districts considered broadly competitive, mostly in the Southwest, California and Florida. Latino voters could be the deciders in competitive races for the U.S. Senate in Texas and Florida. Also in Texas, Latinos could swing the most competitive governorâs race the state has seen in years and, in doing so, elect the first Latina to the stateâs top job.Â

âTrump appealed to their pocketbooks and people were suffering here. I also think people were tired. Weâve been Democratic for over 100 years â why donât we try something different?â said Cecilia HernÃ¡ndez, who founded the local political group Somos STARR this year in response to the big swings to the right sheâs seen in her community.Â

In an interview at the office of her familyâs trash collection business, HernÃ¡ndez said votersâ views are shifting this cycle.Â

âI think along with everything thatâs happening with immigration and with the cost of living today, what Iâve been receiving a lot is, âIâm in the middle,ââ HernÃ¡ndez said. âThey donât want to be seen as far right, and they donât want to be seen as far left, either.â

Latinas stand out in just how much they are feeling the burn of rising costs. They report higher levels of financial stress and are less optimistic about the national economy, according to multiple surveys of Latino voters conducted over the past year.Â

An expansive survey of Latinos conducted in the spring and sponsored by UnidosUS, a Hispanic civil rights and advocacy organization, found that Latinas are more likely than Latino men to say that they have trouble meeting expenses â 23 percent of women vs. 17 percent of men. Men are much more likely to say they can meet their expenses and even have a little left over.

Thirty-eight percent of Latinas voted for Trump in 2024, versus half of Latino men, according to one high-quality analysis, driven by high costs and lack of confidence in the party in power on the economy. The UnidosUS survey of 3,000 Latino voters found that almost a third of Latinas who voted for Trump had regrets about their vote âÂ  seven points more than Latino men.Â

Regret is most striking among young Latinas: 42 percent said they would not vote for him again, a 12-point gap with young Latino men. Latina voters are more likely to register and turn out to vote, and with Latino voters skewing younger, young Latinas wield outsize political power.Â

âLatina women have a large gender pay gap. We also have higher unemployment. We also generally have the responsibility of going to the supermarket and paying the grocery bills and understanding that eggs and and everything else is more expensive,â said Katharine Pichardo, the president and CEO of the Latino Victory Project, which backs progressive Democrats. Latinas are more likely to be closely involved in their kidsâ education and doctorsâ appointments, a frontline view on rising costs that Pichardo said shaped how they voted in 2024 and their views on that vote now.Â

Melissa Morales, the president of Somos Votantes, which does political outreach to Latinos on behalf of Democratic candidates, said Latinas started peeling away from Trump almost immediately in his second term, while Latino men started shifting in the latter part of 2025.Â

While Latinos, like voters overall, broadly rank the cost of living as their top issue, the disparate impact of the administrationâs immigration policies on Latino communities is also registering among Latino voters.Â

A New York Times/Siena poll conducted in mid October found that only a third of Hispanic voters approve of the administrationâs handling of immigration. UnidosUSâ survey found significant gender gaps between Latino men and women. While both groups rank the importance of the issue about the same, Latinas were more likely to oppose policies like ending birthright citizenship and more funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Latinas were also more likely to support banning ICE from sensitive locations like schools and hospitals and to support requiring warrants for enforcement at home or in a workplace.Â

Some of the most dramatic shifts toward Trump and Republicans in 2024 were logged in Texasâ Rio Grande Valley, where Villareal lives. A string of counties in this part of Texas saw double-digit shifts in Trumpâs favor compared with the 2020 election, after significant shifts to the right from 2016 to 2020.Â

Latina voters in the Rio Grande Valley and around Texas will have a big impact on the Texas governorâs race, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa is locked in a dead heat with three-term Gov. Greg Abbott. Hinojosa describes herself as a populist who will tackle corruption and undue influence in government, which she ties to rising costs, weakened public schools and more.Â

Hinojosa rarely acknowledges the history-making potential of her campaign as a Latina in a state that has never elected a Latino to the governorâs mansion. She instead nods to it by saying that sheâd be the first governor from the Rio Grande Valley, which for Texans may as well mean the same thing.Â

Hinojosa, who is bilingual, flexes her Spanglish easily on the stump, telling voters that the most important lesson she ever got came from her mother was the scolding, âNo te dejes.â It doesnât have a direct translation in English.Â

âThe best thing I can come up with is, âKnow your worth and defend it,ââ Hinojosa said in an interview. Asked if the Spanish phrase was connecting with voters, Hinojosa said, âfor sure with Latinos, and 1,000 percent with Latinas.âÂ

âIâve learned on the campaign trail that this is a saying that is mostly passed down through the women in the family,â she added. âAnd I think itâs because of this knowledge that women have for their daughters, grandmothers have for their granddaughters, that the world is tough, and we have to be strong.âÂ

At campaign events in the Rio Grande Valley in September, several voters cited Hinojosaâs identity and approach to politics as a motivating factor.Â

Juanita Vallejo, 40, of Edinburg, Texas, said she sees Hinojosa as an âempowered woman,â and likes her firm stances in support of public schools and curtailing data centers.Â

âI donât want to say it this way, but Iâm going to say it â she wouldnât kiss ass to Trump. I think she would stand up to what is right,â said Rosie Hernandez, 56 of McAllen.Â

Hinojosa is one of the breakout candidates of the cycle, but she has had to plead for funding from national Democrats hesitant to spend in Texas. Earlier this month, a group of influential Latinos in Democratic political circles put pressure on Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who chairs the Democratic Governors Association (DGA), to invest $10 million in the Texas governorâs race. The DGA decided to send $1 million.

Valencia, who signed onto the letter, said Democratsâ investment in Hinojosaâs race has larger implications for the party and sends a message to Latinos. âSheâs a once-in-a-generation candidate from a state that is disproportionately Latino that has been the unicorn that Democrats have chased for decades,â Valencia said.Â

âTo have such a young, dynamic, charismatic Latina candidate in this environment and to not back her is a statement in and of itself, and it says a lot about how certain national Democrats feel about Texas and how they feel about certain candidates.âÂ

Hinojosaâs ability to build enthusiasm for her campaign after starting out with a low profile as a state legislator from Austin could bode well for one the biggest challenges when it comes to Latino voters: turning them out.Â

Latinos had the lowest turnout rates among the major racial and ethnic groups at 51 percent, compared with 71 percent among White voters and 60 percent among Black voters. Nearly 6 million eligible Latinas did not vote in 2024.

During a town hall in Houston with a local Latino influencer this month, Hinojosa mused about the event likely being the first time a candidate for governor hosts an event in Spanish. Before Hinojosa arrived on stage, the host ushered to the microphone a woman who identified herself as a 46-year-old Houston native who had never voted before. Holding a white and orange slip, she said she had registered to vote earlier that day. âQuiero cambio,â she said to cheers. âNo more Trump.âÂ

As both parties look ahead to the 2028 presidential election, theyâll have to contend with the fact that the Latino vote is a swing vote. Whatever gains Democrats make this cycle, they have a lot of ground to make up â especially with Latinas.

Nine days out from Election Day, Villareal said she is planning to vote for Democrats up and down the ballot. She described her vote this time as against Republicans â a register of regret â rather than about enthusiasm for the Democrats on the ticket.Â

âWe have to trust somebody. We have to vote for somebody no matter what,â Villareal said.Â

âAnd obviously, the way things went in 2024 with Republicans, there wasnât a change at all. Itâs just been worse. So weâre gonna try and see.â

#6184. How Travel Credit Cards Are Becoming Full-Trip Companions: Watch Video

Travel credit cards are moving well beyond points and booking. At Skift Global Forum, Capital One Travel’s Sarah Moore said the opportunity lies in remaining useful throughout the trip by combining context, experiences, technology, and trust to build deeper relationships with travelers.

This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner.

Travel credit cards have long competed on points, perks, and booking benefits. For Capital One Travel, the next phase is about extending the relationship further into the trip and finding more ways to stay useful after a customer books.

The company sees an opportunity to connect more parts of the travel journey, from planning and airport support to destination experiences. That approach draws on Capital One’s technology, booking data, travel products, and existing relationship with cardholders as their financial partner.

At Skift Global Forum in New York, Sarah Moore, head of Capital One Travel, discussed how the company is trying to become what she called a “travel companion” for its cardholders, with a role that extends before, during, and after the trip.

The Travel Card’s Next Act: From Earning Points to Erasing Friction

Capital One entered the travel business relatively recently, launching the Capital One Travel booking platform in 2021. Moore said arriving later gave the company an opportunity to look at what already existed and build around the expectations of a modern traveler.

That meant taking a technology-first approach, but also starting with the customer rather than simply recreating the traditional credit card travel model.

“We were able to really see what was out there in the marketplace and understand what the modern traveler was looking for,” Moore said.

That distinction matters as the boundaries between financial services, travel booking, loyalty, and trip planning continue to blur. A travel card may still sit in a traveler’s wallet, but the relationship increasingly extends into the rest of the trip.

For years, booking has been treated as the finish line for many travel companies. Moore sees it more as a starting point.

Capital One Travel wants to remain with customers after the booking transaction, whether that means helping a traveler navigate the airport by surfacing lounge information, providing flight updates, or helping them decide what to do once they reach their destination.

Being useful when something goes wrong can be particularly important, giving a company an opportunity to demonstrate the value of the relationship.

“Knowing when to step up is what builds trust,” Moore said.

For Capital One Travel, those moments can help turn a single booking into a longer-term customer relationship.

Moore also emphasized the importance of collaboration across the travel industry to better support travelers throughout their journeys. No single company can manage every aspect of the travel experience today, making partnerships across the broader ecosystem essential to delivering consistent support to customers throughout their journeys.

Delivering that kind of support also requires a different approach to personalization.

Travel brands have spent years collecting customer data, but Moore said the most useful form of personalization is contextual. The question is not simply who someone is, but what kind of trip they are taking right now.

A traveler taking a weekend trip with a spouse, for example, may want something entirely different from the same traveler on vacation with children.

Moore used her own family as an example. A trip with her husband might call for a relaxing stay at one of Capital One Travel’s Premier Collection hotels. Traveling with her children could mean booking a four-bedroom vacation rental, also available on Capital One Travel, with many homes offering the same luxury benefits found in the Premier and Lifestyle hotel collections. Even within the same family, different travelers may want completely different activities.

That same thinking extends to what travelers actually do once they arrive.

Moore said in a survey conducted by Capital One Travel, more than 70% of travelers are looking at some type of event or live experience, from sports and dining to other forms of cultural immersion. For some travelers, those experiences are increasingly shaping the trip itself rather than simply being added after the flight and hotel are booked.

“Travel is not just a flight and a hotel,” Moore said. “It’s what you’re actually doing when you land and what you’re engaging in when you’re there.”

Capital One has responded by building experiences into its broader cardholder proposition. Moore pointed to partnerships with Major League Baseball and touring artists, as well as more intimate experiences tied to food and culture that can be booked through activities on Capital One Travel.

One example is a culinary–driven trip led by chef José Andrés in his hometown of Asturias, Spain, exclusively for cardholders, giving them a more distinctive and immersive way to experience the destination.

Taken together, those efforts point to a broader shift in what a travel credit card can become. Moore said Capital One is focused on becoming a travel companion that supports cardholders from booking through servicing and the trip itself.

The company launched a dedicated Capital One Travel app within the past year, an example Moore cited of meeting travelers in the channels where they increasingly expect to manage their trips.

AI could push that evolution further. Travelers are increasingly finding inspiration, researching destinations, and making decisions through new interfaces. Moore said Capital One Travel will need to meet them in those places while maintaining the value and trust that come with its role as their financial partner.

That trust also creates an opportunity to use the information Capital One already has more effectively. Transaction data can provide signals about how some customers travel and what they may be looking for next, provided it is used to make the experience easier and more relevant.

For Moore, that is ultimately what “frictionless” travel means: understanding what a traveler needs and making it simple for them to get it.

This shift has implications beyond credit cards. Travel companies across the industry are trying to extend their relationship with customers beyond a single transaction. Doing that effectively requires more than adding another loyalty benefit or digital touchpoint.

It means understanding the context of each trip, being useful when travelers actually need help, and creating access that enhances the experience. It also requires accepting that the traveler, not the brand, is ultimately in control of the relationship.

For Capital One Travel, the opportunity is to make the card and the platform behind it more relevant throughout the journey. If that works, the booking becomes less of an endpoint and more of one moment in a much longer relationship.

So even if you don’t fly JetBlue, their tests of how much more passengers will pay can wind up costing you. A First Bag Starts At $50. A Second Reaches $85. Here’s the new domestic schedule, per bag, each way: Checked bag Paid more than 24 hours ahead Paid within 24 hours First bag, off-peak $50 $60 First bag, peak $55 $70 Second bag, off-peak $70 $75 Second bag, peak $75 $85 Peak pricing is November 19–30, December 17–January 18, and May 20–September 8 next summer. A family of four checking one bag each, without a waiver, pays $440 roundtrip on peak dates even when they pay early. Wait until check-in and it’s $560. On transatlantic Main Base and EvenMore Base fares, the first bag is $80 off-peak or $90 peak when prepaid, rising to $90 or $100 within 24 hours. Standard Main and EvenMore transatlantic fares still include a first bag. Mosaic 1 elite status includes one checked bag and Mosaic 2–4 include two. JetBlue Plus and Premier cardholders have a first checked bag benefit. Those exemptions become a pitch for their credit card since things are worse for everyone else. And while they give you a discount for paying in advance, bag fees are refundable only when the entire booking is canceled before departure. If you pay for an extra bag you don’t wind up checking, you’re out of luck. By putting fear of high prices in passengers, they may generate revenue for services the customer winds up not ever needing and using. JetBlue Keeps Leading The Industry Toward Higher Bag Fees When I covered JetBlue’s increase in March, their cheapest first bag went from $35 to $39. The peak advance price rose to $49. Today’s $50 minimum is 28% higher than that March minimum, and 43% higher than the $35 price before it. In 2018, JetBlue led the move to a $30 first checked bag. United followed that same week. In January 2020, JetBlue went to $35 unless you prepaid. United announced its matching move the next month. In 2024, JetBlue added peak and off-peak baggage pricing, after already raising fees earlier that year. This spring, JetBlue raised fees in late March. United announced another increase days later. JetBlue isn’t the consumer-first airline anymore. When they introduced bag fees in 2015, the first bag was $20 online or at a kiosk, $25 at the counter. They defended their direction by pointing to how much worse other airlines were, declaring: The world is going in a very dramatic direction toward more and more commoditization. That’s not where we’re going. Now they’re leading in the race to the bottom. The Government Encourages This JetBlue tied the spring increase to rising operating costs. But an airline’s bag fee isn’t derived from the fuel needed to carry the bag. Fares and fees are set according to what airlines think customers will pay, subject to competition. Higher bag fees let JetBlue raise the cost of a trip while leaving the advertised airfare alone. They also make it harder to compare the total price across airlines. And the government rewards them for doing it. Domestic air transportation is generally subject to a 7.5% federal excise tax. Separate baggage fees are excluded from that tax. Every dollar an airline moves out of fares and into fees saves them 7.5 cents, even if the total price remains the same. I’ve made this point through previous rounds of JetBlue increases: anyone serious about pushing back on bag fees should start with the tax preference that encourages airlines to move money out of fares and into baggage charges. #6180. Right-wing media and the mystery of Texas’ transgender mailers

On Thursday night, the smear at the heart of the mysterious transgender mailers that have rocked the final weeks of the midterm elections in Texas completed its journey. What began as baseless social media whispers quickly ascended the ladder of conservative influence, jumped into mailboxes across the Lone Star State and ultimately into the comforting prime-time embrace of Fox News.

At a town hall in Fort Worth, a Texas mother of six named Rebekah Smith told Vice President JD Vance that her 11-year-old daughter had received a letter explaining how to transition without her parents ever knowing, and asked how Republicans would keep the government out of her family. “I don’t know who sent that letter to your child,” the vice president said, “but I think the person who sends a letter to an 11-year-old about gender transition, what I call that in my family is a pervert, and that person ought to go to prison.” Host Jesse Watters, never one to let a grievance go to waste, promised that Fox would investigate “this perverted letter.” Vance asked Smith to talk to his staff because he would “like the Department of Justice to investigate that” as well.

Watters rushed to promote the spectacle. “WHOA! Texas MOM tells JD Vance her DAUGHTER received a letter telling her TO TRANSITION TO A BOY,” he posted on X, followed by Vance’s promise. Missing from that framing was the question that should have governed the segment: Who actually sent the material?

Nobody on that stage mentioned that the pamphlet was a fake. Nobody mentioned that the real transgender advocacy group named inside it had disavowed the mailer. Nobody mentioned that sworn testimony filed that same week had tied the text messages that accompanied it to a national Republican organization. The vice president was asking federal prosecutors to chase a forgery that may well have originated in his own party’s orbit — and he was doing it on a network whose viewers had been marinating in that forgery for weeks.

The race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic challenger James Talarico has become a crucible for dark-money maneuvers. As polls show the Republican grip on the Lone Star State slipping, conservative campaigns and their surrogates have resorted to increasingly desperate tactics. In early October, for example, Talarico took a brief hiatus from the campaign trail to recover from a severe case of the flu. Rather than accepting a routine human illness, the right-wing echo chamber treated a temporary absence as evidence of mental illness. Within days, the fabricated scandal has collapsed — yet the machinery of right-wing media simply pivoted to amplifying a more insidious operation designed to trigger visceral outrage.

This second October surprise involved millions of unsolicited text messages and a wave of physical mailers sent to Texas households with materials that directed readers to the website of the Transgender Education Network of

It does not need to survive scrutiny. It just needs to circulate upward.

Texas while inserting provocative advice on child emancipation that the real organization says it never authored or authorized. By flooding the electorate with extreme material disguised as progressive advocacy, right-wing operatives appear to have sought to create a fake controversy that could be weaponized in attack ads and campaign speeches. Vance, for instance, told the Fox News audience that Talarico has “a weird fascination with trans kids,” and that “he’ll probably defend the right of the person sending the letter, not the right of the parent who is rightfully creeped out by this.” Vance claimed that Talarico “has actually called it abusive when parents try to prevent their children from transitioning” and that Paxton “has fought hard to prosecute those people, whereas James Talarico has fought hard to protect those people.” Even the distortion had been laundered by then — Talarico called denying a child’s gender identity abusive, a different claim from saying parents must permit medical transition, but at the top of the ladder the difference no longer exists.

That is how a smear works in the closed ecosystem of the American right. It does not need to survive scrutiny. It just needs to circulate upward. An anonymous account posts it; an influencer adopts it; a donor-funded outlet reports the influencer’s outrage as news; an elected official demands an investigation, and the demand becomes proof the story matters; cable news books the controversy; a vice president promises federal action. Each rung launders the one below it. The correction, when it comes, travels in the opposite direction and arrives nowhere.

The paper trail looks like what you would expect from a covert operation. Texas Transgender Student Union LLC was formed in Wyoming on Sept. 2 through a commercial registered agent that helps owners stay anonymous. After CBS News Texas visited the agent’s address in Sheridan, Wyoming, the agent announced it was resigning. The mailers listed a Houston-area post office box. The Texas Observer reported that the barcode on the envelopes traced to a mail-tracking company that has taken federal campaign money from only one group this year, the National Republican Congressional Committee. The committee said it had nothing to do with the mailers, and the company would not say who paid. CBS News Texas reported that the bulk-mail permit belongs to an Illinois printer owned by the Zerrusen family, who have given heavily to Republican PACs and been photographed with Donald Trump.

When the real Transgender Education Network of Texas filed a petition in Travis County court to unmask the perpetrators behind the impersonation campaign, the partisan safety nets of the Texas judiciary eventually snapped into action. A deposition of Infobip, the messaging company that delivered the texts, which a Travis County judge ordered made public, indicated that the texts were sent on behalf of the Republican Women’s Caucus Fund and a man named John Braun. But on Friday, the Texas Supreme Court, composed entirely of judges appointed by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, issued an administrative stay that blocked its release. Chris Hilton, an attorney who previously served under Paxton, defended him during his impeachment trial and was later pushed out of office amid sexual harassment allegations, argued on behalf of the company that the mailers were not political speech because they named no candidate or party.

Dirty tricks are an old tradition of American politics. This cycle, Republican PACs in Nevada mailed a flyer calling a nonpartisan candidate, Danielle Ford, the “AOC of Nevada,” hoping voters would mistake her for the actual Democratic nominee, Aaron Ford. This week also brought word that the group that funded Cornel West’s 2024 ballot drives raised every dollar through a dark-money network bankrolled by Elon Musk.

The president’s party whines about decoy candidates in Alaska while running them at home. Ratf**king is a long and proud Republican tradition, and the Texas operation fits inside perfectly.

#6178. Why We’ve Been Looking at the Hotel Brands vs. OTAs War All Wrong

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

The hotel industry’s distribution war has an overlooked third party: the owner. New questions about AI, loyalty and customer acquisition could make that imbalance even more consequential.

Maybe we've been looking at the hotel distribution war all wrong, all along.

For years, we at Skift have chronicled the battle between hotel brands and online travel agencies. Hilton and Marriott want guests booking direct; Booking.com and Expedia want those reservations to come through their platforms. Every new technology, most recently AI agents, is assessed by which side it will help.

The fight is real. But the usual framing leaves out a party with a very different balance sheet: the hotel owner.

The owner pays the brand for access to its commercial system and may also pay an OTA when that platform delivers the guest. The brand and the OTA negotiate over the customer, but it is often the property that must absorb the cost of both relationships and still turn a profit.

Hilton’s October 27 results make the distinction clear. The company reported $815 million in third-quarter franchise and licensing revenue, a line that

Tags: artificial intelligence, hotel owners, hotels, OTAs, skift aviation forum, skift commerce summit, the prompt

Skift provides the insights. You make the decisions.

Skift argues the brand-versus-OTA distribution fight leaves out the party that absorbs the cost of both relationships: the hotel owner. Hilton's third-quarter results, reported October 27, showed $815 million in franchise and licensing revenue across a system of 8,683 franchised and licensed properties, 892 managed hotels, and 45 hotels in its ownership segment. Hilton's annual filing states franchise royalties are calculated as a percentage of gross room revenue, with separate program fees for marketing, reservations, technology, and Hilton Honors. In Skift's illustrative example, a $200 room sold through an OTA at a hypothetical 15% commission leaves the owner with a $30 acquisition charge while the royalty is still calculated on the full $200. Hilton's fee economics track revenue flowing through its network; the owner's economics depend on what is left after acquisition costs. MCR Hotels CEO Tyler Morse, who owns and operates 150 hotels including the unflagged TWA Hotel, has argued for years that owners should move away from OTAs and has described hotel ownership as a business of buying reservations. On Hilton's latest earnings call, CEO Chris Nassetta said AI should eventually bring more direct business at lower cost while OTAs remain important for a segment of the business, and cited the RISE system-fee cuts launched in June 2025 — 30 basis points off loyalty costs system-wide and another 50 basis points for hotels meeting a quality threshold, both reductions to system fees rather than royalty rates. Skift's analysis: if AI agents route bookings into brand systems, the owner's test is whether the new channel improves margin after every fee, and that data doesn't exist yet.

A lot of these stylish, boutique hotels enter the points world through curated hotel collections that participate in loyalty programs, giving hotels a wider reach of potential guests without having to adhere to strict brand standards that change the spirit of the property.

One of the pioneers in this space is Design Hotels, a collection of hundreds of independently-owned hotels and resorts dotting the globe, each with its own identity, personality and approach to hospitality.

"Every hotel is picked for its originality [and] the vision that's behind it," Stijn Oyen, managing director at Design Hotels, told TPG, adding that each property has "a strong point of view and cultural connection."

And it's not necessarily easy to make the cut for this collection: According to Oyen, only about 5% of the hotels that apply to join Design Hotels are accepted in an effort to "stay true to the original roots and values of what makes a design hotel."

Then there's the loyalty twist: Marriott actually owns Design Hotels, and many (but not all) of the collection's properties participate in Marriott Bonvoy.

Here's a quick guide to everything you need to know about Design Hotels, plus a few standout properties where you can earn and burn Marriott Bonvoy points.

Related: 12 new boutique hotels worth redeeming your points for

Founded in the early 1990s, Design Hotels was created to bring together independently owned, design-forward hotels that shared a commitment to originality, creativity and local culture.

Today, that collection is more than 300 members strong, with new properties regularly joining. What differentiates the collection is the individuality of each property — each one has its own unique point of view, rather than a prescribed set of standards travelers will see at more traditional hotel brands.

"We're set up around design," Oyen explained. "It's about the vision. It's about being independent with a voice."

Design Hotels became part of Marriott's portfolio following the hotel giant's acquisition of Starwood Hotels & Resorts in 2016, giving Marriott a majority stake in the company. By 2021, Marriott had acquired full ownership of Design Hotels, though the collection continues to operate as a separate entity, with member hotels retaining their individual identities and independence.

The company describes its properties as "design-driven hotels that function as social hubs and spaces for purposeful experiences."

But what does that actually mean? To start, getting into the collection isn't easy, and Design Hotels is looking for one distinguishing factor before choosing a new member: "the originality in its concept."

According to Oyen, only about 5% of applicants pass the test. Hotels are also evaluated on everything from design and sustainability to cultural programming and the property's connection to its local community.

"It's a strong, strong sense of place," Oyen explained, adding that beyond their physical design, the hotels should have vibrant public spaces that attract locals and feel like an extension of the neighborhoods they call home.

It's also about the people. According to Oyen, about 60% of Design Hotels owners are first-time hoteliers, bringing fresh perspectives and new approaches to hospitality. The company calls the creative minds behind its properties "Originals," describing them as "the engines behind pioneering design and revolutionary hospitality," according to the brand's website.

Without rigid brand standards dictating every detail, these hoteliers have the freedom to pursue projects that seasoned hospitality pros might consider too risky. That might be as simple as removing TVs from guest rooms or as dramatic as building a hotel accessible only by cable car, like Vigilius Mountain Resort in Italy's Dolomites.

For Marriott Bonvoy members, Design Hotels offers a truly independent, boutique-like stay while still allowing them to earn and burn points. Something that, frankly, a lot of people don't realize is available to them in the loyalty world.

Just don't forget: Not all Design Hotels participate in Marriott Bonvoy. To see a full list of the 120-plus participating hotels, visit Marriott's dedicated Design Hotels landing page.

For Design Hotels, according to Oyen, the relationship with Marriott is a win-win situation: Hotels gain access to nearly 300 million loyalty members while maintaining their "complete independence."

But because these properties operate differently from traditional Marriott hotels, Bonvoy elite members shouldn't expect all their usual perks to apply.

Here's what members can expect based on their status.

The following Marriott Bonvoy benefits are excluded at Design Hotels:

Set near the beach in Casablanca, Villa Sahrai pays respect to "Casablanca’s Art Deco tradition" across its 56 rooms and public spaces. Be sure to take advantage of the spa and its Moroccan hammam before settling down for food at one of two restaurants or a nightcap at the bar.

How to book: Cash rates from around $160 per night or 34,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

To get to Vigilius Mountain Resort, guests must ascend a private cable car that travels between the mountain hotel and the village it soars above.
