#6175. The Trump Show is on the verge of cancellation

Ahead of Tuesdayâs midterms, Democrats are biting their nails and enduring sleepless nights, wondering whether they will be forced to endure yet another election that has so often characterized the Trump era: close races that seem inevitably to go to the Republicans. All the fundamentals and polls indicate a possible blowout and a big one, but after watching Americans shockingly elect Donald Trump the first time, live through his Big Lie and witness his historic comeback only two years ago, no one can feel confident that this era of chaos, corruption and cruelty might finally be beginning its descent into the dustbin of history. We thought we were here before, and it didnât end well.

There are reasons to be hopeful, though, even if you assume that the polls are underestimating Republican enthusiasm for their leaders once again. While there have been misses in the polling over this past decade, it hasnât manifested in midterms as it has in the races with Trump on the ballot. In those years, the polling was pretty much on the money. Democrats have done very well in all the off-year and special elections this cycle, and although thatâs no guarantee, it has to be considered a good sign.Â

The big difference this time is that Trumpâs approval rating is hovering close to 30%, a lethal number, and he has presided over a high cost of living and a war of choice with Iran, both things he promised would never happen if he were president. The one election he lost in 2020 was the result of his mismanagement of the only crisis he faced, the Covid-19 pandemic, and this second term has solidified the impression among many voters who were inclined to give him the benefit of the doubt anyway, that he simply doesnât know what he is doing.Â

One sign that should give Democrats some real comfort in these last couple of days is Trumpâs performance on the campaign trail. To say the 80-year-old has lost a step is an understatement. Sure, he barnstormed through all the battleground states and even attempted to shore up enthusiasm in places that should not need his presence to get out the vote. But his patented âweaveâ is unraveling at every stop.Â

Trump has taken to doubling down on the weirdness, going on about menâs bodies to a truly bizarre degree, being under the impression that because his trained rally goers will ritualistically cheer anything he says, this is a winning message. His recent comments warning people to stay away from Mar-a-Lago, his private Florida club, because they would be unable to afford the hamburgers could not be more in keeping with his apparent pursuit of Marie Antoinetteâs legacy.Â

After years of ragging on Democrats for bringing celebrities on the campaign trail and bragging that he didnât need any to help him fill up stadiums, the president has invited some to join him at campaign rallies â although one could scarcely call them A-listers.

But most embarrassing for the president is that he is no longer the singular star of the Trump show. As POLITICO reported, after years of ragging on Democrats for bringing celebrities on the campaign trail and bragging that he didnât need any to help him fill up stadiums, the president has invited some to join him at campaign rallies â although one could scarcely call them A-listers. The cast leans heavily on older athletes, from retired NFL players to race car drivers, although Trump did manage to talk at least one genuine country music star, Jason Aldean, to join him in a rally held just a few miles from his home. Rapper Nicki Minaj has become a staple on the trail, and the presidentâs old friend Mike Tyson is often with him. Trump simply canât carry the show by himself anymore.Â

This is the most expensive campaign in history, with Elon Musk alone spending more than $400 million in money he dug out of his couch cushions, but the total spending on both sides has reached upwards of $16 billion, the vast majority of it to benefit the Republicans. The fact is that it doesnât appear to have done them much good. In fact, their spending is almost all coming from large donors like Musk, while their small donor base has shrunk considerably. Thatâs usually a sign of a lack of enthusiasm, and it doesnât bode well for Tuesdayâs results.Â

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

The electionâs stakes are profound. America crossed the Rubicon in 2024 when it invited Trump back into power after he tried to overturn the election, was convicted of fraud, and was revealed to have possessed and leaked classified information after he was out of office. The media and the nationâs elites interpreted that victory as a sign that Trump was some sort of magical superhero, and that it was in all their interests to join with him and reap the rewards. The result has been nothing short of catastrophic, revealing gaping holes in our constitutional order, weaknesses in our democratic system and a void in our society where moral authority used to be. America has never been perfect, and it always falls short of its professed ideals, but this political era has stripped away the belief that we have any at all.Â

The corruption on display, coupled with a lack of concern for the lives of ordinary people, is breathtaking. And while it remains shocking that tens of millions of Americans still support this administration, it seems that a majority may have finally had the veil lifted from their eyes, allowing them to see the incompetence, grift and megalomania for what it is.

Itâs hard to see how a nation founded on the ideas espoused in the Declaration of Independence can survive without even the pretense of ethics or universal values. At the moment, the American creed is simply âto the victor go the spoils,â by which Trump is not just imperiously referring to the foreign countries he seeks to colonize. Heâs talking about America itself.

There can be no more questions about what the Republican Party is capable of, and as weak as he appears on the campaign trail, Trump is clearly frustrated and angry. Reporting suggests that he plans to double down on all of it the minute the election is over. If the American people somehow fail to forcefully repudiate Trump and the oligarchs who use and manipulate him, itâs unlikely weâll get another chance.

Her pants were wet, and she says a flight attendant told her there were no empty seats and she could have paper towels and a tiny bottle of antibacterial cleaning spray to deal with the mess – she couldn’t even have an extra blanket. The passenger shared the story on November 1 and posted the video the following day. Her tweet has been viewed more than 1.6 million times. .@British_Airways ABSOLUTELY disgusted. A passenger may have had an accident on the previous flight. The time between flights is the opportunity to switch cushions. British Airways Has Done This Before In 2017, I wrote about a British Airways passenger flying London to Cape Town who found his seat soaked in urine. In 2018, a British Airways business class passenger headed to Jamaica found his pillow, seat and trousers wet with urine. He was moved away from his wife and offered 40,000 Avios. AirAsia now has a date for Bahrain but less need for it. A Pegasus deal routing Europe traffic through Istanbul undercuts the case for a Gulf hub.

AirAsia is targeting March 2027 for its first passenger flights to Bahrain. It is the group’s first firm timeline for its highly anticipated Gulf hub since the U.S.-Iran war forced it to adjust its plans.

The group gave the new date as it appointed a seven-member, all non-executive board for AirAsia Bahrain on November 1.

“While the geopolitical situation in the region has required us to adjust our initial plans, our commitment to Bahrain has not changed,” said Tony Fernandes, CEO of AirAsia's owner Capital A and adviser to AirAsia Group. “We continue to monitor developments in the region closely and are targeting the commencement of AirAsia flights to Bahrain by March 2027, as conditions allow.”

AirAsia has set March 2027 as its target for the first passenger flights to Bahrain, the first firm timeline for its Gulf hub since the U.S.-Iran war forced the group to adjust its plans. Capital A CEO Tony Fernandes said the commitment to Bahrain has not changed, but framed the date as conditional — "as conditions allow." The plan, signed with Bahrain's transport ministry in November 2025, envisions a Bahrain-registered subsidiary running up to 25 daily flights by 2030 and serving as AirAsia X's bridge from Southeast Asia to Europe and North America. Since then the group has suspended 81 routes and is returning 25 aircraft early as fuel prices climb, and it has shifted its Europe approach toward a codeshare with Pegasus Airlines that routes Southeast Asia–Europe traffic through Istanbul. Only cargo is flying in Bahrain today, via twice-weekly Teleport freighters, with maintenance capabilities planned but no timeline or investment figure disclosed. The March target matches a wider pattern: Wizz Air moved its Abu Dhabi and Dubai restart to March 2027, nearly 20 non-Gulf airlines are still not serving Dubai, and Virgin Atlantic has suspended Dubai flights into 2027.

#6172. James O’Keefe election sting ends in his own felony voter fraud charges

Conservative activist James OâKeefe set out to expose alleged vulnerabilities in Minnesotaâs election system. Now, he faces felony charges stemming from the undercover operation.

OâKeefe, formerly of Project Veritas and current CEO of the OâKeefe Media Group, and conservative influencer Cameron Higby were charged Wednesday with unlawful voting and identity theft after allegedly impersonating registered voters at Minneapolis polling places during the stateâs Aug. 11 primary.

According to Hennepin County prosecutors, the men wore disguises, used fake accents and provided election workers with the names of registered voters without their knowledge or permission. They filmed the encounters and later posted videos claiming to expose weaknesses in Minnesotaâs voter registration procedures.

The operation targeted the stateâs *vouching* system, which allows registered voters to verify the residency of people seeking to register on Election Day. The process requires sworn statements and identifying information from prospective voters.

Neither OâKeefe nor Higby cast a ballot or signed the required vouching oath. Prosecutors contend that misrepresenting their identities while beginning the voting process was itself unlawful.

OâKeefe defended the operation as investigative journalism, calling the prosecution an attack on First Amendment rights. Higby also denied breaking the law, saying the pair intended to expose election vulnerabilities.

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

The charges are the latest controversy involving OâKeefeâs undercover tactics. In 2017, reporters at the Washington Post caught him trying to sell them a false story. In 2009, he collaborated on hidden-camera investigations targeting Planned Parenthood and gained national attention for videos involving the community organization ACORN. He later settled a lawsuit brought by a former ACORN employee for $100,000 without admitting wrongdoing.

But Minnesota officials say the latest operation demonstrated something different from what OâKeefe intended.

Election workers noticed suspicious behavior and reported it, prompting an investigation. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said the stateâs system for identifying and responding to potential misconduct functioned as intended. This vouching process itself accounted for fewer than 0.6% of votes cast in Minnesotaâs 2024 general election, according to state election officials.

OâKeefe and Higby are scheduled to appear in court Nov. 16. Neither has been convicted.

#6170. How Tourism Ireland Is Navigating a More Uncertain Travel Market: Watch Video

Photo Caption: Skift Transatlantic Summit 2026 - Dublin, Ireland

At the Skift Transatlantic Summit, Tourism Ireland Chief Executive Alice Mansergh explained how the island of Ireland is navigating current headwinds by investing in connectivity marketing, market diversification, AI-driven discovery, and the authentic local experiences that can keep the country high on travelers’ wish lists.

This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner.

North America remains one of Ireland’s most valuable visitor markets, but the outlook is getting more complicated. At the Skift Transatlantic Summit, Tourism Ireland Chief Executive Alice Mansergh pointed to continued growth alongside signs of softening demand as travelers contend with higher costs and economic uncertainty.

So far in 2026, Ireland has welcomed 5% more visitors from North America, with spending up 10%. But Mansergh said the past few months have been softer, as travelers think more carefully about their finances and increasingly seek flexible or refundable bookings.

“For all of us, it becomes really important to be at the top of the travel wishlist,” she said.

That challenge is shaping Tourism Ireland’s marketing strategy. Its new “Ireland Goes Beyond” campaign highlights the scenery, culture, heritage, and local experiences that make Ireland worth choosing, even as travelers become more selective about where they spend.

Staying on travelers’ wish lists is only part of the challenge. Ireland also needs to maintain the air connections that bring those travelers to the destination. With jet fuel costs up sharply and fewer Europeans traveling to the U.S., Mansergh said airlines are looking more closely at which transatlantic routes remain profitable.

Tourism Ireland works with carriers to promote strategic routes and stimulate inbound demand. Mansergh summed up the immediate challenge simply: “fill the planes to keep the planes.”

Healthy two-way travel matters, she added, because weaker outbound traffic from Europe can put the same routes that bring North American visitors to Ireland under pressure. “When you lose the connectivity, that can be damaging,” she said.

Those pressures reinforce the importance of a diversified visitor base. North America generates just over a third of Ireland’s inbound overseas revenue, with Europe contributing roughly another third. Britain offers another opportunity, with visitors from Ireland’s nearest neighbor twice as likely to return.

“Now is not the time to be wholly dependent on just one market or another,” Mansergh said.

Beyond traditional marketing and airline partnerships, Tourism Ireland is also adapting to how travelers discover destinations. Its research found that the number of people naming AI as their primary source of travel inspiration has doubled in the past year.

The organization is responding by optimizing its digital content for generative AI. According to Mansergh, information provided by Tourism Ireland now contributes to answers for 19% of queries about the destination across tools including ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

The goal is to influence which experiences AI recommends, particularly lesser-known attractions and local businesses that might otherwise be overlooked.

But visibility in AI search also depends on what travelers are seeing and saying about a destination across the web. “Choose what you want to be famous for,” Mansergh said.

Tourism Ireland has applied that thinking to Halloween, building awareness of the holiday’s roots in the ancient Irish festival of Samhain through its own content and platforms such as Reddit, YouTube, and Tripadvisor.

“You need a bit of a surround sound of people talking about the things you want them to be talking about,” she said.

Technology may be changing how travelers discover Ireland, but the experiences that attract them often have little to do with technology.

“For me, I always want AI to stand for, yes, artificial intelligence, but also authentic Ireland,” she said.

She pointed to sheepdog demonstrations, cider-making farms, and traditional currach-building as examples of experiences that bring travelers closer to local culture while spreading tourism to more regions.

“The more digital we are,” Mansergh said, “the more we crave those authentic touch and feel real moments.”

For 2027, Tourism Ireland plans to keep focusing on connectivity, year-round travel, and emerging opportunities such as “cool-cations.” Taken together, those priorities reflect Tourism Ireland’s approach to a more uncertain market: Protect the connections that bring visitors to Ireland, reach travelers through new channels, and give them compelling reasons to visit.

#6169. $12,000 Buffalo–New York Fares Making Headlines—I’m Finding Nonstops For $337 Roundtrip

A $12,203 airfare between Buffalo and New York about 300 miles each way – is going viral as evidence of how expensive it’s gotten to fly home for the holidays. The TikTok video that started it off though shows a roundtrip price (not one-way) and connecting both directions in Florida (not non-stop). Meanwhile, nonstops on that route seem to start at $337 roundtrip. Kristen Mirand says she was trying to get home to Buffalo and received a notification for a $200 flight from New York. Then she looked at returning, and found five-figure prices with connections in Orlando and Fort Lauderdale. She joked that she’d start walking. The New York Post ran with “Flight from Buffalo to NYC reportedly reached $12K — as holiday airfare hits an all-time high” and suggests higher fuel costs and holiday demand are involved here. ZeroHedge describes a “roughly 90 minute flight,” and launches into airlines keeping fares high after fuel prices fall. It ends with the prospect of airlines “laughing all the way to the bank.” Look at the flights actually displayed in the video: $11,400 roundtrip, returning through Orlando. These are 7 and 9 hour trips from Buffalo to JFK. $12,203 roundtrip, returning through Fort Lauderdale. These are 7 and 8.5 hour trips. Every price is labeled round trip. you’re seeing the cost of the whole ticket when you select a return. This wasn’t a $12,000 nonstop and none of these itineraries gets you there in 90 minutes. I’m seeing nonstop roundtrips around $337 on Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, United Airlines and American Airlines, checking across the New York airports. Even if you want to connect in Florida, Frontier Airlines can be as low as $210 roundtrip. She doesn’t show her dates, but at those prices be flexible! My guess is that the pricing is breaking somewhere as the system puts together this unnatural itinerary. A fare between Buffalo and New York comes with rules about how you can travel and Florida connections aren’t usually included in the routing rules. A search can wind up combining separate fares for different pieces of the trip instead of using the simple fare between the two cities. Bad fare combining or an error putting together the outbound and return can cause weird outcomes. While the last seats on a flight can be expensive, “last seat available” doesn’t seem like the explanation for a $12,000 Buffalo–New York price. Airfares are up. Hopper’s says Thanksgiving domestic roundtrips average $402, up 31%, and Christmas $452, up 23%. Check the dates, cabin, passenger count and currency. Separate searches can get you away from whatever combination generated the nonsense price. For this route I’d also price Amtrak’s Empire Service between Buffalo and New York. Those Florida connections already consume most of the day before you add getting to the airport, security and the trip into Manhattan. #6160. 5 things to watch for in Tuesday’s midterm elections

Midterm elections are almost always referendums on the party in power. That’s especially true this year, when President Donald Trump has repeatedly directed Republican voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.”

But Trump’s sagging poll numbers, driven by cost-of-living concerns and an unpopular war, have helped create a political environment that favors Democrats.

Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales projects Democrats could net four to six seats in the Senate, a scenario considered highly unlikely at the start of the cycle. To succeed, Democrats need to flip seats in several red-leaning states, among them Alaska, Iowa and Kansas. The party would also need to hold its own vulnerable seats in New Hampshire, Minnesota and Georgia.

On the House side, the question seems to be not whether Democrats will take the majority, but rather how big their margin will be. The party needs a net gain of three seats; Inside Elections projects Democrats could wind up winning 20 to 30 seats, a significant number of them in districts that voted for Trump by double digits two years ago.

Here are five things we’ll be watching for as the votes are tallied:

Republicans appeared to win the redistricting wars that defined much of the 2026 election cycle, especially after the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act, which led to new maps in several Southern states. Democrats gained favorable lines in California and Utah, but Republicans redrew more seats in their favor. The overall GOP effort put new districts on the board in places such as Florida and Louisiana but also sought to boost Republicans’ chances of ousting longtime targets, including Reps. Marcy Kaptur of Ohio and Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez of Texas.

While some redrawn districts are clear pickups, many redrawn seats are considered Toss-ups, forcing the GOP to deploy significant resources. Still, if Republicans make the gains they hoped to make in places such as Florida and Texas, it could go a long way in helping them either somehow keep the majority or narrow a Democratic one.

Historic gains among Latino voters helped Trump win the White House in 2024 and boosted GOP candidates in swing districts across the nation. Those victories also influenced Texas Republicans’ redraw of the state’s congressional map, betting that Latino voters would stick with the party. But anger over the president’s immigration policies, coupled with economic anxiety, has driven Trump’s approval numbers among Latinos to historic lows.

Across the South, the Trump-led redistricting push that dismantled House districts with sizable Black populations has fired up Black voters in states such as North Carolina and Louisiana. Black voters could also be key to determining the winner of Michigan’s hard-fought Senate race.

Democrats’ initial midterm target list, released in April 2025, included a few Republican incumbents who represented seats that Trump had carried by double digits the previous year. The number of “reach” battleground races in traditionally red terrain that fit that description has only grown since then. One of the biggest questions heading into election night is how many of those districts Democrats will be competitive in. Wins in those districts would translate into a larger Democratic majority or, at the very least, could help offset losses by Democratic incumbents in redrawn seats.

But flipping these districts would put a bull’s-eye on the Democratic winners, since their seats would likely rank among Republicans’ best pickup opportunities in 2028.

At the start of the midterm cycle, few could have predicted that the Senate battlefield would run through states that Trump carried by double digits in 2024. But concerns over rising prices driven by Trump’s tariff policy and the war in Iran have put several red-state seats in play. In the farm belt states of Iowa and Kansas, soaring diesel and fertilizer costs have GOP candidates on defense. In South Carolina, a divisive Republican primary and an untested first-time candidate have made the race unexpectedly competitive. And in Ohio, the return of a Democratic former senator, coupled with a national environment that is increasingly inhospitable to the GOP, suggests the state could shift from red to purple.

Recent surveys have shown Democrats with the advantage heading into Election Day and Trump’s job approval rating underwater, meaning more voters disapprove of the job he’s doing than approve. All signs point to Democrats retaking the House and potentially winning the Senate majority. That wouldn’t be unexpected — after all, the president’s party almost always loses seats in midterm elections. But polls have been wrong before. In August, some surveys predicted progressive Abdul El-Sayed would notch a double-digit win over Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, but El-Sayed wound up winning by less than a point. Throughout the campaign, Republicans have cautioned against reading too much into the polls, asserting that they typically undercount GOP voters.

#6156. The dark paradox of Israel’s election — and ours

Benjamin Netanyahu didnât win last weekâs election in Israel. But he didnât exactly lose it either. The real loser may have been Israelâs fragile democracy, already corrupted from within, perhaps past the point of no return, by Netanyahuâs decades-long death-grip on power.

On the eve of a momentous election in the United States, the parallels are both inexact and unavoidable. Israelis must now decide what kind of country they will have, or at least what kind they aspire to have. They must decide whose votes actually count, and whether some citizens are more equal than others.Â

Those same questions also confront Americans, both in this weekâs midterm elections and, in a more general sense, on the larger political and historical stage. No doubt it is tempting for liberals and progressives to express outrage at the blatant flaws and contradictions of Israeli democracy. But to invoke the Christian tradition here, it might be better to remove the plank from your own eye before trying to remove the speck from your brotherâs.Â

On the surface, the electoral arithmetic in Israel appears straightforward. Parties opposed to Netanyahuâs far-right government won 67 of the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israelâs parliament. So a majority coalition of anti-Netanyahu forces is clearly achievable, right? You would think so, except that 19 of those 67 seats were won by Israelâs âArab parties,â an all-time high, and that startling fact has thrown the entire political system into confusion.

Netanyahu and his allies have spent the last week airing groundless allegations that the election was fraudulent or rigged, a refrain that Americans are likely to hear a great deal in coming days. What the Zionist far right means is that too many Israeli Arabs â meaning the Palestinian population that remained in Israel after the state was created in 1948 â decided to vote this time, an outcome that no one expected, and that none of the parties representing the Jewish majority particularly wanted.Â

Now, in a masterstroke of historical or perhaps biblical irony, Israelâs Arab minority â which is not a monolithic group in political or cultural terms, and until now has never been electorally significant â holds the balance of power, and perhaps the nationâs future, in its hands.Â

In a masterstroke of historical or perhaps biblical irony, Israelâs Arab minority â which is not a monolithic group in political or cultural terms, and until now has never been electorally significant â holds the balance of power, and perhaps the nationâs future, in its hands.

Gadi Eisenkot, the former general who leads the centrist-Zionist opposition to Netanyahu, promised during the campaign not to form a government with Arab support. Over the last several nights, thousands of demonstrators in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem have urged him to do precisely that, since the only realistic alternative is the grim default setting of Israeli politics: another wobbly right-wing government headed by Netanyahu, which means more brutality and destruction in Gaza, more war with Iran and more settler violence in the West Bank.Â

As Gideon Levy of the left-leaning Israeli newspaper Haaretz explains it,Â

The future of Israel now depends on its Arab citizens and on the attitude of its Jewish citizens toward its Arab ones. Eighty years after the Nakba and the establishment of the Jewish state, Israeli Palestinians may determine its fate. Is there greater historical justice than that?

The electionâs unexpected results are âa cause for rejoicing,â Levy writes, in that they have presented Israelis with a clear choice âbetween a government led by Benjamin Netanyahu and a government that includes the Arab parties.â If the âchange blocâ within the Zionist majority cannot accept a coalition with Arab Israelis, he continues, âthey will make it clear that they are actually the same as Netanyahu, that they prefer even the devil Netanyahu over repressing their racism. â¦ [E]veryone will know that racism is the supreme value in this country, across the board, above any other value.â

That ferocious language certainly does not represent mainstream Israeli opinion, but itâs fair to say the strong emotion beneath Levyâs words is far more widely felt. I donât think itâs possible for a non-Jewish observer (such as myself), however well educated or sympathetic, to understand the anguish felt by Jewish people â wherever they live, and whatever their political views â at the enormous distance between what Israel originally represented to the world, or claimed to represent, and what it represents now.

Iâm old enough to remember when most American liberals and progressives viewed the state of Israel in overwhelmingly positive terms, as a locus of charismatic or heroic renewal for the people Hitler couldnât kill, infused with the spirit of European socialism and, not far below the surface, the collective guilt of the Holocaust. I grew up in one of the most left-liberal corners of America, surrounded by educated adults who supported the civil rights movement, opposed the Vietnam War, hated Richard Nixon and loved Israel. Golda Meir and Moshe Dayan were beloved celebrities; the Six-Day War of 1967 and the Yom Kippur War of 1973, as narrated by U.S. media, were straight-up battles between the forces of light and darkness.Â

That says more about the moral blindness or willful innocence of American liberalism, I must admit, than it says about Israel. In any event, when I saw Joe Bidenâs fateful bear hug with Netanyahu on the tarmac of Ben Gurion Airport in the aftermath of the dreadful Oct. 7 attack, I understood it. I recognized the country Biden was coming from, because I came from there too: It was the Democratic majority of the not-so-distant past, when Israel was embraced as a light to the nations and left-wing radicals who brought up the Palestinian cause were being unreasonable hotheads, if not openly antisemitic and a little bit Nazi.Â

What Israel has become during Netanyahuâs long and destructive reign is now clear to most of the world, and most of all to the many Jewish or Israeli critics who have been speaking difficult truths for many years, often at enormous personal cost. I am disinclined, however, to judge too harshly those who cling to the vision of Israel as an exceptional nation â one that has stumbled, perhaps, but may yet regain its true path.Â

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only by Amanda Marcotte, also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

Like I said earlier, we should mind the plank in our own eye first. Isnât that the same vision that many Americans still cling to? That somehow, on the other side of this dreadful phase of our history â yes, a full decade of Donald Trump, but Iâm afraid the damage goes back a lot further than that â the âindispensable nationâ variously articulated by Abraham Lincoln, John F. Kennedy and Barack Obama is still there, still retrievable, still bending its moral arc toward justice.

#6154. The strange new math behind the price of your groceries

Walmart recently published a list of things it promises not to do to its customers.

âWe price the product, not the person,â Walmart CEO John Furner announced in a September letter to customers. âYour income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay wonât change the price,â he promised. Nor, he said, would the retailerâs AI shopping assistant, Sparky, use information customers shared to raise prices or conceal cheaper options.

This was nice to hear. I hadnât previously considered that telling a computer I needed toilet paper might result in an emergency toilet-paper rate. There is something faintly unnerving about the specificity of a corporate reassurance, particularly when it introduces several possibilities you hadnât thought to worry about.

It made me preemptively nostalgic for the little paper price tag beneath a box of cereal. Thereâs something reassuringly stupid about it. It tells you what the cereal costs. It doesnât know how much money you make, whether youâre in a hurry or what the temperature is outside. Unless an employee comes along with a new sticker, the person reaching for the same box ten minutes later sees the same number. A modest achievement, perhaps, but one Iâm growing increasingly fond of.

The appeal isnât really the paper. Itâs the transparency of the arrangement. As retailers gather more information about their customers and acquire increasingly sophisticated pricing tools, shoppers risk knowing less about why theyâre paying what theyâre paying. The problem isnât simply higher grocery bills. Itâs the possibility of a transaction in which one side can examine the other in exquisite detail, while the other can barely see the rules.

What prompted the letter from Furner is that Walmart is expanding its use of electronic shelf labels, little screens that let employees update prices digitally from a central computer instead of replacing stickers by hand. The change makes sense. Furner points out that updating paper tags is tedious work, and heâd rather employees spend their afternoons helping customers than tending to a small forest of adhesive rectangles. Digital labels can also help ensure the price on the shelf matches the price at checkout.

And electronic labels arenât, in themselves, surge pricing. Walmart says it doesnât use them to change prices according to who is shopping or the time of day. But efficiency is a different question from trust. Making a price easier to change isnât necessarily a problem. Making it harder to understand how that price was reached might be.

Want more great food writing and recipes? Sign up for Salonâs free food newsletter, The Bite.

Weâve already accepted a surprisingly elaborate set of conditions for saving money on groceries. Download the app. Make an account. Remember the password. Clip the digital coupon before you leave home. After handing over our personal information and completing several minor administrative tasks, weâre permitted to save 75 cents on yogurt. The store, meanwhile, gets a rather detailed account of our preferences. What happens when that bargain runs in reverse?

Last December, Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative found that shoppers using Instacart were sometimes shown different prices for identical groceries from the same store at the same time. At one Safeway in Washington, D.C., an 18-ounce box of Signature SELECT Corn Flakes appeared for $2.99, $3.49 and $3.69, depending on whose screen you were looking at.Â

Instacart said the shoppers were assigned to pricing experiments randomly, not sorted by income, demographics or browsing history. It ended the tests after the investigation. That distinction matters, especially because the research didnât establish that anyoneâs personal habits were being used against them. But it demonstrated how quietly prices can diverge when the shopper sees only the number assigned to her. You canât question a difference you have no way of seeing.

I buy a lot of black beans. Enough, presumably, that a supermarketâs software could identify me as a woman with firm opinions about legumes. If that earns me a coupon, wonderful. Iâm considerably less enthusiastic about the possibility of an algorithm deciding that my apparent dependence on black beans means I could stand to pay another 30 cents per can. Itâs one thing to recognize a loyal customer. Itâs another to recognize a captive audience.

Other pricing algorithms raise different questions (McDonaldâs, for instance, faces a lawsuit alleging AI-assisted price coordination among franchises, which the company denies). Prices have always fluctuated; coupons have always rewarded some shoppers more than others. Nor should computers be banished from the business of deciding what things cost. But the supermarket is not an airline, and dinner should not require the same vigilance as booking a flight.

Walmartâs promise is worth taking seriously. The company has drawn a clear line around how it says it will use customer information, and thatâs preferable to leaving shoppers guessing. But itâs a corporate commitment, not a rule every retailer must follow. And the fact that a supermarket now feels obliged to assure us it wonât charge extra because we seem hurried or financially comfortable suggests how strange our expectations have become.

Perhaps itâs naive to want a supermarket not to use what it knows about me against me. Still, I donât need the price tag to know me. I need it to tell me what the cereal costs.

Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., Michiganâs Senate nominee Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and Texas state representative James Talarico, who is running against Paxton. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., was calling for mass arrests of young Republicans when she was asked during a recent appearance about holding the GOP accountable, but that never really caught on either. A last-minute gambit to feign outrage over Barack Obamaâs recent joke comparing Trumpâs White House decor to the Cheesecake Factory fizzled out as well, likely because it simply reminded people of how the current resident is defiling the Peopleâs House.Â

Right-wing social media, especially the Elon Musk-owned X, reads like Stormfront message boards from the 1990s, with Musk himself regularly promoting white nationalist ideas and memes. They want to end professional womenâs sports and return to the sexist delusion that all men are stronger and faster than all women. This much is evident in how real-life right-wingers behave toward the WNBA, such as going so far as to buy tickets so they can throw sex toys at the players.Â

Fox hosts are careful to never say outright that women shouldnât play sports; that, as they well know, could alienate millions of Republican voters, especially women and fathers of female athletes who are more moderate on this issue. Instead, the network attempts to hijack the antipathy many conservatives feel toward female basketball players with their traditional wink-and-nudge coverage, pretending they want to âclean upâ the sport. This preserves the illusion that the right doesnât hate female athletes while portraying the players â the white ones at least â as fragile, helping to reassure an insecure male audience.Â

In the past, this kind of tap dance has worked. Now, as Watters implied, itâs floundering, feeling much too tepid when compared Foxâs online competitors and actual politicians flinging unprintable slurs. Watters suggested as much during another segment, when he argued that Republicans need more âfear pornâ if they want to win.

His use of the word âpornâ is telling. Watters was arguing that it doesnât do to be coy any longer â that only the hard-core stuff will move the base. If your preferred way to watch results roll in is with a crowd, CQ Roll Call’s Nina Heller has a rundown of D.C. bars that will be airing election night results, many of which are offering deals on drinks and food.

â[P]eople are understanding their assignment very, very well.â
